description: Precipitation (metathesis) reaction; purpose: isolate insoluble silver sulfide; key transformation: exchange of anions forming silver sulfide precipitate and soluble rubidium nitrate; typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, protected from light to avoid photoreduction of Ag₂S; solvent: water; no catalyst.

This is a single displacement reaction where fluorine replaces iodine in praseodymium triiodide. The reaction proceeds via a redox mechanism, with fluorine acting as the oxidizing agent and directly displacing iodine as elemental molecules. It typically occurs under high-temperature conditions, often in the molten state, and does not involve a solvent or catalyst.

Oxidation of 5‑hydroxymethyluracil with silver oxide; purpose: convert a hydroxymethyl side chain to a formyl group; key transformation: primary alcohol oxidized to aldehyde; typical conditions: mild heating in aqueous or alcoholic medium with solid Ag₂O as oxidant; solvent: water or methanol; no additional catalyst.

Acid–base neutralization; converts the sodium salt of 4‑fluorobenzoic acid to the free acid. The carboxylate is treated with aqueous hydrochloric acid, typically at 0 °C to room temperature, stirring in water. The reaction yields 4‑fluorobenzoic acid and NaCl, and the product is isolated by acid extraction or crystallization.

General type: skeletal isomerization of a saturated hydrocarbon. Purpose: relocate the methyl substituent to a more thermodynamically favored position, converting 4‑methyloctane to the more stable 2‑methyloctane. Key transformation: intramolecular rearrangement of carbon‑carbon bonds within the alkane chain. Typical conditions: high temperature (300–450 °C) over a solid acid catalyst such as zeolite (e.g., H‑ZSM‑5) or a metal‑oxide catalyst (e.g., Pt/Al₂O₃). Common solvent: none (gas‑ or liquid‑phase flow reactor); the reaction is conducted under pressure to keep the alkane liquid.

General type: acid‑base metathesis (neutralization) between a mineral acid and a metal acetate. Purpose: exchange protons to generate the conjugate base of phosphoric acid and free acetic acid. Key transformation: proton transfer from H₃PO₄ to acetate ion, forming CH₃COOH and LiH₂PO₄. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, stoichiometric amounts. Common solvent/catalyst: water; no additional catalyst required. Reaction is usually carried out with stirring to ensure complete dissolution.

Acid chloride formation; converts a benzoic acid derivative to the acid chloride using thionyl chloride. The carboxylic acid reacts with SOCl₂ (often 1–2 equivalents) under reflux or at 0 °C to room temperature in anhydrous, inert solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform. By‑products are gaseous SO₂ and HCl, which are removed by evaporation. Catalytic DMF may be added to accelerate the reaction.

General type: direct fluorination redox reaction. Purpose: synthesize cerium(III) fluoride while liberating nitrogen gas. Key transformation: fluorine gas oxidizes cerium nitride, converting N³⁻ to N₂ and forming CeF₃. Typical conditions: flow of dry F₂ over solid CeN at elevated temperature (400–600 °C) in a fluorination furnace, often using a nickel or Monel reactor vessel resistant to fluorine corrosion. No solvent; the reaction is gas‑solid.

General type: Swern oxidation (low‑temperature oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde). Purpose: convert citronellol to citronellal without over‑oxidation to the carboxylic acid. Key transformation: activation of dimethyl sulfoxide by oxalyl chloride to form a chlorodimethyl‑sulfonium intermediate, which reacts with the alcohol; triethylamine then abstracts a proton, yielding the aldehyde, dimethyl sulfide, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and triethylammonium chloride. Typical conditions: –78 °C to 0 °C in anhydrous dichloromethane under nitrogen; oxalyl chloride added dropwise, followed by DMSO, then the alcohol, and finally TEA. Common solvents/catalysts: dry CH₂Cl₂; oxalyl chloride acts as activating reagent; TEA serves as base.

SN2 alkylation of a primary amine; 2‑aminoethanol attacks 1‑bromopropane, substituting bromide to form 2‑(propylamino)ethanol and HBr; commonly carried out in an alcoholic solvent (ethanol or isopropanol) with excess amine to neutralize the generated HBr, often under reflux; sometimes a phase‑transfer catalyst (e.g., tetrabutylammonium bromide) or a small amount of KI is used to accelerate the reaction.

Grignard addition to an acyl chloride; phenylmagnesium bromide adds to butyryl chloride to afford 1‑phenylbutan‑1‑one after aqueous work‑up; the Grignard reagent acts as a nucleophilic phenyl donor, adding to the carbonyl of the acyl chloride; reaction run at 0 °C to –20 °C in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) under nitrogen, quenched with dilute acid.

Reaction type: thermal decomposition of a peracid. Purpose: regenerate acetic acid and release oxygen. Key transformation: peracetic acid breaks down to acetic acid and molecular O₂ (often singlet oxygen). Typical conditions: gentle heating (≈50‑70 °C) or catalysis by trace transition‑metal ions (Fe²⁺, Cu²⁺). Solvent: aqueous or neat peracetic acid.

General type: alkaline peroxide oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid. Purpose: oxidize benzaldehyde to benzoic acid. Key transformation: hydrogen peroxide, in the presence of NaOH, generates peroxyanion species that attack the carbonyl carbon of benzaldehyde, ultimately yielding benzoic acid after acid work‑up. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, room temperature to gentle heating (20–60 °C), stoichiometric NaOH and excess H₂O₂; reaction often proceeds in 30 % H₂O₂ solution. Common solvent: water; no additional catalyst required, though trace transition‑metal ions may accelerate the reaction.

Free‑radical aromatic chlorination under photolysis; UV light activates Cl2 to generate chlorine radicals which abstract a hydrogen from the para position of ortho‑xylene and substitute a chlorine atom, yielding 4‑chloro‑1,2‑dimethylbenzene and HCl. Typical conditions: UV irradiation in an inert non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane, ambient to reflux temperature.

Nucleophilic aliphatic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl chloride by fluoride ion. Sodium fluoride provides F⁻ which attacks the carbon bearing the chlorine, displacing Cl⁻ to give 1‑fluorobutane. Reaction is carried out in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF, DMSO) at moderate heat (50‑80 °C) to enhance the rate; no catalyst is required.

Oxidation of cyanide to cyanate; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes CN− to OCN− producing sodium cyanate and water; NaCN + H2O2 → NaOCN + H2O; typically carried out in aqueous alkaline medium at 0–5 °C to avoid over‑oxidation; no catalyst, water solvent.

Catalytic hydrogenation; H2 gas over Pd/C reduces 4‑methylbenzaldehyde to 4‑methylbenzyl alcohol; reaction run in ethanol or EtOAc under 1–5 atm H2 at rt (or mild heating), with 5–10 wt % Pd/C, followed by filtration to remove catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed electrophilic aromatic alkylation (Friedel‑Crafts) and subsequent cyclotrimerization of 2,4,6‑trimethylphenol with formaldehyde to afford cyclotriveratrylene (CTV). Ferric chloride (FeCl₃) acts as the Lewis‑acid catalyst, activating formaldehyde for electrophilic attack on the phenolic ring. The condensation proceeds in a non‑protic solvent such as chloroform or nitrobenzene, often under reflux, followed by cooling to promote cyclization into the macrocyclic CTV structure.

Hydrolysis of thorium oxy‑fluoride (ThOF₂) with water to form thorium dioxide (ThO₂) and hydrofluoric acid. The reaction is a simple acid‑base/oxidation‑reduction transformation, typically performed by stirring ThOF in aqueous solution at elevated temperature (≈150‑200 °C) under pressure to drive off HF. No additional reagents are required.

Type: N‑alkylation via epoxide ring‑opening (nucleophilic addition). Purpose: install two terminal hydroxyl groups on ethylenediamine to give a di‑hydroxy chelating ligand or polymer precursor. Key transformation: the secondary amine nitrogen attacks the less hindered carbon of ethylene oxide, opening the three‑membered ring and forming a β‑hydroxyethyl substituent; repeated with the second amine nitrogen gives N,N′‑bis(2‑hydroxyethyl)ethylenediamine. Typical conditions: ethylene oxide gas or liquid added to a solution of 2‑(2‑aminoethylamino)ethanol in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., THF, acetonitrile) or water; temperature 50–100 °C; excess ethylene oxide; reaction proceeds under mild pressure; no external catalyst required, the amine acts as nucleophile.

Nucleophilic substitution (halogen exchange) using trimethylsilyl iodide; converts a primary alcohol to the corresponding alkyl iodide via a silyl ether intermediate; typically performed under anhydrous conditions in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; inert atmosphere required.

Reverse skeletal isomerization; 2‑methylpentane is converted back to 3‑methylpentane under similar acid‑catalyzed conditions; key transformation methyl shift to give the terminal isomer; typical conditions: 250–350 °C over HZSM‑5 or other solid acid catalyst, gas‑phase, no solvent.

Acid–base neutralization of yttrium oxide with phosphoric acid; the oxide is protonated and reacts to form insoluble yttrium phosphate precipitate and water. Performed in aqueous phosphoric acid (≈1 M), heated to 80–120 °C with stirring to promote complete conversion.

Halogen exchange oxidation of thionyl chloride with elemental fluorine. Fluorine gas reacts with SOCl₂, substituting the two chlorine atoms for fluorine to give thionyl fluoride (SOF₂) while reducing fluorine to chlorine gas (Cl₂). The highly exothermic reaction is performed in a fluorine‑compatible reactor, typically at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) and in an inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is normally employed.

Acid–base neutralization; magnesium oxide acts as a base that deprotonates phosphoric acid, forming the mono‑hydrogen phosphate salt of magnesium and water. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst required; water is both reactant and solvent.

Oxidation (Dess‑Martin periodinane oxidation); the secondary allylic alcohol of pinocarveol is converted to the corresponding ketone, pinocarvone. Conducted at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform under inert atmosphere; Dess‑Martin periodinane is the stoichiometric oxidant; no additional catalyst needed.

Cation exchange (metathesis). Disodium malate is treated with magnesium sulfate in water, resulting in precipitation or solution of magnesium malate and formation of sodium sulfate in solution. Reaction driven by differing solubilities; often performed in aqueous medium with gentle heating to improve exchange. No catalyst needed.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (hydrogenation) of a seven‑membered cyclic ether; oxepane undergoes ring opening under H₂ pressure to give the linear 1,6‑hexanediol. Typical conditions: 50–100 bar H₂, 80–150 °C, using a metal catalyst such as Raney Ni, Pt/C, or Pd/C in a polar protic solvent (e.g., ethanol or methanol) or in the presence of water.

Amination of 2‑chloroacetophenone with dimethylamine; an SN2 substitution of the benzylic chloride by the secondary amine to afford 2‑(dimethylamino)acetophenone while generating HCl. Performed in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or ethanol) with excess dimethylamine; often a base such as triethylamine is added to scavenge the liberated HCl. Useful for installing a dimethylamino group for further synthetic transformations.

Redox (halogenation/oxidation) of bismuth(III) sulfide with bromine; bromine oxidizes sulfide to elemental sulfur while simultaneously converting Bi³⁺ to bismuth tribromide (BiBr₃). Often carried out at 0–25 °C in a non‑reactive solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane) or neat bromine; the reaction is exothermic and may be performed under inert atmosphere to avoid side reactions.

Chromium(VI) oxidation of a benzylic primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid. Sodium dichromate (Na₂Cr₂O₇) in concentrated H₂SO₄ (often 6 M) at 80–100 °C oxidizes 4‑bromobenzyl alcohol through the aldehyde intermediate to 4‑bromobenzoic acid; aqueous sulfuric acid serves as both solvent and acid catalyst.

Oxidation of a diol to a dicarboxylic acid (Jones oxidation); 1,4‑butanediol is oxidized by sodium dichromate in concentrated sulfuric acid to succinic acid, with reduction of Cr(VI) to Cr(III) forming chromium(III) sulfate and water. Conditions: aqueous H₂SO₄ (≈ 4 M), Na₂Cr₂O₇·2H₂O, heated to 70–90 °C for 1–3 h; reaction performed in a glass vessel resistant to acid; no additional catalyst needed.

Reductive amination of phenylacetaldehyde with dimethylamine; sodium cyanoborohydride reduces the in‑situ formed iminium ion to give N,N‑dimethyl‑1‑phenylethanamine; carried out in methanol or ethanol with a catalytic amount of acetic acid, at 0 °C to reflux, under nitrogen.

Photochemical free‑radical chlorination of diethyl ether; UV irradiation generates chlorine radicals that abstract a hydrogen atom from the ether, producing hydrogen chloride and the mono‑chlorinated ether (2‑chloroethyl ethyl ether) as the major product. Typical setup: dilute Cl₂ in ether (or in an inert solvent), UV lamp (254 nm), temperature near ambient, inert atmosphere; reaction limited to low conversion to avoid over‑chlorination.

Type: Grignard reagent preparation. Purpose: generate a nucleophilic organomagnesium species for carbon–carbon bond formation. Key transformation: magnesium inserts oxidatively into the C–Br bond of 1‑bromopropane to give propylmagnesium bromide (CH3CH2CH2MgBr). Typical conditions: anhydrous ethereal solvent (dry diethyl ether or THF), inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar), magnesium turnings activated (e.g., with a pinch of iodine), gentle reflux until the reaction is complete.

Fluorination (free‑radical substitution); purpose is to fully fluorinate trifluoromethane to carbon tetrafluoride, releasing HF; key transformation CHF3 + F2 → CF4 + HF; performed under very low temperature, high‑purity F2 conditions in metal reactors (often nickel); no solvent or catalyst is typically employed.

Fischer esterification; formic acid reacts with n‑butanol in the presence of catalytic sulfuric acid to give butyl formate and water; reflux in the alcohol (or a non‑polar solvent) with removal of water (e.g., Dean‑Stark) drives the equilibrium toward ester formation.

Direct synthesis (combination reaction). Produces calcium iodide for applications like organic synthesis or photography. Calcium metal heated with iodine solid. Reaction proceeds with heating, possibly under inert atmosphere.

Ligand substitution (coordination complex formation); purpose is to prepare the well‑defined Pd(II) catalyst precursor PdCl₂(dppf); key transformation is displacement of two labile acetonitrile ligands by the bidentate diphosphine dppf, yielding PdCl₂(dppf) and releasing MeCN; typically performed in an aprotic solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ or THF under nitrogen, at room temperature to gentle reflux, no additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (esterification) of an acyl fluoride with methanol; purpose is to generate the methyl ester of phenylacetic acid while releasing HF. Key transformation: fluoride is displaced by methoxy to give methyl phenylacetate. Typical conditions: 0 °C to room temperature, often in dry dichloromethane or neat methanol, with a stoichiometric base such as triethylamine or pyridine to neutralize the liberated HF. Reaction proceeds in a few hours under inert atmosphere.

Acid‑base neutralization of permanganic acid with potassium hydroxide; produces potassium permanganate and water; performed in water at ambient temperature using stoichiometric KOH, similar precautions as with the sodium salt.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation); purpose is to convert the weakly acidic sulfathiazole into its more water‑soluble sodium salt; key transformation is deprotonation of the sulfonamide NH by NaOH, producing water and Na⁺ sulfathiazole; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring.

Redox; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes sulfite (H2SO3) to sulfate (H2SO4) while being reduced to water; key transformation: H2SO3 + H2O2 → H2SO4 + H2O; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, usually in acidic medium; no special catalyst required.

Fischer esterification; purpose is to protect the benzylic alcohol as an acetate; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of the alcohol on the protonated carbonyl of acetic acid, forming 4‑methoxybenzyl acetate and water; catalyzed by catalytic H₂SO₄, refluxing in excess acetic acid (or in toluene with azeotropic removal of water) for 1–4 h.

Nucleophilic substitution (Grignard silylation). Provides an aryl‑trimethylsilane useful as a protected aryl moiety or in Hiyama cross‑coupling. Phenylmagnesium bromide attacks bromotrimethylsilane, forming phenyltrimethylsilane and MgBr₂. Conducted in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; moisture‑free conditions are essential, and no extra catalyst is needed.

Double‑replacement metathesis (precipitation) reaction; purpose is to generate an insoluble magnesium hydroxide and a soluble lithium sulfate; key transformation is exchange of anions between LiOH and MgSO₄, yielding Li₂SO₄ (aq) and Mg(OH)₂ (solid); performed in aqueous medium at room temperature with stirring; the Mg(OH)₂ precipitate is filtered off.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration/pinacol rearrangement of a vicinal diol; purpose is to convert 2,3‑dimethyl‑2,3‑butanediol into the corresponding ketone; key transformation involves protonation of a hydroxyl, loss of water to give a carbocation, followed by a 1,2‑methyl shift and formation of 3,3‑dimethyl‑2‑butanone; carried out with concentrated H₂SO₄, heated (80–120 °C), often in the same acidic medium without additional solvent.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an alkyl halide with ammonia; purpose is to synthesize n‑butylamine; key transformation is attack of NH₃ on the primary carbon of n‑butyl chloride, displacing Cl⁻ and forming n‑butylamine with generation of HCl; typically conducted in aqueous or alcoholic NH₃ (excess) at reflux (≈80 °C) or under pressure; the HCl formed is neutralized by the excess ammonia.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (halogenation); chlorination of benzene to give chlorobenzene with HCl as by‑product. Typically carried out with Cl2 in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst such as FeCl3 (or AlCl3) in an inert solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride, dichloromethane) at ambient to mild temperatures.

Direct combination (synthesis) of zinc and tellurium to form zinc telluride, ZnTe. Conducted by heating elemental Zn and Te together in a sealed tube or under inert gas at temperatures above ~500 °C until a homogeneous melt is obtained; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis) driven by insoluble barium sulfate; aqueous solution; Dysprosium(III) sulfate is mixed with barium chloride, producing dysprosium(III) chloride in solution and precipitating BaSO4, which drives the reaction to completion; typically performed by combining equimolar aqueous solutions at room temperature with vigorous stirring; the BaSO4 solid is filtered off; no catalyst needed.

Reductive conversion of niobium dioxide to niobium monoxide using carbon monoxide. CO reduces NbO2 to NbO while being oxidized to CO2. Performed at high temperature (800–1200 °C) under a flow of CO or CO/CO2 mixture; solid‑state reaction, no solvent.

Metallothermic reduction of samarium(III) iodide by sodium; dry Na metal reduces SmI₃ in anhydrous, inert atmosphere (often in THF or liquid ammonia) to produce metallic samarium and sodium iodide; reaction is temperature‑controlled (often 0–50 °C) and conducted in a sealed tube; no catalyst.

Reductive amination of cyclohexanone with ammonia and hydrogen to afford cyclohexylamine and water. Conducted in the presence of a hydrogenation catalyst (e.g., Raney Ni, Pt/C, Pd/C) in an alcohol solvent (methanol, ethanol, or isopropanol) at 80–150 °C under H2 pressure (5–50 bar).

Reaction type: acid-base neutralization. Purpose: preparation of potassium dihydrogen phosphate. Key transformations: phosphorus pentoxide reacts with potassium hydroxide to form potassium dihydrogen phosphate and water. Conditions: aqueous solution with heat; phosphorus pentoxide hydrolyzes to phosphoric acid in water, followed by neutralization with KOH. Solvents: water commonly used.

Acidic redox reaction of potassium permanganate with concentrated hydrochloric acid. Mn(VII) is reduced to Mn(II) chloride while chloride is oxidized to chlorine gas; water and potassium chloride are also formed. Usually carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature or with slight heating; no special catalyst.

Halogen exchange/redox reaction of hydrogen telluride with bromine, producing hydrogen bromide and tellurium dibromide. Typically performed by bubbling Br2 through an aqueous or organic solution of H2Te at low temperature (0–25 °C); inert solvent such as dichloromethane may be used, no additional catalyst.

Double displacement reaction. Synthesis of lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) used as a cathode material in batteries. Involves acid-base exchange between phosphoric acid and lithium/iron(II) acetate. Typically occurs under aqueous conditions at elevated temperatures with pH control to precipitate LiFePO4. Water is a common solvent.

Redox reduction of a high‑valent oxide. Rhenium heptoxide (Re₂O₇) is reduced by hydrogen gas, producing rhenium dioxide and water. Conducted at high temperature (300‑500 °C) under a flow of H₂, often in a quartz tube; no solvent or additional catalyst is needed.

Acid-base reaction. Formation of Imipramine hydrochloride salt enhances pharmacokinetic properties and water solubility. Hydrochloric acid protonates the tertiary amine in Imipramine. Conducted in aqueous or alcoholic solvent (e.g., ethanol, water) at ambient temperature, requiring no catalyst.

Acid-base reaction. Converts Loxoprofen (carboxylic acid) to its soluble sodium salt, producing CO2 and water. Achieved by dissolving Loxoprofen in aqueous sodium bicarbonate solution. Reaction occurs rapidly at ambient temperature without catalysts.

Redox reaction. Reduction of ruthenium(III) chloride to metallic ruthenium using hydrogen gas as the reductant, generating hydrogen chloride as a byproduct. Requires high-temperature and high-pressure H2 conditions; often conducted via thermal decomposition or hydrogen gas flow in the absence of solvents.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution. Bromine acts as an electrophile, reacting with activated sodium phenoxide to form para-bromophenol. Occurs in aqueous or polar solvents (e.g., methanol) with mild conditions. Trace acid may enhance bromine’s electrophilicity, though no catalyst is typically required.

Esterification. Phenol’s hydroxyl group attacks the activated acyl group of 4-aminosalicylic acid, catalyzed by DMAP and activated by DCC, producing phenyl 4-aminosalicylate. Conducted in anhydrous organic solvents (e.g., dichloromethane) at room temperature. DMAP accelerates ester bond formation, while DCC forms inert dicyclohexylurea byproduct.

O‑methylation (alkylation) of phenolic hydroxyls with dimethyl sulfate; purpose is to protect or modify the 3‑ and 4‑hydroxy groups of 3,4‑dihydroxybenzaldehyde, giving 3,4‑dimethoxybenzaldehyde. Key transformation: SN2 attack of phenoxide anion on the methyl group of dimethyl sulfate, forming methoxy substituents. Conditions: base such as K₂CO₃ or NaOH (2 equiv) in an aprotic solvent (acetone or DMF), temperature 0 °C to rt, dimethyl sulfate added dropwise under inert atmosphere; reaction typically run 1–3 h.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution. Acyle oxygen attacked by alcohol to form ester and excess acetic acid. Acetic anhydride serves as activated acetyl source. Acidic conditions (e.g., H2SO4) or basic catalysts (e.g., pyridine) are typical, with solvents like THF or chloroform.

Acation an aromatic amine (nucleophilic acyl substitution); purpose is to introduce an acetyl protecting group on the nitrogen; key transformation: the amine nitrogen attacks acetyl chloride, forming N‑acetyl‑5‑aminosalicylic acid and generating HCl; typical conditions use an organic base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge HCl, solvent dichloromethane or THF, temperature 0 °C to room temperature.

Acid–carbonate reaction (neutralization). Used to prepare cerium(III) fluoride from a carbonate precursor. Cerium carbonate reacts with aqueous hydrofluoric acid, converting CeCO3 to CeF3 while releasing CO2 gas and forming water. Typically carried out in water at ambient to mild heating, with excess HF; HF is handled in a fume hood.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of primary alkyl halide with aqueous ammonia; chloride displaced to give ethylamine and ammonium chloride; reaction carried out under reflux in aqueous ammonia or ethanol/water mixture; moderate heating (~80 °C); no catalyst.

Solid‑state oxidation (redox combustion); purpose is to convert iron(II) oxide to the more stable iron(III) oxide; key transformation: Fe²⁺ is oxidized to Fe³⁺ while O₂ is reduced, yielding Fe₂O₃; typical conditions involve heating FeO in air at 500–800 °C in a furnace, no solvent required.

DCC‑mediated amide coupling; purpose is to synthesize N,N‑diethylm‑toluamide (DEET); key transformation: DCC activates the carboxyl group of 3‑methylbenzoic acid to an O‑acylurea, which is then displaced by N,N‑diethylamine forming the amide and dicyclohexylurea by‑product; typical conditions use dichloromethane as solvent, temperature 0 °C to room temperature, catalytic DMAP, inert atmosphere.

Double‑replacement precipitation; aqueous Cr2(SO4)3 reacts with NaOH, precipitating Cr(OH)3 and forming soluble Na2SO4. Usually carried out at ambient temperature in water; vigorous stirring; no catalyst.

Aminolysis of ethyl cyanate; reaction of ethyl cyanate with ammonia furnishes ethyl carbamate (urethane). Key transformation: nucleophilic addition of NH₃ to the cyanate carbon, forming the carbamate functional group (–OC(O)NH₂). Typical conditions: aqueous or alcoholic solution of NH₃, ambient to mild heating (25–60 °C). Reaction proceeds readily without catalyst; excess ammonia can be used to push equilibrium toward product.

Type: Pinnick oxidation (aldehyde to carboxylic acid); purpose: oxidize octanal to octanoic acid; key transformation: NaClO₂ oxidizes the aldehyde carbonyl to a carboxylate while NaH₂PO₄ buffers the reaction and prevents side reactions; typical conditions: aqueous buffer at pH ≈ 3–4, often with MeCN or t‑BuOH as co‑solvent, 0–25 °C, sometimes 2‑methyl‑2‑butene added as chlorine scavenger; by‑products: NaCl and H₂O.

Catalytic dehydrogenation of a saturated alkane; purpose is to generate an internal alkene; key transformation: removal of two hydrogen atoms from 2,3‑dimethylbutane to give 2,3‑dimethyl‑2‑butene plus molecular H₂; typical conditions are high temperature (300–400 °C) in the gas phase over a metal catalyst such as Pt/Al₂O₃, Cr₂O₃, or supported nickel; no solvent.

Chlorination of a metal nitride; oxidative chlorination that converts solid NbN to volatile NbCl5 while releasing N2 gas. Typically carried out by passing dry Cl2 gas over NbN at 300‑450 °C in a sealed quartz tube or flow reactor; no solvent needed and the reaction is driven by high temperature.

Redox reduction (hydrogen reduction) of vanadium tetrachloride to metallic vanadium; hydrogen gas serves as reductant, producing hydrogen chloride gas. Typically performed at 400‑600 °C under a flow of H₂ in the gas phase, no solvent required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an aldehyde; purpose is to reduce the aldehyde to the corresponding primary alcohol; key transformation: H₂ adds across the C=O bond of tetrahydrofuran‑2‑carbaldehyde forming tetrahydrofurfuryl alcohol; typical conditions use H₂ pressure 1–5 atm, a Pd/C or Raney Ni catalyst, solvent ethanol or methanol, temperature 25–80 °C.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC). 1‑Butanol is converted to butanal while the chromium(VI) species is reduced to Cr(III). Reaction performed in anhydrous dichloromethane (or CH2Cl2) at 0 °C to rt, under inert atmosphere; PCC is the stoichiometric oxidant.

Fischer esterification of a hydroxy‑acid; purpose is to prepare the methacrylate monomer 2‑hydroxyethyl methacrylate; key transformation: condensation of a hydroxyl group of ethylene glycol with methacrylic acid forms an ester bond and releases water; typical conditions employ a strong acid catalyst (p‑toluenesulfonic acid or sulfuric acid), reflux in toluene or benzene with a Dean‑Stark trap to continuously remove water, reaction time 1– hours.

Haloform reaction; oxidative cleavage of a methyl ketone by aqueous sodium hypochlorite under basic conditions (pH ≈ 9‑10) typically at 0‑25 °C; acetone is converted to chloroform, water and sodium acetate; water is the solvent and no added catalyst is needed.

Aminolysis of dimethyl carbonate; ammonia reacts with dimethyl carbonate at elevated temperature (150‑200 °C) in the melt or in liquid ammonia, sometimes with a basic solid support, to give methylamine, methanol and carbon dioxide; purpose is a convenient route to primary alkyl amines; no separate catalyst is required.

Nitric‑acid oxidation of furfural; aqueous nitric acid (concentrated or diluted) refluxes with furfural (80‑120 °C) to oxidize the aldehyde to 2‑furancarboxylic acid while reducing NO₃⁻ to nitrogen oxides; water serves as solvent; often performed without additional catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a nitro group; 2,4‑dichonitrobenzene is reduced with H₂ (1‑5 atm over metal catalyst such as Pd/C, Pt‑O₂, or Raney Ni in a protic solvent (ethanol, methanol) at 25‑80 °C to give 2,4‑dichloroaniline and water; purpose is conversion of nitro aromatics to anilines.

Acid‑base protonation of ammonium selenide; aqueous HCl (≈ 2 equiv) is added to a solution of NH₄₂Se, generating hydrogen selenide gas (H₂Se) and ammonium chloride; reaction is carried out at low temperature (0‑5 °C) to control H₂Se release; no catalyst is required.

Transesterification; used to exchange the alkoxy group of an ester. Propyl octanoate reacts with excess methanol in the presence of a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or base (e.g., NaOH, KOH) at 60–80 °C. The key transformation is the replacement of the propyl group by a methyl group, giving methyl octanoate and 1‑propanol. Typically performed neat (no solvent) or in methanol as both reactant and solvent; removal of the by‑product alcohol drives the equilibrium.

Halide metathesis (double displacement) between ammonium iodide and thulium chloride; three equivalents of NH₄I are with one equivalent of TmCl₃ in aqueous solution. The exchange furnishes ammonium chloride and thulium triiodide, the latter often precipitating due to its low solubility. The reaction proceeds at room temperature with stirring; no special catalyst is required.

Acid–base solid‑state reaction (ammonolysis) used to convert a metal oxide into its chloride; heating anhydrous ammonium chloride with dysprosium oxide at 200–300 °C in a dry tube yields dysprosium(III) chloride with evolution of ammonia gas and water vapour; no solvent, inert atmosphere optional.

Dehydrohalogenation (elimination) reaction; purpose is to convert a trichlorinated alkane into a dichloroalkene; key transformation: removal of HCl from 1,1,2‑trichloroethane yielding 1,2‑dichloroethylene and HCl; typical conditions: strong base such as alcoholic KOH or NaOH, reflux temperature (≈80‑120 °C); common solvent: ethanol or methanol; no metal catalyst required.

Ligand substitution to form a phosphine‑gold(I) complex; triphenylphosphine (PPh₃) is added to a solution of AuCl (gold(I) chloride) in a dry organic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform. The mixture is stirred at ambient temperature under nitrogen, producing the coordination complex AuCl(PPh₃). No by‑products are formed; the reaction is driven by the strong σ‑donation of PPh₃ to Au(I).

Acid–base neutralization/salt metathesis in aqueous solution; citric acid protonates tribasic calcium phosphate, releasing phosphoric acid and forming soluble calcium citrate; usually conducted in water with gentle heating (≤80 °C) and stirring; pH adjusted as needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a nitrile to a primary amine; 2,2‑dimethylpropanenitrile is reduced with H₂ in the presence of a nickel catalyst (e.g., Raney Ni or Ni/Al₂O₃) to give 2,2‑dimethylpropylamine; reaction performed in ethanol or methanol under 1–50 bar H₂ at 80–150 °C.

Redox reduction of palladium(IV) by hydrazine; hydrazine reduces K₂PdCl₆ to metallic palladium while being oxidized to N₂, producing HCl, H₂O and KCl as by‑products; carried out in aqueous acidic medium (often dilute HCl) at ambient temperature with stirring; no external catalyst required.

Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of 2‑pentyl acetate with aqueous NaOH; the ester carbonyl is attacked by hydroxide, yielding 2‑pentanol and sodium acetate. Typically performed in a water/ethanol mixture at reflux (60‑100 °C) with stoichiometric NaOH; no additional catalyst required.

This is a double‑displacement precipitation reaction; aqueous barium iodide reacts with sodium sulfate to form insoluble barium sulfate precipitate and soluble sodium iodide; performed in water at ambient temperature, often used to detect sulfate ions.

Hydrogen reduction of titanium dioxide; purpose is to produce titanium(II) oxide while generating water; H₂ acts as reducing agent, converting Ti⁴⁺ to Ti²⁺ and forming H₂O vapor; typically performed at 800‑900 °C under a stream of hydrogen or H₂/N₂ mixture; solid TiO₂ is heated in the gas phase; no solvent or catalyst required.

Oxidative decomposition of selenium sulfide in the presence of excess oxygen; a redox (combustion) reaction that converts SeS₂ to sulfur dioxide and selenium dioxide. Usually carried out by heating the solid SeS₂ in air or pure O₂ at 200‑400 °C; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of ethyl bromide by methanesulfonic acid in the presence of triethylamine, which scavenges the generated HBr. Forms ethyl methanesulfonate (mesylate) and triethylammonium bromide. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile at 0 °C to room temperature; triethylamine acts as base.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution of a primary alkyl fluoride; aqueous sodium hydroxide (or NaOH in ethanol/water) reacts with 1‑fluorobutane at reflux or elevated temperature. Hydroxide attacks the primary carbon, displacing fluoride to afford 1‑butanol and sodium fluoride. The reaction requires a polaric solvent to solvate the ions and proceeds with inversion of configuration (not relevant for achiral substrate).

Strong oxidative cleavage of estragole with potassium permanganate; purpose is to fully oxidize the side chain to the carboxylic acid 4‑methoxybenzoic acid, with the terminal carbon released as CO₂ and water formed. KMnO₄ oxidizes the alkene and the adjacent methylene to a carboxyl group under basic aqueous conditions. Typical conditions: aqueous KMnO₄ (often 0.1–0.5 M) heated to reflux or kept at 80–100 °C, pH maintained alkaline (NaOH or KOH), followed by acidification of the reaction mixture to precipitate the benzoic acid; no additional catalyst is required.

Acylation of 3‑chloro‑4‑methylaniline with acetic anhydride to give N‑(3‑chloro‑4‑methylphenyl)acetamide and one equivalent of acetic acid. This is a nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation). Usually heated under reflux, either neat acetic anhydride or in a solvent such as pyridine or dichloromethane; a catalytic base (e.g., pyridine or DMAP) can accelerate the reaction.

Reductive conversion of plutonium hexafluoride (PuF₆) by hydrogen gas to plutonium tetrafluoride (PuF₄) with liberation of hydrogen fluoride. A high‑temperature gas‑phase redox reaction (≈300‑500 °C) performed in a fluorine‑compatible reactor; excess H₂ drives reduction, and HF is removed as a by‑product.

Acylation of dimethylamine with propionic anhydride (nucleophilic acyl substitution) to give N,N-dimethylpropanamide; propionic acid is formed as a by‑product. Typically performed at 0‑25 °C in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane with a stoichiometric base (triethylamine or pyridine) to neutralize the acid.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a nitrile; 4‑methoxybenzonitrile is reduced to 4‑methoxybenzylamine under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) with a Pd/C, Raney Ni or Pt catalyst; solvent is ethanol or methanol, temperature ambient to reflux.

Thermal decomposition (calcination) of mixed iron(II)/iron(III) oxalates; purpose is to generate magnetite (Fe3O4). Upon heating (≈300‑400 °C) in an inert or air atmosphere the oxalate ligands oxidatively decompose, releasing CO2 and CO gases while the iron is converted to the mixed‑valent oxide. No solvent or catalyst is required; the reaction is performed in a furnace or on a hot plate.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl bromide with thiocyanate ion; purpose is synthesis of an alkyl thiocyanate. Ammonium thiocyanate is dissolved in a polar protic or aprotic solvent (e.g., ethanol, water, or acetone) and ethyl bromide is added, usually with reflux or gentle heating. The bromide leaves and the SCN⁻ attacks the carbon to give ethyl thiocyanate and ammonium bromide. No additional catalyst is needed.

Acid-base neutralization; calcium hydroxide reacts with acetic acid in aqueous solution to produce calcium acetate and water. Purpose: neutralize the acid and obtain a soluble calcium salt. Key transformation: OH− from Ca(OH)₂ combines with H⁺ from CH₃COOH to form H₂O, while Ca²⁺ pairs with acetate anion. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, room temperature, stirring, stoichiometric amounts; no catalyst required.

Direct combination (synthesis) reaction: elemental chromium is oxidized by fluorine gas to form chromium(VI) fluoride (CrF6). The reaction proceeds by vigorous oxidation at elevated temperatures (typically 300–400 °C) under anhydrous, fluoride‑resistant conditions, often in a fluorine‑compatible reactor. No solvent or catalyst is required; the gases are mixed and heated in the gas phase to afford the high‑oxidation‑state fluoride.

Catalytic hydrogenation (nitrile reduction); reduces the nitrile of 3‑hydroxypropanenitrile to the primary amine, yielding 3‑aminopropanol. Key transformation: –C≡N + 2 H₂ → –CH₂NH₂. Catalyst: Raney nickel (or other supported Ni). Typical conditions: H₂ pressure 30–50 bar, temperature 50–120 °C, reaction time 2–4 h. Solvent: ethanol, methanol, or water; reaction performed in a sealed autoclave.

Alkene isomerization (migration to the thermodynamically favored trans‑alkene); transforms 1‑pentene into trans‑2‑pentene. Commonly carried out with a homogeneous metal catalyst (e.g., Wilkinson’s catalyst RhCl(PPh3)3) or unsupported palladium on carbon under mild H2 pressure, at 30–80 °C in solvents like dichloromethane or toluene; the process equilibrates to the more stable trans internal alkene.

Phosphorus pentachloride mediated cleavage of an ester (dealkylation); purpose is to convert the ester into the corresponding acid chloride (trichloroacetyl chloride) and generate the alkyl chloride (methyl chloride). The reaction is performed in anhydrous, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, typically at 0 °C to reflux under inert atmosphere. POCl3 is formed as a by‑product. No additional catalyst is required.

Acid‑salt metathesis: concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with HgI₂, exchanging anions to produce mercuric sulfate (sparingly soluble) and hydroiodic acid (HI) which may be distilled off. Performed by heating HgI₂ with conc. H₂SO₄.

Same amide‑forming acyl substitution as in #4, but the HCl generated is immediately neutralized by aqueous NaOH, giving the amide, NaCl, and water. Conducted in a biphasic system (e.g., ether/water) with ice‑bath cooling followed by warming; the base ensures quantitative conversion and simplifies work‑up.

Complex‑formation (fluoride complexation) reaction; magnesium fluoride combines with silicon tetrafluoride to give magnesium hexafluorosilicate (MgSiF6). Purpose is preparation of the hexafluorosilicate salt. Key transformation: MgF2 + SiF4 → MgSiF6. Typically conducted in anhydrous HF or at elevated a sealed, dry vessel; inert atmosphere, no catalyst.

Hydrolysis of arsenic pentachloride; purpose is to obtain arsenic acid. The reaction proceeds simply by adding excess of water to AsCl5, usually at room temperature or with gentle warming. Water acts as the nucleophile, replacing each Cl with OH, yielding H3AsO4 and liberating five equivalents of HCl. No catalyst is needed; the reaction occurs in aqueous solution.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution between an amine (aniline) and an acyl fluoride (propanoyl fluoride) to form an amide. The reaction is typically carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt, often in the presence of a base (e.g., pyridine, triethylamine) to capture the generated HF. The result is N‑phenylpropanamide and HF (sealed as a base‑HF adduct). This method provides a mild route to amide formation.

Disproportionation/redox decomposition: Chromium(IV) fluoride thermally decomposes, reducing Cr from +4 to +3 and oxidizing fluoride to elemental fluorine. Typically performed by heating solid CrF4 under an inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst required.

Nucleophilic ring opening of ethylene oxide by n‑butyllithium followed by aqueous work‑up; purpose is to extend the carbon chain and introduce a terminal hydroxyl, yielding 2‑butoxyethanol. BuLi attacks the less hindered carbon of the epoxide, forming a lithium alkoxide which after water quench gives the alcohol and LiOH. Typical conditions: THF solvent, low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) under inert gas, then careful addition of water or dilute acid to protonate the alkoxide.

N‑alkylation via bimolecular nucleophilic substitution (SN2); pyrrolidine attacks the primary carbon of 3‑bromopropionitrile, displacing bromide to give 3‑pyrrolidin‑1‑ylpropanenitrile and HBr. Usually carried out in an aprotic polar solvent such as DMF, acetonitrile or THF, at 0 °C to reflux, with an added base (triethylamine, NaHCO₃) to capture the liberated HBr.

Oxidation of sulfoxide to sulfone: Hydrogen peroxide oxidizes the ethyl‑sulfinyl group of 2‑(ethylsulfinyl)ethanol to the corresponding sulfonyl, yielding water as the only by‑product. Conducted at 0 °C to room temperature in a miscible organic solvent (e.g., MeCN or t‑butanol); often catalyzed by a small amount of acid or base to accelerate H₂O₂ decomposition.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (thioester formation): Methanethiol attacks acetyl fluoride, forming S‑methyl thioacetate and releasing hydrogen fluoride. Reaction is carried out at 0 °C to 25 °C in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, with a stoichiometric base (e.g., pyridine, triethylamine) to capture HF.

Salt metathesis (acid–salt) precipitation; converts yttrium nitrate to yttrium oxalate, leaving nitric acid in solution. Performed in aqueous medium by adding aqueous oxalic acid to Y(NO3)3; Y2(C2O4)3 precipitates due to low solubility; reaction carried out at ≤25 °C to prevent dissolution, no catalyst needed.

Combustion/oxidative decomposition: Praseodymium(III) acetate burns in excess oxygen, oxidizing the organic acetate ligands to CO₂ and H₂O while the metal converts to praseodymium(III) oxide (Pr₂O₃). Requires heating to high temperature (≥500 °C) in a flow of O₂; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Esterification (acetylation) of a diol: Propylene glycol reacts with two equivalents of acetic anhydride to give propylene glycol diacetate and two equivalents of acetic acid. Performed under reflux, often neat or with a catalytic amount of pyridine/DMAP to promote acyl transfer; the by‑product acetic acid is removed by azeotropic distillation or neutralization.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification): Methyl stearate is hydrolyzed by aqueous NaOH to produce sodium stearate (soap) and methanol. Reaction is carried out in water (or water/ethanol mixture) at reflux (≈80 °C) until completion; the mixture is then acidified if free fatty acid is desired. No additional catalyst is required.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of (E)‑benzylidenehydrazine back to benzaldehyde and hydrazine; water adds across the C=N bond, regenerating the aldehyde; conducted in aqueous acidic solution (e.g., 1 M HCl) under reflux.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary bromide by iodide; converts 3‑bromopropan‑1‑ol to 3‑iodopropan‑1‑ol while forming NaBr precipitate. Typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as dry acetone (Finkelstein conditions), reflux or gentle heating; NaI is soluble, NaBr precipitates driving the equilibrium.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) ion‑exchange reaction between copper(II) acetate and sodium bromide; yields copper(II) bromide and sodium acetate. Usually carried out in aqueous medium at ambient temperature; salts remain in solution or precipitate depending on solubility; no catalyst required.

Coupling/condensation reaction activating the phosphate of glycerol‑3‑phosphate with carbonyldiimidazole (CDI) to form α‑glycerylphosphorylcholine; imidazole is released as by‑product. Conducted under anhydrous conditions in aprotic solvents such as DMF or DMSO, often at 0 °C to 40 °C under nitrogen; CDI acts as activating reagent, no external catalyst needed.

Conversion of phenol to aryl chloride using POCl₃ (Pyridine‑mediated chlorination); purpose is to replace the hydroxyl group with chlorine; POCl₃ activates the phenol, pyridine scavenges HCl, yielding 4‑bromophenyl chloride, HCl and pyridinium chloride; typically performed in pyridine as solvent, 0 °C to 25 °C, under inert atmosphere; pyridine acts as base and solvent.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (halogenation); bromine adds to the activated phenol ring at the ortho positions relative to the hydroxyl group, yielding 2,6-dibromo-4-tert-butylphenol and HBr. Typically carried out in an inert organic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride, chloroform or acetic acid at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a catalytic amount of a base (e.g., pyridine) to trap HBr.

Single‑replacement redox reaction in aqueous medium: magnesium metal displaces cadmium from cadmium chloride, giving magnesium chloride in solution and precipitating metallic cadmium. Performed in water, usually with gentle heating to accelerate the reaction; no catalyst is used.

N‑acylation (Schotten‑Baumann amide formation); the amine nitrogen of isopropylamine attacks benzoyl chloride displacing chloride to form N‑benzoylisopropylamine. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature, with a base (e.g., pyridine, triethylamine) to neutralize the generated HCl.

Hydride reduction of the ketone tropinone to the secondary alcohol tropine using lithium aluminium hydride. Performed in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) under inert atmosphere, typically at 0 °C then warmed to reflux; LiAlH4 supplies hydride, converting the carbonyl to an alcohol and leaving the bicyclic amine intact.

Redox (oxidation‑reduction) reaction in concentrated hydrogen bromide where Mo(VI) oxide is reduced to Mo(III) bromide and bromide is oxidized to bromine, with water as by‑product. Carried out by heating MoO₃ directly with excess HBr (often gaseous or concentrated liquid) at elevated temperatures (≈150–200 °C); no additional solvent or catalyst required.

Hydride reduction of the aldehyde group of vanillin to give vanillyl alcohol using lithium aluminium hydride. Conducted in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) under nitrogen, typically at 0 °C to reflux; LiAlH4 reduces the aldehyde to a primary alcohol, leaving the methoxy and phenolic functionalities unchanged.

Oxidative decomposition (combustion) of manganese(II) acetate; heating the solid acetate in excess oxygen decomposes the organic acetate ligands to carbon dioxide and water while the metal is oxidized to manganese(II) oxide. Typically performed by direct heating of the solid in an open flame or furnace at high temperature; no solvent or catalyst required.

Amidation (condensation) of 2,6‑pyridinedicarboxylic acid with ammonia; two equivalents of ammonia react with the two carboxyl groups to give the corresponding diamide (2,6‑pyridinedicarboxamide) with loss of two equivalents of water. Usually carried out by heating the acid with gaseous or aqueous ammonia, often employing an activating agent such as thionyl chloride, SOCl₂, or a carbodiimide to promote the dehydration step.

Catalytic oxidation of a secondary alcohol; 2‑butanol is oxidized by molecular oxygen in the presence of palladium on carbon to give butan‑2‑one (methyl ethyl ketone) and water. Conducted in a solvent such as acetonitrile, toluene, or ethanol at 50–80 °C under an O₂ or air atmosphere, using a few Pd / C as the heterogeneous catalyst.

Selective oxidation of β‑pinene with potassium permanganate; the allylic double bond is oxidized to the ketone verbenone, while KMnO₄ is reduced to MnO₂ precipitate and water is generated. Usually performed in aqueous alkaline solution (often acetate buffer) at 0–25 °C; a biphasic system with dichlorometh can be used to extract the organic product, and the insoluble MnO₂ is filtered off.

Acid–base deprotonation of diphenylphosphine with a strong organolithium; n‑butyllithium abstracts the phosphorus‑hydrogen proton to afford lithium diphenylphosphide and releases n‑butane gas. Carried out at low temperature (‑78 °C to –20 °C) in anhydrous ether or THF under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) to prevent moisture or air attack.

Proton transfer (acid–base) between phosphoric and potassium thiocyanate; the strong acid protonates the thiocyanate ion to give thiocyanic acid (HSCN) and the conjugate base potassium dihydrogen phosphate (KH₂PO₄). Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the reaction is exothermic and the products remain dissolved in water.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a benzylic bromide with water in the presence of aqueous potassium carbonate; the carbonate acts as a mild base to generate hydroxide that displaces bromide, yielding 4‑methoxybenzyl alcohol and potassium bromide. Typically carried out at ambient temperature or gentle reflux in water; no additional catalyst required.

Selective reduction of an aromatic ester to the corresponding aldehyde using diisobutylaluminium hydride (DIBAL‑H). The reaction proceeds at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) in an aprotic ether solvent such as THF or toluene under inert atmosphere, affording p‑nitrobenzaldehyde and methanol as a by‑product. No external catalyst is needed.

Aluminothermic (thermite) reduction of molybdenum(VI) oxide by metallic aluminium. A high‑temperature (≈1000 °C) solid‑state reaction in a furnace produces metallic molybdenum and aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃). Performed under an inert or reducing atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is.

Solid‑gas carbonation of zinc oxide with carbon dioxide to form zinc carbonate. The reaction is an acid‑base process that proceeds more readily in the presence of moisture and at elevated temperature (often 200–300 °C) or under pressure. Conducted in a sealed vessel or furnace; no catalyst required.

Protonolysis (ligand exchange) of tris(dimethylamido)aluminum(III) with hydrogen chloride HCl protonates the dimethylamido groups, releasing dimethylamine and generating aluminum chloride (AlCl₃). The reaction is typically performed in anhydrous organic solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ THF at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst is needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation between aqueous ammonium oxalate and cobalt(II) chloride. Cobalt(II) oxalate precipitates as an insoluble solid while ammonium chloride remains dissolved. The reaction proceeds at room temperature in water; no catalyst is required.

Neutralization reaction. Purpose: Conversion of isothiocyanic acid (HNCS) to sodium thiocyanate (NaSCN). Key transformation: deprotonation of HNCS by NaOH. Conditions: aqueous solution, room temperature. Product includes water as a byproduct. No catalyst required.

Reductive dehalogenation. Zinc serves as reducing agent for removal of a chlorine atom from aromatic ring. Acetic acid provides proton source during cleavage, with concomitant formation of zinc chloride. Requires moderate heating in aqueous or mixed solvent system. Reaction follows cleavage mechanism rather than full reduction to benzene.

Thionation of a primary alcohol to a thiol using phosphorus pentasulfide; purpose is to replace the hydroxyl group with a thiol group, producing hexadecanethiol; key transformation is conversion of the C‑O bond to a C‑S bond with simultaneous formation of phosphoric acid as by‑product; typically carried out by refluxing hexadecanol with P₂S₅ (1.2–1.5 equiv) in anhydrous pyridine or xylene under nitrogen at 100–130 °C; no additional catalyst required.

Free‑radical bromination of 2‑methylhexane; purpose is to introduce a bromine atom at the terminal (C‑1) carbon to give 1‑CH2Br‑2‑methylhexane; the reaction proceeds via homolytic cleavage of Br2 (initiated by UV light or heat) to generate Br· radicals that abstract a hydrogen atom from the alkane and then combine with the resulting carbon radical; typical conditions: dilute Br2 (1–2 equiv) in an inert, non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, UV irradiation or reflux over a peroxide initiator; the process is less selective than chlorination, giving a mixture of primary, secondary and tertiary bromides, with the desired primary product isolated by distillation or chromatography.

Hydrolysis (water‑mediated cleavage); conversion of the prodrug leflunomide to its active metabolite teriflunomide. Key transformation is opening of the isoxazole amide group to give the free carboxylic acid (teriflunomide). Usually performed in aqueous medium at ambient or slightly elevated temperature, often under mildly (pH ≈ 4–5) or neutral conditions; no special catalyst required, water is the reagent and solvent.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; exchange of anions between lead(II) nitrate and cesium sulfate to precipitate insoluble lead sulfate while forming soluble cesium nitrate. Performed by mixing aqueous solutions of the two salts at room temperature; the reaction proceeds spontaneously, and the solid Pb₄ is filtered off. No catalyst needed; water is the reaction medium.

Acid‑carbonate reaction (acid–base neutralization); hydrochloric acid reacts with erbium(III) carbonate, carbon dioxide gas and forming aqueous erbium(III) chloride. The carbonate anion is protonated to CO₂ and H₂O, while Er³⁺ is paired with Cl⁻. Conducted in aqueous HCl, typically at 0 °C to control vigorous gas evolution or at room temperature; stirring is sufficient, no catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (sification); sodium hydroxide attacks the carbonyl carbon of ethyl 3‑methylpentanoate, yielding ethanol and the sodium salt of 3‑methylpentanoic acid. Reaction is carried out in a mixture of water and an alcohol (often ethanol or methanol) under reflux for 1–2 h. After completion the mixture is acidified if the free acid desired; no additional catalyst beyond NaOH is required.

Halogen‑exchange (halogen atom transfer) between iodine monochloride and potassium bromide; bromide attacks ICl, displacing chloride and forming iodine monobromide (IBr) while KCl precipitates. Usually performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or acetonitrile at ambient temperature.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution – Friedel‑Crafts bromination. Aluminum bromide activates bromine, generating a bromonium electrophile that attacks the aromatic ring of 3‑hydroxyacetophenone preferentially at the ortho position to the carbonyl, giving 2‑bromo‑3‑hydroxyacetophenone and HBr as by‑product. Purpose: introduction of a bromine substituent for further functionalisation. Typical conditions: anhydrous AlBr₃ (≈1 equiv) with Br₂ in dry dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride, 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere.

Acid‑base ligand exchange (salt formation); lactic acid donates protons to zirconium oxychloride, generating zirconium lactate coordination polymer and hydrochloric acid as by‑product. Usually carried out in aqueous solution with gentle heating (50–80 °C) to promote dissolution and complexation; the pH is adjusted to favor lactate coordination. No external catalyst is required, water serves as solvent.

Acid‑base neutralization (oxide‑acid reaction): indium(III) oxide reacts with excess glacial acetic acid to form indium(III) acetate and water. The oxide is dissolved by heating the mixture under reflux in glacial acetic acid, which serves both as reactant and solvent. No additional catalyst is required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene: molecular hydrogen adds across the carbon‑carbon double bond of (E)‑2‑methylhept‑3‑ene to afford the saturated alkane 2‑methylheptane. Typical conditions involve H₂ gas (1–5 atm) in the presence of a heterogeneous catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni, with a solvent like ethanol or ethyl acetate, at temperatures of 25–80 °C.

Quaternary alkylation (SN2) of a hydrazine derivative: 1,1‑dimethylhydrazine undergoes nucleophilic substitution with methyl iodide, giving the trimethylhydrazinium iodide salt. The reaction is performed in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile) at 0 °C to room temperature, often neat or with slight excess of methyl iodide; no catalyst is needed.

Conversion of cyclopropylmethanol to cyclopropylmethyl bromide using phosphorus tribromide (PBr3). This is an Sn2 substitution; the reaction is performed at 0 °C to rt in anhydrous ether or dichloromethane under nitrogen. PBr3 reacts with the alcohol to give the bromide and phosphorous acid (H3PO3) as by‑product.

Esterification (condensation) of phosphoric acid with ethanol to give triethyl phosphate; purpose is preparation of a phosphate ester used as flame retardant, plasticizer or solvent; key transformation replaces the three hydroxyl groups of H₃PO₄ with ethoxy groups, releasing three molecules of water; typically performed by refluxing excess ethanol with concentrated phosphoric acid, often with azeotropic removal of water; ethanol serves as both reactant and solvent.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) of ortho‑difluorobenzene with sodium methoxide to afford 2‑fluoroanisole and sodium fluoride; used to introduce a methoxy group onto a fluorinated aromatic ring; methoxide attacks the carbon bearing a fluorine, displacing fluoride; usually carried out in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF DMSO at 80‑130 °C; no additional catalyst required.

Acid–base neutralization; converts the potassium salt of pentanoic acid to the free carboxylic acid. Key transformation: K⁺ is exchanged for H⁺, yielding pentanoic acid and KCl. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; excess HCl is added dropwise and the mixture is stirred. No special catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Transesterification of methyl 2,2‑difluoroacetate with ethanol; exchange of the alkoxy group to give ethyl 2,2‑difluoroacetate and methanol; usually acid (e.g., H2SO4) or base (e.g., NaOMe) catalyzed under reflux with excess ethanol; solvent ethanol (or toluene with azeotropic removal of methanol).

Redox/halogen exchange reaction used in water treatment; hypochlorous acid oxidizes monochloramine to dichloramine while being reduced to water. Occurs in aqueous solution, typically at near‑neutral pH and low temperature (0‑25 °C). No special catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration of imidazole; dinitrogen pentoxide supplies nitronium ion which substitutes at the 4‑position of imidazole, yielding 4‑nitroimidazole and water. Conducted under anhydrous conditions, often in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as nitrobenzene or dichloromethane, at 0‑50 °C. No additional catalyst needed.

Thermal decomposition (calcination) of cadmium carbonate; heating solid CdCO₃ strongly (≈300‑400 °C) in the absence of solvent causes breakdown to cadmium oxide (CdO) solid and release of carbon dioxide gas (CO₂). No catalyst required.

Amidoxime formation (addition of hydroxylamine to a nitrile) where acetonitrile reacts with hydroxylamine sulfate to produce N‑hydroxyacetamidine (acetamidoxime) and sulfuric acid; serves to generate amidoxime functional groups useful in metal chelation and prodrug chemistry; the nitrile carbon is attacked by nucleophilic hydroxylamine followed by tautomerization; commonly performed in aqueous ethanol or water at ambient to reflux temperatures; the generated H₂SO₄ is often neutralized in situ.

Acid–base metathesis of a metal soap; zinc stearate reacts with concentrated nitric acid to liberate stearic acid and form soluble zinc nitrate. Performed in aqueous medium, typically at reflux (80‑100 °C) to ensure complete conversion. No catalyst required; excess acid drives the reaction.

Acid‑base neutralization of beryllium hydroxide with acetic acid to form beryllium acetate; purpose is salt preparation; key transformation: Be(OH)₂ + 2 CH₃COOH → Be(CH₃COO)₂ + 2 H₂O; typical conditions: aqueous solution, ambient or mildly heated (≤50 °C) stirring; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

This is a Fischer esterification forming propyl octanoate from octanoic acid and 1‑propanol. Type: condensation (esterification). Purpose: synthesize the propyl ester of octanoic acid. Key transformation: –COOH + HOPr → –COOPr + H₂O. Typical conditions: excess 1‑propanol, catalytic amount of a strong acid (e.g., 1–2 % H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH), reflux (80–100 °C). Water is removed continuously (Dean–Stark trap or azeotropic distillation) to drive the equilibrium toward product. Solvent often toluene or the alcohol itself.

Oxidative chlorination of chloroform to chloropicrin; concentrated nitric acid oxidizes and chlorinates chloroform, producing trichloronitromethane (chloropicrin) and water. Carried out in a sealed vessel at 70‑90 °C with concentrated (≈ 95 %) nitric acid. Reaction is exothermic; temperature control is critical. No catalyst required.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis); aqueous solutions of barium chloride and rubidium iodate exchange anions to give insoluble barium iodate, which precipitates, and soluble rubidium chloride remains in solution. Conducted at ambient temperature with stirring; the precipitate is filtered and washed. No catalyst needed.

Electrophilic addition of Cl2 across the C=C of 1‑hexene; halogenation gives the vicinal 1,2‑dichlorohexane. Typically carried out at 0 °C to rt in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, under dark conditions to avoid radical side reactions.

Type: Alkylaluminum halide exchangemetathesis). Purpose: Generate methyl chloride and dimethylaluminum chloride for organometallic and Lewis‑acid applications. Key transformation: Chlorine replaces one methyl group on trimethylaluminum, forming CH3Cl and a mixed AlCl/Me species (Me2AlCl). Typical conditions: Conducted under inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar) at low temperature (‑78°C to 0 °C) to control exotherm; dry, aprotic solvent such as toluene or hexanes; no external catalyst required.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification; methanol displaces the 2‑methylbutyl alkoxy group of 2‑methylbutyl acetate, producing methyl acetate and 2‑methyl‑1‑butanol. Typical conditions include catalytic NaOCH₃ or sulfuric acid, reflux in methanol, and continuous removal of methyl acetate (or use of excess methanol) to shift equilibrium.

Type: N‑hydroxymethylation (nucleophilic addition of an amide nitrogen to formaldehyde). Purpose: Produce N‑(hydroxymethyl)formamide, an intermediate for methylol‑urea and resin chemistry. Key transformation: The lone pair on the formamide nitrogen attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon of formaldehyde, yielding a N‑C bond and a new hydroxymethyl group attached to nitrogen. Typical conditions: Mild acid or base catalysis (e.g., acetic acid or NaOH) in aqueous or alcoholic solvent (water, methanol) at ambient temperature; reaction proceeds readily without heating.

Peracid epoxidation of 2‑pentene using performic acid; performed at 0–25 °C in an inert organic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂ or a water/acetone mixture), the alkene is oxidized to 2‑pentyloxirane with formic acid generated as the by‑product.

The reaction involves hydrolysis of a dithiolane acetal under acidic conditions. The general type is acid-catalyzed hydrolysis of acetals/protecting groups. Purpose: regenerate carbonyl compounds (acetaldehyde) from protected thiolane. Conditions: aqueous HCl. Key transformation: cleavage of the dithiolane ring yields the carbonyl group and 1,2-ethanedithiol.

Type: Acid‑base neutralization/halogenation of a metal hydroxide. Purpose: Convert zirconium hydroxide to zirconium(IV) chloride, a common Lewis‑acid catalyst and precursor for Zr‑based materials. Key transformation: Four equivalents of HCl protonate the hydroxide groups, releasing water and substituting chloride for oxide, yielding ZrCl4. Typical conditions: Use concentrated aqueous HCl, heat gently (≈50–80 °C) to drive off water; reaction performed in an inert vessel, no catalyst required.

Type: Oxidative redox reaction (acidic oxidation of sulfide by concentrated nitric acid). Purpose: Produce strontium nitrate, oxidize sulfide to sulfur dioxide, and generate nitrogen oxides as by‑products. Key transformation: Nitrate ions oxidize S²⁻ to SO₂ while being reduced to NO₂; Sr²⁺ is simultaneously nitrated to Sr(NO₃)₂; water is formed from the acid‑base balance. Typical conditions: Excess concentrated HNO₃ (≈68 %); reflux the mixture in a glass vessel equipped with a gas‑scrubbing system; temperature 80–100 °C; no external catalyst needed.

Type: Selective catalytic hydrogenation of an acyl chloride to an aldehyde. Purpose: Synthesize butanal from butanoyl chloride while avoiding over‑reduction to the alcohol. Key transformation: Pd supported on BaSO₄ (Pearlman’s catalyst) adsorbs H₂ and delivers two hydrogen atoms to the carbonyl carbon of the acyl chloride, reducing it to the aldehyde and releasing HCl. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂ pressure, 0–25 °C, solvent such as dry ethanol, ether, or THF; catalyst loading 1–5 % Pd; quinoline may be added as a poison to suppress further reduction to the alcohol.

Type: Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alcohol by phosphorus tribromide. Purpose: Convert 1‑propanol to the corresponding primary alkyl bromide, 1‑bromopropane. Key transformation: PBr₃ reacts with the hydroxyl group to form alkyl phosphite intermediate that collapses, displacing bromide and giving 1‑bromopropane; the by‑product is phosphorous acid (H₃PO₃). Typical conditions: Anhydrous ether or dichloromethane solvent, temperature 0 °C to reflux, inert atmosphere; PBr₃ is used in slight excess (≈1 equiv per 3 alcohol equivalents) and no additional catalyst is required.

Acid‑catalyzed esterification (nitrate ester formation); purpose is to convert ethanol into ethyl nitrate; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of ethanol on the protonated nitric acid generating the nitrate ester and water; typically performed with concentrated HNO₃/H₂SO₄ mixture at 0‑5 °C warmed to 25‑30 °C; sulfuric acid acts as both catalyst and dehydrating agent, no external solvent is required.

Base‑induced elimination (E2) using aqueous base; heated NaOH promotes dehydrohalogenation of 2‑chloropropane to propene. Key transformation: elimination of HCl to form the alkene, producing NaCl and water. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (often 5–10 % w/w) heated to 80–100 °C, sometimes with a phase‑transfer catalyst if a biphasic system is used. No additional catalyst required.

N‑acylation of tert‑butylamine with acetic anhydride to form N‑tert‑butylacetamide and acetic acid as by‑product; a typical amide‑formation (Schotten‑Baumann) reaction carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in a dry aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine, often with a base (e.g., pyridine) to scavenge the generated acid.

Simple acid–base salt formation (protonation of an amide); purpose is to obtain the hydrochloride salt of propionamide for increased solubility or isolation; key transformation is proton transfer from HCl to the carbonyl oxygen or nitrogen of propionamide yielding propionamide·HCl; carried out by stirring propionamide in aqueous or ethanolic HCl at ambient temperature; no additional catalyst required.

Copper(II)‑mediated oxidative cleavage of an alkyl hydroperoxide; purpose is to generate phenol and acetaldehyde from ethyl‑benzene‑hydroperoxide; key transformations involve reduction of Cu(II) to Cu(I) while the O–O bond of the hydroperoxide fragments, producing phenol, acetaldehyde, and CuCl; typically performed in an organic solvent such as acetonitrile or chlorobenzene at 50‑100 °C under inert atmosphere; copper(II) chloride functions as the catalytic oxidant.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (E1 elimination) of 1‑hexanol with concentrated sulfuric acid to give hex‑1‑ene and water; purpose is synthesis of a terminal alkene from a primary alcohol; the hydroxyl group is protonated, water leaves to form a carbocation, then β‑rogen elimination yields the alkene; carried out by heating the alcohol 70‑98 % H₂SO₄ at 140‑180 °C; sulfuric acid acts as both catalyst and solvent; typically performed in a reflux apparatus.

Thermal isomerization (S→N rearrangement) of an alkyl thiocyanate to the corresponding isothiocyanate; purpose is to obtain ethyl isothiocyanate, a useful flavor or synthetic intermediate; key transformation is a 1,3‑sigmatropic shift of the –SCN group to –NCS; performed by heating ethyl thiocyanate at 180‑220 °C, either neat or in a high‑boiling inert solvent such as xylene; no catalyst is required.

Hydrolytic oxidation of a silane (Si–H cleavage); purpose is to produce dimethylsilanol and release hydrogen gas; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of water on the Si‑H bond with simultaneous transfer of hydride to generate H₂; commonly carried out in aqueous base (e.g., NaOH) or with transition‑metal catalysts (Pd, Pt) at 50‑100 °C; the basic medium or metal catalyst facilitates the reaction.

Acid–base neutralization (salt metathesis); converts potassium lactate to free lactic acid while generating potassium hydrogen sulfate. Typically performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; water serves as solvent, no additional catalyst required.

Neutralization of hexafluorosilicic acid with sodium hydroxide to produce sodium hexafluorosilicate and water. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often with stoichiometric NaOH added slowly to control exotherm; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Oxidative fluorination; elemental fluorine adds to rhenium(VI) hexafluoride to give rhenium(VII) heptafluoride. Generally carried out in anhydrous liquid fluorine or HF medium at low temperature (−78 °C to 0 °C) to control reactivity; no separate catalyst is needed.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (amination) of an α‑chloro ester with aqueous NH3; purpose is to replace the chloride with an amino group to give ethyl 2‑aminopropanoate; key transformation: R‑CHCl‑COOEt → R‑CH(NH2)‑COOEt, NH4Cl formed as by‑product; typical conditions: reflux or gentle heating (50‑80 °C) in a mixture of ethanol/water or methanol/water, excess aqueous ammonia; no special catalyst required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) acid‑base reaction between ammonium hydroxide and potassium chromate forming ammonium chromate and potassium hydroxide; used to prepare soluble ammonium chromate salts; involves exchange of cations and anions without redox change; performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; no catalyst needed.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification; glycerol monoacetate reacts with n‑butanol to exchange the acetate group, yielding glycerol and n‑butyl acetate. Typically performed with catalytic NaOH or K₂CO₃ in excess n‑butanol under reflux; removal of butyl acetate drives the equilibrium.

Ozonolysis (oxidative cleavage) of an alkyne; phenylacetylene is cleaved by O₃ in the presence of water to afford benzoic acid and carbon dioxide. Conducted in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane at −78 °C to 0 °C, followed by aqueous work‑up (often with H₂O₂) to reduce ozonides.

Reduction of germanium disulfide with hydrogen; a high‑temperature hydrogenation that reduces GeS₂ to elemental Ge while producing H₂S gas; typically carried out in a sealed tube furnace at 400–600 °C under flowing H₂; no solvent or catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification (ester exchange); acetic acid reacts with methyl lactate to swap the acyl groups, producing lactic acid and methyl acetate. Usually performed under reflux in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., toluene) with a catalytic amount of concentrated H₂SO₄ or p‑toluenesulfonic acid; removal of methyl acetate shifts equilibrium toward products.

Oxidation (dehydrogenation) of a primary alcohol using copper(II) oxide as the stoichiometric oxidant; the alcohol is converted to the corresponding aldehyde while CuO is reduced to metallic copper and water is formed. Typical procedure involves refluxing the isoamyl alcohol with a solid excess of CuO (often 1–2 equivalents) in a high‑boiling, non‑polar solvent such as toluene or xylene, sometimes with a few drops of pyridine to facilitate copper reduction. The reaction is carried out under an inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) to avoid over‑oxidation, and the copper metal precipitates out as a solid.

Strong reduction of an ester (ethyl propionate) with lithium aluminium hydride (LiAlH₄), cleaving both the alkoxy and acyl fragments to give the two corresponding primary alcohols (ethanol from the ethoxy group and 1‑propanol from the propionyl group). The reaction is performed in an aprotic ether solvent (dry diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature, followed by reflux or gentle heating to complete reduction. After the reaction, a careful aqueous work‑up (typically with dilute HCl) quenches excess hydride and isolates the alcohol products.

Copper‑catalyzed Ullmann‑type aryl amination (C–N cross‑coupling) of 1,5‑dichloronaphthalene with ammonia to afford 1,5‑diaminonaphthalene. CuI (often 5–10 mol %) is employed as the catalyst together with 1,10‑phenanthroline as a supporting ligand and potassium carbonate as the base. The reaction is carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as N,N‑dimethylformamide (DMF) or N‑methyl‑2‑pyrrolidone (NMP) at elevated temperatures (120–150 °C) under a sealed tube or inert atmosphere. The amination proceeds through oxidative addition of the aryl chloride Cu(I), transmetalation with ammonia, and reductive elimination to give the aryl amine.

Thermal or catalytic decomposition of hydrazoic acid; the unstable HN₃ breaks down to N₂ and H₂ gases. Usually induced by heating (≈100 °C) or by a metal catalyst (e.g., Cu, Zn) in a flow system to safely vent the gases.

Electrochemical oxidation of bromide in the presence of isocyanuric acid to generate tribromoisocyanuric acid, a solid brominating agent, while releasing hydrogen bromide (HBr) as a by‑product. The process is performed in an aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic electrolyte (often containing a supporting salt such as Na₂SO₄) with a graphite or platinum anode. A constant anodic potential sufficient to oxidize Br⁻ to Br₂ (or Br⁺) is applied; the in‑situ generated bromine reacts with isocyanuric acid to afford the tribromo derivative. The reaction is conducted at room temperature, and the cell is usually operated under stirring with a cathodic reduction (e.g., H⁺ to H₂) to balance the charge.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid using potassium dichromate in sulfuric acid; converts the –CH2OH group of 2‑methyl‑1‑butanol into –COOH, producing water; performed in aqueous H2SO4 under reflux, K2Cr2O7 acts as the oxidant.

Catalytic dehydrogenation of cyclopentane to cyclopentene with concurrent formation of H2; removes two hydrogen atoms from the saturated ring to give the alkene; carried out at 500‑600 °C in the gas phase over metal catalysts such as Pt, Pd or Cr₂O₃; no solvent required.

Grignard addition of 3‑pyridylmagnesium bromide (generated from 3‑bromopyridine and Mg) to formaldehyde, yielding 3‑pyridinemethanol after acidic work‑up; forms a new C–C bond at the carbonyl carbon; performed in anhydrous ether or THF under inert atmosphere at 0 °C to reflux; magnesium serves as the metal source for the organometallic reagent.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (Schotten‑Baumann acylation) of sodium ethoxide with acetyl chloride; yields ethyl acetate and sodium chloride. Ethoxide attacks the carbonyl carbon of acetyl chloride, displacing chloride and forming the ester. Reaction is performed in dry aprotic solvents such as ether or THF at 0–5 °C under inert atmosphere to avoid moisture; no additional catalyst is required.

High‑temperature redox (steam‑reaction) of aluminum with water vapor producing aluminum oxide (Al2O3) and hydrogen gas; performed in a furnace at ≥800 °C under a flow of steam, no catalyst required, the only reagents are solid Al and gaseous H2O.

Hydrolysis of rhodium(III) fluoride by water to give hydrofluoric acid and rhodium(III) oxide; fluoride ligands are replaced by hydroxide, which condenses to the oxide; conducted in aqueous solution, usually with gentle heating; no additional catalyst needed.

Hydrolysis of yttrium iodide with water producing hydrogen iodide and yttrium hydroxide; the metal halide reacts with water to form the corresponding hydroxide and acid; carried out in aqueous medium, often at ambient to mild heating; no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed intramolecular dehydration (cyclodehydration) of 1,3‑butanediol to tetrahydrofuran; one –OH group attacks the carbon bearing the other –OH after protonation, forming the five‑membered ether ring and releasing water; typically performed with concentrated H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH at 150‑180 °C; water is removed to drive the equilibrium.

Base‑catalyzed crossed aldol condensation (Claisen‑Schmidt) of acetone with two equivalents of benzaldehyde in DMF using potassium carbonate; acetone is deprotonated to an enolate, attacks benzaldehyde, and undergoes double dehydration to give the conjugated α,β‑unsaturated diketone dibenzylideneacetone, with water as the only by‑product; typically run at reflux in DMF under mild basic conditions.

Acid‑base neutralisation (salt metathesis) in aqueous solution where disodium succinate reacts with sulfuric acid to protonate the succinate dianion, forming succinic acid and sodium sulfate; performed at room temperature or with gentle heating, no special catalyst required.

Reduction of an allylic ester to the corresponding primary allylic alcohol using lithium aluminium hydride. Type: metal hydride reduction of ester. Purpose: convert 3‑methyl‑2‑butenyl acetate into 3‑methyl‑2‑buten‑1‑ol. Key transformation: ester carbonyl C=O is reduced to CH2OH; the allylic double bond remains unchanged. Typical conditions: dry aprotic ether solvent (THF or diethyl ether), addition of LiAlH4 at 0 °C followed by reflux; quenched with dilute acid or water under inert atmosphere.
