Performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; evolution of CO2 drives the reaction to completion. No catalyst needed.

Double displacement (metathesis) ion‑exchange reaction; calcium chloride exchanges ions with disodium malate to produce calcium malate and sodium chloride. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst; water is the medium.

Protonation (acid–base) reaction forming a salt. Excess sulfuric acid protonates pyridine, producing pyridinium hydrogen sulfate (pyridinium sulfate). Usually conducted by slowly adding conc. H2SO4 to pyridine at 0 °C to control exotherm, then allowing the mixture to warm to room temperature. No catalyst; solvent can be pyridine itself or a non‑reactive solvent such as dichloromethane.

Urea (carbamate) formation via nucleophilic of the amino group of 3,4‑dichloroaniline to the electrophilic carbon of 4‑chlorophenyl isocyanate, producing triclocarban. Usually carried out neat or in a non‑polar solvent (toluene, xylene) at 80–120 °C, sometimes with a catalytic amount of base, and the product precipitates on cooling.

Double displacement precipitation; aqueous NiCl2·6H2O reacts with NaOH to form insoluble Ni(OH)2 precipitate, NaCl in solution and water; carried out in water at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring.

Nucleophilic carboxylation of an organolithium reagent; n‑butyllithium adds to carbon dioxide to form lithium butanoate, a carboxylate salt; performed under inert atmosphere (nitrogen or argon) in dry ethereal solvent such as THF or diethyl ether, typically at −78 °C to 0 °C to control reactivity; the product is isolated after aqueous work‑up.

Thermal decomposition of an inorganic salt. Potassium hexafluoroarsenate (KAsF6) is heated, causing cleavage of the K–AsF6 bond to release volatile arsenic pentafluoride (AsF5) gas and solid potassium fluoride (KF). Requires elevated temperature (≈200–300 °C) under anhydrous, inert atmosphere (e.g., nitrogen or argon). No solvent or catalyst is employed.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (hydrogenation) of a benzylic chloride. Molecular hydrogen in the presence of a metal catalyst (Pd/C, Raney Ni, or PtO2) reduces 2‑chloro‑6‑fluorobenzyl chloride, cleaving the C–Cl bond and forming 2‑chloro‑6‑fluorotoluene with concomitant release of HCl. Reaction is carried out in a suitable solvent such as ethanol, methanol, or THF under H2 pressure (1–5 atm) at 25–80 °C. The catalyst facilitates the substitution of the benzylic chloride by a hydrogen atom.

Knoevenagel condensation of 2‑chlorobenzaldehyde with malononitrile to form 2‑(2‑chlorobenzylidene)malononitrile; a base‑catalyzed carbon–carbon bond‑forming reaction. Typical conditions use a catalytic amount of piperidine or ammonium acetate as base in ethanol or methanol, with the reactants heated under reflux for several hours (2–6 h). Water is eliminated to give the α,β‑unsaturated nitrile product, which precipitates upon cooling and can be filtered.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl bromide by ammonia. Purpose: convert bromoacetaldehyde to 2‑aminoacetaldehyde. Key transformation: NH3 attacks the electrophilic carbon, displacing Br− to give the aminoaldehyde; ammonium bromide forms as a by‑product. Conditions: excess aqueous NH3 at 0–5 °C to limit side reactions, reaction time 1–2 h, solvent water or water/ethanol. No catalyst required.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; used to prepare mercuric cyanide by exchanging anions. Sodium cyanide and mercuric bromide are mixed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the insoluble Hg(CN)₂ precipitates while NaBr remains dissolved. No catalyst required; water is the typical solvent.

Hydroamination (addition of NH₃ across a C=C bond) of cyclopropene to give cyclopropylamine. The strained cyclopropene undergoes nucleophilic attack by ammonia, usually under sealed‑tube conditions with excess NH₃ (liquid ammonia or high‑pressure gas) at 50–120 °C. Transition‑metal catalysts (e.g., Rh, Ir, or Ni complexes) in inert solvents such as THF or toluene are often employed to improve yield.

Double‑displacement precipitation: potassium sulfide reacts with lead(II) nitrate to yield lead(II) sulfide precipitate and soluble potassium nitrate. Conducted in water, usually at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition of a metal phosphate – Chromium(III) phosphate, when heated strongly (typically >800 °C) in a furnace, decomposes to chromium(III) oxide (Cr2O3) and phosphorus pentoxide (P2O5). No solvent or catalyst is used; the reaction proceeds in the solid state under an inert or air atmosphere.

Copper‑mediated Ullmann ether synthesis (C–O cross‑coupling) of phenol with iodobenzene to afford diphenyl ether. Potassium carbonate deprotonates phenol; CuI catalyzes the aryl‑oxygen bond formation in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO or NMP) at 150–200 °C. By‑products are KI and Cu₂O. No additional ligands are strictly required, though catalytic systems may include N‑donor ligands for higher efficiency.

Redox oxidation; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes Se(IV) in selenious acid to Se(VI) forming selenic acid while water is produced; usually conducted in dilute acidic aqueous medium (e.g., H2SO4) at 0‑60 °C, no additional catalyst required.

Acid–base neutralization of a metal oxide. Gallium sesquioxide (Ga₂O₃) reacts with aqueous sulfuric acid, typically under reflux, to give soluble gallium(III) sulfate and water. The reaction proceeds quantitatively in water; heating accelerates dissolution of the oxide.

Oxidation of TEMPO‑hydroxylamine to the nitroxyl radical (TEMPO) using hydrogen peroxide in acetic acid. The mixture is usually stirred at room temperature in a mixed aqueous/acetic acid medium; H₂O₂ serves as the oxidant and generates water as the only by‑product. This protocol is commonly used to generate catalytic TEMPO in situ for subsequent oxidation reactions.

Selective reduction of 2‑mercaptoacetaldehyde to 2‑mercaptoethanol with sodium borohydride. The aldehyde is reduced to a primary alcohol in a protic solvent such as methanol, ethanol, or an aqueous/ethanol mixture, typically at 0–25 °C. NaBH₄ provides hydride without affecting the thiol group; no catalyst is required.

Thermal degradation (thermolysis) of N,N′‑dimethylurea yielding dimethylamine gas and isocyanic acid. Heating the solid to 200–250 °C under reduced pressure causes cleavage of the C–N bond. No catalyst required; performed in a sealed tube or flow reactor.

Esterification (silyl ester formation) with acetic acid; the acidic proton activates the silicon, allowing the ethoxy group to be replaced by an acetate, affording trimethylsilyl acetate and ethanol. Usually performed in an aprotic solvent (CH₂Cl₂ or toluene) with a catalytic amount of a base (pyridine) or a Lewis acid (e.g., ZnCl₂) at rt or gentle reflux.

Nucleophilic carboxylation of a Grignard reagent; converts aylmagnesium chloride into the corresponding carboxylic acid. Hexylmagnesium chloride adds to carbon dioxide to form the magnesium salt of heptanoic acid; subsequent aqueous acidic work‑up protonates the carboxylate, delivering heptanoic acid. Reaction carried out under anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to rt under a CO₂ atmosphere, followed by quench with dilute HCl.

Metalation of naphthalene with lithium metal to give lithium 1‑H‑naphthalen‑1‑ide (lithium naphthalenide); organolithium formation via electron transfer; purpose is to produce a strong reducing agent/nucleophile; lithium turnings added to a solution of naphthalene in dry THF or diethyl ether under nitrogen or argon, usually at 0 °C to room temperature; deep green solution forms; no additional catalyst.

Metathesis (precipitation) reaction in aqueous solution, typically performed at ambient temperature with water as the solvent. Lead(II) formate exchanges its formate anion for hydroxide from NaOH, producing insoluble lead(II) hydroxide precipitate and soluble sodium formate; no catalyst is needed.

Salt metathesis between nitrosyl bromide and silver tetrafluoroborate yielding silver bromide precipitate and nitrosonium tetrafluoroborate; double displacement/halide exchange to prepare the NO⁺ salt for nitrosation; performed in anhydrous, non‑coordinating solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; precipitation of AgBr drives the reaction; no extra catalyst.

Thermite‑type redox (metallothermic reduction); production of metallic ytterbium. Solid Mg reduces YbF3 at high temperature, yielding MgF2 and elemental Yb. Conducted by intimately mixing the powders and heating to 500–800 °C under inert (Ar or N2) atmosphere, often in a sealed crucible or molten‑salt flux; no additional catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification (methanolysis) of phenyl 4‑fluorobenzoate with methanol and catalytic sulfuric acid; ester exchange converting the phenyl ester to methyl 4‑fluorobenzoate and releasing phenol; nucleophilic attack of methanol on the carbonyl followed by phenoxide departure; excess methanol, 1–5 % H₂SO₄, reflux (~65 °C) for several hours, often neat or in methanol solvent; acid acts as catalyst, no other reagents.

Oxidative chlorination of calcium phosphide with chlorine gas to afford phosphorus trichloride and calcium chloride; redox/halogenation inorganic synthesis; purpose is to generate PCl₃ as a useful reagent; solid Ca₃P₂ exposed to dry Cl₂ gas at 200–300 °C in a sealed or flow reactor; no solvent; typically under an inert gas purge; reaction proceeds without added catalyst.

Conversion of 2‑iodobenzoic acid to 2‑iodobenzoyl chloride using thionyl chloride; dehydration/halogenation to form an acid chloride; purpose is to obtain the acyl chloride for subsequent acylation; key replacement of the carboxylic OH by Cl with evolution of SO₂ and HCl; reflux the acid in dry dichloromethane or pyridine with excess SOCl₂, often with catalytic DMF or pyridine; performed under nitrogen or argon; gases are removed as they form.

Acid‑catalyzed cyclization (dehydration). Concentrated phosphoric acid protonates creatine, promoting intramolecular attack of the guanidino nitrogen on the carbonyl carbon, followed by loss of water to give the five‑membered cyclic urea, cyclocreatine. Typically carried out by heating creatine with excess conc. H3PO4 at 100–150 °C; the phosphoric acid acts both as solvent and catalyst.

Halogenolysis/chlorination of an organoborane. Triethylborane reacts with chlorine gas, the B–C bonds are cleaved and each ethyl group is converted to ethyl chloride while boron is converted to boron trichloride (BCl3). Reaction is usually performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an inert, non‑coordinating solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane, under a stream of Cl2.

Hydrolysis (silyl ether cleavage); water replaces the ethoxy group on Me₃Si, yielding trimethylsilanol and ethanol. Typically performed in a mixed organic/aqueous solvent (e.g., THF/H₂O) at room temperature or mild heating; may be catalyzed by a dilute acid or base to accelerate the reaction.

Carbothermal reduction (solid‑state redox). Chromium(VI) oxide is reduced by elemental carbon; carbon is oxidized to CO2 while Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) oxide. Conducted at high temperature (≈1000 °C) in a furnace under an inert atmosphere; the reactants are mixed as powders and heated without solvent.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification (alkoxy exchange). Sodium methoxide attacks the carbonyl of propyl acetate, displacing the propoxide anion and forming methyl acetate; the released propoxide pairs with Na⁺ to give sodium propoxide. Usually carried out in dry methanol or another aprotic polar solvent at reflux (≈65 °C) under anhydrous conditions; excess NaOMe drives the equilibrium.

Redox reduction of osmium tetroxide with hydrogen peroxide; used for detoxification of OsO₄ and simultaneous generation of O₂ gas; OsO₄ + H₂O₂ → OsO₂ + O₂ + H₂O; performed in dilute aqueous H₂O₂ at room temperature; water is the medium, reaction proceeds without added catalyst.

Acid–base neutralization / precipitation: iron(III) hydroxide reacts with phosphoric acid to form iron(III) phosphate precipitate and water. Employed to generate FePO₄ solid or to remove Fe³⁺ from solution. Conducted in water, often with slight heating to improve crystallization; pH is controlled around neutral‑acidic range. No catalyst needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation of diethyl fumarate to diethyl succinate; reduces the C=C double bond of the α,β‑unsaturated diester to a saturated C–C bond; uses H₂ gas (1–5 atm) with Pd/C, PtO₂ or Raney Ni as catalyst; common solvent is ethyl acetate or ethanol; room temperature to 50 °C.

Double displacement precipitation forming lead(II) carbonate and soluble sodium cyanide; aqueous solutions of lead(II) cyanide and sodium carbonate are combined at room temperature, lead carbonate precipitates; water solvent; no catalyst.

General type: sulfidation (gas‑solid reaction). Purpose: conversion of a metal oxide to the corresponding metal sulfide. Key transformation: CrO, replacing oxygen with sulfur to give CrS and water vapor. Typical conditions: pass‑heated CrO (300–500 °C) in a flow reactor; excess H₂S drives the reaction to completion. No solvent; the gas phase serves as reactant.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (E1 elimination) of a tertiary‑like cyclopropanol; purpose is to form the corresponding alkene, 1‑methylcyclopropene; key step is removal of water from the alcohol; usually performed with concentrated H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH at 80–120 °C; solvent can be the acid itself or a polar aprotic solvent like dichloromethane.

Nitrosation to form an alkyl nitrite. Nitrosonium tetrafluoroborate (NO⁺ BF₄⁻) transfers the nitrosonium ion to benzyl alcohol, generating benzyl nitrite and tetrafluoroboric acid as by‑product. The reaction is performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an anhydrous, aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, often under inert atmosphere to avoid moisture.

Salt metathesis (double displacement) to afford zinc azide. Zinc chloride reacts with sodium azide in aqueous solution; Na⁺ exchanges with Zn²⁺, precipitating insoluble zinc azide while forming soluble sodium chloride. Conducted at ambient temperature in water; the zinc azide product is isolated by filtration and washing.

Free‑radical chlorination of vinyl halide (trichloroethylene) leading to substitution of the allylic hydrogen with chlorine and formation of tetrachloroethylene together with HCl. Initiated by UV light or a radical initiator, carried out in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or in the gas phase at elevated temperature (~100 °C).

Acylation (esterification) of 2‑nitrophenol with acetic anhydride to form 2‑nitrophenyl acetate and acetic acid; usually carried out by refluxing the phenol with excess acetic anhydride in a non‑polar solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or toluene) in the presence of a base catalyst such as pyridine or DMAP; temperature 60–80 °C.

Acid–base displacement (proton transfer) reaction; used to generate hydrogen chloride gas and ammonium bisulfate. Key transformation: H2SO4 protonates NH4Cl, releasing HCl and forming NH4HSO4. Typically performed by adding solid NH4Cl to concentrated sulfuric acid at ambient temperature; no solvent required, reaction carried out in a fume hood.

Acid–base (salt metathesis) reaction; used to protonate the perrhenate anion and obtain perrhenic acid; NaReO4 reacts with concentrated HNO3 to give HReO4 and NaNO3; typically performed in aqueous solution, often with heating; water is the solvent.

Thionation of benzophenone to thiobenzophenone using Lawesson’s reagent; the carbonyl oxygen is replaced by sulfur; reaction is conducted under inert atmosphere, refluxing in a high‑boiling non‑polar solvent like toluene or xylene (≈110 °C) for several hours; no additional catalyst needed.

High‑temperature oxidation of germanium diselenide by molecular oxygen; O₂ oxidizes GeSe₂ to germanium dioxide and selenium dioxide; typically performed in a sealed quartz tube or furnace at 400–600 °C in the gas phase; no solvent or catalyst required.

Nucleophilic ring‑opening of ethylene oxide by benzylmagnesium chloride (Grignard reagent) to afford phenethyl alcohol; carried out in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; after addition, the reaction is quenched with aqueous acid to give the alcohol.

Oxidative combustion (redox) of hydrazine; serves as a monopropellant or for laboratory destruction of excess hydrazine. Hydrazine hydrate (N₂H₄·H₂O) reacts with O₂ (often in the gas phase) to produce nitrogen gas and water vapor: 2 N₂H₄ + O₂ → 2 N₂ + 4 H₂O. Requires a catalyst (e.g., Ag, Cu, or Pt) or a spark/ignition source; temperatures typically 200–300 °C; carried out in a flow of inert carrier gas.

Free‑radical chlorination of 2‑methylpentane producing 2‑chloro‑2‑methylpentane and HCl; initiated by UV light or heat in a non‑reactive solvent such as carbon tetrachloride; reaction proceeds via tertiary radical formation; typically conducted at ambient or slightly elevated temperature.

Electrophilic substitution (halogenation) of isoquinoline with bromine; purpose is to install a bromine at the 5‑position for further functionalization. The aromatic ring undergoes attack by Br⁺ generated from Br₂, forming 5‑bromoisoquinoline and releasing HBr. Typical conditions are addition of Br₂ (1 equiv) to a solution of isoquinoline in glacial acetic acid or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; often a Lewis acid catalyst such as FeBr₃ (0.1 equiv) is employed to increase electrophilicity. The reaction is usually quenched with water and the product extracted with an organic solvent.

Nitrosation of a secondary amide. Nitrous acid (generated in situ from NaNO₂/HCl) reacts with N‑methylacetamide to give the N‑nitroso derivative and water. Purpose: introduction of a nitroso group for analytical or synthetic purposes. Key transformation: conversion of the amide nitrogen to an N‑nitroso functionality. Typical conditions: aqueous acidic medium, 0–5 °C, dilute HNO₂. Common solvent: water or water‑acetone mixture.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of pulegone to menthol. Molecular hydrogen adds across the carbonyl and olefinic double bond under metal catalysis, converting the ketone to a secondary alcohol and saturating the ring. Purpose: synthesis of the saturated terpene alcohol menthol. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, Pd/C, Raney Ni or Pt catalyst, ethanol or methanol as solvent, 25–80 °C, reflux if needed.

Oxidative dissolution of gold(III) oxide in concentrated nitric acid to form gold(III) nitrate. Nitric acid oxidizes Au₂O₃, producing Au(NO₃)₃ and water. Purpose: preparation of soluble gold nitrate for further chemistry. Typical conditions: excess conc. HNO₃, reflux at 80–100 °C until complete dissolution. No special solvent beyond the acid is required.

This is a chloromethylation reaction forming chloromethyl methyl ether from formaldehyde and methanol. Hydrogen chloride acts as a catalyst, promoting the protonation of formaldehyde and subsequent nucleophilic attack by methanol while retaining the chlorine. The reaction is typically carried out in anhydrous methanol or a non-reactive solvent at room temperature or slightly elevated temperatures. Concentrated HCl may be used.

Ruthenium tetroxide oxidative cleavage of ortho‑xylene; purpose is to oxidize both benzylic methyl groups to carboxyl groups, affording phthalic acid; key transformation is full oxidation of each –CH₃ to –CO₂H with RuO₄ reduced to RuO₂ and water formed; typical conditions involve RuO₄ in an aqueous organic solvent (e.g., CCl₄/H₂O) at 0‑25 °C, usually catalytic with a co‑oxidant such as NaIO₄; solvents commonly used are dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride with water.

Acylation (acetylation) of isoniazid with acetic anhydride. The hydrazide nitrogen is acylated, yielding N‑acetyl‑isoniazid and acetic acid as by‑product. Purpose: protection or derivatization of the drug molecule. Typical conditions: reflux in pyridine or DMF, 50–80 °C, often with catalytic DMAP. Solvent: pyridine, DMF, or dichloromethane.

Oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC). PCC selectively oxidizes 3‑methylcyclohexan‑1‑ol to the corresponding ketone, 3‑methylcyclohexan‑1‑one, without over‑oxidation to the carboxylic acid. Reactions are usually performed in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, with PCC as the stoichiometric oxidant.

N‑alkylation of N‑methyltryptamine with allyl chloride using sodium hydride. NaH deprotonates the secondary amine, generating a nucleophilic nitrogen that attacks allyl chloride in an SN2 process, releasing H₂ and NaCl and forming N‑methyl‑N‑allyl‑tryptamine. Purpose: introduction of an allyl substituent. Typical conditions: anhydrous DMF or THF, 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar).

SN2 substitution of allyl bromide with nitrate ion from silver nitrate to give allyl nitrate; silver bromide precipitates, shifting equilibrium; carried out in acetone or aqueous acetone at 0 °C to ambient temperature in the dark to avoid photoreduction; Ag⁺ serves as the reactive species, no further catalyst.

Free radical halogenation of acetonitrile; purpose is to introduce a bromine at the α‑carbon to give bromoacetonitrile while generating hydrogen bromide. Key transformation: CH3‑C≡N → Br‑CH2‑C≡N + HBr. Typical conditions: UV light or heat to initiate radicals, dilute bromine in an inert, non‑protic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform; reaction run under nitrogen atmosphere.

Oxidation/chlorination: Chlorine gas oxidizes vanadium(II) chloride to vanadium(IV) chloride (VCl4). Performed under dry, inert atmosphere, typically in a sealed tube or furnace at 150‑200 °C; no solvent needed, chlorine acts as the oxidant.

Carbothermal reduction: Molybdenum trioxide is reduced by carbon to molybdenum dioxide with evolution of carbon monoxide; performed at high temperature (≈800‑1000 °C) in an inert or evacuated atmosphere; solid‑solid reaction, no solvent required.

Phosphorylation/esterification: Phosphorus oxychloride reacts with methanol to form trimethyl phosphate, releasing three equivalents of hydrogen chloride. Carried out at 0‑5 °C to control exotherm, in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane with a base (pyridine or triethylamine) to trap HCl.

Halogen exchange (metathesis) between disulfur dibromide and chlorine. Disulfur dibromide reacts with dry chlorine gas at low temperature (0 °C to room temperature), replacing bromine atoms with chlorine to give disulfur dichloride (S₂Cl₂) and liberating bromine. Typically done in a sealed tube or gas‑flow setup; no solvent or catalyst is needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis): Water attacks propargyl bromide, replacing bromide with hydroxyl to give propargyl alcohol and HBr. Typically performed in aqueous medium with mild heating; proceeds via an SN2 mechanism.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2): Sodium butoxide substitutes 1‑bromopropane, forming 1‑propoxybutane (butyl propyl ether) and sodium bromide. Requires dry, aprotic solvent (THF or DMF), ambient to reflux temperature, under inert atmosphere.

Catalytic dehydrogenation (elimination): Ethylcyclopentane loses H2 to produce 1‑ethylcyclopentene. Conducted with metal catalysts (Pt, Pd, or Pt‑Sn on alumina) at 300‑500 °C under inert gas flow; no additional reagents needed.

Acid‑base double displacement (neutralization): Concentrated nitric acid reacts with magnesium phosphate, yielding phosphoric acid and magnesium nitrate. Performed in aqueous solution with stirring and gentle heating; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base dissolution of zirconium dioxide; purpose is to convert the insoluble oxide into soluble zirconium(IV) sulfate. Key transformation: ZrO2 + 2 H2SO4 → Zr(SO4)2 + 2 H2O. Conditions: excess concentrated H2SO4, heating under aqueous medium; no special catalyst required.

Hydrolytic decomposition of tetrasulfur tetranitride (S₄N₄); vigorous reaction with water cleaves the S–N framework, yielding hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) and ammonia (NH₃) (along with minor sulfur‑oxyanion species). Usually carried out by refluxing S₄N₄ in aqueous media; no catalyst required. Represents a classic hydrolysis of a high‑energy heterocycle.

Suzuki–Miyaura cross‑coupling of 3‑iodophenol with phenylboronic acid; purpose is to construct a biaryl ether (3‑phenylphenol). Key transformation: Ar‑I + Ar′‑B(OH)2 → Ar‑Ar′ + I− + B(OH)3. Typical conditions: Pd catalyst (e.g., Pd(PPh3)4 or PdCl2(PPh3)2), base such as K2CO3 or Na2CO3, mixed solvent (THF/H2O or dioxane/H2O), inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar), temperature 80‑100 °C.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration. Attaches nitro group ortho to ethyl group on benzene ring. Reaction with HNO3/H2SO4 as in reaction 4. Ethyl group is ortho-directing. Competes with para product depending on steric and electronic factors. Sulfuric acid acts as catalyst. Common nitration conditions.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification between isopropyl alcohol and triacetin; purpose is to exchange the acetate ester of glycerol triacetate with an isopropyl group, yielding isopropyl acetate and diacetin. Key transformation: (CH3COO)3C3H5 + CH3CH(OH)CH3 → CH3COOCH(CH3)2 + (CH3COO)2C3H5OH. Typical conditions: catalytic amount of NaOH or acidic catalyst (e.g., H2SO4), reflux in excess isopropanol, removal of water or methanol to drive equilibrium; reaction time2‑6 h.

Acid–base double displacement (metathesis). Sulfate acid protonates the oxalate dianion, exchanging partners to give oxalic acid and potassium sulfate. Typically performed in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to promote dissolution and crystallization of the products. No catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde using a chromium(VI) oxidant; purpose is to convert 1‑hexanol into hexanal; key transformation is oxidation of the –CH2OH group to –CHO while Na2Cr2O7/H2SO4 is reduced to Cr(III); typical conditions are reflux in aqueous sulfuric acid (≈80‑100 °C) often with water as solvent.

Copper‑catalyzed amination (Ullmann‑type) of an aryl chloride; purpose is to produce aniline from chlorobenzene; key transformation is substitution of the aryl chloride by NH3 to give aniline with HCl as by‑product; performed with CuCl (or CuI) as catalyst, often with a base (e.g., K2CO3) at 150‑200 °C in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO or NMP under inert atmosphere.

Fischer esterification of p‑hydroxybenzoic acid with n‑heptanol; purpose is to make heptyl p‑hydroxybenzoate (a paraben); key transformation is condensation of the carboxylic acid and the alcohol to give an ester and water; catalyzed by p‑toluenesulfonic acid, refluxed in toluene (or another high‑boiling solvent) with a Dean‑Stark trap to remove water.

Transmetalation between a Grignard reagent and a dimethyltin dichloride; purpose is to prepare trimethyltin chloride; key transformation is transfer of a methyl group from CH3MgCl to Me2SnCl2 giving Me3SnCl and MgCl2; carried out in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen.

Direct combination (synthesis) reaction; aluminum metal reacts with red phosphorus to afford aluminum phosphide (AlP), employed as a fumigant and semiconductor; conducted at high temperature (~1000 °C) in a sealed furnace under nitrogen or argon; solid‑state reaction, no solvent.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis (saponification) of decyl acetate; purpose is to produce 1‑decanol and sodium acetate; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of OH− on the ester carbonyl, cleaving the C–O bond; performed with aqueous NaOH (often 1 M) and heat (reflux, 60‑100 °C), typically in a water/ethanol mixture.

Acid‑base neutralization of 3‑chloropropan‑1‑amine hydrochloride with NaOH; purpose is to free the amine; key transformation is proton transfer from the ammonium salt to hydroxide forming water, NaCl and the free 3‑chloropropan‑1‑amine; carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature or mild heating, no additional catalyst required.

This is a double displacement (metathesis) reaction, swapping cationic partners between butyrate and hydroxide ions. The amphoteric zinc cation forms insoluble zinc hydroxide precipitate, while sodium butyrate remains in solution. The reaction proceeds in aqueous medium under ambient conditions, driven by the low solubility of zinc hydroxide. Sodium hydroxide serves as a reagent to isolate zinc hydroxide for purification or further reactions.

Intramolecular cyclodehydration (dehydrative cyclization) of N‑acetylanthranilic acid using phosphorus pentoxide as a strong dehydrating agent, affording quinazolin‑4(3H)‑one with loss of water. The reaction is carried out by mixing the acid with excess P₂O₅ and heating (often 150–200 °C) under anhydrous conditions; no additional solvent is required, though a high‑boiling inert liquid (e.g., xylene) may be used to improve mixing.

Chlorination of an alcohol with thionyl chloride (SOCl₂); purpose is to produce an alkyl chloride while generating gaseous by‑products; key transformation: the OH group is replaced by Cl, forming 2,2‑dimethoxyethyl chloride with evolution of SO₂ and HCl gases; typical conditions: anhydrous solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine as base, 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; by‑products are removed by gas vent.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling: 3‑bromo‑2,5‑dimethylthiophene couples with 4‑methoxyphenylboronic acid in the presence of Pd(OAc)₂ as catalyst, tri(o‑tolyl)phosphine as ligand, and K₂CO₃ as base. The reaction is performed under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) in a mixed solvent (e.g., 1,4‑dioxane/H₂O or THF/H₂O) at 80–100 °C, yielding 3‑(4‑methoxyphenyl)-2,5‑dimethylthiophene and potassium bromide as the inorganic by‑product.

Nitrosation of a secondary amine: diethanolamine reacts with nitrous acid (generated in situ from NaNO₂ and HCl) to form N‑nitrosodiethanolamine and water. The reaction is performed in an aqueous acidic medium, kept cold (0–5 °C) to suppress side reactions, and proceeds via formation of the nitrosyl cation which attacks the amine nitrogen.

Acid‑base neutralization: phosphoric acid reacts with lithium hydroxide in aqueous solution to give lithium dihydrogen phosphate and water. The reaction occurs at ambient temperature, is exothermic, and proceeds to completion upon stoichiometric mixing of the acid and base; the resulting salt remains dissolved unless the solution is concentrated and cooled.

Double‑replacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; purpose is to convert calcium sulfate dihydrate and sodium carbonate into insoluble calcium carbonate while forming soluble sodium sulfate; mixing aqueous solutions of CaSO₄·2H₂O and Na₂CO₃ leads to exchange of anions, precipitation of CaCO₃, and release of water; typically carried out at ambient temperature with aqueous media; no special catalyst required; stoichiometry: CaSO₄·2H₂O + Na₂CO₃ → CaCO₃↓ + Na₂SO₄ + 2 H₂O.

Oxidative degradation of arsine by ozone: gaseous arsine (AsH₃) is oxidized by ozone (O₃) to produce arsenic trioxide (As₂O₃), molecular oxygen (O₂) and water. The reaction proceeds rapidly under atmospheric conditions where ozone is present, typically at ambient temperature and pressure; it is an example of a gas‑phase oxidation/combus­tion process.

Hydrolytic cleavage; water adds to the fluorinated ether (fluroxene) cleaving it into acetaldehyde and 2,2,2‑trifluoroethanol. Typically performed under aqueous acidic conditions (e.g., HCl) with reflux; common solvent is water or aqueous methanol.

Acetylation of hydroxylamine using acetic anhydride; similar nucleophilic acyl substitution yielding N‑acetylhydroxylamine and acetic acid as by‑product. Conducted in a non‑protic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane, pyridine) at 0 °C to ambient temperature; pyridine or a tertiary amine often serves as both solvent and acid scavenger. Provides a protected hydroxylamine for subsequent transformations.

Base‑mediated acylation (C‑acylation) of barbituric acid with phenylacetyl chloride in the presence of sodium ethoxide to give the sodium salt of phenobarbital (phenobarbital sodium). Used for the synthesis of the barbiturate drug phenobarbital. Reaction is carried out in dry ethanol under reflux; sodium ethoxide acts as both base and solvent, producing ethanol and NaCl as by‑products.

Acetylation (esterification) of desacetylmetipranolol using acetic anhydride to regenerate metipranolol and release acetic acid. Conducted at 0 °C to ambient temperature in an inert solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine; catalytic amounts of DMAP or pyridine may be added to accelerate acyl transfer.

Strecker synthesis; condensation of butyraldehyde with ammonia and hydrogen cyanide to afford α‑aminobutyronitrile. Carried out in aqueous or alcoholic solution at 0–25 °C; the HCN can be generated in situ from NaCN and HCl. The reaction yields the aminonitrile after simple work‑up.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation); two equivalents of butyric acid react with calcium carbonate to give calcium butanoate, carbon dioxide and water. Performed by stirring the acid and carbonate in water, often with gentle heating to promote CO₂ evolution; no additional solvent is required.

NaBH₄ reduction of a ketone; converts cyclododecanone to the corresponding secondary alcohol, cyclododecanol. Conducted in methanol or ethanol (0.5–1 M), 0 °C to room temperature, 1–2 eq NaBH₄, under nitrogen. Reaction is rapid and selective for the carbonyl.

Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of propyl acetate with tetramethylammonium hydroxide, producing propanol and tetramethylammonium acetate. Reaction proceeds at ambient or mildly elevated temperature in aqueous TMAH solution; the quaternary ammonium base provides the hydroxide nucleophile and the acetate salt remains soluble.

Oxidative roasting of copper arsenide; the metal arsenide is thermally oxidized by excess O₂ to give copper(II) oxide and arsenic trioxide. This is a high‑temperature gas‑solid oxidation performed in a furnace at 400–600 °C under a flow of air or pure oxygen, with no solvent.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification; ethanol exchanges with the methyl ester of 2‑methylpentanoic acid to form the corresponding ethyl ester and methanol. The ionic liquid 1‑butyl‑3‑methylimidazolium tetrafluoroborate acts as both solvent and catalyst. Typical conditions are heating to 60–80 °C, often under reflux, for several hours until equilibrium is reached.

Enzymatic N‑methyltransferase reaction; S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine donates a methyl group to 7‑methylxanthine, producing 3,7‑dimethylxanthine (theophylline) and S‑adenosyl‑L‑homocysteine. Conducted in aqueous buffer (pH 7–8) at 25–37 °C, requiring the appropriate methyltransferase enzyme and often Mg²⁺ as cofactor.

Borrowing‑hydrogen (transfer‑hydrogenation) between ethanol and 4‑isopropylbenzaldehyde; ethanol is dehydrogenated to acetaldehyde while the aldehyde is reduced to the benzylic alcohol. Typically catalyzed by a homogeneous metal complex (e.g., Ru– or Ir‑based) or a solid base/metal catalyst, at 120–150 °C in the neat ethanol or in a high‑boiling solvent such as toluene.

Selenium dioxide benzylic oxidation; the ethyl side chain of 3‑ethylpyridine is oxidized to an aldehyde, giving 3‑pyridinecarboxaldehyde and elemental selenium. The reaction is run in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., 1,4‑dioxane or THF) at 80–120 °C, often under reflux, with stoichiometric SeO₂ and may include a co‑oxidant such as H₂O₂ to regenerate SeO₂.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of vinyl formate; water attacks the vinyl ester, cleaving the C=C bond to afford acetaldehyde and formic acid. The reaction proceeds in aqueous acidic media (e.g., 0.1 M HCl) at ambient to moderate temperatures (20–60 °C), often with gentle stirring; no special solvent is required.

Oxidation (solid‑state): Rh(III) oxide is further oxidized by molecular oxygen to Rh(IV) dioxide. Typically carried out by heating a mixture of Rh2O3 and dry O2 gas at 600–800 °C in a tubular furnace; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification): The ethyl ester of valeric acid reacts with potassium hydroxide, cleaving the ester bond to give ethanol and the potassium salt of valeric acid. Conducted in aqueous KOH (often diluted in ethanol or water) with reflux heating (≈80 °C) until completion; the reaction mixture is then acidified to liberate the carboxylic acid if desired.

Transesterification: Methanol exchanges its methoxy group with the butoxy group of butyl pivalate, producing butanol and methyl pivalate. Usually performed under reflux in excess methanol with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., H2SO4) or base (e.g., NaOCH3) in a solvent‑free or toluene medium; removal of the volatile alcohol drives the equilibrium toward products.

Salt metathesis (acid–base exchange). Fluoride ion from sodium fluoride swaps with chloride ion from ammonium chloride, producing ammonium fluoride and sodium chloride. The reaction proceeds readily in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst or special conditions are required.

Acidic oxidative bromide oxidation (redox): Potassium bromide is oxidized to molecular bromine by potassium permanganate in concentrated sulfuric acid. The mixture is heated gently (≈70–100 °C) under reflux; the acidic medium supplies protons, and Mn(VII) is reduced to Mn(II) while Br⁻ is oxidized to Br₂, with potassium sulfate and manganese sulfate as by‑products.

Peracid epoxidation (Prilezhaev reaction): Ethylene reacts with peracetic acid to form ethylene oxide, with acetic acid generated as the co‑product. Conducted at 0–25 °C in an aprotic organic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, often under inert atmosphere; the peracid acts as the oxidant, delivering an oxygen atom to the C=C bond.

Acid‑mediated redox decomposition of sodium dithionite; the dithionite acts as a reducing agent in acetic acid, generating sulfur dioxide gas and converting acetic acid to sodium acetate; typically carried out in aqueous acidic solution at ambient temperature, no additional catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed alkaline hydrolysis (cleavage) of ethoxymethylformamide; NaOH promotes breakdown of the protected carbonyl to give ethanol, formaldehyde, and sodium formate; usually performed in aqueous NaOH solution with gentle heating (≈50‑80 °C).

Oxidative homocoupling of thiophene using FeCl3 as a Lewis‑acid/oxidant to form 2,2′‑bithiophene; generally carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane or nitrobenzene at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen.

Peroxidase‑catalyzed oxidation of tyrosol with hydrogen peroxide; the enzyme mediates hydroxylation of the phenolic ring, converting tyrosol to 3,4‑dihydroxyphenylethanol while reducing H₂O₂ to water; conducted in aqueous buffer (pH 6‑8) at room temperature, peroxidase serving as the catalyst.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between calcium chloride and sodium lactate; ion exchange produces calcium lactate and sodium chloride; carried out in water at ambient temperature, no special catalyst needed.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) between calcium formate and lead(II) nitrate; leads to formation of soluble calcium nitrate and precipitated lead(II) formate; performed in water with stirring at room temperature; no catalyst required.

Free‑radical chlorination of pentane; radical chain gives substitution at the internal secondary carbon (C‑3) to produce 3‑chloropentane and HCl; same typical conditions as other chlorinations (UV/heat, inert solvent); purpose is to obtain a secondary chlorinated product.

Aldol (Claisen‑Schmidt) condensation of benzaldehyde with acetophenone; base‑catalyzed (NaOH or KOH) in ethanol or methanol, usually performed at 0 °C then warmed to reflux to promote dehydration; key transformation is formation of a C‑C bond between the carbonyl α‑carbon and the aldehyde carbon, yielding the α,β‑unsaturated ketone 1‑phenyl‑2‑propen‑1‑one (chalcone); purpose is to construct conjugated enones for synthetic and materials applications.

Swern oxidation: activation of dimethyl sulfoxide with oxalyl chloride at –78 °C to 0 °C, followed by addition of 4‑methoxybenzyl alcohol and triethylamine; converts the primary alcohol to 4‑methoxybenzaldehyde; reaction is run in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane, under inert atmosphere, and low temperature to suppress side reactions.

Acid–base metathesis (double displacement) reaction; exchanges the acetate ion for nitrate, yielding acetic acid and soluble calcium nitrate. Performed in aqueous medium, often with gentle heating or reflux to distill off the volatile acetic acid; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑base salt hydrolysis (acid liberation); ammonium adipate reacts with aqueous HCl to give free adipic acid and ammonium chloride. The protonation of the adipate anion releases the dicarboxylic acid. Conditions are simple: aqueous HCl, often heated to dissolve the salt; no catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) followed by acid‑base neutralization; used to synthesize nitrilotriacetic acid, a chelating agent. Three equivalents of chloroacetic acid each undergo SN2 attack by ammonia, displacing chloride and forming –CH2COOH substituents on nitrogen; the liberated HCl is neutralized by excess ammonia. Typically performed in aqueous or aqueous‑ethanol solution with excess NH3, heated under reflux (80‑100 °C) for several hours; the reaction mixture is kept basic to trap HCl, and the product is isolated after cooling and crystallization. No catalyst required.

Oxidation (Pinnick oxidation) of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid; converts 5‑formylcytosine to 5‑carboxycytosine for nucleoside modification. Sodium chlorite (NaClO₂) oxidizes the aldehyde while sodium dihydrogen phosphate buffers the solution at pH 3‑4, preventing over‑oxidation. Conducted in water or a water/THF mixture at 0 °C to ambient temperature, often with a chlorine‑dioxide scavenger (e.g., 2‑methyl‑2‑butene). No metal catalyst; reaction is quenched with sodium sulfite and the product is isolated by precipitation or chromatography.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution of an ester by a Grignard reagent; phenylmagnesium bromide attacks octyl acetate, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses, expelling octoxide as octanol and yielding acetophenone. The overall transformation installs a phenyl group onto the carbonyl carbon while cleaving the ester alkoxy fragment. Performed under anhydrous conditions in dry ether or THF, typically at 0 °C to room temperature, under nitrogen or argon atmosphere. The Grignard reagent is added dropwise to the ester solution; after completion the reaction is quenched with aqueous ammonium chloride, and the organic layer is worked up to isolate octanol and acetophenone. No additional catalyst required.

Double‑replacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous solutions of silver cyanide and lead nitrate exchange anions to give soluble silver nitrate and sparingly soluble lead cyanide, which precipitates. Useful for preparing lead cyanide or for analytical removal of silver ions. Carried out at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring; both reactants are dissolved in water (or dilute nitric acid) and mixed, leading to immediate formation of a white Pb(CN)₂ precipitate. The mixture is filtered, and the solid is washed and dried. No catalyst needed.

Acid‑base salt formation (protonation) of a secondary amine; propylhexedrine reacts with hydrogen chloride to produce propylhexedrine hydrochloride, a crystalline salt employed in pharmaceutical formulations. The free base is dissolved in a polar aprotic solvent such as ethanol, methanol, or isopropanol, and anhydrous HCl gas or cold aqueous HCl is added at 0‑5 °C to control exotherm. After stirring, the solvent is removed or the mixture is evaporated to afford the hydrochloride salt, which may be recrystallized from ethanol. No catalyst required.

Neutralization (acid‑base) reaction; phosphorus acid reacts with ammonia to afford ammonium phosphate tribasic, (NH₄)₃PO₄, a common fertilizer and buffer component. Three molar equivalents of gaseous or aqueous NH₃ are added slowly to a cooled (≤30 °C) aqueous solution of H₃PO₄, maintaining vigorous stirring. The resulting solution is cooled further to precipitate the ammonium phosphate, which is filtered, washed with cold water, and dried. The process occurs in water; no catalyst is involved.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis; purpose: convert ethyl 2‑butoxyacetate to its free acid; key transformation: cleavage of the C–O ester bond yielding 2‑butoxyacetic acid and ethanol; typical conditions: aqueous HCl (1–6 M), reflux 80–100 °C for several hours; solvent water (often with a co‑solvent such as acetone); no additional catalyst required.

Halide‑complex formation (metathesis); purpose: generate the soluble tetrachlorocuprate(II) ion; key transformation: exchange of chloride ligands to give K₂[CuCl₄] from KCl and CuCl₂; typical conditions: aqueous solution in excess chloride (often concentrated HCl) at room temperature; solvent water; no special catalyst, high chloride concentration stabilizes the complex.

Condensation (amide formation) via ammonolysis; purpose is to synthesize 2‑oxopropanamide (acetamide) from pyruvic acid; key transformation: the carbonyl carbon of pyruvic acid reacts with NH₃, eliminating water to give the amide; typical conditions: excess ammonia, elevated temperature (0–100 °C); often performed with activation (e.g., conversion to acid chloride or using coupling agents); common solvent: aqueous or alcoholic medium.

Phosphorus pentachloride mediated ester‑to‑acyl‑chloride conversion with concomitant alkyl chloride formation; purpose: produce trichloroacetyl chloride and ethyl chloride; key transformation: PCl₅ replaces the ethoxy group by chloride (forming ethyl chloride) and converts the carbonyl oxygen to POCl₃ while generating the acyl chloride; typical conditions: anhydrous aprotic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂), addition of PCl₅ at 0 °C then warm to rt under inert atmosphere; by‑product POCl₃ removed; no additional catalyst.

Acid–base double displacement (neutralization); purpose: isolate boric acid and ammonium sulfate; key transformation: protonation of borate by H₂SO₄ releasing H₃BO₃ and forming (NH₄)₂SO₄; typical conditions: aqueous mixture, moderate heating (60–80 °C) to drive off excess water; solvent water; no catalyst needed.

Potassium permanganate oxidation of a benzylic methyl group; purpose: oxidize the side chain of 2‑fluorotoluene to a carboxylic acid; key transformation: conversion of –CH₃ to –COOH yielding 2‑fluorobenzoic acid, with MnO₄⁻ reduced to MnO₂; typical conditions: aqueous KMnO₄ in alkaline medium (NaOH), reflux 1–3 h, followed by acid work‑up (HCl) to precipitate product; solvent water; KMnO₄ itself acts as oxidant, no additional catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed methanolysis (transesterification); purpose: replace the acetate group with a methyl ester and free the phenethyl alcohol; key transformation: nucleophilic attack of MeOH on the acetate carbonyl producing methyl acetate and 3,4‑dihydroxyphenylethanol; typical conditions: reflux in MeOH with catalytic acid (e.g., 1–5 % H₂SO₄) for several hours; solvent methanol; acid serves as catalyst.

Catalytic hydration (carbonylation) of carbon monoxide to formic acid. Carbon monoxide reacts with water under high pressure (10–30 MPa) and elevated temperature (150–250 °C) in the presence of an acidic or metal‑based catalyst (e.g., H₂SO₄, Rh or Ir complexes) to give formic acid. The process is a homogeneous or heterogenous catalytic reaction; solvents may include water or mixed water‑organic media.

Transesterification of ethyl methyl carbonate with methanol to afford dimethyl carbonate and ethanol. This reverse process is used to recycle EMC into the more valuable DMC. Typically performed under basic catalysis (e.g., K2CO3, NaOMe) at 100‑150 °C, with azeotropic removal or distillation of ethanol to push the equilibrium toward DMC; reactions may be run bulk or in a refluxing solvent such as toluene.

Amination via SN2 of 1‑bromopropane with ammonium hydroxide to produce 1‑propylamine; carried out in aqueous NH4OH solution under reflux, often with excess ammonia to suppress side reactions; ammonium bromide precipitates as the salt; no catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement precipitation: Silver propionate mixed with sodium chloride precipitates insoluble silver chloride while forming sodium propionate in solution. Performed in water at room temperature; the AgCl precipitate is filtered off.

Acid‑base neutralization. Hydrogen cyanide donates a proton to cesium hydroxide, forming water and cesium cyanide. The reaction occurs in aqueous or alcoholic solution at room temperature with vigorous stirring. No catalyst is required.

Oxidation of a tertiary phosphine to its corresponding phosphine oxide using hydrogen peroxide; serves to generate a stable P=O functional group. Typical conditions: 0 °C to room temperature, inert solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, often with a small amount of acetic acid to promote activation. No metal catalyst needed.

Hydrolysis (acidic or basic) of methyl 3‑hydroxy‑2‑methylpropanoate to regenerate 3‑hydroxy‑2‑methylpropionic acid; purpose is de‑protection of the ester. Key transformation: methyl ester + H₂O → acid + MeOH. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous HCl (acidic hydrolysis) or NaOH (saponification) followed by acid work‑up; temperature 80‑100 °C. Common solvent system: aqueous methanol or THF/water mixture.

Acidic oxidation of 9‑phenanthrol to phenanthrene‑9,10‑dione using sodium dichromate in sulfuric acid; the benzylic alcohol is oxidized to a quinone while dichromate is reduced to Cr³⁺. Typically refluxed in a mixture of conc. H₂SO₄ and aqueous Na₂Cr₂O₇ at 80–100 °C.

Markovnikov acid‑catalyzed hydration of 5‑methyl‑1‑heptene to give 5‑methyl‑2‑heptanol. The reaction proceeds via protonation of the terminal alkene, formation of the more stable secondary carbocation, and nucleophilic attack by water. Conducted in dilute mineral acid (e.g., 5 % H₂SO₄) or via oxymercuration–demercuration (Hg(OAc)₂, NaBH₄) at 0 °C to reflux; solvent is typically water or a water‑organic mixture.

Base‑induced dehydrohalogenation/hydrolysis of 1,2‑dichloro‑1,1,2‑trifluoroethane with aqueous NaOH, yielding 1‑chloro‑1,2,2‑trifluoroethene, NaCl and water. The hydroxide abstracts a β‑hydrogen, eliminating HCl to form the vinyl fluoride and simultaneously displaces the remaining chloride as NaCl. Performed under reflux in aqueous or mixed aqueous/ethanol medium, often 1–2 M NaOH, for 1–2 h.

Esterification (acyl chloride condensation) of hydroxyethyl methacrylate with methacryloyl chloride to give ethylene dimethacrylate; used to prepare cross‑linkable methacrylate monomers. Reaction proceeds via nucleophilic attack of the hydroxyl on the acyl chloride, releasing HCl. Typical conditions: 0 °C to room temperature in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform, with a base such as pyridine, triethylamine, or N‑methylmorpholine to scavenge HCl; inert atmosphere (N₂) is common.

N‑alkylation (SN2) of N‑methylptamine with 1‑iodobutane to afford N‑methyl‑N‑butyltryptamine; a method to extend the alkyl chain on a secondary amine. The iodide is displaced by the amine nitrogen, generating hydrogen iodide as by‑product. Typical conditions: excess amine or a non‑nucleophilic base (e.g., K₂CO₃, NaH) in polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or acetonitrile, 0 °C to reflux; inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of 3‑octanol to give 2‑octene (E/Z mixture) and water; a classic elimination (E1/E2) converting a secondary alcohol to an internal alkene. Common conditions: concentrated H₂SO₄ or p‑toluenesulfonic acid, heating at 150–180 °C; alternatively, solid acid catalysts (e.g., alumina, zeolites) can be used in a flow or batch reactor. No solvent is required in the classic method; if used, an inert hydrocarbon (toluene) may serve as medium.

Acetylation (aryl ester formation) of meta‑cresol with acetyl chloride in the presence of pyridine, yielding 3‑methyl phenyl acetate and pyridinium chloride. The phenolic oxygen attacks the acyl chloride, and pyridine acts as both solvent and HCl scavenger. Typical procedure: 0 °C to ambient temperature in dry pyridine or dichloromethane, under nitrogen; the reaction is usually completed within 1–2 h.

Reaction type: nucleophilic acyl substitution (esterification of an acyl chloride). Purpose: preparation of the allylic acetate. Key transformation: the hydroxyl of 3‑methyl‑2‑buten‑1‑ol attacks the carbonyl carbon of acetyl chloride, chloride leaves and the ester 3‑methylbut‑2‑enyl acetate is formed with liberation of HCl. Typical conditions: anhydrous environment, 0 °C to room temperature, often in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF with a base (triethylamine or pyridine) to scavenge the generated HCl.

Precipitation of metal sulfide (acidic sulfide exchange); H₂S gas reacts with SnCl₄ to produce tin(IV) sulfide (SnS₂) and HCl; key transformation is formation of insoluble SnS₂ precipitate; carried out in aqueous solution with H₂S bubbled through, often at room temperature or slight warming; water is the solvent, no catalyst.

Oxidation; hydrogen‑peroxide mediated oxidation of triethylphosphine to triethylphosphine oxide; the P(III) is oxidized to P=O while H₂O₂ is reduced to water; carried out at 0 °C to 25 °C to control exotherm, commonly in an inert organic solvent (e.g., THF, dichloromethane) or a biphasic aqueous/organic system; no additional catalyst is needed.

Nucleophilic substitution of 2‑chloro‑2‑methylbutane with ammonia to produce 2‑methyl‑2‑butanamine (tert‑butyl‑amine derivative) and HCl. The reaction proceeds by SN1 (or SN2 for secondary chloride) mechanism depending on conditions. Common laboratory conditions: excess gaseous or aqueous NH₃ (or NH₃ in ethanol), reflux in ethanol or methanol for several hours; the HCl formed is neutralized by excess NH₃ or by adding a base such as NaHCO₃.

Oxidation; air oxidation of a trialkylphosphine to the corresponding phosphine oxide; the P(III) center is converted to P=O; typically performed at room temperature or with gentle heating, often in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane, tetrahydrofuran or acetonitrile; no catalyst is required, although light or trace metal impurities can accelerate the reaction.

Periodate oxidation (glycol cleavage) of the vicinal diol (2S‑propane‑1,2‑diol) to produce one equivalent of methanal and one equivalent of ethanal, together with sodium iodate and water. Reaction type: oxidative cleavage of a 1,2‑diol. Conditions: NaIO₄ (1.0‑1.5 eq) in a mixture of water and a miscible organic co‑solvent (e.g., THF), pH neutral to slightly basic, 0‑25 °C, usually performed under dark conditions.

Carbothermic synthesis of hafnium carbide (HfC) from elemental hafnium and carbon. This high‑temperature solid‑state reaction forms a refractory metal carbide with very high melting point. Typical conditions: mixing hafnium powder with carbon (graphite) in stoichiometric ratio, heating under inert gas (Ar) or vacuum to 1800–2100 °C for several hours; often performed in a graphite crucible to avoid oxidation.

Acid–base neutralization: silver(I) oxide reacts with strong perchloric acid to give soluble silver perchlorate and water; typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring.

Hydride reduction of an ester (LiEt3BH, “Superhydride”) to give the corresponding alcohols. The reagent delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon of tert‑butyl acetate, cleaving the C–O bond; after work‑up the alkoxy fragment forms tert‑butanol and the acyl fragment becomes ethanol. Usually performed in dry THF at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen; 1.5–2 eq LiEt3BH are used, followed by aqueous quench. No catalyst.

High‑temperature solid‑state fluorination (metathesis): silica is converted to volatile silicon tetrafluoride while calcium fluoride supplies fluoride, producing calcium oxide as a solid residue; carried out in a sealed tube or furnace at 400–600 °C, no solvent, inert atmosphere often used.

Metathesis (anion exchange); purpose is to obtain silver tetrafluoroborate as a non‑coordinating anion source; key transformation: Ag⁺ swaps NO₃⁻ for BF₄⁻, forming AgBF₄ and HNO₃; typical conditions: dry aprotic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile or CH₂Cl₂) under inert atmosphere, low temperature to avoid decomposition.

Redox oxidation of selenium by concentrated sulfuric acid: selenium is oxidized to selenium dioxide and the acid is reduced to sulfur dioxide, with water formed; conducted by adding elemental selenium to conc. H₂SO₄ and heating under reflux in a glass apparatus, no additional solvent.

Acid–base/complexation reaction: ferric oxide reacts with citric acid, protonating the oxide to water and chelating Fe³⁺ to form ferric citrate; usually carried out in aqueous solution with heating to dissolve the oxide and promote complex formation.

Free‑radical halogenation: chlorine abstracts hydrogen from methylcyclopentane, generating a carbon radical that combines with chlorine to afford 1‑chloro‑1‑methylcyclopentane and HCl; requires UV light or heat as initiator, performed in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde. Neopentyl alcohol is converted to 2,2-dimethylpropanal by removal of two hydrogens and formation of a carbonyl group. Typical reagents include PCC, Dess‑Martin periodinane, or Swern oxidation conditions, usually performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or pyridine at 0 °C to room temperature.

Nitrosation of a secondary amino acid; purpose is to form an N‑nitroso derivative for analytical or synthetic use. L‑Proline reacts with nitrous acid (generated in situ from NaNO₂/HCl) to give N‑nitroso‑L‑proline and water. Reaction is carried out at 0–5 °C in aqueous acidic solution (pH ≈ 3) to minimize side reactions; the acid both generates HNO₂ and protonates the amine.

Double‑displacement metathesis precipitation: the chloride of silver chloride exchanges with the bromide of 1‑ethyl‑3‑methylimidazolium bromide, precipitating insoluble silver bromide and yielding 1‑ethyl‑3‑methylimidazolium chloride in solution; conducted in water or a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile) with stirring at room temperature.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; exchanges sulfide and chloride ions to form sodium chloride and calcium sulfide. Typically carried out in aqueous solution with stirring at ambient temperature; no catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Reductive amination; primary amine (isopropylamine) condenses with a ketone (3,4‑methylenedioxyphenyl‑2‑propanone) to give an imine which is reduced by sodium cyanoborohydride to the corresponding secondary amine (3,4‑methylenedioxy‑N‑isopropylamphetamine). Conducted in methanol or ethanol, often buffered to pH 5‑6 with acetic acid; ambient to mild heating; NaBH₃CN is the reducing agent.

Hydrohalogenation (Markovnikov addition of HCl) of an alkene; HCl adds across the double bond of 4‑methyl‑1‑pentene to give 2‑chloro‑4‑methylpentane. Performed in aqueous or gaseous HCl, usually at 0 °C to room temperature; no additional catalyst required; solvent can be dichloromethane or ethanol.

Quaternary ammonium salt formation via SN2 alkylation; tributylamine attacks benzyl chloride, displacing chloride to give benzyltributylammonium chloride. Reaction run in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane, often under reflux; no catalyst needed.

Multi‑component condensation/cyclization (acridine synthesis); cyclohexanone, 2‑aminobenzaldehyde, and ammonium acetate condense, lose water and cyclize to afford 9‑amino‑1,2,3,4‑tetrahydroacridine. Typically performed in refluxing ethanol or acetic acid with ammonium acetate acting as a catalyst/solvent; reaction time 2‑6 h; yields heterocyclic aromatic amine.

Oxidation (redox) of thallium(I) sulfide by molecular oxygen; solid Tl₂S reacts with O₂ at elevated temperature to produce sulfur dioxide gas and thallium(I) oxide solid. Conducted by heating the mixture in air or pure O₂ flow (200‑400 °C); no solvent; solid‑gas reaction.

Double displacement/precipitation reaction; used to isolate insoluble gadolinium phosphate, often for ceramics or phosphor precursors. An aqueous solution of gadolinium chloride is mixed with phosphoric acid, the phosphate anion replaces chloride and GdPO₄ precipitates while HCl remains in solution. Typical conditions: dilute aqueous medium, moderate heating (≈50–80 °C) to improve crystallinity, vigorous stirring. No catalyst; water is the solvent.

Acid‑base (neutralization) reaction; sodium hydride reacts with acetic acid to give sodium acetate and hydrogen gas; carried out in dry ether or THF, often at 0 °C to rt, under inert atmosphere; no catalyst required.

Type: N‑acylation (amide formation) of an aromatic amine. Purpose: Protect the amino group of anthranilic acid as an acetyl amide. Key transformation: The amine of anthranilic acid attacks acetic anhydride, forming N‑acetylanthranilic acid and releasing one equivalent of acetic acid. Typical conditions: Reflux in an inert organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or THF) with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge the generated acid. Often performed at 0 °C to room temperature then warmed to 50–80 °C. No metal catalyst needed.

Type: nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide‑formation) using carbonyldiimidazole (CDI). Purpose: convert cyanoacetic acid into its hydrazide, a useful precursor for heterocycle synthesis. Key transformation: CDI activates the carboxyl group to an O‑acylimidazole, which is displaced by hydrazine to give cyanoacetic acid hydrazide and liberates imidazole. Typical conditions: anhydrous aprotic solvent (e.g., THF, DMF, or DCM), 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere, stoichiometric excess of CDI and hydrazine. No additional catalyst required; imidazole is formed as a by‑product.

Grignard addition to an acyl bromide; phenylmagnesium bromide adds to 2‑bromoacetyl bromide to afford 2‑bromoacetophenone after aqueous work‑up, with MgBr₂ as by‑product. Reaction proceeds via nucleophilic addition of the phenyl carbanion to the carbonyl. Performed under inert atmosphere in anhydrous Et₂O or THF at –78 °C to 0 °C; no external catalyst required.

Ozonolysis of a styrene‑type double bond; 1‑ethenyl‑2‑methylbenzene reacts with ozone to form an ozonide that is reduced to give 2‑methylbenzaldehyde and formaldehyde; the reaction is carried out in dichloromethane at –78 °C, followed by a reductive work‑up with zinc/acetic acid (or an oxidative work‑up with H₂O₂) to cleave the ozonide.

Aminolysis of a methyl ester to form an amide; methyl (2S)-2‑amino‑3‑methylbutanoate reacts with excess ammonia to give the corresponding amide and methanol; performed in aqueous or alcoholic ammonia solution under reflux (often in methanol or ethanol); no additional catalyst required.

Type: Wolff–Kishner reduction (hydrazone‑based deoxygenation of a ketone). Purpose: Reduce the carbonyl of acetophenone to the corresponding alkane, yielding ethylbenzene. Key transformation: Acetophenone condenses with hydrazine to form the phenylhydrazone, which under strongly basic conditions (NaOH) and high temperature decomposes, eliminating nitrogen and forming the alkane. Typical conditions: Hydrazine hydrate (excess), aqueous NaOH (≈5 M), high boiling solvent such as ethylene glycol or diethylene glycol, heated to 180–200 °C for several hours under nitrogen. No metal catalyst required.

Type: Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (deacetylation) of an N‑acetyl indole. Purpose: Remove the acetyl protecting group to liberate serotonin. Key transformation: The amide bond of N‑acetylserotonin is protonated by HCl, allowing water (from the aqueous acid) to attack the carbonyl and release acetic acid, restoring the free indole‑amine (serotonin). Typical conditions: Reflux in dilute aqueous hydrochloric acid (1–3 M) for 1–3 h; the reaction can be performed in a mixed solvent (e.g., water/ethanol) to improve solubility. No catalyst beyond the acid.

Type: Reductive iodination/decomposition of a metal carbonyl. Purpose: Convert nickel carbonyl to nickel(II) iodide while liberating carbon monoxide and hydrogen gas. Key transformation: Two equivalents of HI reduce Ni(CO)4, displacing CO ligands as free CO and generating H2 from the reduction of protons; the nickel is oxidized to NiI2. Typical conditions: Anrous HI (excess) under inert atmosphere, mild heating (50–100 °C). Reaction often carried out in a sealed tube or pressure vessel; no additional catalyst is required.

Type: Reppe acetylene carbonylation (heterogeneous metal‑catalyzed C‑C bond formation). Purpose: Synthesize ethyl acrylate from simple C1 and C2 building blocks. Key transformation: Acetylene inserts into a metal‑carbonyl complex, reacts with CO and ethanol to give the ester ethyl acrylate, with regeneration of the metal catalyst. Typical conditions: High pressure (10–30 atm CO, 5–10 atm acetylene), temperature 150–200 °C, solvent often 1,2‑dichloroethane or heptane, catalytic system based on nickel carbonyl or cobalt carbonyl with an iodide promoter (e.g., NaI). Reaction conducted in a stainless‑steel autoclave.

Acid‑catalyzed cleavage (Hock rearrangement) of cumene hydroperoxide to give phenol and acetone. Industrial route for phenol production. Conducted at 295‑350 °C in the presence of strong mineral acid (e.g., 60 % H₂SO₄) or solid acid catalysts such as zeolites; reaction is bulk or in inert organic solvent.

Oxidation‑reduction reaction: Iodine is oxidized to iodic acid (HIO₃) by potassium permanganate in concentrated sulfuric acid. Used to prepare HIO₃. Performed in aqueous H₂SO₄ at 0‑80 °C; MnO₄⁻ reduces to Mn²⁺ forming MnSO₄, K⁺ combines with sulfate to give K₂SO₄. No additional catalyst needed.
Base‑induced E2 elimination; potassium tert‑butoxide abstracts a β‑hydrogen from 1‑bromoheptane, producing 1‑heptene and KBr. Carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as THF or DMSO at 50–80 °C.

Alkoxide‑acid metathesis producing aluminum phosphate; purpose is to synthesize AlPO₄ or to replace isopropoxide ligands. Aluminum isopropoxide reacts with H₃PO₄, the proton transfers to the alkoxide generating isopropanol and forming AlPO₄ network. Typically carried out under inert atmosphere (N₂) in a non‑coordinating solvent such as toluene or THF, with gentle reflux (≈120 °C) to remove isopropanol; no additional catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution/glycidylation: Triethylene glycol is deprotonated by Na₂CO₃ and reacts with epichlorohydrin to form the diglycidyl ether (triethylene glycol diglycidyl ether) while NaCl, CO₂ and H₂O are produced. Provides an epoxy monomer for resin synthesis. Carried out in polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetone, THF, or dimethyl carbonate) at 50‑80 °C under reflux; Na₂CO₃ acts as base and HCl scavenger.

Acylation (amide formation) of 6‑aminopenicillanic acid with phenoxyacetyl chloride to give phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin V). Reaction purpose is antibiotic synthesis. Conducted in anhydrous dichloromethane or ether at 0 °C to room temperature in the presence of a tertiary amine base (e.g., triethylamine) to capture HCl; no metal catalyst required.

Ester hydrolysis with decarboxylation; purpose is to break chloromethyl methyl carbonate into smaller molecules; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of water on the carbonate carbonyl, yielding methanol, chloromethanol, and carbon dioxide; carried out in aqueous media, often acid‑ or base‑catalyzed, at room temperature; water serves as both reactant and solvent.

Acid–base/oxide neutralization; preparation of palladium(II) chloride. Palladium(II) oxide reacts with aqueous hydrochloric acid, typically at room temperature or with gentle heating, to give soluble PdCl₂ and water. Reaction performed in water; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base double‑displacement: Cadmium tellurite reacts with sulfuric acid, producing soluble cadmium sulfate and free tellurous acid (H₂TeO₃). Used to convert the insoluble tellurite salt into the acid form. Performed in water with gentle heating; no catalyst needed.

Elimination (E1) dehydration of tert‑butyl alcohol to give isobutylene; purpose is to generate the alkene; typically performed with a strong acid catalyst such as concentrated H₂SO₄ or HCl in anhydrous chlorobenzene as solvent, heated under reflux; water is produced as by‑product.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of primary bromides by hydroxide to afford a 1,4‑diol; 1,4‑dibromobutane is refluxed in aqueous NaOH (or NaOH/ethanol) at 80–100 °C, typically using excess NaOH, yielding 1,4‑butanediol and NaBr.

Condensation (pyrophosphorylation) between diethyl chlorophosphate and sodium diethyl phosphate to form tetraethyl pyrophosphate; purpose is synthesis of a P–O–P bonded ester; carried out in a dry aprotic solvent (e.g., THF, benzene) at 0 °C to rt; sodium chloride precipitates; no additional catalyst required.

Thermal cis‑trans isomerization of dimethyl fumarate to dimethyl maleate promoted by potassium carbonate; heated in refluxing solvent (e.g., toluene) or neat with K₂CO₃, effecting the conversion from the trans (fumarate) to the cis (maleate) isomer.

Oxidation of dimethyl sulfoxide to dimethyl sulfone using potassium dichromate in sulfuric acid; purpose is to convert a sulfoxide to the corresponding sulfone; conducted in aqueous H₂SO₄ at 0–25 °C under vigorous stirring; chromium(VI) is reduced to chromium(III) sulfate as a by‑product.

Hydrolytic cleavage (hydrolysis) of phenyl N‑phenylcarbamate to phenol, aniline and carbon dioxide; purpose is to release the constituent amine and phenol; carried out in water with acid or base catalysis, usually heated (e.g., reflux) to accelerate decomposition; CO₂ is evolved gas.

Amide‑bond formation (CDI‑mediated coupling) of N‑methylglycine (sarcosine) with lauric acid to give N‑lauroylsarcosine; purpose is synthesis of a surfactant‑type amide; performed in anhydrous solvent such as DMF or DCM at 0 °C to rt; carbonyldiimidazole activates the acid, releasing CO₂ and imidazole as by‑products.

Fischer esterification of 1‑phenylethanol with acetic acid to afford phenylethyl acetate; purpose is preparation of the ester; typical conditions involve reflux in excess acetic acid with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑toluenesulfonic acid); water is removed to drive equilibrium toward product.

Halogen exchange (fluorination) on a cyclophosphazene ring; replaces each chlorine atom with fluorine to give hexafluorocyclotriphosphazene while precipitating silver chloride. Typically carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF at elevated temperature (80‑120 °C) with stoichiometric AgF; the insoluble AgCl is removed by filtration.

Dehydrogenation of propane to propyne; an oxidative dehydrogenation reaction used to generate alkynes from alkanes. Key transformation: C₃H₈ → C₃H₄ + 2 H₂. Typically performed at 500‑650 °C in the gas phase over metal oxide catalysts such as Cr₂₃, MnOₓ, or Pt‑based systems, often with a slight oxygen or steam diluent to prevent coke formation. No solvent; high‑temperature flow reactor.

Curtius rearrangement of a carboxylic acid; phenylpropionic acid is converted to its acyl azide using diphenylphosphoryl azide, which upon heating rearranges to an isocyanate that is hydrolyzed by water to the primary amine (3‑phenylpropylamine) with loss of carbon dioxide. Conducted in an inert organic solvent (toluene, dichloromethane) at 60‑100 °C; water is present either as a co‑solvent or added after the rearrangement; no external catalyst is required.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification; the secondary alcohol of menthol attacks ethyl isovalerate, displacing ethanol and forming menthyl isovalerate. Usually performed under reflux in a solvent such as toluene or cyclohexane with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., p‑TsOH) or an enzyme (lipase); removal of the volatile ethanol drives the equilibrium to completion.

Acid–base metathesis reaction; purpose is to generate bromous acid in situ; key transformation: protonation of bromite ion by hydrochloric acid to give HBrO₂ while sodium exchanges to chloride forming NaCl; typical condition: dilute aqueous HCl at low temperature (0–25 °C) to avoid decomposition of HBrO₂; solvent: water; no catalyst required.

Acid–base neutralization (salt metathesis); phosphoric acid protonates the hydrogen phosphate of disodium hydrogen phosphate, yielding two equivalents of sodium dihydrogen phosphate. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; stirring until complete dissolution gives the sodium dihydrogen phosphate salt.

Type: redox oxidation of manganese dioxide to permanganate using ozone in alkaline medium. Purpose: generate calcium permanganate (Ca(MnO4)2) as a strong oxidizer. Key transformation: O3 oxidizes Mn(IV) in MnO2 to Mn(VII) forming permanganate ion; concomitantly ozone is reduced to O2, and water is formed. Typical conditions: aqueous calcium hydroxide solution (basic), low temperature (0–25 °C) to control ozone decomposition, continuous ozone bubbling. No additional catalyst; reaction is conducted in a glass reactor under stirring.

Alkylation (O‑methylation) of para‑aminophenol using dimethyl sulfate; purpose is to convert the phenolic OH into a methoxy group, yielding 4‑methoxyaniline with methyl hydrogen sulfate as by‑product. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of phenoxide on the electrophilic methyl of dimethyl sulfate, forming an O‑Me bond and releasing CH₃SO₄H. Typical conditions: anhydrous medium, inorganic base (e.g., Na₂CO₃, K₂CO₃) or pyridine, temperature 0 °C to reflux, solvent such as acetone or acetonitrile.

Sulfation of dodecyl alcohol with sulfamic acid; purpose is to prepare a dodecyl hydrogen sulfate (alkyl sulfate) as a surfactant precursor, liberating ammonia. Key transformation: replacement of the hydroxyl hydrogen of the alcohol by the bisulfate moiety (–OSO₃H) from NH₂SO₃H, producing NH₃. Typical conditions: heating the neat mixture or in a high‑boiling solvent (e.g., toluene) at 150–200 °C under inert atmosphere; excess sulfamic acid drives the reaction to completion.

Swern oxidation of perillyl alcohol to perillaldehyde using dimethyl sulfoxide, oxalyl chloride and triethylamine. Purpose is selective oxidation of a primary allylic alcohol to the corresponding aldehyde without over‑oxidation. Key transformations: activation of DMSO by oxalyl chloride to form a chlorodimethyl‑sulfonium intermediate, nucleophilic attack by the alcohol, and elimination by triethylamine to give the aldehyde and dimethyl sulfide. Typical conditions: −78 °C to 0 °C in anhydrous dichloromethane; oxalyl chloride added to DMSO, then alcohol, followed by triethylamine addition; work‑up with aqueous NH₄Cl.

Double‑displacement precipitation analogous to reaction 2, but using potassium hydroxide. ZnCl₂ + KOH in water yields precipitated Zn(OH)₂ and soluble KCl. Ambient temperature, aqueous medium; no catalyst needed.

Double dehydrohalogenation of 1,3‑dichlorobutane with aqueous KOH to form buta‑1,3‑diene; a bimolecular E2 elimination reaction. Key transformation: ClCH₂CH₂CH₂Cl + 2 KOH → CH₂=CH‑CH=CH₂ + 2 KCl + 2 H₂O. Performed by the aqueous KOH suspension (often reflux) to 80‑100 °C. Water is the solvent; excess KOH drives the elimination.

Solid‑state redox comproportionation of copper(II) oxide with metallic copper to afford copper(I) oxide (Cu₂O). Purpose is to obtain Cu(I) oxide from readily available CuO and Cu metal. Key transformation: reduction of Cu²⁺ in CuO by Cu⁰, with simultaneous oxidation of Cu⁰ to Cu⁺, yielding Cu₂O. Typical conditions: intimate mixing of powders, heating at 200–300 °C in air or inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst required, sometimes a small amount of flux (e.g., Na₂CO₃) is added to improve contact.

Metathesis (acid‑base salt exchange) between sodium bicarbonate and ammonium methanesulfonate producing ammonium bicarbonate and sodium methanesulfonate. Purpose is to generate the inorganic ammonium bicarbonate salt and the sodium sulfonate. Key transformation: proton transfer from NH₄⁺ to HCO₃⁻ and exchange of the sulfonate anion with Na⁺. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the reaction proceeds spontaneously and is often used for purification or isolation of the desired salt.

Selective reduction of a ketone using sodium borohydride; reduces the carbonyl of 2‑chloroacetophenone to the secondary alcohol 1‑(2‑chlorophenyl)ethanol while leaving the aryl chloride intact; usually performed in a protic solvent like methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature; no catalyst required.

Acid-base neutralization forming scandium phosphate; purpose is preparation of the inorganic salt; key transformation is proton transfer from phosphoric acid to scandium hydroxide yielding water and ScPO4; generally performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

General type: condensation (oxime formation). Purpose: convert an aldehyde into its corresponding oxime for protection or further transformation. Key transformation: nucleophilic addition of hydroxylamine to the carbonyl carbon followed by loss of water to give the syn‑benzaldehyde oxime. Typical conditions: benzaldehyde is dissolved in ethanol or methanol, hydroxylamine hydrochloride (or free hydroxylamine) is added with a base such as pyridine or NaOAc to maintain pH 5–6, reaction is kept at 0 °C to room temperature for 1–3 h, and water is removed (e.g., azeotropic distillation) to drive the equilibrium.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (ester formation); sodium butan‑1‑olate reacts with acetyl chloride in a dry solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or THF) at 0‑25 °C under nitrogen to afford butyl acetate and NaCl; no catalyst needed.

Direct halogenation of uranium metal with bromine gas to give uranium tetrabromide (UBr₄). Purpose is synthesis of a metal bromide. Key transformation: U⁰ + 2 Br₂ → UBr₄. Typical conditions: stoichiometric Br₂ passed over solid uranium in a sealed quartz tube or crucible, heated to 300–400 °C under an inert atmosphere; no solvent.

Catalytic skeletal isomerization of n‑octane to 3‑methylheptane; purpose is to increase octane rating by producing a branched isomer; key transformation is migration of a methyl group along the carbon chain; typically carried out in the gas phase over solid acid catalysts such as Pt‑loaded zeolite Y, sulfated zirconia or zeolite ZSM‑5 at 300–500 °C; no solvent needed.

Iron(II)‑mediated oxidation of cyclohexyl hydroperoxide to cyclohexanone; purpose is to generate the ketone while oxidizing Fe(II) to Fe(III); key transformation is cleavage of the O–O bond and transfer of an oxygen atom to the cyclohexyl group; commonly performed in aqueous or polar organic media (e.g., methanol/water) at 0–25 °C under inert atmosphere; iron(II) sulfate acts as catalyst, no additional reagents required.

Acid‑mediated salt metathesis to free the 1‑oxide of pyridine‑2‑thiol from its zinc salt; addition of hydrochloric acid protonates the pyrithione anion and displaces zinc as ZnCl₂, liberating neutral 2‑pyridinethiol 1‑oxide. The reaction is carried out in aqueous HCl (0.5–2 M) at room temperature or with gentle heating (≤50 °C); the mixture may be stirred in water or a water/ethanol blend, and the ZnCl₂ salt remains in solution while the free pyrithione can be extracted into an organic solvent such as ethyl acetate.
