Thermal dehydration (condensation) of iron(III) oxide‑hydroxide to give anhydrous iron(III) oxide; purpose is to obtain the oxide material; key transformation is loss of water from FeO(OH) to form Fe₂O₃; commonly carried out by heating the solid in air at 300–400 °C, no solvent required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 1‑chloropropane by azide ion to afford 1‑azidopropane; purpose is preparation of an alkyl azide for further functionalization (e.g., click chemistry); key transformation is displacement of chloride by N₃⁻; usually performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO or acetone at 50–80 °C with excess NaN₃.

Hydrolysis (nucleophilic substitution) of N‑bromophthalimide with aqueous NaOH to give N‑hydroxyphthalimide and NaBr; purpose is to generate the N‑hydroxy derivative used as a radical initiator or oxidant; key transformation is replacement of the N‑Br bond by N‑OH; carried out in water or dilute aqueous NaOH at 0 °C to room temperature, often with simple stirring.

Acid‑catalyzed esterification (Fischer esterification) of isopropanol with acetic acid to form isopropyl acetate; sulfuric acid acts as the strong acid catalyst and dehydrating agent; purpose is synthesis of an ester solvent; key transformation is condensation of the alcohol and carboxylic acid with loss of water; performed by refluxing the mixture (often neat acetic acid serving as solvent) with catalytic H₂SO₄, optionally using a Dean‑Stark trap to remove water.

Oxidation of copper(I) chloride to copper(II) chloride by chlorine gas; redox oxidation; Cu⁺ is oxidized to Cu²⁺ while Cl₂ is reduced to Cl⁻, yielding CuCl₂; carried out in aqueous solution of CuCl with chlorine gas bubbled through at room temperature, often in water or dilute HCl; no catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction between ammonium chromate and lead nitrate in aqueous solution; purpose is to isolate insoluble lead(II) chromate pigment; key transformation is exchange of the anions producing solid PbCrO₄ and soluble NH₄NO₃; typically carried out by mixing the two aqueous solutions at room temperature, allowing the yellow PbCrO₄ precipitate to form and be filtered.

Ester hydrolysis (acid- or base‑catalyzed) converting a methyl aminocyclopropane‑1‑carboxylate to the corresponding carboxylic acid and methanol; typical conditions use aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) or aqueous base (NaOH) at reflux, with water as solvent; work‑up isolates 1‑aminocyclopropane‑1‑carboxylic acid after removal of methanol.

Oxidative dehydrogenation of a primary amine to an imine using copper(II) oxide as a solid oxidant. Isopropylamine is heated with CuO, which abstracts two hydrogen atoms to afford 2‑propanimine (acetone imine) plus water; the copper is reduced from Cu(II) to Cu(I) or Cu(0). Typical procedure: 150–200 °C, solid‑state or high‑boiling solvent (e.g., o‑xylene), inert atmosphere to avoid over‑oxidation.

Acid–base neutralization forming sodium iodate; aqueous sodium hydroxide neutralizes iodic acid to give water and NaIO₃; typically carried out in dilute aqueous solution at ambient temperature, followed by crystallization of the iodate salt from the filtrate.

High‑temperature solid‑state metathesis (double replacement) producing antimony(III) telluride and sodium bromide; stoichiometric SbBr₃ and Na₂Te are intimately mixed and heated in a sealed tube or furnace (≈500–800 °C) under inert gas; the reaction yields Sb₂Te₃ as a solid product and NaBr as a by‑product, which can be removed by washing with hot water.

Oxidation of a phosphorothioate to the corresponding phosphate; potassium peroxymonosulfate (Oxone) oxidizes the P=S moiety of O,O‑diethyl O‑4‑nitrophenyl phosphorothioate to P=O, affording O,O‑diethyl O‑4‑nitrophenyl phosphate; performed in aqueous acetone or methanol at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a buffer to maintain pH, and the product is isolated after aqueous work‑up.

Simple acid‑base neutralization forming an ammonium salt. Hydrogen chloride protonates diisopropylamine, giving diisopropylammonium chloride. The reaction proceeds at room temperature, usually in a nonprotic solvent such as ether or dichloromethane, and the solid salt precipitates upon completion.

Redox reduction of iodine(V) oxide (I2O5) by hydrogen gas; hydrogen serves as the reducing agent, converting I2O5 to elemental iodine while forming water. Typically carried out in the gas phase at elevated temperatures (≈200–300 °C) under an inert atmosphere; no solvent required.

Condensation (addition) of ammonia to cyanamide yielding cyanoguanidine (dicyandiamide). The reaction proceeds via nucleophilic attack of NH3 on the nitrile carbon of cyanamide, followed by proton transfers. Conducted under heating (≈120–150 °C) in the presence of excess gaseous ammonia or aqueous ammonia solution; often performed neat or in a high‑boiling solvent such as ethanol.

Reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol using lithium aluminium hydride; purpose is to convert hexanoic acid into 1‑hexanol. Key transformation is the replacement of the –COOH group by a –CH2 group. Typically performed under anhydrous conditions in dry diethyl ether or THF at 0 °C to reflux, with 1–3 equiv LiAlH4 under nitrogen; work‑up with aqueous acid to quench excess hydride.

Alcohol acylation of ketene with ethanol to form ethyl acetate; a concerted addition of the alcohol O‑H across the ketene double bond (esterification). Usually performed neat or in a dry inert solvent (e.g., toluene) at 0–25 °C; no catalyst is needed, though a base such as pyridine can be added to scavenge the generated HCl if trace impurities are present.

Wurtz coupling of 1‑bromobutane using metallic sodium to form a C8 alkane (octane) and sodium bromide as by‑product. Requires anhydrous, aprotic solvent (dry diethyl ether or THF), reflux conditions, and an inert atmosphere to prevent sodium oxidation.

Acid decomposition of carbonate; produces dysprosium trifluoride while releasing CO2; Dy2(CO3)3 + 6 HF → 2 DyF3 + 3 CO2 + 3 H2O; performed in aqueous HF at mild temperature (room temperature to 60 °C), often under stirring to vent CO2.

General type: thermal or enzymatic decarboxylation of an α‑amino acid. Purpose: convert the amino acid into the corresponding primary amine. Key transformation: removal of the carboxyl group as CO₂, forming isobutylamine (2‑methyl‑propyl‑NH₂). Typical conditions: heating of L‑leucine (often 150–200 °C) or using a decarboxylase enzyme; sometimes solid acid catalysts (e.g., zeolites) are employed. Common solvents/catalysts: neat or in high‑boiling inert solvent (e.g., o‑xylene); enzyme preparations use aqueous buffer.

Friedel‑Crafts alkylation of benzothiophene with methyl chloride using aluminum chloride as Lewis acid catalyst, yielding 2‑methyl‑1‑benzothiophene; performed in dry, non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂ or CS₂) at 0–25 °C under anhydrous conditions, with hydrogen chloride generated as a by‑product.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of butyrohydrazide (butyric acid hydrazide) to regenerate butyric acid and release hydrazine. Performed in aqueous acidic medium (e.g., 1–2 M HCl) with heating under reflux; water acts as both solvent and reactant.

Enzymatic N‑methyltransferase reaction wherein S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine (SAM) donates a methyl group to the indole nitrogen of serotonin, producing N‑methylserotonin and S‑adenosyl‑L‑homocysteine. Occurs under physiological pH (≈7.4) in the presence of the appropriate methyltransferase enzyme; typically carried out in buffered aqueous solution (phosphate buffer) at 25–37 °C.

Double displacement precipitation (metathesis) reaction in aqueous solution; purpose is to exchange anions, precipitating copper(II) phosphate (insoluble) while forming soluble sodium bromide; typically carried out by mixing aqueous solutions of sodium phosphate and copper(II) bromide at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

This is an aluminothermic reduction of uranium(III) chloride, where aluminium metal reduces UCl3 to uranium metal while forming aluminium chloride. The process is used for bulk uranium preparation. It is performed at elevated temperatures (≈700–900 °C) in a sealed crucible under inert atmosphere; the reaction may be carried out in a molten salt medium (e.g., NaCl–KCl eutectic) to improve mixing, and no additional catalyst is required.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of 2‑ethylfuran to 2‑ethyltetrahydrofuran; purpose is to saturate the furan ring; key transformation is addition of H₂ across the two C=C bonds of the heterocycle; performed under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) in the presence of a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni, using an alcohol solvent (e.g., ethanol or methanol) at 25–80 °C.

Double displacement/acid‑base neutralization in water; sodium hydroxide reacts with magnesium phosphate to give sodium phosphate in solution and precipitate magnesium hydroxide; typically conducted by dissolving NaOH and magnesium phosphate in water, stirring at room temperature; no catalyst needed; water is the solvent.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution of acetyl chloride with sodium hydrosulfide; NaSH attacks the carbonyl, replacing chloride and yielding thioacetic acid and NaCl. Typically carried out in a biphasic water/THF or aqueous ethanol mixture at 0 °C to rt; no additional catalyst required.

Metathesis (double displacement) reaction in aqueous medium; calcium perchlorate exchanges its anion with lead carbonate, precipitating insoluble calcium carbonate while forming soluble lead(II) perchlorate; performed by mixing aqueous solutions of the two salts at ambient temperature with stirring; water solvent, no catalyst.

Fischer esterification of creatine with methanol catalyzed by p‑toluenesulfonic acid; purpose is to convert the carboxyl group of creatine into a methyl ester; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of methanol on the activated carbonyl followed by loss of water; reaction is refluxed in excess methanol with a catalytic amount of p‑TsOH (typically 1–10 mol %) at 60–80 °C; removal of water drives equilibrium; no additional solvent needed beyond methanol.

Acid‑base neutralization of metasilicic (silicic) acid with sodium hydroxide to form sodium metasilicate and water; carried out in aqueous solution, usually at mild heating (30–60 °C) to ensure dissolution; stoichiometric NaOH (2 equivalents) is added to the acid solution with stirring; water is both solvent and product; no catalyst required.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (halide exchange) using potassium fluoride; converts 1‑bromohexane to 1‑fluorohexane; typically carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 80‑120 °C, sometimes with a phase‑transfer catalyst; potassium bromide precipitates as the inorganic by‑product.

Catalytic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide in basic medium (redox reaction) mediated by nickel(II) nitrate; hydrogen peroxide is reduced to water while molecular oxygen evolves; nickel(II) is precipitated as Ni(OH)₂ and nitrate forms NaNO₃; performed in aqueous NaOH solution at ambient temperature with Ni(NO₃)₂ acting as catalyst.

Duff ortho‑formylation of a phenol using hexamethylenetetramine (HMTA) under strong acid. 4‑Methylphenol reacts with HMTA in trifluoroacetic acid; the acid protonates HMTA, generating an electrophilic iminium intermediate that attacks the ortho positions of the activated aromatic ring. Hydrolysis of the intermediate releases two equivalents of formaldehyde that become aldehyde substituents, producing 2,6‑diformyl‑4‑methylphenol, with by‑products ammonium trifluoroacetate, water and formaldehyde. Conditions: excess TFA, reflux (80–100 °C) for several hours; no metal catalyst needed.

Enzymatic O‑methyltransferase reaction; S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine transfers a methyl group to the 7‑hydroxy position of 2,4‑dihydroxy‑1,4‑benzoxazin‑3‑one, yielding the 7‑methoxy product and S‑adenosyl‑L‑homocysteine; conducted in aqueous buffer (pH 7‑8) at 25‑37 °C with the appropriate methyltransferase; no organic solvents required.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of 2‑propoxyethyl acetate to acetic acid and 2‑propoxyethanol; an ester saponification (water‑mediated cleavage) used to regenerate the alcohol; typical conditions involve refluxing the ester in aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) or aqueous base (NaOH) for 1‑3 h, followed by neutralization if basic conditions are used; water serves as the solvent.

Sandmeyer‑type diazotization‑halogenation; 3‑aminopyridine is converted to its diazonium chloride with NaNO₂/HCl at 0‑5 °C, then chloride replaces the diazonium group to give 3‑chloropyridine; copper(I) chloride is normally added as catalyst; reaction performed in aqueous acidic medium and the product extracted into an organic solvent such as ether.

Thermal decomposition of a metal sulfate; purpose is to convert the sulfate to the corresponding oxide and release sulfur trioxide gas; key transformation: gadolinium(III) sulfate breaks down upon heating to produce solid gadolinium(III) oxide and gaseous SO3; typical conditions: high temperature (≈1000–1100 °C) in a furnace, often in air or an inert atmosphere; no solvent; the reaction may be carried out in a ceramic crucible, and SO3 is vented or trapped.

Metal halide reduction; purpose is to prepare tin tetrahydride (SnH4) from tin tetrachloride; LiAlH4 transfers hydride to SnCl4 forming SnH4 while AlCl3 and LiCl are generated as by‑products; typically carried out in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere at 0 °C to reflux, no catalyst required.

Selective reduction of the cyclic disulfide in lipoic acid to dihydrolipoic acid using sodium borohydride; NaBH₄ delivers hydride in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature; sodium metaborate is generated as by‑product; the carboxylic acid moiety remains unchanged under these conditions.

Metathesis or ligand exchange reaction. Purpose to synthesize organocadmium and zinc sulfide compounds. Key transformation involves replacement of sulfide (S²⁻) ligand on cadmium with methyl groups from dimethylzinc. Conducted in inert atmosphere, often in non-polar or coordinating solvents (e.g., toluene, ethers) at elevated temperatures.

Organometallic synthesis; nucleophilic substitution/alkylation of GeCl4 with MeLi to afford tetramethylgermanium. Performed under inert atmosphere at –78 °C to 0 °C in dry ether or THF; lithium chloride precipitates and is removed.

Reaction type: strong reduction of a nitrile to a primary amine. Purpose: synthesize 2‑phenoxyethylamine from the corresponding nitrile. Key transformation: –C≡N → –CH2NH2 (nitrile carbon reduced by four electrons). Typical conditions: LiAlH4 (1–2 equiv) in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether), under inert atmosphere, 0 °C to reflux; reaction quenched carefully with water/alcohol. No additional catalyst required.

High‑temperature metallothermic reduction; silica is reduced by elemental beryllium to give silicon and beryllium oxide. Conducted in a furnace at ~1500 °C in an inert or vacuum atmosphere; solid‑state reaction with no solvent.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a (Z)-alkene; H2 adds across the C=C of oct‑4‑ene to produce n‑octane. Typical conditions: H2 gas (1–5 atm), Pd/C, PtO2 or Raney Ni catalyst, solvent such as ethanol or ether, temperature 25–80 °C.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) in aqueous solution; silver acetate reacts with nitrous acid to exchange anions, yielding acetic acid and soluble silver nitrite. Carried out in water at 0–25 °C, no special catalyst required.

Strong‑base induced elimination (E2) of a secondary alkyl halide; potassium tert‑butoxide removes a β‑hydrogen from 2‑iodoheptane to afford hept‑2‑ene and KI; carried out in an aprotic polar solvent such as THF or DMSO at 0‑25 °C under inert atmosphere, using KOtBu (≈1.5‑2 equiv).

Condensation (esterification) of methyl hydrogen sulfate with methanol to afford dimethyl sulfate and water. The alcohol attacks the sulfonic acid functionality, eliminating water. Typically carried out by refluxing methanol (or a methanol/solvent mixture) with methyl bisulfate, optionally with a Dean‑Stark trap to remove water. Provides a route to dimethyl sulfate from the monomethyl sulfate precursor.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation (electrophilic aromatic substitution); benzene attacks the electrophilic carbonyl of phthalic anhydride in the presence of AlCl3 to form o‑benzoylbenzoic acid. Conducted in anhydrous, non‑protic solvent (e.g., CH2Cl2, CS2) at 0 °C to reflux under inert atmosphere; AlCl3 acts as Lewis‑acid catalyst.

Redox (oxidation‑reduction) in basic solution; bromine is reduced to bromide while selenite is oxidized to selenate, producing water and sodium salts. Performed in aqueous NaOH at ambient temperature; no catalyst needed.

Oxidative decomposition (combustion‑type) of formyl cyanide with molecular oxygen; purpose is to fully oxidize the aldehyde carbon to CO₂ while releasing hydrogen cyanide from the cyanide group; key transformation: HCOCN + O₂ → CO₂ + HCN; typical conditions involve heating under an oxygen atmosphere, often in the gas phase or in a sealed tube; no specific solvent or catalyst is required, although metal oxide catalysts can accelerate the oxidation.

Catalytic hydrogenation of (Z)-3‑methyl‑2‑hexene; purpose is to saturate the carbon‑carbon double bond to give the corresponding alkane; key transformation: C=C → C–C by addition of H₂; typical conditions use H₂ gas (1–5 atm) with a transition‑metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni in an inert solvent (ethanol, ethyl acetate or THF) at 25–80 °C.

Oxidation of 1‑phenylethanol to acetophenone using 1‑hydroxy‑1,2‑benziodoxol‑3(1H)-one (IBX); purpose is to convert a secondary benzylic alcohol into a ketone; key transformation: secondary alcohol → ketone with concomitant reduction of the hypervalent iodine to 2‑iodobenzoic acid; typical conditions are room temperature to 40 °C in a polar aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile, often under a nitrogen atmosphere; no additional catalyst is required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) alkylation of a carboxylate – lithium benzoate reacts with methyl iodide to form methyl benzoate and lithium iodide. The benzoate anion attacks the electrophilic methyl carbon of MeI, displacing iodide. Usually carried out in a dry aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF, under reflux and an inert atmosphere to avoid moisture. Excess methyl iodide and sometimes a phase‑transfer catalyst are used to improve yield.

This is a thermal decomposition reaction. Magnesium aluminate (MgAl2O4) breaks down into magnesium oxide (MgO) and aluminum oxide (Al2O3) when heated to high temperatures (>1000°C). No solvent or catalyst is involved.

Staudinger reduction of 2‑azidoacetamide with triphenylphosphine; azide is converted to 2‑aminoacetamide while triphenylphosphine is oxidized to Ph3P=O; generally run at room temperature in THF or CH2Cl2 under nitrogen.

Halogenation (substitution) of an alkoxide with PCl₅; sodium butoxide is converted to butyl chloride while generating NaCl and POCl₃. Performed at 0 °C to rt in inert, non‑protic solvents such as CH₂Cl₂ or CHCl₃; reaction often under nitrogen.

Hydrolysis of an acyl fluoride; water attacks acetyl fluoride yielding acetic acid and HF; usually done in aqueous media at ambient temperature; HF may be neutralized with a base (e.g., NaHCO₃) if isolation is desired.

Acid‑catalyzed ether cleavage of 1‑ethoxypropane with hydroiodic acid; HI protonates the ether oxygen, followed by SN2 attack of iodide on the ethyl side, producing iodoethane and 1‑propanol. Typically carried out in excess HI, refluxing the mixture; no additional catalyst required.

Halogenation/quench of ethyllithium with elemental iodine; purpose is to generate the corresponding alkyl halide (ethyl iodide) and lithium iodide; key transformation: R‑Li + I₂ → R‑I + LiI; typical conditions are low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) in an aprotic ether solvent such as THF, under inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) to prevent side reactions; the reaction is usually performed dropwise to control exotherm.

Acid‑base neutralization forming the hydrochloride salt of minaprine; purpose is to increase the drug’s water solubility and stability for pharmaceutical use; key transformation: amine (minaprine) + HCl → minaprine·HCl (ionic salt); typical conditions involve dissolving minaprine in a minimal amount of ethanol or water and adding aqueous HCl (1 M) at 0–25 °C, followed by stirring and possible gentle heating to ensure complete salt formation; the product is isolated by evaporation or precipitation.

Condensation of isocyanic acid with thiourea to afford dithiobiuret. The nucleophilic amino group of thiourea attacks the carbon of HNCO, forming a new C–N bond and ultimately yielding the sulfur‑containing urea analogue after loss of water. Usually performed in water or ethanol at 0–50 °C, often under inert atmosphere to avoid side reactions; no additional catalyst is required.

Metathesis/acid‑base reaction; used to dissolve insoluble nickel(II) oxalate and generate soluble nickel(II) sulfate while liberating oxalic acid. Key transformation: exchange of anions (oxalate ↔ sulfate). Typically performed in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating and stirring; no catalyst required. Common solvent: water.

Metathesis/precipitation (double‑displacement). Silver methanesulfonate exchanges its anion with chloride from sodium chloride, precipitating insoluble silver chloride while forming soluble sodium methanesulfonate. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the silver chloride solid is filtered off. No catalyst.

Thermal decomposition / rearrangement of thiosulfinate to disulfide. Diallyl thiosulfinate spontaneously collapses on mild heating (room temperature to 50 °C) in an inert organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or ether) to give diallyl disulfide. No catalyst is needed; the reaction proceeds via reduction of the S=O bond and formation of an S–S bond. Purpose: generation of the characteristic garlic flavour disulfide.

Reductive dehalogenation (hydrogenolysis); purpose is to remove the iodine substituent from iodobenzene to produce benzene. Key transformation: cleavage of the C–I bond and formation of H–I. Conducted under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) with a metal hydrogenation catalyst such as palladium on carbon (Pd/C) or Raney nickel, in an alcohol solvent (e.g., ethanol) at 25–80 °C.

Direct metal fluorination (redox) reaction; transforms metallic uranium into uranium tetrafluoride while generating hydrogen gas; uranium metal reacts with gaseous HF, oxidizing U(0) to U(IV) and reducing HF to H2; typical conditions are 300‑500 °C under a controlled HF flow, sometimes diluted with an inert gas; performed in a sealed reactor; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base/fluorination of lutetium oxide with hydrofluoric acid to afford lutetium fluoride; carried out in aqueous or anhydrous HF, often under reflux; water is the medium, no catalyst; key transformation: Lu₂O₃ + 6 HF → 2 LuF₃ + 3 H₂O.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction; aqueous solution of scandium fluoride mixed with sodium hydroxide yields insoluble scandium hydroxide precipitate and soluble sodium fluoride; performed at ambient temperature with stirring, no catalyst required.

Solid‑state synthesis (direct combination) of a gallium chalcogenide; elemental gallium and tellurium are heated together to produce gallium telluride (commonly Ga₂Te₃); usually performed in an inert atmosphere (argon) at 500–700 °C in a sealed tube or crucible; no solvent or catalyst.

Thermal decomposition (calcination); solid ammonium phosphomolybdate is heated strongly (≈300–400 °C) in a furnace, causing breakdown to molybdenum trioxide, phosphorus pentoxide (or phosphoric oxide species), with release of ammonia and water vapor; no solvent; air or inert atmosphere may be used; provides metal oxides for further processing.

Robinson tropinone synthesis (multicomponent Mannich/condensation). Purpose: construct the bicyclic tropinone framework from simple precursors. Key transformations: (a) formation of an iminium ion from methylamine and succinaldehyde, (b) nucleophilic addition of acetone enolate to the iminium (Mannich step), and (c) intramolecular cyclization/condensation that yields the bicyclic tropinone and eliminates water. Typical conditions: reflux in methanol or ethanol with a catalytic amount of HCl (0.1–0.5 M), 4–8 h; the reaction is generally performed under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation. Common solvent: methanol (acts as both solvent and participant in azeotropic removal of water).

Oxidation of cis‑3,7‑dimethyl‑2,6‑octadien‑1‑ol with PCC; purpose is to convert the primary allylic alcohol to the corresponding aldehyde. Key transformation: PCC oxidizes the –CH₂OH group to –CHO, giving cis‑3,7‑dimethyl‑2,6‑octadienal. Typical conditions: dichloromethane solvent, 0 °C to ambient temperature, anhydrous environment; reaction completes within 1–2 h. No additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution/hydrolysis of vicinal dibromide; purpose is to convert 1,2‑dibromobutane into the corresponding 1,2‑butanediol. Key transformation: replacement of each Br by OH, precipitation of AgBr. Carried out by adding silver oxide (Ag₂O) to an aqueous or alcoholic suspension of the dibromide, often with mild heating (40–60 °C). No additional catalyst; solvent typically water or ethanol.

Direct oxidative fluorination (halogenation); purpose is to convert the binary compound AlSb into its high‑oxidation‑state fluorides. Key transformation: fluorine oxidizes aluminum to AlF₃ and antimony to SbF₅. Reaction is highly exothermic, performed in the gas phase or in an inert fluorinated solvent at low temperatures (−78 °C to 0 °C) to control vigor. No catalyst; fluorine gas is the sole reagent.

Oxidative cleavage/oxidation with potassium permanganate; oxidizes the allylic double bond of isosafrole to a β‑keto carbonyl, yielding 3,4‑methylenedioxyphenylacetone; MnO₂ precipitates as by‑product; generally carried out in aqueous or acetone medium, cold to moderate temperature (0–25 °C) then warmed, often under neutral to slightly basic conditions; excess KMnO₄ is filtered off as MnO₂.

type: double‑displacement (metathesis) ion‑exchange. Purpose: preparation of manganese(II) lactate salt from inexpensive precursors. Key transformation: exchange of nitrate anions from Mn(NO₃)₂ with lactate anions from sodium lactate, yielding NaNO₃ and Mn(lactate)₂ in solution. Typical conditions: dissolve both salts in water, mix at room temperature or slightly elevated temperature (20–60 °C) with vigorous stirring; the reaction proceeds spontaneously, no catalyst needed. The products remain in aqueous solution and can be isolated by evaporation or crystallisation.

Williamson ether synthesis (nucleophilic substitution, SN2). Purpose: form an aryl ether by O‑alkylation of phenol. Key transformation: phenoxide anion attacks 1,2‑dibromoethane, displacing bromide to give 2‑bromoethoxybenzene and HBr (often trapped by base). Typical conditions: phenol deprotonated with K₂CO₃ or NaOH, polar aprotic solvent (acetone, DMF), reflux 60–80 °C. Catalyst: base to generate phenoxide.

Acetyl chloride acylation of an alcohol. The hydroxyl group of ethyl 6‑hydroxyhexanoate is converted to an acetate ester (ethyl 6‑acetoxyhexanoate) with acetyl chloride; hydrogen chloride is generated as a by‑product. The reaction is usually performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane, with a non‑nucleophilic base (triethylamine, pyridine) present to neutralize HCl and prevent side‑reactions.

Transfer hydrogenation using formic acid as hydrogen donor over Pd/C; purpose is to reduce the conjugated double bonds of trans‑resveratrol to give dihydroresveratrol. Key transformation: formic acid decomposes on Pd surface to H₂ (or hydride) and CO₂; the hydrogen adds across the C=C bonds of resveratrol, producing the saturated dihydro derivative and releasing CO₂. Typical conditions: Pd/C (5–10 wt %), formic acid (1–2 equiv), solvent such as ethanol or MeCN, temperature 25–80 °C, atmospheric pressure. No external hydrogen gas needed.

Partial reduction of an ester to an aldehyde using diisobutyl‑aluminium hydride (DIBAL‑H); purpose is to stop at the aldehyde stage; key transformation: methyl 3‑methylbutanoate + DIBAL‑H → 3‑methylbutanal + methanol; performed at low temperature (≈ ‑78 °C) in dry THF; stoichiometric amount of DIBAL‑H, inert atmosphere; quench with methanol or aqueous acid at low temperature.

Oxidation (hydroxylation) of allopurinol to oxypurinol using hydrogen peroxide; used to convert the parent drug into its active metabolite; key transformation is insertion of an OH group at the C‑8 position of the purine ring while reducing H2O2 to water; typically performed in aqueous buffer (pH 7–8) at ambient temperature, often catalyzed by a peroxidase enzyme or a metal catalyst such as Fe‑EDTA to enhance rate.

Acid–base metathesis; purpose is to convert insoluble silver thiocyanate into soluble silver nitrate while generating thiocyanic acid; key transformation: AgSCN + HNO₃ → AgNO₃ (aq) + HSCN; typical conditions: dilute aqueous acid, room temperature or slight warming; solvent: water; no catalyst needed.

Formation of aryl chloroformate – phosgene reacts with phenol to produce phenyl chloroformate and hydrogen chloride. This is analogous to the alcohol case, involving nucleophilic attack of the phenoxide on phosgene. A stoichiometric base (pyridine, triethylamine) is used to neutralize HCl; the reaction is performed at 0 °C to room temperature in dry dichloromethane or toluene under nitrogen.

Aminolysis of butyl acetate with aniline to give N‑phenyl acetamide (acetanilide) and n‑butanol; a nucleophilic acyl substitution useful for preparing secondary amides from esters; the ester carbonyl is attacked by aniline, forming the amide and releasing the alcohol; commonly carried out by heating the neat reactants or in a high‑boiling inert solvent (toluene, xylene) under reflux, sometimes with removal of butanol to drive equilibrium; no additional catalyst is required, though a slight excess of aniline can improve yield.

Thermal decomposition (disproportionation) of oxygen difluoride to molecular oxygen and fluorine; serves as a method to generate F2 gas in situ; the O–F bonds break homolytically, yielding O2 and 2 F· radicals that combine to F2; requires elevated temperature (typically > 200 °C) or photolytic activation (UV irradiation); usually performed in an inert gas stream under controlled pressure; no solvent or catalyst is employed.

Hydrogen reduction of chromium(IV) dioxide to chromium(III) oxide (Cr2O3) with formation of water; a solid‑gas redox reaction used in metallurgy for producing Cr2O3 or for catalyst preparation; H2 serves as the reductant, converting CrO2 to Cr2O3 while being oxidized to H2O; conducted in a flow of hydrogen at high temperature (500–800 °C) in a tubular furnace; no solvent; catalyst is not required as the reaction is heterogeneous on the solid oxide surface.

Wet carbonate‑mediated SN2 hydrolysis of a primary bromo ether; aqueous Na₂CO₃ provides hydroxide that displaces bromide to afford 2‑methoxyethanol, with concomitant formation of NaBr, CO₂ and water; the reaction is performed in a mixed water/organic medium (often ethanol/water) under reflux.

Metathesis/halide exchange reaction; used to synthesize boron cyanide (B(CN)3) by replacing chloride ligands on BCl3 with cyanide; key transformation is BCl3 + 3 KCN → B(CN)3 + 3 KCl; performed under anhydrous, inert atmosphere (dry N2 or Ar) in a polar aprotic solvent such as THF or acetonitrile, often refluxed; no catalyst required.

Catalytic oxidation of carbamazepine to oxcarbazepine using hydrogen peroxide and sodium tungstate; an oxidative functional‑group transformation that introduces a carbonyl at the 10‑position, converting the dihydro‑azepine to the 10‑oxo derivative; Na2WO4 activates H2O2 to generate peroxotungstate species that perform selective oxygen insertion; typically run in aqueous medium (or mixed water/acetone) at 0–25 °C, pH 7–8, with 1–2 equiv of 30 % H2O2 and catalytic Na2WO4 (0.1–1 mol %). By‑products are water; the reaction proceeds under mild conditions without metal‑organic reagents.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification of methyl phenidate with ethanol to give ethyl phenidate and methanol; the methyl ester is exchanged for an ethyl ester using p‑toluenesulfonic acid as a Brønsted acid catalyst; the mechanism involves protonation of the carbonyl, nucleophilic attack by ethanol, formation of a tetrahedral intermediate, and release of methanol; carried out by refluxing methyl phenidate in excess ethanol (2–5 equiv) with a catalytic amount of TsOH (≈5 mol %) for 2–6 h; removal of methanol (e.g., by azeotropic distillation) drives the equilibrium to the ethyl ester.

Hydrolysis (sol‑gel) of tetramethyl orthosilicate. Water cleaves the Si‑OCH₃ bonds, producing methanol and silica. Used to generate SiO₂ networks or colloidal silica. Typically performed in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic media, often acid (e.g., HCl) or base (e.g., NH₃) catalyzed, at ambient temperature to reflux. No special solvent required beyond water; the reaction proceeds readily.

Selenium dioxide oxidation (allylic oxidation). SeO₂ selectively oxidizes the allylic C‑H of perillene to give perillaldehyde. Employed to introduce an aldehyde function adjacent to a double bond. Commonly carried out in refluxing 1,4‑dioxane or tert‑butanol, sometimes with a catalytic amount of water, at 80–100 °C. No additional catalyst; SeO₂ itself acts as the oxidant.

Acid–base neutralization (phenoxide protonation). Hydrochloric acid protonates sodium 2,4,6‑trimethylphenolate to afford 2,4,6‑trimethylphenol and sodium chloride. Simple salt‑metathesis used to generate the free phenol. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature, no catalyst required.

Fischer esterification of caffeic acid with methanol. The carboxylic acid group of caffeic acid reacts with methanol to form methyl caffeate and water. Used to protect the acid or to modify polarity. Typically refluxed in excess methanol with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) and removal of water (Dean‑Stark trap). No special solvent beyond methanol.

Metathesis/complexation forming calcium tetrafluoroborate. Boron trifluoride reacts with calcium fluoride to generate Ca(BF₄)₂. Performed under anhydrous conditions, often in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dry dichloromethane, diethyl ether, or liquid HF at low temperature (0 °C to rt). No additional catalyst; the reaction proceeds via fluoride exchange.

Acid‑base precipitation (double displacement) reaction in water; aluminum sulfate reacts with sodium carbonate, producing insoluble aluminum hydroxide precipitate, soluble sodium sulfate, and carbon dioxide gas from carbonate decomposition. Typically carried out by mixing aqueous solutions at room temperature with vigorous stirring; no catalyst required.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis). Aqueous potassium phosphate reacts with calcium chloride to precipitate calcium phosphate while forming soluble potassium chloride. Used for removal of calcium or preparation of calcium phosphate salts. Conducted in water at ambient temperature; the insoluble Ca₃(PO₄)₂ precipitates and is filtered. No catalyst required.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction in aqueous solution; exchange of K⁺ and Fe²⁺ ions; ferrous carbonate precipitates while potassium fumarate stays soluble; typically performed at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Transmetallation/organometallic synthesis; methylmagnesium chloride transfers methyl groups to gallium trichloride forming volatile trimethylgallium and MgCl₂; carried out under anhydrous conditions in dry ether or THF under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar); low to moderate temperature (0–25 °C); no additional catalyst.

Acid‑base reaction producing hydrogen sulfide; phosphoric acid protonates sulfide ion of strontium sulfide, liberating H₂S gas and yielding strontium phosphate which precipitates; carried out in aqueous solution, often chilled to control H₂S evolution, no catalyst needed.

Acid–base neutralization forming a pharmaceutical salt; nicotinic acid reacts with HCl to give niacin hydrochloride; performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; water is the solvent; no catalyst needed.

Ring‑opening transesterification/decarboxylation of ethylene carbonate with diethylene glycol producing triethylene glycol and CO₂; typically conducted at elevated temperature (120–180 °C) under reduced pressure to remove CO₂; catalyzed by basic salts (e.g., K₂CO₃) or metal alkoxides; often solvent‑free or in excess diol.

Hydrolytic decomposition of dioxygen difluoride; purpose is to neutralize O2F2 or generate hydrogen fluoride. Key transformation: O2F2 reacts with water to give molecular oxygen and HF (O2F2 + H2O → O2 + 2 HF). Typical conditions: performed at low temperature (–78 °C to 0 °C) because O2F2 is extremely reactive; aqueous medium; reaction is highly exothermic; no catalyst.

Dehydrative condensation of methanol with phosphorus pentoxide yielding trimethyl phosphate and water; P₂O₅ acts as a strong dehydrating agent; reaction performed under anhydrous conditions, usually by adding excess dry methanol to P₂O₅ and warming (50–80 °C); no solvent, no catalyst beyond P₂O₅.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysishydrolysis of methacrylate ester) giving 4‑hydroxybenzoic acid and methacrylic acid; carried out in aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) with heating (reflux, 80–100 °C); water is the reaction medium; no additional catalyst required.

Acid–base neutralization; sodium bicarbonate neutralizes glycine·HCl, liberating CO₂ and forming free glycine, water and NaCl. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Strong reduction of an ester; LiAlH₄ reduces sec‑butyl acetate to the two corresponding alcohols, ethanol (from the acetyl group) and sec‑butanol (from the alkoxy side). Conducted under anhydrous conditions in ether or THF, usually at 0 °C to reflux, with inert atmosphere.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) in aqueous solution; cyanide ion replaces bromide, converting CuBr to cuprous cyanide (CuCN) and forming NaBr. Reaction is done in water, often at ambient temperature with excess NaCN; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base metathesis (salt exchange); copper(I) azide reacts with aqueous HCl to give copper(I) chloride precipitate and hydrazoic acid gas; purpose is preparation of HN₃; key transformation CuN₃ + HCl → CuCl(s) + HN₃(g); conditions: dilute HCl (≈1 M) at 0–5 °C in water, inert atmosphere; solvent is water; low temperature needed to avoid explosive decomposition.

Peracid oxidation of citronellal (oxidative cyclisation) – peroxyacetic acid transfers an oxygen to the allylic double bond of citronellal, inducing intramolecular epoxide formation and rearrangement to give rose oxide; acetic acid is formed as by‑product. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt in anhydrous dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride, inert atmosphere, reaction time 1–3 h.

Peracid epoxidation; meta‑chloroperoxybenzoic acid adds an oxygen across the C=C bond of 1‑cyclooctene to give 1,2‑epoxycyclooctane. Carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane, from 0 °C to room temperature, in the dark; no additional catalyst needed.

Acid–base exchange (neutralization); excess sulfuric acid protonates sodium phosphate, yielding phosphoric acid and three equivalents of sodium bisulfate. Performed in aqueous medium, often with gentle heating to ensure complete conversion; no catalyst required.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution; purpose is to replace the benzylic bromide with a cyano group to give 4‑chlorobenzyl cyanide; key transformation: C–Br bond displaced by CN⁻ forming C–CN; typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, NaCN (1–2 eq) at 0 °C to room temperature; work‑up with water to precipitate NaBr.

Oxidation of a sulfide to a sulfoxide; ac acid reacts with hydrogen peroxide to generate peracetic acid in situ, which oxidizes diethyl sulfide to diethyl sulfoxide, producing water as by‑product. Typical conditions involve stirring the mixture in glacial acetic acid at 0–25 °C; the reaction proceeds without added metal catalysts.

Redox (carbothermic reduction): Carbon reduces thallium(I) oxide to metallic thallium while being oxidized to carbon dioxide. Typically carried out in a high‑temperature furnace (≈800‑1000 °C) under an inert atmosphere; solid‑state reaction with no solvent or catalyst required.

Reaction type: catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene. Purpose: saturate the C=C bond of but‑1‑enylbenzene to afford the fully reduced alkylbenzene. Key transformation: addition of H₂ across the double bond converts the vinyl side chain to a saturated n‑butyl group, yielding 1‑phenylbutane. Typical conditions: expose the substrate to H₂ gas (1–5 atm) in the presence of a heterogeneous catalyst such as Pd/C (10 %), PtO₂, or Raney Ni, in a solvent like ethanol, ethyl acetate, or THF, at ambient temperature to 80 °C. Reaction time varies from 1 h to several hours depending on pressure and catalyst loading.

Double displacement precipitation; ammonium oxalate supplies oxalate ion that reacts with BeCl2 to give insoluble BeC2O4 and soluble NH4Cl; carried out in water at room temperature or with gentle heating; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Double‑displacement/precipitation (metathesis): Ammonium oxalate reacts with calcium nitrate in aqueous solution to precipitate insoluble calcium oxalate, while ammonium nitrate remains dissolved. Conducted at room temperature in water with stirring; filtration isolates the calcium oxalate solid.

Oxidative conversion (KMnO₄ oxidation): 2‑Acetylnaphthalene is oxidized by potassium permanganate to naphthoic acid by cleaving the side‑chain methyl group to a carboxyl group. Performed in aqueous alkaline medium (e.g., NaOH) with KMnO₄ under reflux, followed by acid work‑up; water is the solvent, no added catalyst.

Halogenation of ethanol by phosphorus triiodide (PI₃) to convert the primary alcohol into ethyl iodide with concomitant formation of phosphorous acid (H₃PO₃). Reaction proceeds via SN2 attack of iodide on the activated alcohol; performed in dry ether or another aprotic solvent at 0–25 °C under an inert atmosphere, with PI₃ generated in situ from red phosphorus and iodine.

Oxidation. Converts an alkyl group to a carboxylic acid functional group. Purpose: Synthesis of 2-naphthoic acid from 2-methylnaphthalene. Key transformation: Oxidation of the methyl group (-CH3) to a carboxylic acid (-COOH) under strongly oxidizing conditions. Reaction conditions: Heated aqueous potassium permanganate (KMnO4) solution. Solvents: Water with basic conditions (e.g., potassium hydroxide). Manganese dioxide (MnO2) precipitates as a byproduct.

Esterification (condensation) of phosphorous acid: Two equivalents of isopropanol react with phosphorous acid to form di‑isopropyl phosphite with loss of two equivalents of water. Usually carried out under reflux in anhydrous toluene or benzene using a Dean–Stark apparatus to remove water; a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) may be employed to promote the condensation.

Transesterification / nucleophilic substitution: Sodium methoxide attacks dimethyl carbonate, yielding sodium methyl carbonate and methanol. The reaction proceeds in a polar aprotic solvent such as THF or dimethyl sulfoxide at ambient or slightly elevated temperature; the methoxide anion serves as both nucleophile and base, no external catalyst needed.

Acid‑chloride formation (Vilsmeier‑type activation): Heptanoic acid is converted to heptanoyl chloride using oxalyl chloride. The reaction is performed in anhydrous dichloromethane (or another inert organic solvent) at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a catalytic amount of DMF to generate the reactive Vilsmeier intermediate. By‑products are gaseous CO, CO₂ and HCl, which are removed from the reaction mixture.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; purpose: to isolate calcium as insoluble calcium oxalate; key transformation: CaCO3 + (NH4)2C2O4 → CaC2O4(s) + (NH4)2CO3; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst, water as solvent.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) alkylation; purpose: synthesis of ethyl iodide; key transformation: I⁻ attacks ethyl triflate, displacing triflate to give EtI and NaOTf; typical conditions: dry polar aprotic solvent (acetone, DMF, DMSO) at room temperature to reflux under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst.

Transamidation between N‑acetylpiperidine and methylamine; the reaction swaps the nitrogen substituent on the carbonyl, producing N‑methylacetamide and freeing piperidine. Typically requires excess methylamine (often as a gas or in aqueous solution) and heating (reflux) to drive the equilibrium toward products. Solvents such as toluene, acetonitrile, or even neat methylamine can be used; acid or base catalysts are occasionally added (e.g., catalytic amounts of TiCl₄ or NaOH) to accelerate the exchange.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alcohol with hydrogen bromide; converts 1‑propanol to 1‑bromopropane by protonating the hydroxyl group and displacement with bromide ion, yielding water as by‑product. Typically carried out by bubbling gaseous HBr through the alcohol or using a concentrated aqueous HBr solution, often refluxed at 45‑80 °C; sometimes a catalyst such as ZnBr₂ or a dehydrating agent (e.g., P₂O₅) is added to drive the reaction to completion.

Reaction type: acid‑base salt formation (hydrochloride salt preparation). Purpose: convert the free base of 3‑chloromethamphetamine into a more stable, water‑soluble hydrochloride salt for storage or pharmaceutical use. Key transformation: the amine nitrogen is protonated by hydrochloric acid, forming 3‑chloromethamphetamine·HCl. Typical conditions: stir the free‑base amine with anhydrous HCl gas or concentrated aqueous HCl at 0 °C to room temperature for 1–2 h. Common solvent: ethanol, isopropanol or methanol; the product often precipitates and is filtered.

High‑temperature oxidation (combustion) of lithium ferrosilicon; purpose: conversion of alloy to silica, lithium oxide and iron(III) oxide; key transformation: Li‑Fe‑Si alloy + O2 → SiO2 + Li2O + Fe2O3; conducted in a furnace at several hundred to >1000 °C in an oxygen or air atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst required.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; purpose: to precipitate barium sulfate; key transformation: BaF2 + Rb2SO4 → BaSO4(s) + 2 RbF; carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature; no catalyst, water as solvent.

Redox (metal‑oxide formation) – Magnesium metal reduces nitrogen dioxide while being oxidized to MgO, producing nitric oxide. Typically carried out by passing NO2 gas over heated Mg powder (≈300–500 °C) in an inert atmosphere; no solvent, solid‑gas contact.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; purpose: to precipitate lead(II) oxalate and produce acetic acid; key transformation: Pb(CH3COO)2 + H2C2O4 → PbC2O4(s) + 2 CH3COOH; typically done in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst, water as solvent.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (nitration); purpose is to install a nitro group para to the methyl substituent on toluene. Key transformation: HNO3/H2SO4 generates the nitronium ion (NO2⁺) which attacks the aromatic ring, yielding 1‑methyl‑4‑nitrobenzene and water. Typical conditions: mixed concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids, temperature controlled at 0‑50 °C; the acid mixture serves as both solvent and reagent.

Ligand exchange / chelation (coordination) reaction; iminodiacetic acid acts as a bidentate ligand that displaces sulfate from copper(II) sulfate, forming copper(II) iminodiacetate complex and generating sulfuric acid; performed in aqueous solution, often at room temperature or with gentle heating; pH is adjusted (slightly acidic) to keep the ligand deprotonated; no additional catalyst is needed.

Hydrolytic decomposition of a carbamate (carbamate hydrolysis with decarboxylation); purpose is to generate β‑alanine from N‑carbamoyl‑β‑alanine. Key transformation: cleavage of the N‑C(=O) bond, release of CO₂ and NH₃, yielding free β‑alanine. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, heating to 80‑120 °C, often under slightly acidic (≈0.1 M HCl) or basic (≈0.1 M NaOH) conditions to accelerate the reaction; solvent is water or aqueous methanol. No metal catalyst is required.

Swern oxidation; converts the allylic primary alcohol trans‑2‑methyl‑2‑buten‑1‑ol to the corresponding aldehyde trans‑2‑methyl‑2‑butenal. Key steps are activation of DMSO with oxalyl chloride at 0 °C, formation of the alkoxysulfonium intermediate, and deprotonation by triethylamine. Typical conditions: anhydrous CH₂Cl₂, 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere; reagents added sequentially under dry conditions.

Copper‑catalyzed thiolation (nucleophilic substitution); replaces the bromide of benzyl bromide with a thiol group to give benzyl mercaptan. Sodium hydrosulfide generates HS⁻, which attacks the benzylic carbon, while CuI facilitates formation of a reactive organocopper intermediate. Usually performed in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or DMSO at 50–80 °C under nitrogen.

Metal‑acid redox (single‑displacement) reaction; terbium metal reduces hydrogen bromide, producing hydrogen gas and terbium(III) bromide. The reaction is carried out by heating elemental terbium in concentrated aqueous or gaseous HBr (often refluxing) with no additional solvent required.

Electrophilic aromatic bromination; the activated phenolic rings of 2,2′‑biphenol undergo substitution by four equivalents of Br₂ to give 2,2′‑dihydroxy‑3,3′,5,5′‑tetrabromobiphenyl, with evolution of four equivalents of HBr. Typical conditions: Br₂ added dropwise to a solution of biphenol in CCl₄, CHCl₃ or AcOH at 0 °C to rt; reaction may be accelerated by a Lewis acid catalyst such as FeBr₃, though the phenol is sufficiently activating.

Transesterification (ester exchange); converts methyl hydrogen carbonate to ethyl methyl carbonate by exchanging the alkoxy group; driven by removal of water; typically performed with excess ethanol, acid (e.g., H2SO4) or base (e.g., NaOH) catalyst at reflux; common solvent is ethanol itself.

Double SN2 alkylation of ethylenediamine; two equivalents of benzyl chloride react with ethylenediamine in basic aqueous medium (2 eq NaOH) to give N,N′‑dibenzylethylenediamine (benzathine), together with NaCl and water. Conducted in refluxing ethanol/water or aqueous ethanol, often under nitrogen, with NaOH serving both to deprotonate the amine and to neutralize HCl formed.

DCC‑mediated Steglich esterification; dicyclohexylcarbodiimide activates hexanoic acid to form an O‑acylisourea intermediate which reacts with ethanol to afford ethyl hexanoate. By‑product dicyclohexylurea precipitates out. Typical conditions: anhydrous CH₂Cl₂ or THF, 0 °C to rt, under inert atmosphere; catalytic DMAP is frequently added to accelerate acyl transfer.

Reduction of N‑tert‑butylformamide with lithium aluminum hydride, cleaving the amide to afford tert‑butylamine and methanol. Performed in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) under an inert atmosphere, typically at 0 °C initially and then warmed to reflux, with careful quenching of excess LAH after completion.

Fischer esterification; purpose: form a methyl ester from a carboxylic acid. 2‑Propylpentanoic acid is reacted with excess methanol in the presence of catalytic H₂SO₄ (reflux) to give methyl 2‑propylpentanoate and water. Removal of water (e.g., Dean‑Stark) drives the equilibrium toward ester formation.

N‑bromosuccinimide synthesis – electrophilic bromination (halogenation) of succinimide in basic aqueous medium. Sodium hydroxide neutralizes the HBr formed, giving N‑bromosuccinimide, NaBr and water. Purpose: prepare NBS, a convenient source of bromine radicals for allylic/benzylic bromination. Typical conditions: 0 °C to room temperature, aqueous NaOH (≈1 M), slow addition of Br2 with stirring; often performed in water or water/acetone mixture. No catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization to generate tribasic potassium phosphate. Potassium hydroxide deprotonates the dibasic phosphate anion (HPO4²⁻) to give PO4³⁻ (K3PO4) and water. Purpose: produce a strongly basic phosphate buffer or dry inorganic base. Conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature; reagents are mixed stoichiometrically, often under stirring. No special catalyst; water is the solvent.

Halogen exchange (Halex) fluorination of hexachloroethane. Hydrogen fluoride replaces two chlorine atoms with fluorine, yielding 1,1,2,2‑tetrachloro‑1,2‑difluoroethane and HCl as by‑product. Purpose: prepare mixed‑halogen ethane used as refrigerant or intermediate. Typical conditions: excess anhydrous HF gas at elevated temperature (300–400 °C), often in a sealed nickel or quartz reactor; catalysts such as SbF5 or pyridinium poly‑HF can accelerate the exchange. No organic solvent; reaction medium is gaseous HF.

Transesterification of 2‑ethylbutyl acetate with ethanol, producing ethyl acetate and 2‑ethylbutanol. Similar conditions to reaction 3: catalytic amount of acid (H2SO4) or base, reflux in excess ethanol, often 60–80 °C. Ethanol serves as solvent and reactant; removal of ethyl acetate can shift equilibrium.

Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of 1‑adamantyl acetate. Aqueous NaOH attacks the ester carbonyl, yielding 1‑adamantyl alcohol and sodium acetate; water is consumed, and the acetate anion is regenerated as NaOAc. Purpose: deprotect the acetate protecting group to liberate the free alcohol. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) heated to reflux (80–100 °C) for 1–3 h, often in a water/methanol mixture to improve solubility. No catalyst required.

Double‑displacement precipitation between ammonium thiocyanate and mercury(II) oxalate; yields mercuric dithiocyanate (Hg(SCN)₂) and soluble ammonium oxalate (NH₄)₂C₂O₄. Conducted in water at room temperature; HgC₂O₄ precipitates upon addition of NH₄SCN, then the solid mercury thiocyanate forms and is collected, while the ammonium oxalate remains in solution.

Phosgene scavenging by silver oxide. Phosgene (COCl₂) reacts with solid Ag₂O, undergoing nucleophilic attack of oxide on the carbonyl carbon; each Cl is transferred to silver, forming AgCl precipitate, while the carbonyl is oxidized to CO₂ gas. Purpose: safely destroy phosgene to avoid toxicity. Conditions: performed in anhydrous inert solvent (e.g., dry CH₂Cl₂ or CCl₄) at 0 °C to room temperature, under a fume hood; solid Ag₂O is added gradually to a of phosgene. No catalyst beyond the oxide itself.

Acid‑base neutralization; solid mercury(II) oxide reacts with aqueous hydrochloric acid to produce soluble mercuric chloride (HgCl₂) and water. Used in preparation of HgCl₂ solutions or in analytical precipitation of mercury. Reaction performed in water at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring; excess acid ensures complete dissolution. No special catalyst required.

Condensation to form imepitoin – nucleophilic acyl substitution between imidazolidin‑2‑one (hydantoin) and 6‑aminonicotinic acid (or its activated derivative) producing a urea‑type linkage and releasing water. Purpose: assemble the heterocyclic core of the anti‑epileptic drug imepitoin. Typical laboratory conditions: activate the carboxylic acid (e.g., as acid chloride, mixed anhydride, or using carbodiimide coupling reagents such as DCC/EDC) in an aprotic solvent (DMF, DCM, or THF), maintain temperature 0 °C to 25 °C, then add the hydantoin nucleophile; after completion, work‑up yields imepitoin and water. Catalysts are not required, but coupling agents facilitate dehydration.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; used to convert nickel(II) acetate to nickel(II) iodide while generating acetic acid. Key transformation: exchange of acetate ligands for iodide ligands. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required; water serves as solvent.

Aqueous citrate reduction (Turkevich method) of chloroauric acid; boiling HAuCl₄ solution is reduced by trisodium citrate, producing metallic Au nanoparticles, NaCl, citric acid and water; performed in water at reflux (~100 °C), citrate serves as reducing and stabilizing agent, no additional catalyst.

Acid–base neutralization of carbon dioxide with a strong base; forms rubidium carbonate and water. Key transformation: CO2 is hydrated to carbonic acid and deprotonated by RbOH, yielding carbonate. Conducted in aqueous rubidium hydroxide solution at room temperature or mild heating; no catalyst needed.

Redox/solid‑state synthesis of aluminum arsenide from arsine and aluminum metal. Key transformation: AsH3 decomposes, delivering arsenic that reacts with Al to form AlAs, releasing H2 gas. Carried out in a sealed quartz tube or high‑temperature furnace (300–600 °C) under inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst required.

Double displacement/acid‑base reaction; sulfuric acid reacts with lead(II) chromate to precipitate lead(II) sulfate and generate chromic acid in solution. Key transformation: exchange of sulfate for chromate anions. Performed in aqueous medium, often at room temperature; stirring may be used; no catalyst.

Thermal decomposition (calcination) of yttrium(III) acetate hydrate to yttrium(III) oxide. Key transformation: organic acetate groups break down to volatile acetic acid (and water) while the metal centers consolidate into Y2O3. Conducted by heating the solid precursor in air or inert gas at 300–500 °C; no solvent, catalyst, or additional reagents required.

Hydrogen reduction of germanium dioxide to elemental germanium. Key transformation: GeO2 is reduced by H2 to Ge metal with formation of water vapor. Performed in a flowing hydrogen atmosphere at elevated temperatures (400–600 °C) in a tubular furnace; no catalyst, but the reaction may be carried out on a porous GeO2 bed.

SN2-type chlorination of a secondary alcohol using phosphorus pentachloride. The hydroxyl group of 2‑butanol is replaced by chloride, forming 2‑chlorobutane; phosphorus pentachloride is reduced to phosphorus oxychloride (POCl₃) and HCl is generated. Typically carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to reflux, often with pyridine as an HCl scavenger.

Transesterification; methyl methacrylate exchanges its methoxy group for a butoxy group, yielding butyl methacrylate and methanol. Catalyzed by an acid (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or a base (e.g., sodium methoxide). Reaction is refluxed, often with excess 1‑butanol and continuous removal of methanol to shift equilibrium toward product.

Fischer esterification of 3‑methylbut‑3‑enoic acid with methanol to give methyl 3‑methylbut‑3‑enoate; acid‑catalyzed condensation that eliminates water; typically reflux in methanol with catalytic H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH.

Metathesis/acid‑base exchange between scandium acetate and hydrochloric acid. The acetate ligands are protonated to give acetic acid, while scandium is converted to scandium chloride. Performed in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to drive off volatile acetic acid; no special catalyst required.

Intramolecular cyclocondensation forming an oxazolidin‑2‑one. 2‑Aminoethanol attacks the carbonyl of ethyl chloroformate, displacing chloride and ethanol, then cyclizes to the five‑membered heterocycle with release of HCl. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as THF or dichloromethane at 0–25 °C; a base (e.g., triethylamine) is commonly added to neutralize HCl, though the stoichiometry shown produces HCl.

Acid‑carbonate neutralization producing a metal lactate salt. Lactic acid protonates manganese carbonate; CO₂ and H₂O evolve, and the resulting manganese lactate remains in solution. Usually carried out in water with gentle heating; no catalyst required.

Reaction type: alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of an amide. Purpose: cleavage of the N‑aryl amide bond to liberate 4‑nitroaniline and generate the sodium salt of 3‑oxobutanoic acid. Key transformation: hydroxide ion attacks the carbonyl carbon of the amide, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to release the amine (4‑nitroaniline) and produce the carboxylate (sodium 3‑oxobutanoate). Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH solution (1–2 M), reflux heating (80–100 °C) for several hours; the reaction mixture is then cooled and the products are isolated by acidification (to precipitate the aniline) and evaporation (to obtain the sodium salt). No additional catalyst is required.

Double‑replacement/precipitation of a lanthanide hydroxide. Hydroxide ions from NaOH replace oxalate ligands of cerium(III) oxalate, forming soluble sodium oxalate and insoluble cerium(III) hydroxide precipitate. Conducted in water, typically at ambient temperature or with mild heating to ensure complete reaction; no catalyst required.

Double‑replacement (metathesis) reaction in aqueous solution; cation exchange converts soluble sodium metaborate and calcium chloride into insoluble calcium metaborate precipitate and soluble sodium chloride. Typically performed by mixing aqueous solutions of the two salts at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Acid–base protonation (salt formation) of the basic amine idazoxan with hydrogen chloride to give idazoxan·HCl. The reaction is used to prepare a crystalline hydrochloride salt that often has improved stability and solubility for pharmaceutical handling. Conducted by adding gaseous or aqueous HCl to a solution of idazoxan (commonly in ethanol, methanol, or water) at room temperature; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation) – Ammonia reacts with aqueous tungstic acid (H₂WO₄) to give ammonium tungstate as the salt and water. Conducted in water at ambient or mildly elevated temperature; the mixture is stirred until all acid is neutralized, then the ammonium tungstate precipitates or remains in solution.

Condensation/cyclization (thiazole formation) between 2‑chloroacetophenone and methyl thiourea to afford clomethiazole. The reaction proceeds via nucleophilic substitution of the chloride by the thiourea nitrogen, followed by intramolecular cyclization to the thiazole ring. Typical conditions involve refluxing the reactants in ethanol or methanol (often 1–2 M) with a catalytic amount of pyridine or triethylamine as base, for 2–6 h under inert atmosphere; no metal catalyst is needed.

Ester hydrolysis (reverse Fischer esterification); water cleaves the acetate ester back to the alcohol and acetic acid. Key transformation: 3‑bromopropyl acetate + H₂O → 3‑bromopropan‑1‑ol + CH₃COOH. Typical conditions: aqueous acid or base (e.g., 1 M HCl or NaOH), heating under reflux; acid catalysis is common for mild conditions; aqueous medium serves as solvent.

Oxidative roasting (high‑temperature oxidation) of indium(III) sulfide with oxygen to give indium(III) oxide and sulfur dioxide gas. Conducted in a furnace at 600–900 °C with a continuous flow of dry air or pure O2; the solid sulfide is heated in the presence of the oxidant, and the reaction proceeds without solvents or catalysts.

Williamson ether synthesis via deprotonation and SN2 alkylation; purpose is to attach a methoxy group to the fluoropropanol, preserving the fluorine; key steps are deprotonation of the alcohol by NaH to form the alkoxide, SN2 attack on methyl iodide to give 1‑fluoro‑2‑methoxypropane, with evolution of H₂ and formation of NaI; performed in dry THF or DMF under nitrogen, typically at 0 °C to rt, using excess NaH and methyl iodide.

Solid–gas sulfidation; used to convert indium oxide to indium sulfide. The oxide is reduced and sulfur is introduced, forming In2S3 and H2O. Typically carried out at 600–800 °C in a flow of H2S (often diluted with inert gas) in a sealed or quartz tube; no solvent, inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation.

Acid‑silicate reaction (fluorination) of lithium disilicate with hydrofluoric acid, producing volatile silicon tetrafluoride and lithium fluoride as salts, along with water. Performed by adding concentrated HF to powdered Li2Si2O5 under reflux or in a heated, closed PTFE vessel (150–200 °C) to drive off SiF4 gas; no catalyst is required, and the medium is aqueous HF or HF/ethanol mixture.

Halogen exchange fluorination of selenium trioxide with hydrogen fluoride to generate seleninyl fluoride (SeO₂F₂) and water; carried out in anhydrous HF or in a sealed vessel at low temperature (‑20 °C to 0 °C) under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

General type: Acetyl chloride acylation (esterification) of an alcohol. Purpose: Rapid formation of the acetate ester from phenylethanol. Key transformation: Phenylethanol oxygen attacks acetyl chloride, displacing chloride and giving 1‑phenylethyl acetate while producing HCl. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt, dry dichloromethane or chloroform as solvent; a stoichiometric base such as pyridine, triethylamine, or sodium carbonate is added to neutralize HCl and drive the reaction forward. No metal catalyst required.

Transesterification: methyl 2-chloro-2-methylpropanoate reacts with ethanol to exchange the alkoxy group, producing ethyl 2-chloro-2-methylpropanoate and methanol; typically acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or base (NaOEt) catalyzed, reflux in excess ethanol with removal of methanol to drive equilibrium.

Selective ester to aldehyde reduction; DIBAL‑H reduces methyl gallate (methyl 3,4,5‑trihydroxybenzoate) to 3,4,5‑trihydroxybenzaldehyde while leaving phenolic OH groups untouched. Typically performed at –78 °C in dry THF or toluene, followed by aqueous work‑up; no additional catalyst required.

Complete ester reduction; LiAlH₄ reduces methyl pivalate (methyl 2,2‑dimethylpropanoate) to the corresponding primary alcohol, 2,2‑dimethyl‑1‑propanol, and liberates methanol from the ester alkoxy fragment. Conducted in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere, refluxing, then carefully quenched with water; no extra catalyst needed.

Halide exchange (SN2) using a silver salt; ethyl iodide reacts with AgSCN, the thiocyanate ion displaces iodide to give ethyl thiocyanate while AgI precipitates, driving the reaction forward. Usually carried out in refluxing acetone or ethanol at room temperature or mild heating; the insoluble AgI is removed by filtration.

Carbodiimide‑mediated anhydride formation; dicyclohexylcarbodiimide (DCC) activates the two carboxyl groups of malonic acid, promoting intramolecular dehydration to give malonic anhydride (oxetane‑2,5‑dione). The by‑product dicyclohexylurea precipitates. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt in dry dichloromethane (or CH₂Cl₂), often with catalytic DMAP; reaction is performed under nitrogen.

Thermite‑type aluminothermic reduction; chromium(III) oxide (Cr₂O₃) is reduced by powdered aluminum at high temperature to produce metallic chromium and aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃). The reaction is initiated by ignition (e.g., Mg fuse) and proceeds at >1500 °C in the solid state; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Carbothermic chlorination/reduction; vanadium(III) oxide (V₂O₃) reacts with carbon and chlorine gas at elevated temperatures (≈600–800 °C) to yield vanadium(III) chloride (VCl₃) and carbon monoxide. The process is a solid‑state high‑temperature synthesis of a metal halide; conducted in a sealed furnace or tube under an inert atmosphere.

Eschweiler–Clarke methylation of 4‑bromoamphetamine using formaldehyde and formic acid; the amine forms an iminium intermediate with formaldehyde that is reduced by formic acid, yielding p‑bromomethamphetamine with water and CO₂ as by‑products; conducted in aqueous formic acid, heated under reflux for several hours.

Nucleophilic substitution at silicon (S_N2) where iodide is displaced by azide to give trimethylsilyl azide; used to prepare a protected azide reagent. Conducted in anhydrous polar aprotic solvent (e.g., THF, DMF) at 0 °C to room temperature; no catalyst required.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction; base-induced hydrolysis of an inorganic salt. Aqueous KOH converts mercuric bromide into soluble potassium bromide while insoluble mercury(II) hydroxide precipitates. Usually performed in water at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required.

N‑alkylation (SN2) of thiosemicarbazide with methyl iodide to afford N‑methyl thiosemicarbazide, with hydrogen iodide generated as by‑product. Typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF, often in the presence of a base (triethylamine, NaHCO₃) to scavenge HI, at ambient temperature.

O‑methylation of the phenolic hydroxyl of 2‑hydroxyestradiol using methyl trifluoromethanesulfonate (methyl triflate), yielding 2‑methoxyestradiol and triflic acid. Carried out under strictly anhydrous conditions in a halogenated solvent (CH₂Cl₂ or CHCl₃) at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) with a non‑nucleophilic base (pyridine, 2,6‑lutidine) to capture the generated acid.

Acid‑base salt formation; hydroxylamine is protonated by concentrated sulfuric acid forming hydroxylamine sulfate with release of water; typically carried out in aqueous medium at 0‑5 °C to control exotherm, no special catalyst required.

Chlorination of indium(III) oxide; Cl₂ gas reacts with In₂O₃ at high temperature to give indium(III) chloride (InCl₃) and O₂. Conducted at 500‑800 °C in a dry gas stream; solid‑state redox reaction, no catalyst.

Acid–base reaction forming tin(II) acetate from tin(II) oxide and acetic acid, with water as by‑product. Usually performed by refluxing tin(II) oxide in excess glacial acetic acid under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Reaction type: salt formation / alkylation of tertiary amine; purpose: generate a stable ionic salt of the strong methylating agent; key transformation: nucleophilic attack of triethylamine nitrogen on MeOTf giving triethylammonium triflate; typical conditions: add MeOTf dropwise to a solution of Et3N in anhydrous CH2Cl2 at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen; no additional catalyst needed.

Acyl‑chloride esterification (Schotten‑Baumann reaction) of 1‑pentadecanol with benzoyl chloride; intended to give pentadecyl benzoate. The alcohol nucleophilically attacks the carbonyl of benzoyl chloride, releasing HCl. Typical procedure: dissolve 1‑pentadecanol in dry dichloromethane, cool to 0 °C, add benzoyl chloride (1.1 equiv) dropwise, and stir in the presence of a base such as pyridine or triethylamine (1.2 equiv) to scavenge HCl. Reaction proceeds at 0 °C to rt for 1–2 h. Work‑up involves washing with dilute HCl, water, brine, drying (Na₂SO₄), and purification by column chromatography distillation.

High‑temperature solid‑state acid–base (salt metathesis) conversion of scandium oxide to scandium chloride, releasing ammonia and water. Reaction is carried out by heating a mixture of Sc₂O₃ and NH₄Cl (often sealed in a tube) at 200–300 °C; no catalyst is employed.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction. Aqueous potassium hydroxide displaces chloride from mercury(II) chloride, forming soluble potassium chloride and insoluble mercury(II) hydroxide precipitate. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, stirring; water is the solvent and no additional catalyst is required.

Double‑replacement (metathesis) reaction. Aqueous hydrochloric acid exchanges anions with cadmium nitrate, yielding soluble cadmium chloride and nitric acid. Conducted in water at room temperature with vigorous mixing; no catalyst needed.

Nitro‑group reduction. Sodium dithionite (Na₂S₂O₄) reduces 2‑nitropyridine to 2‑aminopyridine, converting the –NO₂ group to –NH₂. Usually performed in aqueous alkaline medium (e.g., NaOH or carbonate buffer) at 50–80 °C; the reaction proceeds without added metal catalysts, water being the solvent.

Acylation (acetylation) of an amine. Tryptamine reacts with acetic anhydride, transferring an acetyl group to the nitrogen to give N‑acetyltryptamine and one equivalent of acetic acid as by‑product. Commonly carried out neat or in a non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge the generated acid; mild heating (0–25 °C) is typical.

Acid‑catalyzed ether cleavage / esterification. Dimethyl ether reacts with acetic acid under strong acid conditions (e.g., catalytic H₂SO₄) to give methyl acetate and methanol. The process requires heating (reflux) and anhydrous conditions; sulfuric acid serves both as catalyst and dehydrating agent, with the reaction medium typically being the acetic acid–ether mixture itself.

Sodium dithionite reduction of an azo compound. Purpose: chemically reduce azobenzene to hydrazobenzene under mild aqueous conditions. Key transformation: Na₂S₂O₄ generates sulfite radicals that transfer electrons to the –N=N– group, yielding the –NH–NH– product. Typical conditions: aqueous buffer (pH ≈ 7–8), room temperature, 1–2 eq sodium dithionite, reaction completed within minutes to an hour; product extracted with organic solvent.

Reaction type: condensation (addition) forming a cyclic ureide (diazolidinylurea). Purpose: synthesis of the preservative diazolidinylurea from urea and hydroxymethylurea. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of the –NH2 of urea on the carbonyl carbon of hydroxymethylurea followed by cyclization and loss of water. Typical conditions: aqueous or mixed‑water medium, pH 4‑6, moderate heating (50‑80 °C) for several hours. No special catalyst is required; the reaction proceeds under acid‑catalyzed conditions.

Acid‑base neutralization; converts sparingly soluble lanthanum trihydroxide into water‑soluble lanthanum sulfate; the hydroxide groups are protonated to give water and La³⁺ coordinates with SO₄²⁻; usually performed in aqueous solution at room temperature or with gentle heating (≤50 °C) to aid dissolution; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required, excess H₂SO₄ may be added to drive the reaction to completion.

Reaction type: Friedel‑Crafts alkylation (trichloromethylation) of benzene. Purpose: introduction of a CCl₃ group to give benzotrichloride. Key transformation: generation of the trichloromethyl carbocation from chloroform by AlCl₃, electrophilic aromatic substitution on benzene, and liberation of HCl. Typical conditions: anhydrous AlCl₃ (1–2 equiv) in a dry, nonprotic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride, chloroform, or dichloromethane; temperature kept low (0‑5 °C) on addition, then gentle reflux for 1‑2 h. Reaction is moisture‑sensitive.

Reaction type: reduction of an oxime to an amine using lithium aluminium hydride. Purpose: convert the hydroxyimino‑methyl substituent to a primary amino group, yielding 4‑aminobenzene‑1,3‑diol. Key transformation: LiAlH₄ delivers hydride to the C=N bond, followed by protonation to give the –NH₂ functionality. Typical conditions: LiAlH₄ (2‑3 equiv) in dry diethyl ether or THF under nitrogen, addition at 0 °C then reflux (≈70 °C) for 2‑4 h. Quench with careful addition of water or dilute acid at low temperature.

Reaction type: enzymatic N‑methyltransferase reaction. Purpose: methylate the primary amine of tyramine to produce N‑methyltyramine. Key transformation: transfer of the methyl group from S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine (SAM) to the nitrogen of tyramine, producing S‑adenosyl‑L‑homocysteine (SAH) as by‑product. Typical conditions: aqueous buffer (pH 7‑8), presence of tyramine N‑methyltransferase enzyme, Mg²⁺ as cofactor may be required, temperature 30‑37 °C, reaction time minutes to hours. No organic solvents are required.

Oxidation of bis(2‑chloroethyl) sulfide (mustard gas) with ozone to the corresponding sulfone, bis(2‑chloroethyl) sulfone, with release of O₂. Performed by bubbling O₃ through a solution of the sulfide in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to –78 °C; work‑up quenches excess ozone. No catalyst.

Reaction type: catalytic aerobic oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone. Purpose: convert 2‑octanol to 2‑octanone. Key transformation: Cu(II) chloride activates molecular oxygen, forming a Cu‑oxo species that abstracts hydrogen from the alcohol, yielding the ketone and water while regenerating Cu(II). Typical conditions: CuCl₂ (5‑10 mol %), base such as pyridine or NaHCO₃, solvent e.g., acetonitrile or DMSO, O₂ balloon or flow, temperature 80‑120 °C, reaction time 2‑6 h. Sometimes a ligand (e.g., bipyridine) is added to improve turnover.

Reaction type: redox (disproportionation). Purpose: neutralization of nitrogen dioxide in basic conditions. Key transformations: nitrogen dioxide (N in +4) is simultaneously oxidized to nitrate (+5) and reduced to nitrite (+3). Conditions: aqueous potassium hydroxide solution, room temperature or mild heating.

Reaction type: acid‑base reaction (oxide dissolution) forming a metal fluoride. Purpose: preparation of rhodium(III) fluoride from rhodium(III) oxide. Key transformation: protonation of oxide by HF, followed by replacement of O²⁻ with F⁻, yielding RhF₃ and water. Typical conditions: excess hydrofluoric acid (6 equiv), temperature 100‑150 °C, often performed in sealed PTFE reactors or under reflux of liquid HF; no additional catalyst required. Reaction produces water as by‑product.

The general type is a double displacement (metathesis) reaction. Purpose is to synthesize copper(II) chloride and nitric acid. Key transformation involves copper nitrate reacting with hydrochloric acid to exchange anions. Conditions occur in aqueous solution, typically with heating. Solvent is water, and no catalyst is required.

General type: solid‑state oxidation (metal‑oxide redox). Purpose: increases the oxidation state of vanadium oxide for subsequent use or material preparation. Key transformation: V²⁺O (VO) + ½ O₂ → V³⁺O (V₂O₃). Typical conditions: the powdered vanadium(II) oxide is heated in a flow of dry oxygen or air at temperatures of 300–500 °C; the reaction is conducted in a ceramic or quartz tube. No solvent is used; the process may be carried out in a furnace under controlled atmosphere.

Transesterification of ethyl 2‑cyanoacrylate with methanol; the ester alkoxy group is exchanged, yielding methyl 2‑cyanoacrylate and ethanol. Catalyzed by a small amount of acid (e.g., p‑TsOH) or base (e.g., NaOMe) using excess methanol as solvent, refluxed until equilibrium is reached.

Oxidative cleavage of a polyunsaturated fatty acid methyl ester using potassium permanganate; purpose is to break the C=C bonds to generate shorter carboxylic acids (nonanoic acid and methyl azelate). Key transformation: KMnO4 oxidatively cleaves each double bond to carbonyl groups, ultimately yielding carboxylic acids after work‑up. Typical conditions: aqueous KMnO4 (often in alkaline medium) heated gently, followed by acidification; common solvent is water or water/acetone mixture.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction in aqueous solution; cobalt(II) nitrate reacts with perchloric acid to exchange anions, yielding cobalt(II) perchlorate and nitric acid. Performed at room temperature or with gentle cooling; water is the solvent; no catalyst required.

Base‑mediated saponification; ethyl 4‑fluorobenzoate reacts with aqueous NaOH to give sodium 4‑fluorobenzoate and ethanol; usually carried out at reflux in a water/ethanol mixture; the carboxylate salt is isolated after acidification if the free acid is desired.

Ester formation from an acid chloride (acyl substitution) with methanol; purpose is synthesis of methyl heptanoate. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of methanol on heptanoyl chloride carbonyl, releasing chloride as HCl which is usually trapped by a base.
