Esterification (Fischer esterification) of propionic acid with 2‑phenylethanol to give 2‑phenylethyl propionate; acid‑catalyzed condensation with loss of water; typically performed by refluxing the substrates in an aprotic solvent such as toluene or benzene with catalytic H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH and removal of water using a Dean–Stark apparatus.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification); phenyl 2‑fluoroacetate is cleaved by aqueous NaOH to sodium 2‑fluoroacetate and phenol; reflux in water (often with ethanol as co‑solvent); water serves as solvent; acidification after reaction isolates phenol if desired.

Ozonolysis (oxidative cleavage) of 2,3‑dimethylpent‑1‑ene; ozone adds across the C=C to form a molozonide which fragments on work‑up to give aldehydes. The double bond is cleaved to formaldehyde (from the terminal carbon) and 2‑methylbutanal (from the internal fragment). Typical conditions: O3 passed through a solution of the alkene in a non‑protic solvent (CH2Cl2 or CCl4) at –78 °C to 0 °C, followed by reductive work‑up with aqueous work‑up (often dimethyl sulfide or water) to isolate the aldehydes.

Base‑promoted elimination (E2) of 2‑bromobutanoic acid with NaOH; hydroxide abstracts a β‑hydrogen while bromide leaves, forming the α,β‑unsaturated carboxylic acid but‑2‑enoic acid (crotonic acid) and NaBr, with water as a by‑product. Conducted in aqueous NaOH, usually heated (reflux) to drive the elimination; no special catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization of propionic acid with potassium bicarbonate; the carboxylic acid protonates the bicarbonate, releasing CO2 and H2O and forming potassium propionate. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the evolution of CO2 drives the reaction to completion. No catalyst needed.

Metathesis/precipitation (complexation) reaction between sodium oxalate and europium(III) nitrate in water, yielding the insoluble coordination compound diuropium trioxalate, Eu2(C2O4)3, and soluble sodium nitrate. The reaction is usually carried out in aqueous solution with mild heating and stirring; the product precipitates on cooling and is isolated by filtration. No additional catalyst required.

Precipitation of ytterbium oxalate by reaction of Yb(OH)3 with oxalic acid; purpose is to isolate Yb2(C2O4)3·nH2O as a solid. Two equivalents of Yb(OH)3 combine with three equivalents of H2C2O4, releasing six molecules of water and forming the oxalate salt. Carried out in dilute aqueous solution at ambient or slightly elevated temperature; the reaction proceeds without added catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 1,7‑dibromoheptane with sodium cyanide; each bromide is displaced by cyanide to give 1,7‑heptanedinitrile and NaBr. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at elevated temperature (80–120 °C) to promote substitution; the reaction may be done under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation of CN⁻.

Precipitation of a metal sulfide; hydrogen sulfide gas is bubbled through an aqueous lead(II) acetate solution, producing black lead(II) sulfide precipitate and acetic acid; typically done at 0–25 °C in water as the solvent.

Ester aminolysis of methyl decanoate with ammonia; ammonia attacks the carbonyl carbon, displacing methanol and forming decanamide. Typically performed by bubbling gaseous or aqueous NH3 into the ester or by refluxing the ester with excess liquid NH3 (or aqueous NH3) at 100–150 °C; the reaction proceeds without additional catalyst, although a small amount of base can be used to neutralize the generated methanol.

Metal‑acid displacement reaction; purpose is to obtain thulium(III) chloride and hydrogen gas; thulium metal is oxidized to Tm³⁺ with concurrent proton reduction to H₂; performed in dilute hydrochloric acid (≈1 M) at room temperature or with slight warming; aqueous system, no catalyst needed.

Acid‑metal redox (acid digestion). Concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with barium aluminide, liberating hydrogen gas and converting the metal components into their sulfate salts (barium sulfate and aluminum sulfate). Typically carried out in aqueous H₂SO₄ with heating under reflux; water is the solvent and no special catalyst is required.

Electrophilic methylation using diazomethane. Diazomethane transfers a methyl group to the N‑7 position of guanine, producing 7‑methylguanine and nitrogen gas as the by‑product. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as dimethyl sulfoxide or methanol at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; no catalyst is needed.

Wittig olefination; methyltriphenylphosphonium bromide is deprotonated (commonly with n‑BuLi or NaHMDS) to form the phosphorus ylide Ph3P=CH2, which reacts with 4‑methylbenzaldehyde to give 4‑methylstyrene (p‑methylstyrene) and triphenylphosphine oxide. Typical conditions: THF as solvent, inert atmosphere, 0 °C to rt, ylide generated in situ, aldehyde added dropwise, reaction proceeds 1–2 h. The reaction is chemoselective for the aldehyde carbonyl and yields the terminal alkene.

Double displacement precipitation; used to exchange cations and form insoluble barium sulfate, which precipitates out of solution; key transformation is Ba²⁺ replacing Mg²⁺ to give BaSO₄(s) and Mg(NO₃)₂(aq); typically carried out in aqueous medium at room temperature or mild heating; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

LiAlH₄ reduction of an ester; lithium aluminum hydride reduces butyl formate to the corresponding primary alcohols, n‑butanol (from the alkoxy fragment) and methanol (from the formyl fragment); carried out in dry ether or THF at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen.

Reductive amination. Indole‑3‑acetaldehyde is condensed with dibutylamine, and the imine intermediate is reduced in situ by sodium cyanoborohydride to give N,N‑dibutyltryptamine. The reaction is usually performed in methanol or dichloromethane with a weak acid (e.g., acetic acid) to facilitate imine formation, at 0 °C to ambient temperature.

SN2 alkylation of cyanide with ethyl chloride yielding propionitrile and NH₄Cl; typical conditions involve a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO) and heating (50–100 °C); aqueous work‑up isolates ammonium chloride; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization and salt formation. Hexafluoroantimonyic acid is neutralized by potassium carbonate, producing carbon dioxide, water, and the potassium hexafluoroantimonate salt. The reaction proceeds in aqueous solution at room temperature; no catalyst is required.

Ester reduction to alcohols. Lithium aluminium hydride reduces the propyl ester of p‑hydroxybenzoic acid (propylparaben) to the corresponding benzyl alcohol and propanol. Performed in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere, typically at reflux; LiAlH₄ acts as the reducing agent, no additional catalyst needed.

Reductive dehalogenation (metal‑mediated). Sodium metal effects dehalogenation of 1,2‑dibromo‑1,1,2,2‑tetrachloroethane, producing tetrachloroethylene and sodium bromide. The reaction is carried out in dry ether (e.g., THF) under reflux with freshly cut sodium; no catalyst other than the alkali metal is required.

Fischer esterification; 3‑methylbutanoic acid and propyl alcohol combine to form propyl 3‑methylbutanoate and water. Conducted by refluxing the acid and alcohol with an acid catalyst such as H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH, often with removal of water (e.g., Dean–Stark) to drive the equilibrium.

General type: Strecker-type multicomponent synthesis of an α‑amino acid. Purpose: preparation of isoserine (2‑amino‑3‑hydroxypropionic acid). Key transformation: condensation of glycolaldehyde with ammonia and hydrogen cyanide to give an α‑aminonitrile intermediate, followed by acidic or basic hydrolysis to the amino acid. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, pH≈1–2 for hydrolysis, temperature 0 °C to reflux; often performed in water or methanol solvent. No special catalyst required.

General type: Friedel‑Crafts acylation (electrophilic aromatic substitution) of a heteroaromatic ring. Purpose: installation of an acetyl carbonyl at the 2‑position of furan. Key transformations: generation of the acylium ion from acetyl chloride by coordination to AlCl₃, electrophilic attack of the acylium on furan to give 2‑acetylfuran, regeneration of AlCl₃. Typical conditions: anhydrous solvent such as dichloromethane, carbon tetrachloride or nitrobenzene; temperature 0 °C to reflux; inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar). Catalyst: aluminum chloride (Lewis acid).

General type: redox (oxidation‑reduction) reaction in aqueous solution. Purpose: reduction of bromate to bromide while bisulfite is oxidized to sulfate. Key transformations: BrO₃⁻ is reduced to Br⁻; HSO₃⁻ is oxidized to SO₄²⁻ (present as NaHSO₄). Typical conditions: aqueous acidic medium (often dilute H₂SO₄) at room temperature to gentle heating; no external catalyst required.

General type: salt/complex formation (Lewis acid‑base adduct). Purpose: preparation of the non‑coordinating anion hexafluoroarsenate. Key transformations: addition of a fluoride ion to AsF₅ to generate the octahedral [AsF₆]⁻ anion, which pairs with K⁺ to give K[AsF₆]. Typical conditions: anhydrous hydrogen fluoride or liquid HF as solvent, low temperature (‑20 °C to 0 °C), inert atmosphere; no catalyst needed.

General type: halogen exchange (redox) reaction between a silicon tetrahalide and elemental halogen. Purpose: conversion of SiI₄ to SiCl₄ with concomitant formation of iodine. Key transformations: chlorine oxidizes iodide bound to silicon, producing SiCl₄ and elemental I₂. Typical conditions: gas‑phase or sealed‑tube reaction at elevated temperature (150–300 °C); inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride can be used; no catalyst required.

Double‑displacement precipitation; analogous to (1) but with potassium counter‑ion; forms silver sulfate precipitate and soluble potassium fluoride: 2 AgF + K₂SO₄ → Ag₂SO₄ ↓ + 2 KF; performed in water, typically at room temperature; precipitation of Ag₂SO₄ shifts equilibrium; no catalyst required.

General type: multicomponent Strecker‑type decarboxylative amination leading to β‑amino acid formation. Purpose: synthesis of β‑alanine from simple precursors. Key transformations: malonic acid undergoes condensation with ammonia and hydrogen cyanide to form a β‑aminonitrile intermediate, which then decarboxylates and hydrolyzes to give β‑alanine; overall release of CO₂. Typical conditions: aqueous or alcoholic medium, heating (80–120 °C), often under mildly acidic or neutral pH; no special catalyst beyond the acidity of the medium.

Nitrile hydrolysis; converts butyronitrile to butyric acid while releasing ammonia. Typical acid‑catalyzed or base‑catalyzed aqueous hydrolysis at reflux (120–180 °C). Common conditions: dilute H₂SO₄ or NaOH in water; solvents often water or water‑ethanol mixtures; removal of excess ammonia by gas stripping if needed.

Silane reduction of boron trichloride (hydride transfer); yields boron hydride (commonly diborane, B₂H₆) and silicon tetrachloride. Performed under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) at low to moderate temperature (0–80 °C). Anhydrous, aprotic solvents such as diethyl ether or THF are used; no additional catalyst required, but the reaction is driven by the strong Si–Cl bond formation.

Selenium dioxide oxidation (benzylic oxidation); oxidation of indane to 1‑indanone by replacing the benzylic C‑H with a carbonyl group; SeO₂ (1–1.5 eq) in a high‑boiling aprotic solvent such as 1,4‑dioxane or acetic acid, heated to 80–120 °C under reflux; typically performed under nitrogen.

Intramolecular cyclocondensation of an aldehyde with a β‑amino alcohol to form a 2‑phenyl‑oxazolidine. The amino group adds to benzaldehyde, followed by intramolecular attack of the hydroxyl on the iminium carbon and loss of water. Usually carried out under reflux in toluene or xylene with a Dean‑Stark trap to remove water; catalytic amounts of a weak acid (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid) accelerate the cyclization.

Heterogeneous esterification of nicotinic acid with benzyl alcohol to give benzyl nicotinate. Titanium dioxide acts as a solid acid catalyst (or photocatalyst under UV light). Reaction is run under reflux (≈120 °C) in a high‑boiling solvent such as toluene or anisole, often with a Dean‑Stark apparatus to continuously remove the water byproduct.

Ester aminolysis (amide formation) where sec‑butyl formate reacts with ammonia to afford sec‑butanol and formamide. Typically performed in a sealed pressure tube or autoclave with excess gaseous or aqueous NH₃ at 100–130 °C. No catalyst is required; the reaction proceeds via nucleophilic attack of NH₃ on the carbonyl carbon followed by elimination of the alkoxide.

Potassium permanganate oxidation: strong oxidant converts a benzylic primary alcohol to the corresponding carboxylic acid. Purpose is to obtain 2‑ethoxybenzoic acid from the alcohol. Key transformation is the six‑electron oxidation of the –CH2OH group to –CO2H, with reduction of Mn(VII) to MnO2. Typical conditions: aqueous alkaline medium (e.g., KMnO4 (3–5 equiv) in dilute NaOH), heating under reflux (50–80 °C) for several hours until the purple color disappears. After reaction, the mixture is acidified (HCl) to precipitate the acid, filtered, and purified. Common solvent is water; sometimes a co‑sol such as acetone is used to improve solubility.
Acid–oxide neutralization; thallium oxide reacts with aqueous hydrobromic acid to produce thallium(I) bromide and water; carried out at room temperature in aqueous HBr solution; no catalyst needed.

Type: catalytic dehydration/dehydrogenation of a vicinal diol to a ketone. Purpose: convert 2,3‑butanediol into butan‑2‑one (methyl ethyl ketone) with loss of water. Key transformation: removal of one molecule of water (two hydrogens and one oxygen) from the diol, forming the carbonyl group at C‑2. Typical conditions: solid acid catalyst (e.g., H₂SO₄, Amberlyst‑15) or metal catalyst (e.g., copper chromite, Raney nickel) at 150–200 °C under atmospheric pressure. Common solvent: toluene dipolar aprotic solvents; sometimes the reaction is performed solvent‑free. No stoichiometric reagents are required beyond the catalyst.

Reduction of a sulfoxide to a sulfide using zinc dust; metal‑mediated deoxygenation that converts R‑S(=O)‑R′ into R‑S‑R′ with formation of ZnO; typically carried out under reflux in a dry polar aprotic solvent such as THF or ethanol under an inert atmosphere.

Aminolysis of an ester with ammonia to give the corresponding primary amide and the leaving alcohol; propyl 2‑methylpentanoate reacts with NH₃ to afford 2‑methylpentanamide and propanol; performed in excess aqueous or alcoholic ammonia, usually heated to reflux (50–100 °C) to drive the equilibrium.

Intramolecular cyclocondensation of 2‑aminothiophenol with an aldehyde to form a benzothiazole heterocycle; condensation followed by dehydration eliminates water and builds the thiazole ring; commonly performed in refluxing polyphosphoric acid, acetic acid, or with a Lewis acid (e.g., I₂) at 80–130 °C.

Double silylation of acetylene to give 1,2‑bis(trimethylsilyl)acetylene; acetylene is deprotonated with NaNH₂ in liquid NH₃ or dry THF (often at –78 °C to 0 °C) to generate the acetylide, which is then trapped with trimethylsilyl chloride; reaction is moisture‑free and run under nitrogen or argon.

Fischer esterification of cyclopropanecarboxylic acid with methanol to afford methyl cyclopropanecarboxylate and water; acid‑catalyzed condensation typically uses catalytic H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH, refluxing excess MeOH (65–80 °C) and removal of water (e.g., Dean‑Stark) to drive completion.

Type: Chemoselective reduction of an aldehyde (hydride reduction). Purpose: Reduce the aldehyde to a primary alcohol while leaving the C=C double bond untouched. Key transformation: NaBH₄ delivers a hydride to the carbonyl carbon of pent‑4‑enal, giving pent‑4‑en‑1‑ol. Typical conditions: MeOH or EtOH as solvent, 0 °C to rt, 1.0–1.5 equiv NaBH₄, reaction time 1–2 h. No transition‑metal catalyst required.

Silicon‑Fluorine metathesis (nucleophilic substitution at silicon); converts a Si–F bond into a Si–C bond while precipitating LiF. Methyllithium attacks methylfluorosilane, yielding dimethylsilane and lithium fluoride. Conducted in dry THF or Et2O at 0 °C to room temperature under inert gas; excess MeLi often used to drive reaction to completion.

Direct combination (synthesis) of tetraphosphorus with sodium to form sodium phosphide; high‑temperature solid‑state reaction carried out in a dry, inert atmosphere using molten sodium (≈200‑300 °C); no solvent required; by‑product is none.

Acyl substitution (esterification) of 2‑bromoethanol with acetic anhydride yielding 2‑bromoethyl acetate and acetic acid; typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane, using pyridine or DMAP as a base to capture the generated acid.

Oxidation of acetone by Oxone (potassium peroxymonosulfate) to generate dimethyldioxirane (DMDO) while reducing Oxone to potassium sulfate and potassium bisulfate; conducted in an acetone/water mixture at 0 °C to rt; DMDO is formed in situ as a powerful epoxidizing oxidant; no additional catalyst required.

Electrophilic halogen addition (anti‑addition) across a carbon–carbon double bond; chlorine adds to trans‑2‑pentene to give the vicinal dichloride 2,3‑dichloropentane. Conducted by bubbling Cl₂ gas through an inert, non‑polar solvent such as CCl₄ or CH₂Cl₂ at 0 °C to room temperature; no catalyst required.

Formation of 9‑fluorenylmethyl chloroformate from 9‑fluorenylmethanol using triphosgene (a solid phosgene equivalent); reaction is a chloroformate synthesis (acyl chloride analogue); carried out in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt under inert gas, with a base such as triethylamine to trap HCl; gaseous by‑products are CO₂ and HCl.

Reductive alkylation of naphthalene using lithium naphthalenide and ethyl bromide to afford ethyl naphthalene and lithium bromide; proceeds via single‑electron transfer and radical coupling; performed in dry THF at –78 °C to 0 °C under inert atmosphere; lithium naphthalenide is generated in situ from naphthalene and lithium metal.

Williamson‑type O‑alkylation of maltol with ethyl iodide under basic conditions to give ethyl maltol; reaction is done in aqueous or alcoholic solution with NaOH (or similar base) at reflux; produces NaI and water as by‑products; phase‑transfer catalysts (e.g., tetrabutylammonium bromide) are often employed to improve yields.

Metathesis (acid‑base exchange) reaction; converts potassium selenate to selenic acid while forming potassium bisulfate. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient to modest temperature; excess sulfuric acid drives the equilibrium toward products. No special catalyst required; water acts as solvent.

Base‑catalyzed etherification (nucleophilic substitution) of triethylene glycol with epichlorohydrin to give the diglycidyl ether; sodium hydroxide deprotonates the diol, and tetrabutylammonium bromide serves as a phase‑transfer catalyst to shuttle hydroxide into the organic phase. Reaction is usually performed at 50‑80 °C in a biphasic system (water/organic solvent such as dichloromethane or toluene). Water and NaCl are formed as by‑products.

Acid‑base displacement (salt metathesis) where dilute nitric acid protonates calcium stearate, liberate stearic acid and generate calcium nitrate in solution. Conducted in aqueous medium, often with gentle heating to improve dissolution; no additional catalyst required.

Double‑displacement/acid decomposition of ammonium tetrachloroplatinate(II) with dilute sulfuric acid, yielding platinum(II) chloride precipitate and ammonium sulfate in solution together with liberated HCl gas. Performed in aqueous solution at room temperature or slightly warmed; stirring ensures complete reaction; no extra catalyst needed.

Simple acid‑base neutralization (salt formation) of betaxolol base with hydrochloric acid to produce betaxolol hydrochloride. Usually carried out in aqueous or methanolic solution at ambient temperature; crystallization of the hydrochloride salt follows evaporation; no catalyst needed.

Precipitation/metal‑acetylide formation: acetylene gas reacts with aqueous silver nitrate to give silver acetylide (AgC≡CH) precipitate and nitric acid. Conducted by bubbling acetylene through cold AgNO3 solution under inert atmosphere; useful for preparing explosive silver acetylide. No catalyst; water is the medium.

acid‑halogen exchange (acid‑base) of antimony trioxide with hydrogen chloride to form antimony trichloride and water; purpose is synthesis of volatile SbCl3; key transformation: Sb2O3 + 6 HCl → 2 SbCl3 + 3 H2O; typical conditions: reflux Sb2O3 with concentrated HCl gas or aqueous HCl, often in a non‑reactive solvent (e.g., carbon disulfide or benzene) to azeotropically remove SbCl3; temperature 100‑120 °C.

Coordination/salt formation: copper(II) oxide reacts with two equivalents of glycine, deprotonating the amino acid and coordinating the metal to give copper(II) glycinate and water; typically performed in aqueous or water‑ethanol medium under reflux, no catalyst required.

Grignard addition to ester: methylmagnesium bromide adds twice to methyl phenylacetate, first forming a ketone intermediate and then a tertiary alkoxide which, after acidic work‑up, yields 2‑methyl‑2‑phenylpropan‑1‑ol and methanol; carried out under inert atmosphere in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) from 0 °C to reflux, no catalyst.
Acid‑base neutralisation: aqueous HCl protonates decylamine to produce decylammonium chloride salt; performed at room temperature in water, no additional solvent or catalyst needed.

LAH reduction of ketone: lithium aluminium hydride reduces 2‑tetralone to the secondary alcohol 2‑tetralol; conducted in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) under nitrogen, cooled then warmed to reflux, quenched with water or dilute acid, no catalyst.

High‑temperature solid‑state synthesis of europium silicide: elemental europium reacts with silicon in a 1:2 ratio to form EuSi₂, performed in a sealed tube or inert‑gas furnace at 800–1000 °C; no solvent or catalyst, inert atmosphere required.

Williamson ether synthesis (O‑methylation): a base deprotonates isobutanol to isobutoxide, which attacks dimethyl sulfate in an SN2 step to give isobutyl methyl ether; commonly run in anhydrous acetone or DMF with NaOH, K₂CO₃ or NaH as base at 0 °C to reflux, no metal catalyst.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (acylation) of acetylhydrazine with acetyl chloride; triethylamine acts as base to neutralize HCl, yielding N,N′‑diacetylhydrazine. Typically performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen; no additional catalyst required.

Acid–hydride (acid‑base) reaction; purpose is to liberate hydrogen gas and form a soluble magnesium salt; MgH2 reacts with aqueous HCl, yielding MgCl2 in solution and H2 gas; reaction is rapid at room temperature, generates effervescence; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification) of the methyl ester of (‑)-ecgonine; water attacks the carbonyl, producing methanol and the free carboxylic acid (‑)-ecgonine. Commonly carried out in aqueous acidic medium (e.g., 1 M HCl) with reflux heating, often using a mixture of water and a miscible organic solvent such as methanol.

Metal‑halogen exchange to generate sec‑butyl lithium, an organolithium reagent; elemental lithium inserts into the C–Cl bond, forming sec‑butyl lithium and lithium chloride. Conducted in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) under inert atmosphere; no catalyst needed.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation); purpose is removal of an aryl chlorine to give the corresponding ether; key transformation is cleavage of the C–Cl bond and addition of H₂ to form anisole while releasing HCl; typical conditions are 1–5 atm H₂ gas, Pd/C (5–10 % on carbon) as catalyst, in an alcohol solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate at reflux temperature.

Knoevenagel‑type condensation followed by cyclization (Pechmann condensation) between malonic acid and salicylaldehyde, releasing CO₂ and water and forming a coumarin ring system. Typically performed by heating the reactants in a polar aprotic solvent such as pyridine or in excess acetic anhydride, often with a catalytic amount of p‑toluenesulfonic acid or sulfuric acid.

Aqueous double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; purpose is to precipitate calcium carbonate and generate soluble potassium chloride; carbonate anion exchanges between K2CO3 and CaCl2 to form insoluble CaCO3; conducted in water at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst required.

Oxidation of fenbendazole with meta‑chloroperbenzoic acid (mCPBA) to give oxfendazole (sulfoxide); the peracid transfers an oxygen atom to the thioether, and is reduced to meta‑chlorobenzoic acid. Usually carried out in dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; no additional catalyst required.

Type: nucleophilic acyl substitution (esterification using an acyl chloride). Purpose: synthesis of phenyl 2‑propylpentanoate. Key transformation: phenoxide attacks the carbonyl carbon of 2‑propylpentanoyl chloride, displaces chloride and forms the ester; HCl is generated. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere, solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, 1‑2 equiv of a base (pyridine, triethylamine, or DMAP) to trap HCl.

Same transformation as #1 but using potassium hydroxide. Hydroxide ion from KOH substitutes bromide on 2‑bromopropane to give isopropanol. Typical conditions: aqueous KOH (5–10 %), reflux temperature (≈80 °C). Often performed in an alcohol–water mixed solvent (e.g., ethanol/water) to dissolve both reagents. No catalyst needed.

Acid‑salt reaction: nickel(II) sulfide reacts with aqueous hydrochloric acid, protonating sulfide to release H₂S gas and forming soluble nickel(II) chloride; typically done in dilute HCl at room temperature or mild heating, water as solvent, no catalyst.

Pictet‑Spengler cyclization; phenethylamine condenses with glyoxylic acid (an α‑oxoacid) to give an iminium intermediate that cyclizes onto the aromatic ring, producing 1,2,3,4‑tetrahydroisoquinoline‑1‑carboxylic acid. Conducted under acidic conditions (e.g., 6 N HCl or AcOH) at 60–100 °C in aqueous methanol or ethanol. The carboxyl group is installed at the C‑1 position of the isoquinoline scaffold.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between ammonium oxalate and magnesium sulfate in aqueous solution, swapping cations to afford magnesium oxalate and ammonium sulfate. Performed by mixing aqueous solutions of the two salts at ambient temperature with stirring; the reaction proceeds without catalyst and may be driven to completion by crystallization of one product.

Oxidation of aol a quinone; H2O2 serves as the oxidant converting 2‑methoxyphenol into 2‑methoxy‑1,4‑benzoquinone with formation of water. Typically carried out in aqueous or water‑acetone mixture at 0–25 °C, often under mildly basic conditions (e.g., NaOH) or with a catalytic amount of transition‑metal ion (Fe, Ti) to accelerate peroxide activation.

Acid–base reaction of a metal carbonate with hydrobromic acid; produces nickel(II) bromide, carbon dioxide gas, and water; performed in aqueous HBr, often with stirring and gentle heating to promote CO2 evolution.

Acid‑base neutralization / salt hydrolysis; O‑methylhydroxylammonium chloride is treated with aqueous NaOH to liberate the free base O‑methylhydroxylamine, producing water and NaCl as by‑products. Conducted in water at ambient temperature, usually with careful temperature control to avoid exotherm; no catalyst required.

Condensation / solid‑state ion‑exchange forming a metal‑oxygen framework; potassium hydroxide reacts with titanium(IV) hydroxide, eliminating water and yielding potassium titanate (K2TiO3 or related phase). Performed under high‑temperature conditions (200–300 °C) in a dry melt or hydrothermal autoclave; the reaction proceeds without additional solvent or catalyst.

Halogen exchange (Finkelstein‑type SN2) of a primary bromide with fluoride; potassium fluoride substitutes one bromide in 1,2‑dibromoethane to give 2‑fluoroethyl bromide and potassium bromide. Requires a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO or acetone, often with a crown ether (18‑crown‑6) to solubilize KF, and is heated (50–100 °C) to drive the reaction.

Nucleophilic substitution forming a silyl azide; sodium azide displaces bromide from trimethylsilyl bromide, producing trimethylsilyl azide and NaBr. Conducted in dry THF or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; the reaction proceeds readily without added catalyst, but anhydrous conditions are essential to prevent azide hydrolysis.

Thioether formation via SN2 substitution; phenyl mercaptan (deprotonated to phenylthiolate) attacks benzyl bromide, yielding benzyl phenyl sulfide and HBr. Typically performed in an aprotic solvent such as acetone, DMF or acetonitrile with a base (e.g., K2CO3, NaH) to generate the thiolate; reflux or mild heating (30–60 °C) promotes completion.

Acid‑base neutralization of peroxydisulfuric acid with sodium hydroxide forming sodium persulfate, an oxidizing salt; key transformation is deprotonation of H2S2O8 to give water and Na2S2O8; carried out in aqueous solution, usually 0–10 °C to limit decomposition; no catalyst required.

Sonogashira palladium‑copper cross‑coupling between 2‑bromo‑6‑methylpyridine and phenylacetylene using Pd(0) and CuI with triethylamine as base; forms a C(sp2)‑C(sp) bond yielding 2‑methyl‑6‑(phenylethynyl)pyridine; typical conditions: anhydrous amine solvent (Et3N) or THF/DMF, inert atmosphere, 50–80 °C; Pd(0)/CuI catalyst system essential.

Acid‑catalyzed cyclocondensation; o‑phenylenediamine condenses with glyoxal in the presence of HCl to afford 2‑hydroxybenzimidazole and water. Typical conditions: aqueous HCl (1–3 M), heating to reflux (often in ethanol/water).

Electrophilic bromination/oxidative cyclization of 2‑aminothiophenol with N‑bromosuccinimide producing 2‑bromo‑benzothiazole and succinimide; NBS supplies Br⁺ and acts as oxidant, enabling intramolecular attack of thiol on brominated imine; usually performed in dry dichloromethane or acetonitrile at room temperature or mild reflux; no metal catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution of benzoyl chloride by sodium phenolate to give phenyl benzoate (aromatic ester) and NaCl; reaction class: esterification from acid chloride; commonly run in aprotic solvents such as acetone, THF, or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; phenoxide anion serves as nucleophile, no additional catalyst required.

Simple acid‑base neutralization between acetic acid and dimethylamine forming dimethylammonium acetate; produces an ammonium acetate salt; carried out in aqueous or alcoholic solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst or special conditions needed.

Hydrolysis/neutralization of boron tribromide with aqueous sodium hydroxide yielding sodium metaborate and sodium bromide; exothermic reaction typically performed by adding BBr₃ dropwise to cold (0 °C) NaOH solution; aqueous medium; no catalyst required.

Buchwald‑Hartwig C–N cross‑coupling; installs a 4‑chlorophenyl group onto piperazine to give 1‑(4‑chlorophenyl)piperazine. Key transformation is Pd‑catalyzed aryl‑nitrogen bond formation via oxidative addition of 4‑chloroiodobenzene, transmetalation with the deprotonated piperazine (NaOtBu), and reductive elimination. Typical conditions: inert atmosphere, dry aprotic solvent (toluene, dioxane, or DMF), 80–120 °C, Pd(OAc)₂ (5 mol %) with tri‑tert‑butylphosphine (10‑20 mol %) as ligand, NaOtBu as base. By‑products are NaI and acetic acid from acetate ligand.

Salt metathesis (double‑displacement) between AlCl₃ and lithium dimethylamide to generate tris(dimethylamido)aluminum(III) and LiCl. Key transformation replaces chloride ligands on Al³⁺ with dimethylamido groups. Typical conditions: dry THF or Et₂O, 0 °C to room temperature, stoichiometric amounts, inert atmosphere. No catalyst required; LiCl precipitates and is removed by filtration.

Staudinger reduction of an azide with triphenylphosphine. The azide (3‑azidopropionitrile) reacts with Ph₃P to give 3‑aminopropionitrile, nitrogen gas, and triphenylphosphine oxide. Key steps: nucleophilic attack of phosphine on azide, formation of iminophosphorane intermediate, hydrolysis to amine. Typical conditions: THF or toluene, ambient to gentle heating (25–50 °C), inert atmosphere, reaction time 1–12 h. No additional catalyst; the phosphine itself drives the reduction.

Acid–base neutralization forming ammonium sulfamate. Sulfamic acid (NH₂SO₃H) reacts with aqueous ammonium hydroxide (NH₄OH) to give the ammonium salt NH₄SO₃NH₂ and water. Key transformation is proton transfer from the acidic –SO₃H to the ammonium ion. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at 0–25 °C, stoichiometric amounts, vigorous stirring. No catalyst required.

Base‑induced dehydrohalogenation of 1‑chloro‑1,1‑difluoroethane with solid calcium hydroxide (dry base) to produce 1,1‑difluoroethene; purpose similar to reaction 0, forming the alkene by HCl elimination; key step is loss of HCl to generate the C=C bond; conditions generally employ Ca(OH)₂ under reflux or melt, occasionally in a polar solvent like ethanol, no catalyst needed.

Alcohol‑exchange transesterification of methyl propiolate with ethanol to give ethyl propiolate and methanol; acid catalysts (e.g., H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) or basic catalysts (NaOEt) are employed; refluxing ethanol in excess drives the equilibrium, solvent may be the ethanol itself.

Thallium(III) nitrate oxidation: Tl(NO3)3 oxidizes 2,4‑dichlorobenzyl alcohol to the corresponding aldehyde, reducing Tl(III) to Tl(I) nitrate; performed in dry acetonitrile (or CH2Cl2) at ambient temperature, generally under inert atmosphere, no extra catalyst.

Oxide‑acid reaction (salt formation). Lead(II) oxide (PbO) reacts with hydrogen bromide (HBr) to afford lead(II) bromide (PbBr₂) and water. Key transformation is protonation of the oxide to water and simultaneous formation of the metal halide. Typical conditions: refluxing aqueous HBr (concentrated), temperature 80–100 °C, excess HBr to drive completion. No catalyst needed; solid PbBr₂ precipitates.

Thermal decomposition (denitration) of an alkyl nitrate; benzyl nitrate decomposes upon heating to produce benzyl alcohol and nitrogen dioxide. Reaction type: radical or thermal decomposition of an organic nitrate. Typical conditions: heating at 150–200 °C in an inert solvent (e.g., toluene or xylene) or under reduced pressure; sometimes catalyzed by metal oxides. No catalyst is strictly necessary, but metal nitrate catalysts can facilitate the process.

Fischer esterification; the carboxyl group of 4‑methyl‑2‑oxovaleric acid reacts with ethanol to form ethyl 4‑methyl‑2‑oxovalerate, releasing water. Typically performed by refluxing the acid (1–2 equiv) with excess ethanol (solvent) and a catalytic amount of concentrated H₂SO₄ or p‑toluenesulfonic acid at 78 °C for 4–8 h, followed by removal of excess ethanol and neutralization. Purpose: conversion of the keto‑acid into a more volatile ester for purification or further synthetic steps.

Redox (disproportionation) reaction between hydrogen selenide and iodine. H₂Se is oxidized to elemental selenium (Se⁰) while I₂ is reduced to hydrogen iodide (HI). Overall: H₂Se + I₂ → Se + 2 HI. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, ambient temperature, dark or low light to avoid side photochemistry, stoichiometric amounts. No catalyst required; the reaction proceeds spontaneously.

Base‑catalyzed amidic hydrolysis (saponification). Sodium hydroxide hydrolyzes prop‑2‑ynamide, cleaving the C–N amide bond to generate the prop‑2‑ynoate carboxylate (as its sodium salt) and liberating ammonia. Typically performed in aqueous NaOH solution with heating (reflux) to drive the reaction to completion.

Acidic oxidative oxidation of a primary alcohol. Concentrated sulfuric acid provides the aqueous medium while potassium dichromate acts as the oxidant, converting ethanol to acetic acid with concomitant reduction of Cr(VI) to Cr(III). The reaction is carried out under reflux in a warm acidic solution, producing water, potassium sulfate and chromium(III) sulfate as by‑products.

Ester saponification (base‑mediated hydrolysis). Aqueous sodium hydroxide attacks the carbonyl carbon of prop‑2‑ynyl benzoate, breaking the ester linkage to give propargyl alcohol and the benzoate anion, which is isolated as sodium benzoate. Conducted in aqueous NaOH, usually with heating (reflux) to ensure complete hydrolysis.

Hydrolysis of a silyl ether. Water reacts with ethoxy(dimethyl)silane, cleaving the Si–O ether bond to produce dimethylsilanol and ethanol. The transformation proceeds readily in the presence of trace acid or base and can be performed at ambient temperature in a mixed aqueous/organic solvent system.

Reaction type: nucleophilic acyl substitution (carbamate formation) using phosgene as a carbonyl chloride source; purpose: synthesis of alkyl carbamates as protecting groups or intermediates; key transformation: hexanol attacks phosgene to give a chloroformate intermediate, which is then aminated by ammonia to afford hexyl carbamate while releasing HCl; typical conditions: low temperature (0 °C to room temperature) in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, with a base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) to scavenge the generated HCl.

Metal‑catalyzed reduction of arsenic trioxide to arsine. Hydrogen gas in the presence of a copper catalyst reduces As₂O₃, forming arsine gas (AsH₃) and water as the only stoichiometric by‑product. The reaction requires elevated temperature and pressure of H₂ (typically several atmospheres) and is carried out in a sealed reactor, often with a small amount of liquid medium to facilitate contact.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an α,β‑unsaturated aldehyde; purpose is to saturate the C=C bond of crotonaldehyde to give butyraldehyde. Key transformation: H₂ adds across the C=C double bond while the carbonyl remains intact. Typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm) with a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, Raney Ni; temperature 0 °C to 50 °C. Common solvents: ethanol, methanol, ethyl acetate.

Selective reduction of a carboxylic acid to an aldehyde using DIBAL‑H; converts γ‑aminobutyric acid to 4‑aminobutanal while leaving the amine unchanged; key transformation –COOH → –CHO; performed in dry THF or toluene at –78 °C under nitrogen, 1 equiv DIBAL‑H, then quenched with MeOH/H₂O; no catalyst required

Metal‑acid redox (single displacement) reaction; purpose is to generate hydrogen gas and a neodymium(III) bromide salt. Key transformation: Nd⁰ is oxidized to Nd³⁺ while H⁺ from HBr is reduced to H₂. Typical conditions: excess aqueous HBr (conc.) added to Nd metal pieces, stirring, often warmed gently to accelerate. No special catalyst; water is the solvent.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction in aqueous solution; purpose is to exchange cations to form magnesium benzoate. Key transformation: Na⁺ pairs with Cl⁻ to give NaCl, while Mg²⁺ pairs with benzoate anions to give Mg(benzoate)₂. Typical conditions: aqueous solutions of NaBenzoate and MgCl₂ mixed at ambient temperature; may be stirred to completion. Solvent: water; product may precipitate if less soluble.

Halogen exchange / nucleophilic substitution (halogenation) reaction; purpose is to convert dichloroiodomethane to chloroform while releasing hydrogen iodide. Key transformation: I⁻ is displaced by Cl⁻ from HCl, and successive chlorination yields CHCl₃. Typical conditions: excess gaseous or aqueous HCl, reflux temperature (≈80–100 °C). Solvent often a non‑nucleophilic medium such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform itself; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑base (neutralization) reaction of a metal carbonate with a strong acid; purpose is to dissolve cobalt(II) carbonate and generate the perchlorate salt. Key transformation: CoCO₃ reacts with HClO₄, producing CO₂ gas, H₂O, and soluble Co(ClO₄)₂. Typical conditions: aqueous perchloric acid (conc.) added to solid CoCO₃ at room temperature, with gentle stirring. Solvent: water; evolution of CO₂ drives the reaction forward.

Single‑displacement redox reaction; purpose is to reduce mercuric chloride to elemental mercury and precipitate silver chloride. Key transformation: Ag⁰ oxidized to Ag⁺, forming insoluble AgCl; Hg²⁺ reduced to Hg⁰. Typical conditions: aqueous HgCl₂ solution mixed with solid silver at ambient temperature; stirring promotes complete precipitation. Solvent: water; the black metallic mercury separates, while white AgCl precipitate can be filtered.

Catalytic oxidation of 1‑pentanol to pentanal using molecular oxygen and palladium on carbon; purpose is to convert a primary alcohol into the corresponding aldehyde; key transformation is removal of two hydrogen atoms from the alcohol to form the carbonyl group; typical conditions involve bubbling O₂ through a suspension of Pd/C (5–10 % wt) in a solvent such as toluene, acetonitrile or ethanol at 25–80 °C, often under ambient pressure; no additional catalyst is required.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis) between silver perchlorate and sodium selenide; purpose is to prepare insoluble silver selenide while forming soluble sodium perchlorate; key transformation is exchange of Ag⁺ and Na⁺ ions, precipitating Ag₂Se; performed in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; water is the common solvent and no catalyst is needed.

Gas‑phase synthesis of carbonyl sulfide; combines CO and H2S to give COS and H2. Employed for commercial COS production which is a raw material for pesticides and polymers. Reaction: CO + H2S → COS + H2. Usually carried out at 400–600 °C in a quartz reactor; catalysts such as alumina, silica, or metal oxides (e.g., ZnO) can improve conversion. No solvent; gases flow continuously.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amidation) of acetyl chloride with methylamine in the presence of pyridine; purpose is synthesis of N‑methyl‑acetamide; key transformation is attack of the amine on the acyl chloride to form the amide and capture of the liberated HCl by pyridine, giving pyridinium chloride; typically carried out at 0–5 °C in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, then allowed to warm to room temperature; pyridine acts as a base, no additional catalyst required.

Salt metathesis/acid‑base exchange between hydrochloric acid and erbium(III) acetate; purpose is to generate erbium(III) chloride and free acetic acid; key transformation is proton transfer from HCl to acetate ions, producing AcOH and ErCl₃; conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or with gentle heating; water is the solvent and no catalyst is employed.

Fluorination/complexation to form trisodium hexafluoroaluminate (Na₃AlF₆) from aluminum oxide, sodium fluoride and hydrofluoric acid; purpose is preparation of a fluoro‑aluminate salt (e.g., cryolite component); key transformation involves conversion of Al₂O₃ to the [AlF₆]³⁻ complex by reaction with excess NaF and HF, releasing water; typically performed in concentrated aqueous HF (or molten HF/NaF mixture) at 80–150 °C; no catalyst is required.

Double‑displacement/acid‑base reaction between hydrochloric acid and scandium sulfate; purpose is to convert scandium sulfate to scandium chloride while regenerating sulfuric acid; key transformation is exchange of Cl⁻ and SO₄²⁻ ions, producing ScCl₃ and H₂SO₄; carried out in aqueous solution, often with heating to drive the equilibrium; water serves as the solvent and no catalyst is necessary.

S‑alkylation of 2‑aminoethanethiol with methyl iodide to produce S‑methylcysteamine and HI; the thiolate attacks the methyl carbon via an SN2 pathway; performed under basic conditions (NaH or Na₂CO₃) in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or acetonitrile, often at ambient temperature or mild heating.

Metathesis (double displacement) reaction in aqueous solution; ferric chloride exchanges chloride with calcium ferrocyanide, precipitating iron(III) ferrocyanide and forming soluble calcium chloride; carried out at ambient temperature in water, no catalyst required.

Oxidative conversion of 1,4‑dihydroxynaphthalene to 1,4‑naphthoquinone using ceric ammonium nitrate (CAN); CAN acts as a one‑electron oxidant oxidizing both phenolic groups to carbonyls; typically performed in a MeCN/H₂O mixture at 0–25 °C, no additional catalyst.

Staudinger reduction of an azide to an amine; triphenylphosphine reacts with the azido group of 2′,3′‑dideoxy‑3′‑azidocytidine forming an iminophosphorane that hydrolyzes with water to give 3′‑amino‑2′,3′‑dideoxycytidine and triphenylphosphine oxide; conducted in an aprotic solvent such as THF or toluene at rt‑50 °C, stoichiometric PPh₃, no metal catalyst.

Type: Double displacement (metathesis) in aqueous solution. Purpose: preparation of cerous sulfate (Ce₂(SO₄)₃) and sodium chloride from inexpensive salts. Key transformation: exchange of cations between Na₂SO₄ and CeCl₃, yielding 6 NaCl and 1 Ce₂(SO₄)₃ as a precipitate or soluble species depending on concentration and temperature. Typical conditions: dissolve both salts in water, heat gently (50–80 °C) with stirring to ensure complete ion exchange, then cool to allow crystallization of cerous sulfate. No special catalyst is required; pH is usually neutral.

Gattermann–Koch formylation (electrophilic aromatic substitution); CO and HCl generate a formyl electrophile in the presence of AlCl₃/CuCl Lewis‑acid catalyst, which adds to 1,3,5‑trimethylbenzene to afford 2,4,6‑trimethylbenzaldehyde; carried out under CO/HCl pressure (1–5 atm) at 0–30 °C in dry CH₂Cl₂ or CCl₄, AlCl₃ and CuCl are required.

Direct combination (synthesis) reaction; chlorine gas oxidizes elemental lead to form lead(II) chloride; typically performed by passing dry Cl₂ over heated lead (≈200–300 °C) in a sealed vessel, no solvent or catalyst.

Type: acid–base neutralization (hydroxide dissolution). Purpose: preparation of soluble ferric acetate. Key transformation: the hydroxide of iron(III) reacts with acetic acid, producing water and ferric acetate in solution. Typical conditions: addition of aqueous or glacial acetic acid to Fe(OH)₃ at ambient temperature with stirring; gentle heating (≤80 °C) can accelerate dissolution. No catalyst needed.

Acid‑base protonation (salt metathesis). Sodium methyl mercaptan is protonated by hydrochloric acid to afford methanethiol (CH₃SH) and sodium chloride. Typically performed in aqueous solution at 0 °C to temperature; no special catalyst is required.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) precipitation. Erbium sulfate reacts with hydrofluoric acid, yielding insoluble erbium trifluoride and sulfuric acid in solution. Usually performed by adding solid Er2(SO4)3 to cold concentrated HF (≈ 48 % w/w) under stirring; the fluoride precipitates and is filtered. No catalyst; HF/H2O mixture is the solvent.

Diazomethylation (esterification). Diazomethane reacts with pyridine‑4‑carboxylic acid to give the methyl ester methyl pyridine‑4‑carboxylate (methyl nicotinate). Conducted in dry ether or THF at 0 °C to ambient temperature under inert atmosphere; excess diazometh is quenched with a weak acid. No catalyst is needed.

Double‑displacement metathesis precipitation. Sodium carbonate exchanges anions with copper arsenate, yielding insoluble copper carbonate precipitate and soluble sodium arsenate. Carried out in aqueous solution with gentle heating and stirring; the copper carbonate is isolated by filtration. No catalyst is employed.

Lithium aluminium hydride reduction of an ethyl ester to a primary benzylic alcohol. Purpose: transform the ester side chain into a benzyl alcohol. Key transformation: hydride attack on the ester carbonyl followed by collapse to an aldehyde intermediate and further reduction to the alcohol; the ethoxy group is released as ethanol. Typical conditions: dry THF or diethyl ether, 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen, quench with aqueous Na₂SO₄ or water. No additional catalyst.

Anhydride hydrolysis / partial neutralization. Phthalic anhydride reacts with potassium hydroxide to form potassium hydrogen phthalate and water. Usually performed in aqueous KOH at ambient or slightly elevated temperature; no catalyst is required.

Thermal or catalytic cracking of 2,2,3,3‑tetramethylbutane to give 2‑methylpropane (isobutane) and 2‑methylprop‑1‑ene (isobutene). Conducted at 400–500 °C over a solid acid catalyst such as zeolite or alumina; solvent‑free conditions are typical. No additional reagents are needed.

Wacker oxidation of 2‑octene to 2‑octanone. The internal alkene is oxidized by a PdCl₂/CuCl₂ catalytic system in an aqueous organic solvent (e.g., DMF, acetonitrile, or water) oxygenair) at 50–80 °C, producing the methyl ketone 2‑octanone. Palladium(II) and copper(II) act as catalysts, with O₂ as the terminal oxidant.

Electrochemical oxidation of sodium chlorite in aqueous solution; anode-driven conversion of ClO2− to ClO2 with simultaneous formation of NaOH. Used to generate chlorine dioxide for bleaching or disinfection. Conducted in a water electrolyte, inert anode, controlled current, temperature below 25 °C; no additional catalyst.

Peracid oxidation of N,N‑dimethylaniline with peracetic acid; generates the same N‑oxide product while peracetic acid is reduced to acetic acid; typical conditions are 0 °C to 25 °C in a mixture of acetic acid/water or dichloromethane; 1.1–1.2 equivalents of peracetic acid are used.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of methyl bromide by methyl selenol, yielding dimethyl selenide and HBr. Serves to form organoselenium compounds. Typically performed in aprotic solvents such as THF or diethyl ether at 0–25 °C under inert atmosphere; no catalyst required.

Acid–base metathesis (double displacement) between sulfuric acid and manganese(II) acetate producing manganese(II) sulfate and freeing acetic acid. Carried out in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to distill off volatile acetic acid; no catalyst needed.

Fischer esterification of propanol with pentanoic acid to give propyl pentanoate and water. Acid-catalyzed condensation; common catalysts are concentrated H2SO4 or p‑toluenesulfonic acid. Reaction run under reflux in toluene or excess acid, with water removale., Dean‑Stark) to drive equilibrium.

Redox reaction in acidic medium where potassium dichromate oxidizes hydrogen peroxide; dichromate is reduced from Cr(VI) to Cr(III) and H2O2 decomposes to water and O2, yielding potassium sulfate and chromium(III) sulfate. Conducted in aqueous H2SO4 solution at ambient temperature; dichromate itself acts as oxidant, no extra catalyst.

Conversion of 4‑chlorobenzenesulfonic acid to the corresponding sulfonyl chloride using phosphorus pentachloride; PCl5 chlorinates and dehydrates the sulfonic acid, producing HCl and phosphorus oxychloride as by‑products. Performed in anhydrous, inert solvent (e.g., CH2Cl2) at 0 °C to room temperature; no additional catalyst.

Selective reduction of a carboxylic acid to an aldehyde using diisobutylaluminum hydride (DIBAL‑H); purpose is to convert caffeic acid to the corresponding aldehyde while preserving the phenolic groups and conjugated double bond; key transformation is COOH → CHO; typical conditions: 1.0–1.2 equiv DIBAL‑H in dry THF at –78 °C to 0 °C under nitrogen, slow addition, quench with methanol/water; solvent: anhydrous THF; no additional catalyst.

Formation of a phosphorochloridate by amination of phosphorus trichloride; purpose is preparation of dimethylphosphoramidic dichloride; key transformation is PCl₃ + (CH₃)₂NH → (CH₃)₂N‑PCl₂ + [CH₃)₂NH₂]Cl (dimethylammonium chloride); typical conditions: dropwise addition of dry PCl₃ to a solution of dimethylamine in dry dichloromethane or ether at 0 °C under nitrogen, inert atmosphere; by‑product precipitates as an ammonium salt; solvent: dry CH₂Cl₂ (or Et₂O); no external catalyst.

Simple acid‑base exchange (neutralization) between hydroiodic acid and ammonium acetate; purpose is to generate ammonium iodide and acetic acid; key transformation is HI + NH₄OAc → NH₄I + HOAc; typical conditions: aqueous solution, ambient temperature, stirring until complete dissolution; solvent: water; no catalyst required.

Carbonate formation via the phosgene equivalent triphosgene reacting with phenol; purpose is synthesis of diphenyl carbonate; key transformation is 2 PhOH + COCl₂ → PhO‑CO‑OPh with liberation of 2 HCl (triphosgene provides three equivalents of COCl₂, thus 6 PhOH → 3 PhO‑CO‑OPh + 6 HCl); typical conditions: phenol (often as sodium phenoxide or in the presence of a base such as pyridine or triethylamine) added dropwise to a solution of triphosgene in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, base scavenges HCl; solvent: CH₂Cl₂ or THF; base (pyridine, TEA) acts as HCl scavenger.

Condensation of hydroxylammonium acetate (source of hydroxylamine) with benzaldehyde to give benzaldehyde oxime; a classic oxime‑formation reaction; key transformation: C6H5CHO + NH2OH·CH3CO2⁻ → C6H5CH=NOH + CH3CO2H; carried out at 0–25 °C to room temperature in methanol, ethanol or aqueous ethanol; mildly acidic (generated acetic acid) medium suffices, no external catalyst required.

Transamidation of dimethylformamide with methylamine; purpose is exchange of the dimethylamino group for a methylamino group to give N‑methylformamide; key transformation is DMF + MeNH₂ → MeNHCHO + Me₂NH; typical conditions: excess methylamine (gas or aqueous solution) heated to 80–120 °C in a sealed tube or refluxing solvent such as toluene, removal of volatile dimethylamine drives the equilibrium; sometimes a Lewis acid (e.g., ZnCl₂) or base (pyridine) is employed as catalyst; solvent can be none (neat) or toluene; catalyst optional.

Oxidation (peroxide oxidation of sulfide). tert‑Butyl hydroperoxide acts as oxidant, reducing to tert‑butanol while diphenyl sulfide is oxidized to diphenyl sulfone. Typically carried out at 0 °C to rt in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane; no metal catalyst is required, though acids or Lewis acids can accelerate the process.

Synthesis reaction. Purpose is to form lanthanum aluminate (LaAlO3) from oxides. Key transformations: combination of lanthanum and aluminum oxides. High-temperature calcination required (>1000°C). No solvent. No catalyst.

Oxidation (Jones oxidation of a primary alcohol). Chromic acid (generated from CrO₃/H₂SO₄) oxidizes the terminal primary alcohol of 5‑hydroxy‑2‑pentanone to a carboxylic acid, giving 4‑oxopentanoic acid. Reaction is performed in acetone, usually at 0 °C to rt, and the mixture is quenched with water after completion.

Free‑radical halogenation (benzylic chlorination). Chlorine under UV light abstracts a benzylic hydrogen of 1‑chlorodiphenylmethane, forming a benzylic radical that captures Cl₂ to give dichlorodiphenylmethane and HCl. Conducted in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, 0 °C to reflux, with UV irradiation as the radical initiator.

Transmetallation (Grignard reagent with HgCl₂). Two equivalents of ethylmagnesium bromide react with mercury(II) chloride, transferring the ethyl groups to mercury to form diethylmercury while the magnesium salts (MgBr₂ and MgCl₂) remain in solution. Performed in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) under an inert atmosphere at 0 °C to rt.
hydrolysis reaction; converts silicon tetrafluoride to silicon dioxide and hydrogen fluoride; water acts as a nucleophile; occurs spontaneously under ambient conditions; water as solvent.

Reductive dehalogenation (Wurtz‑type coupling) of vicinal dihalide by zinc metal, producing ethylene and zinc halides (ZnBr₂, ZnI₂); carried out with zinc dust in dry ether or THF under reflux, sometimes with a catalytic amount of iodine to activate the metal.

SN2 alkylation; highly reactive methyl iodide is displaced by acetate from cesium acetate to form methyl acetate and cesium iodide; can proceed at room temperature or mild heating in DMF or acetone; cesium acetate is the nucleophile, no catalyst required.

Cyclocondensation (condensation–cyclization) of urea with glyoxal to form 2,4‑oxazolidinedione; water is eliminated. The reaction creates a five‑membered heterocycle containing both amide and lactone functionalities. Usually performed in a polar protic solvent such as ethanol or water, often under reflux (80–100 °C); acid (e.g., p‑TsOH) or base catalysts can be used to accelerate the condensation, but the reaction can proceed uncatalyzed.

Redox (metal oxidation by nitrogen trichloride). Nitrogen trichloride oxidizes copper metal; copper is reduced to Cu(II) chloride and NCl₃ is reduced to nitrogen gas. The reaction proceeds readily at ambient temperature in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic media; no additional catalyst is required.

Acid‑base hydrolysis of a metal azide; converts rubidium azide to soluble rubidium hydroxide and volatile hydrazoic acid; occurs in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water acts as both solvent and reactant; mild stirring is sufficient.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2 displacement by nitrite). Silver nitrite reacts with 1,3‑dichloropropane; the nitrite anion displaces one chloride in an SN2 fashion, precipitating AgCl and yielding 1‑chloro‑3‑nitropropane. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF at reflux or ambient temperature; the insoluble AgCl is filtered off after completion.

Redox oxidation of hypophosphoric acid by potassium permanganate in acidic medium; Mn(VII) oxidizes the phosphorus center and is itself reduced to Mn(II), producing phosphoric acid, manganese(II) sulfate, potassium sulfate and water. Conducted in concentrated H2SO4, often with the permanganate added portionwise while maintaining the temperature below 80 °C; aqueous sulfuric acid serves as both solvent and acid medium.

Base‑catalyzed thioester hydrolysis (saponification). Sodium hydroxide attacks the carbonyl of S‑ethyl thioacetate, cleaving the C–S bond and forming sodium thioacetate while the ethoxy group is released as ethanol. Usually performed in aqueous or mixed water/ethanol solution at ambient temperature or under gentle reflux; no additional catalyst is required.

Double displacement (acid–base) precipitation reaction; hydroxide ions displace sulfate to give mercury(II) hydroxide precipitate and soluble sodium sulfate. Carried out in aqueous solution, often at room temperature; no catalyst needed; water serves as the solvent.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of phenyl acetate (ester cleavage); water attacks the carbonyl carbon of phenyl acetate under acidic conditions (e.g., 5–10 % sulfuric acid) and heat to afford phenol and acetic acid; reflux in a mixture of water and a co‑solvent such as ethanol or toluene is common to improve miscibility.

Condensation cyclization to a heterocycle; acetylacetone (a 1,3‑diketone) condenses with hydrazine hydrochloride to give pyrazole, releasing water and forming ammonium chloride; usually refluxed in ethanol or acetic acid with a mild base such as sodium acetate to neutralize HCl, temperature 80–100 °C; solvent ethanol (or methanol) and optional acid/base catalyst.

Alkaline oxidative conversion of a benzylic methyl group to a carboxylic acid (KMnO4 oxidation). Potassium permanganate in aqueous alkaline medium oxidizes the toluene side chain of 2,4‑dichlorotoluene to 2,4‑dichlorobenzoic acid, while the Mn(VII) is reduced to MnO2 and KOH is formed. Typical conditions: reflux in water or water/acetone mixture with excess KMnO4, neutral to mildly basic pH; solid MnO2 precipitates and is filtered off.

Direct combination (redox) of metallic silver with chlorine gas to form silver(I) chloride. Each chlorine molecule accepts electrons from two silver atoms, yielding the insoluble white AgCl solid. The reaction proceeds spontaneously at room temperature in the gas phase or in an inert moist atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is needed, though it is often carried out in a dry flask or under a slight vacuum to collect the precipitate.

Acid‑base complexation producing sodium hexafluorostannate(IV). Tin(IV) oxide dissolves in hydrofluoric acid; sodium fluoride provides the counter‑cations, and the overall process yields Na2SnF6 with water as a by‑product. Conducted in concentrated aqueous HF (often in a PTFE‑lined vessel) at low to moderate temperature (0–50 °C) with vigorous stirring; the reaction is exothermic and requires careful handling of HF.

Oxidation of Fe(II) to Fe(III) by nitric acid (redox acid reaction). Fe²⁺ from iron(II) sulfate is oxidized to Fe³⁺, while HNO₃ is reduced to nitrogen dioxide gas. The reaction is performed in aqueous solution, usually with dilute HNO₃ at room temperature or slight heating; NO₂ evolves as a brown gas and water is formed alongside Fe₂(SO₄)₃.

Thermally induced urea hydrolysis leading to precipitation of scandium oxide nanoparticles. Upon heating, urea decomposes to generate NH₃ and CO₂, which raise the pH and cause hydrolysis of scandium nitrate to Sc(OH)₃, subsequently dehydrating to Sc₂O₃ nanocrystals. Typical procedure: aqueous solution of scandium nitrate and excess urea heated to 80–120 °C for several hours; the resulting oxide nanopowder is collected by filtration and washing. No external catalyst is required.

N‑alkylation (SN2) of p‑phenylenediamine with methyl iodide; purpose: introduce two methyl groups to give N,N‑dimethyl‑p‑phenylenediamine; key transformation: nucleophilic attack of amine nitrogen on CH3I displacing I− and forming HI; typical conditions: reflux in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or acetonitrile, often with a mild base (e.g., Na2CO3) to neutralize HI, temperature 80–120 °C.

NaBH₄ reduction of a carbonyl: 2‑(methylamino)‑1‑phenylethanone is treated with sodium borohydride in methanol or ethanol (0 °C to rt) to selectively reduce the ketone to the secondary alcohol 2‑(methylamino)‑1‑phenylethanol; the amine remains unchanged.

Oxidation of benzaldehyde to benzoic acid using in‑situ generated peroxyformic acid (formic acid + H2O2); purpose: convert aldehyde to carboxylic acid; key transformation: oxygen transfer from peroxyformic acid to the aldehyde, yielding benzoic acid, CO2 and H2O; typical conditions: aqueous solution of 30 % H2O2 and excess formic acid, 0–25 °C, acidic pH, no additional catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of 4‑nitroaniline to p‑phenylenediamine; purpose is to generate the diamine for polymer or dye synthesis; key transformation: 4‑nitroaniline + 3 H₂ → p‑phenylenediamine + 2 H₂O; conditions: hydrogen gas (1–5 atm) with 5–10 % Pd/C catalyst, solvent ethanol or methanol, room temperature to 50 °C; catalyst Pd on carbon, solvent polar protic.

Acid‑base metathesis between sulfuric acid and calcium thioglycolate; purpose: liberate free thioglycolic acid; key transformation: protonation of thioglycolate anion, precipitation of calcium sulfate and release of thioglycolic acid; typical conditions: aqueous medium, addition of dilute H2SO4 at room temperature with stirring; solid CaSO4 separates out.

Hydrolysis of phenyl 2,2,2-trichloroacetate ester to yield phenol and 2,2,2-trichloroacetic acid; spontaneous or acid/base-catalyzed cleavage occurs under aqueous conditions, with water acting as the nucleophile to break the ester bond.

General type: intramolecular cyclodehydration (lactam formation). Purpose: conversion of L‑glutamic acid to pyrrolidone‑carboxylic acid (5‑oxoproline). Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of the side‑chain carboxylate on the α‑carboxyl carbon with loss of water, forming a five‑membered lactam ring. Typical conditions: heating the amino acid at 150–200 °C, often in the presence of an acid catalyst (e.g., HCl) or a dehydrating agent such as acetic anhydride; solvent-free or in a high‑boiling solvent. No metal catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of glycerol to hydroxyacetone (acetol); purpose: convert a triol into a ketone by removing water; key transformation: protonation of a secondary hydroxyl, elimination of water and 1,2‑hydride shift yielding CH3‑C(=O)‑CH2‑OH; typical conditions: dilute H2SO4 (5–10 %), temperature 180–210 °C, often in a sealed reactor or with a water‑removing trap; glycerol itself acts as the solvent.

Oxidation of 4‑(trifluoromethyl)phenyllithium with molecular oxygen to 4‑(trifluoromethyl)phenol; purpose: generate phenol from the organolithium precursor; key transformation: O2 insertion into the C‑Li bond forming a lithium peroxide intermediate that upon aqueous work‑up gives the phenol; typical conditions: ether solvent (THF or diethyl ether), –78 °C to 0 °C under inert atmosphere, slow introduction of O2 or air, followed by quench with dilute NH4Cl or water.

Strong reduction of an ester with lithium aluminium hydride (LiAlH₄); purpose is to cleave the phenyl ester into the corresponding alcohols. Key transformation: LiAlH₄ reduces the carbonyl and simultaneously cleaves the C–Oaryl bond, giving phenol from the phenoxy fragment and 3‑chloropropanol from the acyl fragment. Typical conditions: anhydrous THF or diethyl ether, LiAlH₄ (2–3 equiv) added at 0 °C under nitrogen, then the mixture is refluxed for 2–4 h. Quench with water/NaOH cautiously at low temperature.

Neutralization (acid‑base) reaction: caesium oxide reacts with sulfuric acid to afford caesium sulfate and water (Cs2SO4 + H2O). Usually carried out in aqueous solution, added slowly with cooling to control exotherm; no additional catalyst needed.

Acid–base double displacement; converts insoluble cobalt carbonate to soluble cobalt thiocyanate while releasing CO₂; typically performed in aqueous solution with gentle heating to evolve gas, no catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed redox (iodide/iodate) reaction: iodide ions are oxidized by iodate in the presence of sulfuric acid, producing elemental iodine, water and potassium sulfate. Used in iodometric titrations and analytical generation of I₂. Carried out in aqueous solution, typically at room temperature, with excess dilute H₂SO₄ as the acidic medium.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene; purpose is to saturate ethylene to ethane; ethylene reacts with hydrogen in the presence of a metal catalyst such as nickel, palladium or platinum under pressure (1‑5 atm) and moderate temperature (30‑150 °C); performed in the gas phase, typically solvent‑free; catalyst is essential.

Metal‑mediated reductive dehalogenation: zinc dust reduces 1,2,2‑tribromopropane, eliminating two bromine atoms and forming the allylic bromide 1‑bromo‑2‑propene while zinc is converted to ZnBr₂. Conducted under anhydrous conditions (dry ether or THF) at reflux, using stoichiometric Zn metal as the reducing agent.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification: ethanol exchanges the alkoxy group of methyl p‑hydroxybenzoate (methylparaben) to give ethyl p‑hydroxybenzoate and methanol. Catalyzed by a strong acid such as H₂SO₄, the reaction is refluxed in excess ethanol, and methanol is removed (e.g., by azeotropic distillation) to drive the equilibrium toward product formation.

α‑Chlorination of acetophenone with N‑chlorosuccinimide (NCS); an electrophilic halogenation of the enolizable ketone α‑position. The enol form of acetophenone reacts with NCS to afford 2‑chloroacetophenone and succinimide as by‑product. Typical conditions: dichloromethane (or CHCl₃) at 0 °C to rt, often with a catalytic amount of acid or base to generate the enol. Used to introduce a functional handle for further substitution.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification of a methyl ester: 1‑propanol reacts with methyl valerate, swapping the methoxy group for a propoxy group to afford propyl valerate and methanol. Typical conditions involve reflux in a suitable solvent (often the excess alcohol itself) with a catalytic amount of acid (H₂SO₄) or a base (e.g., NaOCH₃), and continuous removal of methanol to shift the equilibrium.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification: isopropylparaben is treated with excess ethanol and catalytic sulfuric acid, converting it to ethylparaben and isopropanol; typical conditions are ethanol as solvent, 1–5 % H₂SO₄, reflux for 4–8 h, with removal of isopropanol to favor product formation.

Electrophilic aromatic halogenation (multiple substitution): benzene undergoes successive chlorination with excess Cl₂, each step replacing a hydrogen atom with chlorine and forming HCl as by‑product, ultimately yielding hexachlorobenzene. The reaction is performed at elevated temperature (often 150‑200 °C) with a Lewis acid catalyst such as FeCl₃ or AlCl₃, or under UV irradiation, in a non‑polar solvent or neat chlorine.

Thermal decarboxylation of a carboxylic acid: heating 1‑adamantanecarboxylic acid induces loss of CO₂ to give adamantane. The process typically requires temperatures of 200‑300 °C and may be facilitated by a metal catalyst (e.g., Cu or Zn salts) or conducted under reduced pressure; no solvent is usually employed.

N‑alkylation (SN2) of the primary amine in tryptamine with ethyl bromide; potassium carbonate acts as a mild base to deprotonate the amine and scavenge HBr. Typically carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or acetonitrile at 0 °C to reflux, yielding N‑ethyltryptamine as the product.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2) of ethyl bromide with sodium ethoxide; purpose is to form a symmetrical ether (diethyl ether). Ethoxide attacks the carbon bearing bromine, displacing Br⁻ to give diethyl ether and NaBr. Typical reaction: ethanol (solvent and source of ethoxide) with NaOEt, reflux under dry conditions.

Halogenolysis/chlorination of yttrium phosphide with chlorine gas; the metal phosphide is cleaved to give phosphorus trichloride and yttrium(III) chloride. Usually performed in a sealed tube or flow reactor at elevated temperatures (200–400 °C) under an inert atmosphere; no solvent is required as the reaction is gas‑solid.

Single replacement (acid‑metal) reaction; nickel metal reacts with dilute sulfuric acid in aqueous solution at room temperature or with gentle heating to produce nickel(II) sulfate dissolved in water and hydrogen gas released; no catalyst required, water is the solvent.

Acylation (Schotten‑Baumann reaction) of para‑aminobenzoic acid with acetyl chloride; triethylamine serves as a base to capture the generated HCl, forming triethylammonium chloride. Conducted in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature, affording para‑acetamidobenzoic acid.

Benzylic oxidation of 4‑bromotoluene to the aldehyde using selenium dioxide; SeO₂ abstracts hydrogen from the methyl group and is reduced to elemental selenium. The reaction is typically run in a high‑boiling polar aprotic solvent (e.g., 1,4‑dioxane or 1,2‑dichloroethane) at 80–120 °C under reflux, delivering 4‑bromobenzaldehyde.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation) using an acid chloride; acetyl chloride acylates aniline to give acetanilide while releasing HCl; usually carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent (CH₂Cl₂, THF) with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to neutralize HCl and improve yield.

Enzymatic O‑methyltransferase (SAM‑dependent) methylation of luteolin; S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine (SAM) donates a methyl group to a phenolic hydroxyl of luteolin, producing the methylated flavonoid Okanin and S‑adenosyl‑L‑homocysteine (SAH). Conducted in aqueous buffer (pH 7–8) at 25–37 °C, often with Mg²⁺ as cofactor, and requires the specific methyltransferase enzyme.

Aqueous double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis) between trisodium citrate and silver nitrate; silver ions exchange with sodium ions to form sparingly soluble silver citrate precipitate while sodium nitrate remains in solution. Performed at ambient temperature in water; the mixture is stirred until the silver citrate fully precipitates and is then filtered.

Oxidative degradation (Fenton-type oxidation). Purpose: conversion of caffeine to the more oxidized metabolite 1,3,7‑trimethyluric acid. Key transformation: hydroxyl radicals generated from H2O2 (in presence of Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺) attack the imidazole ring of caffeine, introducing oxy‑functionalities and cleaving N‑C bonds to give the uric‑acid derivative while reducing peroxide to water. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, acidic pH (≈3), Fe²⁺ catalyst (often FeSO₄), 20‑60 °C, reaction time 30 min–2 h. Common solvent: water; sometimes small amount of methanol to improve solubility.

Halide‑selenide metathesis (solid‑state exchange). Purpose: synthesis of a niobium selenide (Nb–Se) material. Key transformation: chloride ligands of NbCl₅ are displaced by selenide ions from Na₂Se, forming NaCl as by‑product and generating NbSeₓ (often NbSe₂) as the target solid. Typical conditions: dry, inert atmosphere; reagents mixed and heated (300‑600 °C) in a sealed tube or ampoule to promote diffusion; sometimes a slight excess of Na₂Se is used. Solvent: none (solid‑state), or high‑boiling non‑coordinating solvent (e.g., quinoline) if carried out in melt.

Reductive metal‑halide exchange (metal reduction). Purpose: preparation of europium(II) bromide from the trivalent salt. Key transformation: elemental lithium donates electrons to EuBr₃, reducing Eu³⁺ to Eu²⁺ and forming LiBr; overall stoichiometry gives EuBr₂ and LiBr. Typical conditions: anhydrous, aprotic solvent such as THF or diethyl ether under inert atmosphere (argon); low temperature (0 °C to –78 °C) to control vigorous reactivity; lithium added gradually as a dispersion or ribbon. No additional catalyst required.

Mannich condensation (β‑amino ketone formation). Purpose: construction of 4-(piperidin‑1‑yl)butan‑2‑one, a β‑amino ketone useful as a building block. Key transformation: piperidine reacts with formaldehyde to generate an iminium ion, which is then attacked by the enol form of acetone, yielding the new C–C bond and installing the piperidyl substituent at the β‑position of the carbonyl. Typical conditions: reflux in an alcohol solvent (ethanol or methanol) or in acetonitrile; catalyst is the secondary amine itself; reaction time 2‑6 h; often performed under nitrogen to avoid oxidation.

Allylic oxidation with selenium dioxide; transforms the secondary allylic alcohol linalool into the conjugated aldehydes geranial/nereal (collectively citral). Reaction uses SeO₂ (1–2 eq) in refluxing 1,4‑dioxane or tert‑butanol/H₂O (1:1) at 80–100 °C, often with a catalytic amount of hydrogen peroxide to re‑oxidize reduced selenium. Gives a mixture of citral isomers.

Metathesis precipitation; nickel(II) nitrate aqueous solution is treated with potassium cyanide, producing insoluble Ni(CN)2 precipitate and soluble KNO3; carried out at low to moderate temperature in water, careful cyanide handling, no catalyst.

Double displacement (acid-carbonate reaction). Produces lead nitrate for applications like pigment or battery materials. Carbonate neutralizes nitric acid, releasing CO₂ and water. Typically occurs at ambient temperature in aqueous solution.

Redox reduction of iodine by sodium peroxide; iodine is reduced to iodide and peroxide is oxidized to O2; reaction proceeds in aqueous or alcoholic solution, often warmed slightly to improve rate; no catalyst; provides a method to generate NaI while evolving oxygen.

Ligand exchange / acid‑base metathesis (metal fluoride formation). Purpose: conversion of a chromium(III) acetate complex to the corresponding fluoride salt. Key transformation: fluoride ions from HF replace acetate ligands bound to Cr³⁺, producing chromic fluoride (often CrF₃ or hydrated CrF₃) and liberating acetic acid. Typical conditions: aqueous HF (or aqueous NH₄HF₂) at 0‑25 °C; careful addition of Cr(OAc)₃ to avoid excessive heat; reaction proceeds rapidly with evolution of acidic vapors. Solvent: water; excess HF ensures complete ligand substitution.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an α‑halo ester; methylamine displaces the bromide on ethyl chloroacetate to form an α‑amino ester. Key transformation: CH₂Cl–COOEt → CH₂NHCH₃–COOEt, producing ethyl 2‑(methylamino)acetate and NaCl (or HCl neutralized). Typical conditions: excess methylamine (often as a gas or in solution), solvent such as ethanol or THF, temperature 0 °C to reflux to control side reactions; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization with gas evolution. Purpose: generation of the sodium salt of pyruvic acid (sodium pyruvate) for biochemical use. Key transformation: the acidic proton of pyruvic acid is abstracted by bicarbonate, forming carbonic acid that decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O, while the pyruvate anion pairs with Na⁺. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature; stoichiometric NaH₃ added dropwise with stirring; CO₂ bubbles off as reaction proceeds. No catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (acylation of a silyl‑protected amine). Bis(trimethylsilyl)amine attacks trifluoroacetyl chloride to give bis(trimethylsilyl)trifluoro‑acetamide and HCl. Typically run in anhydrous aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to room temperature; a tertiary amine base (triethylamine or pyridine) is often added to neutralize the generated HCl.

Salt metathesis (ligand exchange) to form a metallocene: sodium cyclopentadienide reacts with cobalt(II) chloride in dry THF or diethyl ether under nitrogen, yielding bis(cyclopentadienyl)cobalt (cobaltocene) and sodium chloride. Typical procedure: 2 equiv NaCp, stir at room temperature to reflux for several hours, inert atmosphere, filtration to remove salts.

Acid–base neutralization / salt formation. Sulfur dioxide gas is absorbed in aqueous potassium hydroxide to form potassium bisulfite (KHSO₃). Conducted in water at low to ambient temperature, often with vigorous stirring to maximize gas dissolution.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution of an alkyl halide by ammonia. Ammonia displaces bromide from propargyl bromide, producing propargylamine and HBr (often captured as ammonium bromide). Carried out in aqueous or alcoholic ammonia solution, typically at 0 °C to reflux, using excess ammonia to drive the reaction to completion.

Acid‑catalyzed electrophilic addition (Markovnikov hydration) of a terminal alkene. 1‑Nonene reacts with water in the presence of dilute sulfuric acid to give 2‑nonanol via protonation of the double bond and subsequent nucleophilic attack by water. Performed at reflux (≈100 °C) in aqueous H₂SO₄, often with the reaction mixture stirred for several hours.

Oxidation of a primary allylic alcohol to an aldehyde using Dess‑Martin periodinane. Trans‑2‑methyl‑2‑buten‑1‑ol is converted to trans‑2‑methyl‑2‑butenal under mild, neutral conditions. The reaction is typically performed in dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, under nitrogen, with 1.0–1.2 equiv of DMP and no additional catalyst.

Acid dissolution of samarium oxide with nitric acid; produces samarium(III) nitrate. Purpose: preparation of nitrate salt, often used as oxidizer or precursor. Key transformation: Sm2O3 + 6 HNO3 → 2 Sm(NO3)3 + 3 H2O. Typical conditions: aqueous HNO3 (conc. 1–6 M), heating under reflux (60–90 °C) to accelerate dissolution. Solvent: water; reaction proceeds without added catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an αβ‑unsaturated ketone. Carvone is hydrogenated over palladium on carbon (Pd/C) to selectively reduce the C=C double bond, yielding dihydrocarvone while leaving the carbonyl intact. Conducted in a protic solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, at room temperature to 50 °C, under 1–5 atm H₂ pressure.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde using Dess‑Martin periodinane; transforms 2‑ethylhexanol into 2‑ethylhexanal. The reaction is performed at 0 °C to ambient temperature in a dry, non‑protic solvent (commonly dichloromethane or chloroform) under nitrogen.
