No additional catalyst is required; the periodinane reagent acts as the oxidant and by‑product is iodobenzene dioxide.

Double displacement precipitation (alkaline precipitation); reaction of cadmium chloride with aqueous ammonium hydroxide produces cadmium hydroxide precipitate and ammonium chloride; performed in water, often at room temperature; excess NH4OH keeps solution basic, no catalyst needed.

Pinner-type imidate formation (acid‑catalyzed addition of an alcohol to a nitrile); ethanol reacts with acetonitrile in the presence of hydrochloric acid to give ethyl acetimidate hydrochloride. The mixture is refluxed in anhydrous ethanol (or a suitable alcohol solvent) with gaseous or aqueous HCl; the reaction proceeds at 60–80 °C until conversion is complete, after which the salt precipitates.

Hydrolysis of a metal halide; molybdenum pentachloride reacts with water to produce molybdenum trioxide solid and liberates hydrogen chloride gas. Conducted by slow addition of aqueous water to MoCl₅ under cooling (0–25 °C) or by stirring a suspension of MoCl₅ in water; the reaction is exothermic and no additional reagents are required.

Redox oxidation of ferrous to ferric ion by nitrous acid in acidic medium; ferrous sulfate is oxidized to ferric sulfate while nitrous acid is reduced to nitric oxide gas, with water as a by‑product. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at 0–25 °C, using an in‑situ generated nitrous acid (NaNO₂ + HCl) and excess HCl to maintain acidity. The evolution of NO gas is observed; the reaction is stoichiometric and does not need external catalysts.

Acetylation of a phenolic ester (esterification/acetylation) using acetic anhydride; methyl salicylate’s phenolic OH is acetylated to give methyl acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin analog) while producing acetic acid. Pyridine serves as both solvent and base to scavenge the generated acid; the reaction is refluxed at 80–100 °C for 1–3 h under nitrogen. After cooling, the product is isolated by filtration or extraction, and the pyridine‑acetic acid mixture is washed away.

Metathesis/precipitation (double displacement); aqueous barium nitrate mixed with ammonium oxalate precipitates insoluble barium oxalate while ammonium nitrate remains in solution; carried out at ambient temperature in water; no catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of 2,4‑dinitrotoluene to 2,4‑diaminotoluene; nitro groups are hydrogenated to amines using H₂ gas in the presence of a metal catalyst (Pd/C, Pt, Raney Ni) in ethanol or methanol under several bar pressure; purpose is to obtain the diamine for dyes, polymers or explosives; key transformation: –NO₂ to –NH₂; typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, 25–80 °C.

Redox reduction of AuCl₃ to metallic gold by sodium ascorbate; the ascorbate acts as a two‑electron donor, being oxidized to dehydroascorbic acid while Au³⁺ is reduced to Au⁰; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often mildly acidic; purpose is preparation of gold nanoparticles or bulk gold; typical solvent: water; no external catalyst required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (ester aminolysis) of ethyl benzoate with hydrazine hydrate to afford benzohydrazide ethanol. Purpose is preparation of the benzoic acid hydrazide. Key transformation is replacement of the ethoxy group by –NHNH₂. Typical conditions: excess hydrazine hydrate, reflux in ethanol or methanol (80‑100 °C) for 2‑6 h. No catalyst required; solvent often serves as both reactant and medium.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) between sodium oxalate and lithium iodide to exchange counter‑ions, yielding NaI and lithium oxalate; usually carried out in aqueous solution with stirring; heating can improve crystallization of the less‑soluble lithium oxalate; no catalyst needed.

Acid–base salt metathesis of cerium(III) chloride with nitric acid to form cerium(III) nitrate and release hydrochloric acid (often as gas); performed in aqueous solution, low to moderate temperature (0–25 °C) to avoid decomposition; purpose is preparation of soluble cerium nitrate for further chemistry; no catalyst required.

Copper‑catalyzed carbene O‑H insertion using ethyl diazoacetate and phenol; Cu(OAc)₂ generates a metal‑carbene from the diazo compound, which inserts into the phenolic O‑H bond to give ethyl 2‑phenoxyacetate with loss of N₂; typical conditions: 5–10 mol % Cu(OAc)₂, dichloromethane or acetonitrile, 0–25 °C, inert atmosphere; purpose is C‑O bond formation and synthesis of phenoxy‑acetate esters.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution of fluoroacetyl chloride with aqueous ammonia to afford fluoroacetamide and HCl; the reaction is usually run at 0–5 °C in a mixed water/organic solvent (e.g., THF) to control HCl evolution; excess NH₃ or a base (NaHCO₃) may be added to neutralize acid; purpose is preparation of the fluorinated amide.

Aqueous hydrolysis/disproportionation of trichloroisocyanuric acid; generates the less‑chlorinated derivative and free hypochlorous acid. Water attacks the chlorine atoms, yielding dichloroisocyanuric acid and HOCl. Reaction proceeds at room temperature in water; no additional reagents or catalysts are needed.

Hydration/hydrolysis of calcium aluminate; water cleaves the Al–O–Ca bonds, forming calcium hydroxide and aluminum hydroxide precipitate. Occurs readily in aqueous suspension, often near neutral pH and ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Enzymatic aldose‑ketose isomerization of D‑xylose‑5‑phosphate to D‑xylulose‑5‑phosphate catalyzed by phosphopentose isomerase; purpose is interconversion of pentose phosphates in the pentose‑phosphate pathway; occurs in aqueous buffer at physiological pH (≈7.5) and temperature (≈37 °C) with the enzyme, no organic solvent required.

Acid‑base neutralization with gas evolution; sodium bicarbonate deprotonates the triethylammonium bromide salt, releasing CO₂ and H₂O and liberating free triethylamine while forming sodium bromide. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature; stirring is sufficient, no catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization of a secondary amine hydrochloride with carbonate; sodium carbonate reacts with dibutylammonium chloride, producing CO₂, H₂O, dibutylamine, and sodium chloride. Typically carried out in water with mild heating to accelerate CO₂ evolution; no catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; hydroxide ions from potassium hydroxide replace perchlorate ions on magnesium, precipitating magnesium hydroxide while forming soluble potassium perchlorate. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no additional catalyst is required.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; exchanges cations between calcium nitrate and sodium lactate to form calcium lactate and sodium nitrate. Usually performed in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; no catalyst required. The reaction proceeds via solubility differences, as calcium lactate is less soluble and can precipitate, facilitating separation.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (acidaponification); purpose: obtain the free carboxylic acid from a methyl ester. Methyl 2‑propylpentanoate is refluxed with water and catalytic H₂SO₄ (often in a mixture of aqueous acid and a co‑solvent such as toluene) to give 2‑propylpentanoic acid and methanol.

Type: intramolecular cyclodehydration/condensation using carbodiimide activation. Purpose: synthesize 3H‑1,3‑benzoxazol‑2‑one heterocycle from anthranilic acid. Key transformation: anthranilic acid reacts with carbonyl diimidazole (CDI) to form an activated imidazolide; intramolecular attack of the ortho‑amino group on the activated carbonyl yields cyclization and release of imidazole. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt, 1–2 equiv CDI, inert atmosphere, dry solvent (DMF, DCM or THF); reaction proceeds 1–4 h. No additional catalyst needed.

Acidic fluoride substitution; manganese(III) oxide is treated with aqueous hydrofluoric acid, converting the oxide to soluble manganese(III) fluoride while water is formed (Mn₂O₃ + 6 HF → 2 MnF₃ + 3 H₂O); performed under reflux or gentle heating in HF solution; no additional catalyst, but careful handling of HF is required.

Type: reductive methylation (Eschweiler–Clarke reaction). Purpose: convert a primary amine to the corresponding N,N‑dimethyl tertiary amine. Key transformation: 2‑phenylethylamine undergoes successive condensation with formaldehyde to give an iminium intermediate, which is reduced by formic acid (hydride donor) to install a methyl group the sequence repeats to give N,N‑dimethylphenylethylamine, with CO2 and H2O as by‑products. Typical conditions: aqueous or MeCN solvent, excess formaldehyde (≈2 eq) and formic acid (≈3 eq), reflux 80–100 °C for 4–12 h. No metal catalyst required.

Type: base‑induced dehydrohalogenation (E2 elimination). Purpose: generate an α,β‑unsaturated nitrile from a β‑halo nitrile. Key transformation: potassium tert‑butoxide abstracts a β‑hydrogen from 4‑bromobronitrile, expelling bromide to form 3‑butenenitrile; the tert‑butoxide is protonated, giving tert‑butanol, and KBr is formed as a salt. Typical conditions: dry aprotic solvent (THF, DMSO), 0 °C to rt, 1 equiv KOtBu, inert atmosphere; reaction completes within 30 min to 2 h. No additional catalyst.

Type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alcohol by hydrogen halide. Purpose: convert ethanol to ethyl iodide. Key transformation: protonation of ethanol by HI, followed by backside attack of I⁻ on the methyl carbon to displace water, yielding iodoethane and water. Typical conditions: excess HI (48 % aqueous or anhydrous), reflux60–80 °C with a catalytic amount of red phosphorus to regenerate HI; reaction time 1–3 h. Solvent can be the ethanol itself; no extra catalyst.

Combination (synthesis) reaction: elemental caesium metal reacts directly with oxygen gas to give caesium oxide (Cs2O). The process is highly exothermic, occurs spontaneously at ambient temperature in dry air, and requires no solvent or catalyst.

Reduction; LiAlH4 reduces both nitrile groups of pyridine‑2,6‑dicarbonitrile to primary amines, yielding 2,6‑diamino­pyridine; useful for preparing diamine precursors for heterocycle synthesis; carried out under anhydrous conditions in dry ether or THF, refluxing under nitrogen; excess LiAlH4 is added portionwise and the reaction is quenched with water or a dilute acid; no additional catalyst is required.

Reaction type: amide (formyl) hydrolysis (acidic or basic); purpose: removal of the formyl protecting group to regenerate DL‑methionine; key transformation: water attacks the carbonyl of the N‑formyl group, cleaving the C–N bond to give DL‑methionine and formic acid; typical conditions: aqueous acidic medium (e.g., 1 M HCl) or dilute NaOH, heating at 50–80 °C for several hours; solvent: water or water/ethanol mixture.

Type: chlorination of hydroxyl groups using phosphorus pentachloride. Purpose: replace the three ring‑OH groups of cyanuric acid with chlorine to obtain cyanuric chloride. Key transformation: each OH reacts with PCl₅ to give POCl₃, HCl and the corresponding C‑Cl bond; overall three equivalents produce cyanuric chloride, three equivalents of POCl₃ and three equivalents of HCl. Typical conditions: dry, non‑protic solvent (CS₂, CH₂Cl₂, or dry benzene), 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen; stoichiometric PCl₅ (3 eq) added slowly. No additional catalyst.

Halogen‑lithium exchange (metal‑halogen exchange). Treatment of 1‑bromonaphthalene with n‑butyllithium replaces the bromine with lithium to give 1‑naphthyllithium. Performed under inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar) at low temperature (−78 °C) in anhydrous THF; the reaction is usually stirred for 30 min to 1 h before quenching. No additional catalyst required.

Type: peracid epoxidation (Prilezhaev oxidation). Purpose: form a vinyl epoxide (vinyloxirane) from 1,3‑butadiene. Key transformation: one of the C=C bonds of 1,3‑butadiene reacts with meta‑chloroperbenzoic acid (m‑CPBA) to give the corresponding epoxide; the oxidant is reduced to meta‑chlorobenzoic acid. Typical conditions: dilute solution of 1,3‑butadiene in dry dichloromethane, 0 °C to rt, 1.1–1.5 eq m‑CPBA, inert atmosphere; reaction complete in 1–2 h. No metal catalyst required.

Metathesis precipitation of a metal sulfide; purpose is to synthesize praseodymium(III) sulfide; aqueous PrCl₃ is reacted with Na₂S solution, yielding Pr₂S₃ solid and NaCl in solution; performed under inert atmosphere or nitrogen to avoid oxidation of sulfide, often at 60‑80 °C with stirring; no catalyst; the sulfide precipitates and is filtered and washed.

Fischer esterification; synthesizes tert‑butyl hexanoate from hexanoic acid; key transformation: carboxylic acid + tert‑butanol → tert‑butyl hexanoate + water; typical conditions: reflux with a strong acid catalyst such as concentrated H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH, often in toluene or benzene using a Dean‑Stark apparatus to remove water; common solvent/catalyst: toluene, H₂SO₄.

Double displacement/precipitation reaction; aqueous reaction of ErCl3 with NH4OH produces insoluble Er(OH)3 and soluble NH4Cl; carried out in water at room temperature with stirring; no catalyst needed.

Type: Nucleophilic substitution (SN2). Purpose: introduce a cyano group for later functional group interconversion. Key transformation: cyanide ion replaces the chloride on the benzylic carbon, yielding 4‑fluorobenzyl cyanide and NaCl. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO, or acetonitrile, NaCN (often as aqueous solution or dissolved in the solvent), temperature from room temperature to 80 °C, reaction under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation.

Type: reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol using lithium aluminium hydride. Purpose: convert cyclobutanecarboxylic acid into cyclobutylmethanol. Key transformation: –CO₂H group is reduced to –CH₂OH, with LiAlH₄ delivering hydride to the carbonyl carbon. Typical conditions: LiAlH₄ (1–2 equiv) added to a dry ether solvent (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere (N₂) at 0 °C then warmed to reflux; reaction quenched with careful hydrolysis (water then dilute acid). No additional catalyst required.

Type: acid–base gas absorption forming a metal bisulfite salt. Purpose: capture sulfur dioxide as a soluble calcium sulfite/bisulfite for further use. Key transformation: SO₂ dissolves in water to give H₂SO₃, which reacts with Ca(OH)₂ to form Ca(HSO₃)₂. Typical conditions: aqueous slurry of calcium hydroxide at ambient temperature, SO₂ gas bubbled through the mixture; product precipitates or remains in solution and can be isolated by evaporation. No special catalyst; water is the solvent.

Type: double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Purpose: exchange halide ligands to generate insoluble copper(I) iodide. Key transformation: KI + CuCl → KCl (soluble) + CuI (insoluble). Typical conditions: aqueous solution of KI and CuCl at room temperature; stirring promotes precipitation of white CuI, which is filtered off. No catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Type: thermal decomposition (pyrolysis) of a phenyl carbamate. Purpose: cleave phenyl N‑phenylcarbamate into phenol and phenyl isocyanate. Key transformation: the N‑C(O)O bond breaks, releasing phenol (Ar‑OH) and forming phenyl isocyanate (Ph‑N=C=O). Typical conditions: heating the carbamate neat or in a high‑boiling inert solvent (e.g., diphenyl ether) at 200–250 °C under nitrogen; volatile phenol and isocyanate are distilled off. No catalyst required.

Type: metal‑water single‑replacement (hydrolysis) redox reaction. Purpose: generate hydrogen gas and a lanthanide hydroxide from elemental gadolinium. Key transformation: Gd(s) oxidized to Gd³⁺, water reduced to H₂, yielding Gd(OH)₃ solid. Typical conditions: finely divided gadolinium added to hot water or passed steam; reaction proceeds slowly at room temperature but rapidly with heated/steam water. Reaction medium is aqueous; no catalyst needed.

Hydride reduction of tellurium dioxide by sodium borohydride, producing hydrogen telluride (H2Te), hydrogen gas, and sodium metaborate. Conducted in a protic solvent (e.g., ethanol or water–ethanol mixture) at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation of H2Te. Excess NaBH4 ensures complete reduction; the by‑product NaBO2 remains dissolved.

Copper‑catalyzed cyanation (Rosenmund‑von Braun type) of an aryl bromide; 2‑bromo‑3‑methylphenol is converted to 2‑cyano‑3‑methylphenol, with CuBr as by‑product; carried out in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or DMSO at 120–180 °C, often with CuCN (1–2 equiv).

Base‑mediated saponification of a tert‑butyl ester; converts the ester into the sodium carboxylate while generating tert‑butanol. Key transformation: C(O)O‑tert‑Bu + NaOH → RCOONa + t‑BuOH. Conducted in aqueous NaOH (often 0.5–2 M) with an organic co‑solvent (ethanol, methanol, or THF) at reflux or 60–80 °C until completion; no additional catalyst required.

Isomerization of 1,3‑butadiene to 1,2‑butadiene (allene); reaction type is double‑bond migration (alkene‑allene rearrangement); converts a conjugated diene into an allene; commonly performed with transition‑metal catalysts such as Pd, Ni, or CuCl, or with strong base; conditions involve elevated temperatures (150–250 °C) in the gas phase or high‑pressure flow reactors, often without solvent.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 2,3‑dimethyl‑1‑hexene to 2,3‑dimethylhexane; type: addition of H₂ across a carbon‑carbon double bond to saturate the alkene; typical catalysts include Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni; reaction is run in an alcoholic solvent (ethanol or methanol) or ethyl acetate under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) at 25–80 °C.

Alkaline leaching (base‑mediated dissolution) of cassiterite (SnO₂) with sodium hydroxide to give sodium stannate; reaction type: acid‑base neutralization and solid‑liquid conversion; key transformation is SnO₂ + 2 NaOH → Na₂SnO₃ + H₂O; performed in aqueous NaOH (10–20 % w/w) at 80–120 °C with vigorous stirring; no external catalyst needed.

N‑alkylation (O‑ethylation) of morphine using ethyl trifluoromethanesulfonate in the presence of triethylamine; reaction type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2) forming ethyl‑morphine ether and triethylammonium triflate; typically carried out in dry dichloromethane or acetonitrile at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; no metal catalyst required.

Metathesis/precipitation double‑displacement between cobalt(II) carbonate and ammonium oxalate; reaction type: salt metathesis leading to insoluble cobalt oxalate; key transformation is CoCO₃ + (NH₄)₂C₂O₄ → CoC₂O₄↓ + (NH₄)₂CO₃; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; cobalt oxalate precipitates and is filtered, no catalyst needed.

Esterification (condensation) of phthalic anhydride with 1‑butanol to give dibutyl phthalate; ionic liquid 1‑butyl‑3‑methylimidazolium chloride acts as both solvent and catalyst. Key transformation: two –OH groups of butanol replace the anhydride carbonyl oxygens, forming two ester linkages and releasing water. Typically performed under reflux (80‑120 °C) with removal of water to drive equilibrium; solvent‑free or using the ionic liquid itself; inert atmosphere may be used.

Dimerization (dehydrogenative coupling) of dimethylarsine to tetramethyldiarsine; an As–As bond is formed while two hydrogen atoms are eliminated (often as H₂). Reaction type: self‑coupling of a secondary arsine. Conducted by gentle heating (50‑100 °C) under inert gas, usually in the gas phase or in a non‑coordinating solvent (e.g., toluene); no added catalyst is required, though trace transition‑metal salts can accelerate the process.

Acid‑base neutralization of calcium carbonate with hydrochloric acid, producing carbonic acid and calcium chloride. Carbonic acid rapidly decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; excess HCl ensures complete conversion. No special catalyst; water is the solvent.

Mannich reaction (amine‑formalaldehyde condensation) of indole with dimethylamine and formaldehyde to afford gramine (3‑(dimethylaminomethyl)indole) and water. Key steps: formation of an iminium ion from dimethylamine and formaldehyde, followed by electrophilic attack on the C‑3 position of indole. Usually performed in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to reflux; mildly acidic conditions (acetic acid or a catalytic amount of HCl) promote iminium generation.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration of benzene using dinitrogen pentoxide (N₂O₅) as the nitrating agent; nitronium ion (NO₂⁺) is generated in situ, attacking benzene to give nitrobenzene, with nitric acid as a by‑product. Conducted at low temperature (0‑30 °C) in a mixed acid medium (often sulfuric acid or fuming nitric acid) to control reaction rate and minimize poly‑nitration.

Transesterification of dimethyl carbonate with ethanol; used to prepare mixed carbonate ethyl methyl carbonate while releasing methanol. The reaction exchanges a methyl group of the carbonate for an ethyl group. Typically catalyzed by a base (e.g., K2CO3, NaOMe) or an acid (e.g., H2SO4) at 80‑120 °C, often with continuous removal of methanol to drive the equilibrium; can be performed neat or in an inert solvent such as toluene.

Alkoxide exchange (metathesis) between methanol and sodium propoxide, yielding propanol and sodium methoxide. This proton transfer equilibrates the two alkoxides; performed in anhydrous aprotic solvents such as THF or diethyl ether under inert atmosphere, typically at room temperature. No catalyst is required.

Type: cyanohydrin formation (nucleophilic addition of HCN to a carbonyl). Purpose: generate 2‑hydroxy‑2‑phenylacetonitrile from acetophenone. Key transformation: cyanide ion attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that is protonated to give the α‑hydroxy nitrile. Typical conditions: NaCN (1.1 equiv) added to a solution of acetophenone in water/ethanol at 0 °C, then dilute HCl (0.5–1 M) is added to provide HCN in situ; reaction stirred 30 min‑1 h at 0–5 °C, then neutralized and extracted.

N‑alkylation (SN2) of the secondary amine; methyl iodide alkylates tetrahydroquinoline to give N‑methyl‑1,2,3,4‑tetrahydroquinoline, generating HI as a by‑product. The reaction is usually carried out in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF or acetonitrile) at reflux, in the presence of a base (e.g., K₂CO₃, NaHCO₃) to neutralize HI.

Metathesis between silver fluoride and potassium chloride. Type: double‑displacement (exchange) reaction. Purpose: precipitation of silver chloride from a mixture containing AgF, yielding soluble potassium fluoride. Key transformation: AgF + KCl → AgCl↓ + KF. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, ambient temperature; precipitation driven by the low solubility of AgCl. Common solvents/catalysts: water; no catalyst needed.

Acid–base precipitation (metathesis); used to prepare insoluble yttrium phosphate while liberating acetic acid; key transformation is exchange of acetate and phosphate ions; typically carried out in aqueous solution with stoichiometric phosphoric acid added to a solution of yttrium acetate, heated gently to ensure dissolution; no catalyst required; water is the common solvent and the precipitated yttrium phosphate is filtered and washed.

Quinone reduction; employed to obtain the hydroquinone (1,2‑dihydroxynaphthalene) from 1,2‑naphthoquinone; sodium dithionite donates two electrons and two protons, converting the carbonyl groups to hydroxyls; performed in aqueous alkaline medium (pH 7‑9) at ambient to 50 °C; inert atmosphere optional; water is the solvent; no additional catalyst is needed.

Acid–base neutralization (salt precipitation). Thallium(I) hydroxide reacts with phosphoric acid to produce thallium(I) phosphate and water. The reaction is performed in water, usually with slight heating to aid dissolution of the acid and to promote precipitation of the sparingly soluble Tl₃PO₄. No catalyst required; water serves as the reaction medium.

Gas absorption/neutralization precipitation; fundamental step in flue‑gas desulfurization to capture SO₂ as calcium sulfite; sulfur dioxide dissolves in water to form sulfite which reacts with calcium oxide (lime) to give solid CaSO₃; conducted in an aqueous slurry of CaO at room temperature with vigorous stirring; water is the reaction medium; no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of a tertiary alcohol; tert‑butyl alcohol loses water to generate isobutylene, with toluene serving as a dry, non‑participating solvent; typically uses a strong acid catalyst such as concentrated H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH, or solid acid (e.g., Al₂O₃) at 80‑120 °C; the reaction yields isobutylene gas and water; toluene is the common solvent; catalyst is essential.

Condensation (biguanide formation); o‑toluidine nucleophilically attacks cyanoguan, forming o‑tolylbiguanide and liberating ammonia; generally carried out in ethanol or water under reflux, sometimes with a base (e.g., Na₂CO₃) to neutralize the released NH₃; reaction temperature 80‑120 °C; no metal catalyst required; solvent is ethanol or aqueous medium.

This is an acid-base metathesis reaction where phosphorous acid reacts with lead(II) acetate to form lead phosphite, acetic acid, and water. It occurs in aqueous solution without requiring catalysts. The reaction proceeds at mild temperatures (e.g., room temperature) with the release of acetic acid as a product.

Carbodiimide‑mediated esterification (Steglich esterification); DCC activates cyclopentanecarboxylic acid to an O‑acyl‑urea intermediate which reacts with ethanol to give ethyl cyclopentanecarboxylate, while dicyclohexylurea precipitates as by‑product; performed in dry dichloromethane (or THF) at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen; catalytic DMAP often added to accelerate acyl transfer; no metal catalyst; DCC and DMAP are the reagents that drive the transformation.

Reduction of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol; NaBH4 selectively reduces the aldehyde group of 3,4-dihydroxybenzaldehyde to give hydroxytyrosol; typically performed in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature, often under inert atmosphere, with aqueous work‑up to remove excess hydride.

This thermal decomposition breaks down nickel carbonate into nickel oxide and carbon dioxide. It is typically performed by heating nickel carbonate in a solid-state reaction at elevated temperatures (usually above 300°C) to drive off carbon dioxide.

Acid–base (metathesis) reaction in aqueous solution; nitric acid protonates ammonium selenite, yielding selenous acid and ammonium nitrate. Usually performed at room temperature in water; no special catalyst required.

Free‑radical chlorination of mandelic acid; Cl₂ under UV light or heat abstracts the α‑hydrogen and substitutes chlorine at the α‑carbon, producing 2‑chloromandelic acid and HCl. Conducted in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane, initiated by light or heat.

Electrophilic aromatic iodination (halogenation) of 5‑chloro‑8‑hydroxyquinoline to give clioquinol; I₂ (generated I⁺ species with KI) reacts in glacial acetic acid, replacing a hydrogen with iodine at the 7‑position and releasing HI. Reaction typically refluxes in acetic acid; KI assists in forming ICl/I⁺.

Sodium borohydride reduction of an aromatic aldehyde; 4‑(dimethylamino)benzaldehyde is dissolved in MeOH (or EtOH) and NaBH4 is added at 0 °C to rt, selectively reducing the aldehyde to 4‑(dimethylamino)benzyl alcohol; the by‑product is sodium borate after aqueous work‑up.

Oxidation (Jones oxidation) of anthrone to anthraquinone using chromic acid (H₂CrO₄/CrO₃ in aqueous sulfuric acid). The secondary carbonyl is oxidized to a quinone, water is formed. Performed at 0–25 °C in acetone/water mixture; no additional catalyst needed.

Direct oxidative chlorination of bismuth antimonide; chlorine gas oxidizes Bi and Sb from 0 to +3, forming BiCl₃ and SbCl₃. Conducted by passing dry Cl₂ over the solid at elevated temperature (≈200–400 °C) in a sealed tube or flow reactor; no solvent or catalyst required.

Single‑displacement acid‑metal reaction; purpose is to generate strontium perchlorate and hydrogen gas. Sr(s) is oxidized to Sr²⁺ while H⁺ from aqueous perchloric acid is reduced to H₂. Typically carried out in dilute HClO₄ solution at 0‑25 °C with vigorous stirring; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

High‑temperature oxidative roasting of indium(III) selenide; O₂ oxidizes Se to volatile SeO₂ and In to In₂O₃. Carried out in a furnace at 600–800 °C under a flow of air or pure O₂; no solvent, catalyst, or additives needed.

Reduction of nitrosobenzene to phenylhydroxylamine; zinc dust acts as a chemical reductant in glacial acetic acid, typically under reflux. The nitroso group (–N=O) is reduced to the hydroxylamine (–NHOH) without affecting the aromatic ring. Used to prepare phenylhydroxylamine for azo‑dye synthesis or as an intermediate in Fischer–Hepp rearrangements. Reaction is carried out in acetic acid solvent; no additional catalyst required.

High‑temperature redox (single‑displacement) of a metal with steam; hot magnesium metal reacts with H₂O(g) to give MgO and H₂ gas; carried out in a steam tube furnace at >500 °C; inert atmosphere not required, no solvent or catalyst.

Acid displacement (or salt metathesis) of potassium hexachloroplatinate(IV) with concentrated sulfuric acid, producing potassium sulfate, hydrogen chloride gas, and platinum tetrachloride (PtCl4). Usually performed by heating a mixture of K2[PtCl6] and 98 % H2SO4 at 80–120 °C. HCl evolves as a gas and is often trapped; the solid PtCl4 can be isolated by filtration. No external catalyst needed.

Double displacement precipitation with ammonium phosphate and lutetium nitrate; purpose: synthesize lutetium phosphate while forming ammonium nitrate by‑product; key transformation: Lu(NO₃)₃ + (NH₄)₃PO₄ → LuPO₄ + 3 NH₄NO₃; typical conditions: aqueous medium, ambient to slightly elevated temperature (≈60 °C) with stirring; water solvent; no catalyst required.

Acid–base gas absorption reaction where sulfur dioxide (SO2) reacts with aqueous potassium carbonate (K2CO3). The acidic oxide is protonated and converts the carbonate to carbon dioxide (CO2) and potassium sulfite (K2SO3). Conducted at ambient temperature in water; the CO2 gas is released, and the aqueous solution contains K2SO3. No catalyst required.

Radical hydrogen‑atom abstraction: a hydrogen atom attacks acetylene, abstracting a hydrogen to generate the ethynyl radical (C₂H) and molecular hydrogen. This gas‑phase radical addition step occurs under high‑temperature or photolytic conditions that produce H atoms (e.g., UV photolysis of H₂). No solvent; a radical initiator may be used.

Acid–base neutralization and gas evolution; ammonium hydrogen sulfate is treated with aqueous sodium hydroxide, producing sodium hydrogen sulfate, water, and liberating ammonia gas. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature or with gentle heating; the reaction proceeds without additional catalysts.

High‑temperature thermal decomposition (pyrolysis) of cadmium sulfide (CdS) into elemental cadmium vapor and elemental sulfur vapor. Requires temperatures above ~1500 °C under an inert or reduced‑pressure atmosphere to prevent oxidation. The process is used for purification of Cd or S and for vapor‑phase deposition techniques. No solvent or catalyst; only heat.

Halogen‑exchange/acyl‑chloride formation: hydrogen chloride reacts with trifluoroacetic anhydride to give trifluoroacetic acid and trifluoroacetyl chloride. Typically performed at 0–25 °C in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, often with a base (e.g., pyridine) to scavenge the generated HCl and drive the reaction forward. Provides a convenient route to the highly reactive acyl chloride.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration of vanillin using the mixed acid system of concentrated nitric acid and sulfuric acid. The mixture generates the nitronium ion (NO2⁺), which substitutes at the 5‑position of the aromatic ring, yielding 5‑nitrovanillin and water. Reaction is carried out at 0–5 °C initially, then allowed to warm to 20–30 °C, usually in sulfuric acid as solvent. No external catalyst; temperature control is critical to avoid over‑nitration or oxidation.

N‑carbamoylation (cyanogen bromide mediated) of glycine; purpose is conversion of the α‑amino group into an N‑carbamoyl functionality yielding hydantoic acid. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of the amino nitrogen on CNBr forming an N‑cyanamide intermediate, which hydrolyzes with water to give the carbamoyl carbonyl and releases HBr. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, temperature 0 °C to ambient, pH buffered mildly basic to neutral; no additional catalyst required. Common solvent: water (occasionally mixed with a miscible organic co‑solvent).

Metathesis precipitation forming insoluble NdF3 from Nd(NO3)3 and NaF, with NaNO3 remaining in solution; typical conditions involve aqueous medium, often mildly heated to ensure dissolution, followed by filtration of the NdF3 precipitate.

Acid‑base (neutralization) reaction; converts sodium oxide and hydrogen sulfide into sodium sulfide with water as by‑product; conducted at elevated temperature in the gas or solid phase; no solvent or catalyst.

High‑temperature solid‑state synthesis (acidic oxide neutralization); silica reacts with molten KOH to yield potassium silicate (e.g., K₂SiO₃) and water vapor. Requires temperatures above ~300 °C; performed without solvent and without a catalyst.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification of an ethyl β‑keto ester; purpose is to replace the ethoxy group with a methoxy group, giving methyl 3‑oxopentanoate; key steps involve methoxide attack on the carbonyl and formation of sodium ethoxide as by‑product; typical conditions: methanol as solvent, 0.1–0.2 eq sodium methoxide, reflux (≈65 °C) for 1–3 h under nitrogen.

Copper(II) chloride‑catalyzed acetylation (Fischer‑type esterification) of 2‑pentanol with acetic anhydride. Purpose is synthesis of the secondary acetate ester, 2‑pentyl acetate. Key transformation: the hydroxyl oxygen attacks one carbonyl of acetic anhydride, displacing acetate; CuCl₂ acts as a Lewis acid to activate the anhydride and promote ester formation, generating one equivalent of acetic acid as by‑product. Typical conditions: reflux in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine, 1–2 equiv of CuCl₂, reaction time 1–4 h. Solvent often pyridine which also scavenges the formed acid.

Grignard nucleophilic substitution on dimethylgermane dichloride. Purpose is preparation of tetra‑methylgermane. Key transformation: two equivalents of methylmagnesium chloride transfer methyl groups the germanium center, displacing both chloride ligands as MgCl₂. Reaction type is a Grignard transmetallation/alkyl‑metal halide substitution. Typical conditions: anhydrous ethereal solvent (diethyl ether or THF), inert atmosphere (N₂), 0 °C to reflux, stoichiometric amounts of reagents. No additional catalyst.

Grignard addition to a carbonyl; acetophenone reacts with phenylmagnesium bromide (1 eq) in dry Et₂O or THF at 0 °C to rt; nucleophilic attack forms a tertiary alkoxide which on aqueous NH₄Cl work‑up gives 1,1‑diphenylpropan‑2‑ol; anhydrous ether solvent and inert atmosphere required.

Copper(II) bromide‑catalyzed oxidative bromination of 2‑methoxyphenylbor acid with hydrogen peroxide (Chan–Lam type halogenation). Purpose is synthesis of 2‑bromoanisole. Key transformation: Cu(II) is reduced by H₂O₂ to Cu(I), which then reacts with the aryl‑B(OH)₂ to form a Cu‑aryl intermediate; oxidative rebound with Br⁻ yields the aryl bromide and regenerates Cu(II). By‑products are water and boric acid. Typical conditions: aqueous or mixed aqueous/organic solvent (e.g., MeCN/H₂O), temperature 25–50 °C, catalytic CuBr₂ (5–10 mol %). Base (e.g., Na₂CO₃) is often added to keep the boronic acid soluble.

Condensation of sulfuric acid with sulfur trioxide to give disulfuric acid (pyrosulfuric acid, H₂S₂O₇). Purpose is preparation of a stronger sulfonating agent (oleum). Key transformation: electrophilic addition of SO₃ to the hydroxyl group of H₂SO₄, forming the anhydride linkage S‑O‑S. Typical conditions: low temperature (0–25 °C) under anhydrous conditions, usually performed in the gas‑phase or in a dry glass apparatus; no solvent, the reagents are combined directly. The reaction is exothermic and often carried out with careful temperature control.

Peracid epoxidation (Prilezhaev oxidation) of acrylamide using peroxytrifluoroac acid. Purpose is conversion of the vinyl double bond to the epoxy ring, yielding glycidamide. Key transformation: concerted transfer of an oxygen atom from the peroxyacid to the C=C bond, forming the three‑membered epoxide and releasing trifluoroacetic acid. Typical conditions: dilute solution of peroxytrifluoroacetic acid in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, 0 °C to room temperature, reaction time 1–2 h. The peracid is generated in situ or used freshly due to its instability.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (halogenation); replaces a hydrogen on the aromatic ring of 2‑methylphenol with chlorine to give 4‑chloro‑2‑methylphenol while generating HCl. Typically carried out with Cl₂ in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst such as FeCl₃ or AlCl₃, at 0 °C to room temperature, in a non‑polar solvent like carbon tetrachloride or chloroform.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an alkyl halide by azide; potassium azide displaces iodide in iodoethane to form ethyl azide and potassium iodide. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF or DMSO) at ambient temperature or mild heating; often performed under nitrogen to avoid moisture.

Deoxyfluorination of primary alcohols using diethylaminosulfur trifluoride (DAST). Benzyl alcohol is converted to benzyl fluoride while DAST is reduced to diethylamine, sulfur dioxide, and hydrogen fluoride. The reaction is carried out at 0 °C to rt in anhydrous CH₂Cl₂ or THF under nitrogen; care is taken to exclude moisture because DAST is moisture sensitive.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation) of a long‑chain alkyl bromide; hydrogen gas in the presence of a metal catalyst (Pd/C, Raney Ni, or PtO₂) reduces nonadecyl bromide to nonadecane, releasing hydrogen bromide. Conducted under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) at 25–80 °C in solvents such as ethanol, THF, or ethyl acetate.

Halide–acetate metathesis (acid‑base ligand exchange) between acetic acid and niobium(V) bromide. The Br⁻ ligands are displaced by acetate to afford niobium(V) acetate, releasing hydrogen bromide gas. Conducted in a dry, non‑coordinating solvent such as bromobenzene or toluene at reflux, often under an inert atmosphere to collect HBr.

Benzylic free‑radical bromination (side‑chain substitution); two bromine molecules abstract hydrogen atoms from the methyl groups of o‑xylene, forming o‑bis(bromomethyl)benzene and two equivalents of HBr. Reaction proceeds under UV light or heat in an inert, non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, with the temperature kept below 50 °C to limit over‑bromination.

Condensation/cyclization (intramolecular Mannich-type reaction). Ethylene diamine reacts with formaldehyde to form a six‑membered heterocycle (piperazine) with loss of water. Typically carried out in aqueous or alcoholic solution at reflux, often under mildly acidic conditions (e.g., a few drops of acetic acid) to promote imine formation, and the water formed is removed by azeotropic distillation or Dean‑Stark trap.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation. Barium chloride exchanges anions with stearate, producing insoluble barium stearate which precipitates and soluble sodium chloride remaining in solution. Conducted in aqueous medium at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring; the solid barium stearate is filtered and washed. No catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution – sulfonation. Sulfur trioxide (often as fuming sulfuric acid) attacks the para position of toluene, yielding para‑toluenesulfonic acid. Reaction performed at 0–50 °C in concentrated H₂SO₄ or SO₃/H₂SO₄ mixture, with careful temperature control to avoid polysulfonation. Work‑up involves quenching with ice water and isolation of the acid by crystallization.

Acid‑base (deprotonation) neutralization. The acidic NH of 5,5‑diphenylhydantoin is deprotonated by sodium hydroxide, giving the corresponding sodium salt and water. Typically carried out in aqueous NaOH solution at room temperature, often with mild heating to ensure complete dissolution. No special catalyst; the reaction is driven by stoichiometric base.

Base‑catalyzed thioester hydrolysis (saponification). Sodium hydroxide cleaves allyl thioacetate, producing the thiol (allyl mercaptan) and sodium acetate. Conducted in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑ethanol medium, usually at 50–80 °C for several hours. The thiol can be extracted with an organic solvent (e.g., diethyl ether) after neutralization. No additional catalyst needed.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (N‑demethylation) of codeine, cleaving the N‑methyl group to give norcodeine and releasing methane. Conducted with hydrogen gas (1–5 atm) over a palladium‑on‑carbon (Pd/C) or Raney nickel catalyst in a solvent such as methanol or ethanol, at 25–60 °C. The reaction selectively removes the methyl substituent from the nitrogen, producing the demethylated alkaloid and CH4 as the volatile by‑product.

Metallothermic reduction: zirconium tetrachloride is reduced by sodium metal to give zirconium metal and sodium chloride. Purpose is preparation of Zr metal. Conducted at high temperature (≈600–800 °C) in a sealed, dry, inert atmosphere (argon). Sodium and ZrCl4 are mixed as solids or in a molten salt medium; no additional solvent.

Oxidation of thymine with selenium dioxide; converts the 5‑methyl group of thymine to an aldehyde, producing 5‑formyluracil while reducing SeO2 to elemental selenium and generating water. Typical conditions: reflux in a polar organic solvent such as dioxane‑water or DMF, 1–2 equivalents SeO2, inert atmosphere, no additional catalyst.

Double displacement (metathesis) acid‑base reaction; purpose is to exchange the anions of hydrobromic acid and calcium nitrate to generate free nitric acid and calcium bromide. Key transformation: 2 HBr + Ca(NO₃)₂ → 2 HNO₃ + CaBr₂. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or with mild heating; no catalyst needed; water is the solvent and the products remain in solution (HNO₃ may be distilled off).

Halogenation of phenoxyethanol with phosphorus pentachloride; a nucleophilic substitution that replaces the hydroxyl group with chlorine to give 2‑chloro‑1‑phenoxyethane, with formation of phosphorus oxychloride as by‑product. Conducted under anhydrous conditions, typically in dichloromethane or toluene at 0 °C to reflux; excess PCl5 is used, no additional catalyst.

Reduction of tungsten(VI) chloride by sodium metal; sodium donates electrons to WCl6, reducing it to tungsten(V) chloride (WCl5) and forming sodium chloride. Usually carried out in dry THF or diethyl ether under inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) at low temperature (‑78 °C to room temperature); solid‑state or solution‑phase reduction, no catalyst.

Acylation of isobutylamine with acetic anhydride; nucleophilic attack of the amine on the anhydride furnishes N‑isobutylide and acetic acid as by‑product. Typical procedure: add 1 equiv acetic anhydride to the amine in a solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine, stir at 0 °C to rt; reaction proceeds without catalyst, though pyridine can act as base to scavenge the acid.

Salt formation of oxprenolol with hydrochloric acid; protonation of the basic amine gives oxprenolol hydrochloride. Performed by dissolving oxprenolol in ethanol, isopropanol or water and adding aqueous or gaseous HCl at 0 °C to rt, followed by crystallization; no catalyst required.

Nitrous acid mediated deamination (oxidative deamination) of isocytosine, converting the exocyclic amino group into a carbonyl, releasing nitrogen gas and water to give uracil; typically performed in aqueous acidic medium at 0‑25 °C.

Oxidation-reduction reaction; concentrated sulfuric acid oxidizes H2Se to elemental selenium and SO2, with water as a byproduct; requires strong acidic and oxidizing conditions; typically carried out by adding H2Se to concentrated H2SO4 under controlled temperature.

Fischer esterification of diethylene glycol with acetic acid; general type = acid‑catalyzed esterification; purpose = obtain the same mono‑acetate as above; key transformation = one hydroxyl of the diol reacts with acetic acid, water is eliminated, giving 2‑(2‑hydroxyethoxy)ethyl acetate; typical conditions = reflux diethylene glycol with excess acetic acid in the presence of a strong acid catalyst (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑toluenesulfonic acid) at 100–120 °C, continuously removing water (e.g., Dean‑Stark trap) to shift equilibrium; common solvents/catalysts = often performed without an added solvent (acetic acid acts as both reactant and solvent) or in toluene with a catalytic amount of acid.

Acidic redox reaction where potassium permanganate oxidizes Fe(II) to Fe(III) while being reduced from Mn(VII) to Mn(II) in excess HCl, yielding KCl, water, FeCl₃ and MnCl₂; carried out in aqueous hydrochloric acid, ambient temperature, with stirring.

Acid–base reaction; nickel(II) oxide dissolves in hydrogen chloride to form nickel(II) chloride and water; usually carried out in aqueous HCl solution with heating to accelerate dissolution; water is the solvent and no catalyst is employed.

Acid–base neutralization; purpose: convert magnesium carbonate to a soluble magnesium salt while releasing CO₂; key transformation: MgCO₃ + 2 HClO₃ → Mg(ClO₃)₂ + CO₂ + H₂O; typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature or with gentle heating to drive off CO₂; solvent: water; no catalyst required.

Oxidation of diethyl sulfide to diethyl sulfoxide using sodium hypochlorite (bleach); reaction proceeds in aqueous NaOCl, often buffered to pH 8‑9, at 0‑25 °C, producing NaCl and water as by‑products.

Metallothermic reduction of zirconium tetrachloride with lithium metal to give elemental zirconium and lithium chloride; performed under inert atmosphere (Ar or N₂), dry conditions, typically in a sealed tube or molten lithium at elevated temperatures (≈300‑500 °C).

Acid‑catalyzed ester cleavage with hydrogen bromide (hydrohalogenation); HBr protonates the carbonyl oxygen of propyl formate, bromide attacks the alkyl carbon displacing formate to afford 1‑propyl bromide and formic acid; reflux in concentrated aqueous HBr, no additional catalyst.

Fischer esterification of nicotinic (pyridine‑3‑carboxylic) acid with 2‑butoxyethanol catalyzed by sulfuric acid; reflux in excess alcohol or an inert solvent (toluene) with water removal (Dean‑Stark) affords 2‑butoxyethyl 3‑pyridinecarboxylate and water.

DCC‑mediated carbodiimide coupling of salicylic acid with 4‑tert‑butylphenol to form p‑tert‑butylphenyl salicylate, producing dicyclohexylurea as by‑product; conducted in anhydrous dichloromethane (or DMF) at 0 °C then warmed to room temperature under nitrogen.

Acid–base neutralization/precipitation. Salicylic acid (a phenolic carboxylic acid) reacts with basic bismuth oxide to protonate the oxide and form water while the bismuth cation coordinates two salicylate anions, giving bismuth subsalicylate precipitate. Typically performed in aqueous medium, often by heating a suspension of bismuth oxide in water and adding dissolved salicylic acid; the product isolates as a solid after cooling and filtration.

Crossed aldol (base‑catalyzed) condensation between acetaldehyde and the enolate of ethyl phenylacetate. Deprotonation of ethyl phenylacetate (usually with NaOEt or NaOH in ethanol) generates the nucleophilic enolate, which attacks the carbonyl carbon of acetaldehyde, forming a β‑hydroxy ester (ethyl 3‑hydroxy‑3‑phenylbutanoate). Reaction is carried out in ethanol or methanol at 0 °C to rt; mild base catalyst; work‑up involves acidification and extraction.

Base‑mediated hydrolysis (saponification) of an acid chloride; benzoyl chloride reacts with aqueous NaOH to give sodium benzoate, NaCl and water; purpose is to neutralize the acyl chloride and form the benzoate salt; performed at room temperature or mild heating in water with excess NaOH, stirring until completion.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt metathesis) of disodium ethylenediaminetetraacetate with sulfuric acid. Two equivalents of H₂SO₄ protonate the tetravalent carboxylate groups, yielding free ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) and sodium sulfate as by‑product. Performed in aqueous solution with gentle heating to ensure complete protonation and dissolution of the salts.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) in aqueous solution. Cobalt(II) chromate exchanges its anion with carbonate from ammonium carbonate, yielding insoluble cobalt(II) carbonate precipitate and soluble ammonium chromate. Reaction proceeds at ambient temperature in water; stirring promotes complete exchange; product filtered and washed.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction. Copper(II) chloride exchanges its chloride anions with benzoate from potassium benzoate, forming copper(II) benzoate (sparingly soluble) and potassium chloride in solution. Usually carried out in aqueous medium, often with gentle heating to ensure dissolution of reagents; copper(II) benzoate precipitates on cooling and is isolated by filtration.

Fischer esterification of methacrylic acid with ethanol; purpose is synthesis of the ester ethyl methacrylate. Key transformation: condensation of a carboxylic acid and an alcohol to form an ester and water. Typical conditions: reflux of methacrylic acid and excess ethanol in the presence of a catalytic amount of concentrated H2SO4 (≈1–5 %); removal of water (e.g., Dean‑Stark trap) to drive equilibrium. Common solvent: none required beyond the reactants, but inert solvent (toluene) can be used.

Ion‑exchange (salt metathesis) base generation. Sodium hydroxide displaces chloride from choline chloride, producing sodium, a quaternary ammonium base. Conducted in water at room temperature; the mixture is typically concentrated and choline hydroxide is isolated as an aqueous solution or lyophilized product.

General type: thermal decomposition (redox). Purpose: generate metallic silver and oxygen gas. Key transformation: decomposition of Ag2O to 2 Ag^0 and O2. Typical conditions: heating above 300 °C in a closed vessel or flow apparatus; no solvent or catalyst.

Sulfidation/reduction: Hydrogen sulfide reduces molybdenum trioxide to molybdenum disulfide, releasing water. Purpose is preparation of MoS2 from MoO3. Key transformation: MoO3 + H2S → MoS2 + H2O. Typical conditions are passage of H2S gas over MoO3 at 300‑600 °C in a flowing inert carrier gas; gas‑phase reaction with no solvent or catalyst.

Iodination/reduction synthesis: TeO2 reacts with excess HI to give TeI4 and water. Performed in a sealed tube at 150‑250 °C, using gaseous or liquid HI; excess HI drives conversion, and no separate solvent is needed.

Tosylation of a primary alcohol; conversion of pentan‑1‑ol to the pentyl p‑toluenesulfonate ester using p‑toluenesulfonyl chloride as the sulfonylating agent and pyridine as both solvent and base. Reaction is usually performed at 0 °C to room temperature in pyridine (or dichloromethane with pyridine) to scavenge HCl, yielding pyridinium chloride as a by‑product.

General type: O‑methylation (alkyl carbonate methylation) using dimethyl carbonate as green methylating agent. Purpose: convert catechol to veratrole (1,2‑dimethoxybenzene). Key transformation: two phenolic OH groups are methylated, yielding CO2 as by‑product. Typical conditions: reaction conducted at 120–150 °C in the ionic liquid 1‑butyl‑3‑methylimidazolium chloride, which acts as both solvent and catalyst; the ionic liquid may be recycled.

Alkali‑metal reduction (single‑displacement). Sodium metal reduces UCl₄ to uranium metal, producing NaCl as the only by‑product. Reaction performed in anhydrous, oxygen‑free conditions, usually in a sealed stainless‑steel or tantalum tube; the mixture may be heated to melt sodium (≈98 °C) or to 200–300 °C to promote contact. No solvent is required; sometimes dry aromatic hydrocarbons (e.g., THF) are used as a carrier to improve mixing.

General type: high‑temperature thermolysis/solid‑state synthesis of a metal silicide. Purpose: form iron silicide from silane and iron pentacarbonyl. Key transformation: Si–H bonds react with Fe(CO)5, releasing CO and H2 and depositing FeSi. Typical conditions: sealed tube or furnace heating to 200–400 °C under inert atmosphere (argon); no solvent, and the reaction proceeds via gas‑phase intermediates.

Hydrogenation of an α‑amino aldehyde to the corresponding β‑amino alcohol; purpose is reduction of the aldehyde carbonyl to a primary alcohol while leaving the amine unchanged. Typical conditions: 2‑amino‑3‑methylbutanal dissolved in methanol or ethanol, Pd/C (5–10 % w/w) or Raney Ni as catalyst, H₂ pressure 1–3 atm, temperature 25–50 °C, 2–6 h. Product is 2‑amino‑3‑methylbutan‑1‑ol.

Acid‑catalyzed acetal hydrolysis (deprotection); the 1,3‑dioxolane protecting group on 4‑pyridinecarboxaldehyde is cleaved by water to regenerate the aldehyde and release 1,2‑ethanediol; performed with dilute aqueous acid (e.g., HCl or p‑TsOH) at mild temperature; common solvent mixtures include THF/H2O or MeOH/H2O.

General type: catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dechlorination). Purpose: partial dechlorination of hexachlorobenzene to pentachlorobenzene, producing HCl. Key transformation: one C–Cl bond is replaced by C–H, releasing HCl. Typical conditions: H2 gas (1–5 atm) with a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, Raney Ni, or a Cu‑Cl/Al2O3 system; temperature 150–250 °C; reaction performed in an organic solvent like toluene or hexane.

Friedel‑Crafts acid‑catalyzed alkylation of phenol with isobutylene; electrophilic aromatic substitution installs a tert‑butyl group giving 2‑tert‑butylphenol. Performed with phosphoric acid (or other solid Brønsted acid) as the catalyst, usually neat or in a non‑coordinating solvent (e.g., toluene) at 80–130 °C under a stream of isobutylene gas; no external metal catalyst required.

Salt metathesis. Reaction between nickel acetate and sodium carbonate in aqueous solution produces nickel carbonate precipitate and sodium acetate. Progresses under ambient conditions without catalysts, driven by insolubility of nickel carbonate.

Electrophilic nitrosation of urea; a nitrosyl chloride reagent delivers a nitroso group to the nitrogen of urea, forming an N‑nitrosourea and liberating HCl. Typically carried out in a dry non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a base such as pyridine to scavenge the generated HCl.

Nucleophilic substitution followed by intramolecular cyclization (ring‑closure) to form a piperazine derivative; purpose is to couple 4‑methylphenylhydrazine with 1,2‑dibromoethane, generating 1‑(p‑tolyl)piperazine with loss of HBr. Key transformation: 4‑Me‑PhNHNH₂ + BrCH₂CH₂Br → 1‑(p‑tolyl)piperazine + 2 HBr. Typically performed in ethanol or isopropanol under reflux, using a base such as Na₂CO₃ or triethylamine to neutralize the liberated HBr; no transition‑metal catalyst is required.

N‑ethylation of ketene to produce N‑ethylacetamide; analogous nucleophilic addition of ethylamine to ketene; forms a secondary amide; typical conditions involve a polar aprotic or alcoholic solvent (e.g., THF, methanol) at 0 °C to 25 °C, often under nitrogen; no catalyst needed.

Acidic hydrolysis of metaphosphoric (polyphosphoric) acid; water cleaves the P‑O‑P bonds to yield orthophosphoric acid. Usually performed by adding water to the polyacid and heating gently (50–80 °C) until dissolution is complete; no special catalyst is required.

Electrophilic nitro‑ylation (nitronium ion reaction) of urea; purpose is to N‑nitrosate urea forming nitrourea while generating tetrafluoroboric acid from the BF₄⁻ counter‑ion. Key transformation: (NH₂)₂CO + NO₂⁺ BF₄⁻ → (NH₂)CONO₂ + HBF₄. Conducted in anhydrous, aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane at low temperature (‑20 °C to 0 °C) under inert atmosphere; the reaction proceeds without additional catalyst, but the nitronium tetrafluoroborate is itself a strong electrophile.

Acid‑catalyzed ketal formation (protecting the carbonyl of ethyl acetoacetate) with ethylene glycol; sulfuric acid protonates the carbonyl, enabling nucleophilic attack by ethylene glycol and subsequent loss of water to give the ethylene glycol ketal of the β‑keto ester. Typical conditions: catalytic H₂SO₄ (1–5 mol %), reflux in toluene or benzene, and removal of water by a Dean‑Stark trap.

Synthesis (combination) reaction; elemental lead reacts directly with elemental sulfur to form lead(II) sulfide (galena, PbS). Typically performed by mixing solid Pb and S and heating to 400–600 °C in a furnace under an inert atmosphere; no solvent is used.

Chlorination/dehydration reaction; boric acid is converted to boron trichloride by thionyl chloride, which acts as a chlorinating agent and also generates HCl and SO₂ gases. The transformation replaces –OH groups with –Cl, yielding BCl₃ gas. Conducted under anhydrous conditions, often in a dry inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chlorobenzene, at 0 °C to reflux; gases are removed continuously.

Alcoholysis (condensation) of silicon tetrachloride; four molecules of ethanol react with SiCl₄, with pyridine acting as a base to capture the liberated HCl, forming tetraethoxysilane (TEOS) and four equivalents of pyridinium chloride. Reaction is performed under anhydrous, inert atmosphere (e.g., N₂) in a dry aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or toluene, at 0 °C to room temperature. Pyridine is used in stoichiometric excess to drive HCl removal.

Oxidation of a thioether to a sulfone; purpose is to convert tetrahydrothiophene into the cyclic sulfone sulfolane while generating acetic acid as by‑product. Key transformation: insertion of two oxygen atoms onto the sulfur (R‑S‑R → R‑S(=O)₂‑R). Typical conditions: peracetic acid (30 % aqueous) added dropwise to a solution of tetrahydrothiophene in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetic acid, temperature 0 °C to room temperature, stirring 1–4 h. No additional catalyst required; work‑up with aqueous base removes excess peracid.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (hydrolytic cleavage); water attacks allyl phenylacetate to regenerate phenylacetic acid and release allyl alcohol; carried out in aqueous HCl or H₂SO₄ at reflux temperature, often in a mixture of water and a miscible organic solvent (e.g., THF or dioxane) to improve miscibility.

Simple acid‑base neutralization forming the ammonium salt tributylammonium chloride. Usually performed by mixing stoichiometric HCl with tributylamine in a suitable solvent such as ethanol, methanol, or dichloromethane at ambient temperature; the reaction proceeds quantitatively without catalyst.

Selective reduction (hydride reduction of aldehyde); sodium borohydride reduces 2‑methoxybenzaldehyde to 2‑methoxybenzyl alcohol; carried out in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature, followed by aqueous work‑up.

Double‑displacement (precipitation) reaction; aqueous sodium hydroxide reacts with YbBr₃ to form a precipitate of ytterbium hydroxide and soluble sodium bromide. Performed in water at ambient temperature; stirring sufficient, no catalyst needed.

Association (dimerization) of alkali metal atoms; two gaseous rubidium atoms combine to form a dirubidium (Rb₂) diatomic molecule. Observed under high‑temperature vapor conditions (e.g., in an oven or molecular beam) at low pressures where collisions are infrequent; no solvent or catalyst is involved.

Combination (solid‑state synthesis) of a metal and a non‑metal to form a binary sulfide; heating elemental indium with elemental sulfur (often 500–800 °C) under inert atmosphere or vacuum, no solvent, yields indium(III) sulfide (In₂S₃).

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (acetyl transfer) in which acetylimidazole serves as an acetyl donor to isoamyl alcohol; the alcohol attacks the carbonyl forming isoamyl acetate and releasing imidazole; typically performed at room temperature or slight warming in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, no catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of a trihalomethane; hydrogen gas reduces chloroform over palladium on carbon, cleaving one C–Cl bond to give dichloromethane and hydrogen chloride; carried out under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) at 0–50 °C in a protic or aprotic solvent (e.g., ethanol, ethyl acetate).
Double displacement reaction; generates hydrogen selenide and sodium sulfate via acid treatment; selenide protonation to volatile H2Se; aqueous sulfuric acid, room temperature; no catalyst.

Direct combination (halogenation) to prepare a binary selenium chloride; chlorine gas is bubbled into molten or dissolved selenium at low temperature (often –78 °C to 0 °C) in an inert, non‑reactive solvent such as carbon tetrachloride, affording diselenium dichloride (Se₂Cl₂).

Halogen exchange (redox metathesis) where chlorine oxidizes iodide in titanium diiodide to elemental iodine while chloride replaces iodide to give titanium dichloride; typically conducted in a dry, inert solvent (e.g., CCl₄ or CH₂Cl₂) at 0–25 °C under a chlorine atmosphere, no catalyst required.

Reaction type: Weinreb‑amide to aromatic ketone via Grignard addition. Purpose: synthesize acetophenone. Key transformation: phenylmagnesium bromide adds to the Weinreb amide, forming a chelated magnesium complex; aqueous work‑up releases acetophenone and N‑methoxy‑N‑methylamine. Typical conditions: anhydrous ether or THF, -78 °C to 0 °C, nitrogen atmosphere, 1–2 h. No catalyst needed.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution of a primary alkyl chloride by sulfite ion; sodium sulfite reacts with (3‑chloropropyl)trimethylsilane in aqueous or polar aprotic medium (e.g., DMF/H₂O) at 50–80 °C, producing sodium chloride and sodium 3‑(trimethylsilyl)‑1‑propanesulfonate.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) ion‑exchange between sodium carbonate and potassium metaphosphate in aqueous solution, swapping the cations to give potassium carbonate and sodium metaphosphate. Conducted in water at moderate temperature (20–50 °C); the reaction is driven to completion by crystallization or removal of one product; no catalyst required.

Condensation (aminal formation) of 1,3,5‑trioxane with ammonium hydroxide to give hexamethylenetetramine (urotropine) and water. This is a base‑catalyzed cyclocondensation of formaldehyde equivalents with ammonia, employed for synthesis of the heterocyclic aminal. Conducted in aqueous NH₄OH, refluxing (≈100 °C) for several hours; often performed in a sealed tube or under reflux with vigorous stirring. No additional catalyst required.

Alpha‑bromination of 2‑butanone using sodium hypobromite (NaOBr). Electrophilic substitution at the carbonyl α‑position to afford 1‑bromo‑2‑butanone with concomitant formation of NaOH. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOBr generated in situ from NaBr/NaOCl, reaction kept cold (0–5 °C) initially, then allowed to warm to room temperature; pH is controlled to avoid over‑bromination. No external catalyst needed.

Acid‑induced cleavage of trimethylsilyldiazomethane to generate diazomethane and trimethylsilyl chloride. Serves as a convenient method to release the highly reactive diazomethane gas. Performed by adding gaseous or aqueous HCl (often in ether or dichloromethane) to a solution of TMS‑diazomethane at 0 °C under inert atmosphere; the mixture is then distilled or extracted to isolate diazomethane. No catalyst beyond the acid.
Acid‑base neutralization; hydrogen bromide reacts with ammonium hydroxide (aqueous NH4OH) to afford ammonium bromide and water; performed in water at normal temperature, no catalyst needed.

N‑methylation (SN2 alkylation) of 4‑phenyl‑1,2,3,6‑tetrahydropyridine with methyl trifluoromethanesulfonate in the presence of triethylamine. The strong methylating agent transfers a methyl group to the nitrogen, while triethylamine scavenges the generated triflate acid. Conducted in anhydrous aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; reaction time ranges from minutes to a few hours. No additional catalyst required.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to a strained ketone using sodium hypochlorite (bleach). Key transformation: cyclopropanol → cyclopropanone with NaOCl acting as the oxidant, generating NaCl and H2O as by‑products. Typically carried out in a biphasic mixture of water and an organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0–25 °C; pH buffered (often NaHCO3) to avoid over‑oxidation.

Double‑displacement (precipitation) reaction: barium chloride reacts with lithium carbonate to form soluble lithium chloride and highly insoluble barium carbonate, which precipitates. This reaction is often used to remove barium ions or to produce barium carbonate. Conducted in aqueous solution, typically at room temperature; the barium carbonate is collected by filtration. No catalyst is required.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction between sulfuric acid and barium selenate, producing selenic acid (H₂SeO₄) and insoluble barium sulfate (BaSO₄). Used to generate strong selenic acid in situ while removing barium as a filterable solid. Performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; the mixture is stirred until BaSO₄ precipitates fully, then filtered to obtain the acidic filtrate. No catalyst needed.

Reaction type: Electrophilic aromatic substitution (chlorination). Purpose: Synthesis of polychlorinated dibenzofurans. Key transformation: Introduction of four chlorine atoms at positions 2,3,7,8 of dibenzofuran. Conditions: Iron(III) chloride acts as a catalyst to activate chlorine gas, likely requiring an inert atmosphere and elevated temperature. Solvent: Possibly chlorinated hydrocarbons.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) quaternization of trimethylphosphine with methyl iodide to give tetramethylphosphonium iodide; usually performed in an aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile, THF or dichloromethane at rt to reflux; no catalyst required

Reaction type: Electrophilic aromatic substitution (nitration). Purpose: Site-specific nitration of 8-hydroxyquinoline. Key transformation: Nitro group introduced at position 5 of quinoline via acetylation-controlled activation. Conditions: Nitric acid activated by acetic anhydride under acidic conditions. Catalyst: Acetic acid/acetate species may control regioselectivity.

Reaction type: Acid-catalyzed ester hydrolysis. Purpose: Cleavage of methyl ester to phenylacetic acid. Key transformation: Bimolecular hydrolysis of methyl phenylacetate yielding methanol and phenylacetic acid. Conditions: Dilute aqueous HCl at reflux. Solvent: Water.

Reaction type: N-oxide reduction. Purpose: Conversion of 2-methylpyridine N-oxide to 2-methylpyridine. Key transformation: Deoxygenation of the N-oxide group using zinc dust. Conditions: Zinc in acetic acid as both solvent and proton donor under reflux. Catalyst: Electron transfer from zinc activates the reduction.

Reaction type: Metathesis/halogenation. Purpose: Conversion of iron(III) acetate to iron(III) bromide. Key transformation: Exchange of acetate and bromide ions. Conditions: Stoichiometric excess of hydrobromic acid in aqueous solution at ambient temperature. Solvent: Water.

Hydrolysis of a phenyl phosphate ester; purpose is to break the P–OAr bond and liberate phenol. Phenyl dihydrogen phosphate decomposes to phenol and phosphoric acid upon heating in aqueous or mildly acidic medium. Typical conditions are reflux in water or a water‑methanol mixture; no additional catalyst is required.

Free‑radical halogenation; photochemical substitution of a secondary hydrogen in propane with bromine under UV light (often in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride); produces 2‑bromopropane and HBr as a by‑product; used for preparing alkyl bromides.

Ester aminolysis with methylamine to give a secondary amide. Methylamine nucleophilically replaces the butyl group of n‑butyl hexanoate, producing N‑methylhexanamide and n‑butanol. Carried out with excess methylamine (gas or 2‑M solution in ethanol) under reflux (70–100 °C) in a solvent like ethanol or toluene; optionally a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or base can be used to improve conversion.

Conversion of 2‑furancarboxylic acid to 2‑furoyl chloride using phosphorus pentachloride; acid chloride formed with by‑products POCl₃ and HCl; reaction performed in anhydrous chlorinated solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride) at reflux or room temperature; excess PCl₅ is used.

Acid–base reaction with carbonate decomposition; copper(II) carbonate reacts with boric acid, releasing carbon dioxide and water while forming copper(II) borate; performed in aqueous solution with heating to drive off CO₂ (≈60–100 °C), after which the copper borate precipitates; no catalyst needed.

Reaction type: Hydrazone formation (nucleophilic addition-elimination). Purpose: Formation of acetone hydrazone from ketone and hydrazine. Key transformation: Condensation of hydrazine with acetone carbonyl group. Conditions: Reflux in aqueous/ethanolic medium. Catalyst: Protonation by H+ from hydrochloride salt accelerates reaction.

Disproportionation (redox) of bromous acid; purpose: produce higher‑oxidation bromic acid and lower‑oxidation hypobromous acid; key transformation: 2 HBrO2 → HBrO3 + HBrO; typical conditions: aqueous solution, often mildly heated or in the presence of acid; solvent: water.

Acid leaching / salt metathesis: Zinc chromite (ZnCr₂O₄) is dissolved by concentrated hydrochloric acid, converting the oxide framework into soluble zinc chloride and chromium(III) chloride while producing water. Typically performed by refluxing the solid in aqueous HCl (excess) at 80‑100 °C; no special catalyst is required. The reaction is used for recovering metal chlorides from mixed oxides.

Strong oxidative cleavage of 1,3‑propanediol by potassium permanganate in alkaline aqueous medium; the diol is oxidized to malondialdehyde while MnO₄⁻ is reduced to insoluble MnO₂ and K⁺ forms KOH. Typical conditions: aqueous KOH solution, KMnO₄ added portionwise at 0–25 °C to control over‑oxidation, then stirred at room temperature; the MnO₂ precipitate is filtered off to isolate the aldehyde product.

Double displacement precipitation: cobalt(II) chloride reacts with sodium carbonate to form insoluble cobalt(II) carbonate and sodium chloride; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the solvent.

Ullmann ether synthesis (aryl‑alkyl ether formation): Copper‑catalyzed coupling of chlorobenzene with sodium ethoxide yields ethyl phenyl ether. The reaction proceeds via oxidative addition of the aryl chloride to a Cu(I) species, transmetalation with ethoxide, and reductive elimination to form the C–O bond. Typical conditions: CuI or CuBr (5‑10 mol %), NaOEt (1.2 eq), polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, heated to 120‑150 °C under inert atmosphere. No external base beyond the alkoxide is required; NaCl is the by‑product.

DCC‑mediated amidation (carboxylic acid activation): Isonicotinic acid is activated by dicyclohexylcarbodiimide (DCC) to form an O‑acylurea intermediate, which then reacts with hydrazine to give isoniazid (pyridine‑4‑carboxylic acid hydrazide). The reaction is an amide‑bond forming coupling, often performed in dry dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature. Catalytic DMAP may be added to accelerate. Dicyclohexylurea precipitates and is filtered off.

Direct amidation of iodoacetic acid with ammonia: Ammonia nucleophilically attacks the carbonyl carbon of iodoacetic acid, displacing water to form iodoacetamide and releasing a molecule of water. Because simple carboxylic acids are poor acyl donors, the reaction is usually carried out under reflux in excess aqueous ammonia or in the presence of a coupling agent (e.g., EDC) to drive amide formation. Typical conditions: aqueous NH₃ (10‑20 M), heat to 80‑100 °C for several hours; the product precipitates on cooling.

Azo coupling (electrophilic azo condensation); purpose is to form an azo‑dye linking phenyl diazonium to the enol form of acetylacetone; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of the enol on the diazonium N₂⁺, creating an N=N bond and yielding 3‑phenylazoacetylacetone while generating tetrafluoroboric acid; typical conditions: cold acidic medium (0–5 °C) in glacial acetic acid or AcOH/H₂O mixture; no metal catalyst required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution with a Grignard reagent; MeMgBr adds to the carbonyl of benzyl thioacetate, displacing the benzyl thiolate to afford acetone; the liberated thiolate is protonated during work‑up to give benzyl mercaptan. Performed under anhydrous conditions in ether or THF, typically at 0 °C to reflux, using 1.5–2 equiv of MeMgBr.

Iron‑catalyzed oxidative phenol coupling (Fenton‑type oxidation); purpose is to synthesize 4,4′‑dihydroxybiphenyl from phenol; key transformation involves Fe²⁺/H₂O₂ generation of phenoxy radicals that couple at the para positions to give the biphenyl diol, with Fe²⁺ oxidized to Fe³⁺; performed in aqueous solution, often at ambient temperature, slightly acidic to neutral pH; catalyst: catalytic FeSO₄ (iron(II) sulfate); solvent: water.

Negishi cross‑coupling of an aryl halide with an organozinc reagent; purpose is to construct the C‑C bond of 4‑phenylpyridine; key steps are transmetalation of phenylzinc bromide to Pd(0) (Pd(PPh₃)₄), followed by reductive elimination replacing the iodine on 4‑iodopyridine with phenyl; typical conditions: inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar), anhydrous THF as solvent, 50–80 °C; catalyst: tetrakis(triphenylphosphine)palladium(0); no additional base required.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; aqueous NaOH solution reacts with dysprosium fluoride to exchange anions, forming soluble sodium fluoride and insoluble dysprosium hydroxide precipitate; typically performed in water at or slightly elevated temperature, no special catalyst required.

N‑alkylation of 1‑methylxanthine via SN2 substitution; purpose is to prepare the phosphodiesterase inhibitor 3‑isobutyl‑1‑methylxanthine (IBMX); key transformation is nucleophilic attack of the xanthine nitrogen on isobutyl iodide displacing iodide; typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, base (e.g., K₂CO₃ or NaH) to deprotonate the nitrogen, reflux temperature, inert atmosphere; no metal catalyst required.

Base‑induced precipitation; aqueous ammonia provides OH⁻ which reacts with Nd³⁺ to form neodymium hydroxide precipitate, while acetate is converted to ammonium acetate in solution. Carried out in aqueous medium at room temperature or slightly elevated temperature; no catalyst.

Double‑displacement ionic exchange in aqueous medium; purpose is to form strontium diiodate from strontium nitrate and sodium iodate; key transformation swaps the anions: Sr(NO₃)₂ + 2 NaIO₃ → Sr(IO₃)₂ + 2 NaNO₃; performed in water at ambient temperature; no catalyst needed.

Substitution of phenolic OH by chlorine using thionyl chloride; 2‑chlorophenol reacts with SOCl₂ (usually in the presence of pyridine or another base) at 0 °C to reflux, converting the OH to Cl and producing 1,2‑dichlorobenzene along with sulfur dioxide and hydrogen chloride gases.

Double‑displacement/precipitation reaction of sodium fluoride with magnesium sulfate; forms poorly soluble magnesium fluoride (MgF2) precipitate and sodium sulfate stays dissolved; carried out in water, often with gentle heating to improve precipitation.

Electrophilic addition of chlorine across the C=C bond of propene; purpose is preparation of a vicinal dichloride; key transformation CH2=CH‑CH3 + Cl2 → CH2Cl‑CHCl‑CH3 (1,2‑dichloropropane); typical conditions room temperature in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform; no catalyst needed

Dehydrative conversion of an amide to a nitrile using thionyl chloride; purpose is synthesis of benzonitrile from benzamide; key transformation C6H5‑C(=O)‑NH2 → C6H5‑C≡N with evolution of 2 HCl and SO2; typical conditions reflux in anhydrous solvent (dry dichloromethane or pyridine) under nitrogen, pyridine often used to trap HCl; moisture‑free environment required

Oxidation (combustion) of cerium(III) sulfide; solid Ce2S3 reacts with O2 at elevated temperature (typically >400 °C) to give cerium dioxide (CeO2) solid and gaseous SO2; carried out in air or pure O2 flow; no catalyst needed.

Oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid with concentrated nitric acid; purpose is conversion of 2,3,6‑trichlorobenzaldehyde to the corresponding acid; key transformation Ar‑CHO → Ar‑COOH with formation of H2O and 2 NO2; typical conditions dropwise addition of aldehyde to cold (0–25 °C) conc. HNO3 then stirring at 40–60 °C until gas evolution ceases; reaction carried out in the acid medium, no external solvent necessary
Acid‑base neutralization; proton from tetrafluoroboric acid reacts with potassium hydroxide to give water and potassium tetrafluoroborate; carried out in water at ambient conditions; no catalyst.

Formation of a tri‑acid chloride from 1,3,5‑benzenetricarboxylic acid using thionyl chloride; purpose is preparation of 1,3,5‑benzenetricarbonyl chloride for further coupling; key transformation three –COOH groups → three –COCl groups, releasing 3 HCl and 3 SO2; typical conditions excess SOCl2, reflux in dry solvent (e.g., dry dichloromethane or toluene) or neat, often with catalytic DMF; performed under inert atmosphere and removal of volatile by‑products yields the acid chloride

Catalytic hydrogenation of 1,2,3,4‑tetrahydroisoquinoline to decahydroisoquinoline; purpose is full saturation of the heterocycle; key transformation C9H11N + 3 H2 → C9H15N; typical conditions hydrogen pressure 1–5 atm, palladium on carbon (10 % Pd/C) or Raney Ni as catalyst, solvent such as ethanol or methanol, temperature 25–80 °C; reaction reduces the remaining aromatic double bond to give the fully saturated product

Phosgenation (acylation) of p‑phenylenediamine with phosgene to form terephthalamide; purpose is to synthesize an aromatic diamide. Key transformation: each –NH₂ group attacks COCl₂, yielding two amide bonds and releasing two equivalents of HCl. Typical conditions: low temperature (0 °C to room temp) in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, with a base (e.g., triethylamine or pyridine) to trap HCl.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification between salicylic acid and ethyl acetate producing ethyl salicylate and acetic acid; used to prepare aromatic esters. Key transformation: exchange of the alkoxy group of ethyl acetate with the phenolic acid, driven by removal of acetic acid. Conditions: excess ethyl acetate, catalytic sulfuric acid, reflux (≈78 °C) in a sealed or reflux apparatus; removal of volatile acetic acid (e.g., by distillation) shifts equilibrium.

Base‑catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis (alkaline hydrolysis). Converts the –CN of 2‑fluoroacetonitrile to a carboxylate, yielding sodium 2‑fluoroacetate and ammonium hydroxide. Typically carried out in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) at reflux (≈80‑100 °C) for 1–4 h; water (or water/ethanol) is the solvent, no additional catalyst needed.

Conversion of anthranilic acid to anthranilamide via thionyl chloride activation (in‑situ acid chloride formation) followed by amidation with aqueous ammonia; purpose is amide synthesis. Key steps: anthranilic acid reacts with SOCl₂ to give the corresponding acid chloride, releasing SO₂ and HCl; subsequent addition of aqueous NH₃ converts the acid chloride to the primary amide, generating additional HCl.
