Acidic dichromate oxidation of 3,4,5‑trimethoxybenzyl alcohol to 3,4,5‑trimethoxybenzoic acid; potassium dichromate in sulfuric acid oxidizes the benzylic primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid, reducing Cr(VI) to Cr(III); reaction carried out under reflux in aqueous H₂SO₄ (often with a co‑solvent like acetone); chromium(III) sulfate precipitates as a by‑product.

Hydrogenation reduction; catalytic hydrogenation of aromatic nitro groups to amines using H₂ and Pd/C; converts 2,4‑dinitrophenol to 2,4‑diaminophenol; typically performed in ethanol or methanol under 1–5 atm H₂ at 25–60 °C; Pd on carbon serves as the catalyst.

Acid–base salt formation; reaction of terbium(III) oxide with aqueous hydrofluoric acid to give terbium(III) fluoride and water; essentially a dissolution/neutralization process; carried out in aqueous HF solution at ambient temperature with careful safety controls; no additional catalyst required.

Double‑displacement precipitation; barium carbonate reacts with ammonium oxalate in water to precipitate insoluble barium oxalate while ammonium carbonate remains soluble; performed in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; no catalyst needed.

Sulfide precipitation (acid‑base type); employed to obtain cadmium sulfide, a colored semiconductor material. H₂S gas reacts with Cd(OH)₂, replacing OH⁻ with S²⁻ to give CdS (insoluble) and water. Typically carried out by passing H₂S through an aqueous slurry of Cd(OH)₂ under slightly acidic conditions to keep H₂S in solution; ambient temperature; water as solvent; no catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition; heating magnesium hydrogen sulfate causes loss of volatile sulfuric acid, yielding magnesium sulfate solid; usually performed by slowly raising temperature to 200–250 °C under dry conditions; no solvent or catalyst required.

Amide hydrolysis; aqueous hydrolysis of bucetin (an acetanilide derivative) cleaves the amide bond to give acetic acid and 4‑ethoxyaniline; can be carried out under acidic or basic conditions, typically refluxing in dilute HCl or NaOH aqueous solution (or with a buffer) at 80–120 °C; catalyst is the acid or base used.

Formation of an alkyl chloroformate; 2‑ethylhexanol reacts with phosgene to give 2‑ethylhexyl carbonochloridate and hydrogen chloride; carried out at 0–5 °C in dry non‑protic solvent (e.g., CH2Cl2, CCl4) in the presence of a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge HCl.

SN1 hydrolysis of a tertiary alkyl bromide; water acts as nucleophile to replace Br, yielding 3‑methyl‑3‑pentanol and HBr; typically carried out in aqueous medium or water/THF mixture under reflux or gentle heating.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) on 2‑fluoropyridine; NaOMe displaces fluoride to give 2‑methoxypyridine and NaF; performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, often at reflux temperature.

Oxidative condensation of benzaldehyde with pyrrole to form a dipyrrin scaffold; p‑toluenesulfonic acid protonates the aldehyde, DDQ serves as the oxidant to dehydrogenate the intermediate, affording the dipyrrin; usually run in dichloromethane under inert atmosphere, at room temperature to gentle reflux.

Hypervalent iodine oxidation of benzyl alcohol to benzaldehyde; 1‑hydroxy‑1,2‑benziodoxol‑3(1H)‑one (BI‑OH) acts as the oxidant, producing benzaldehyde and 2‑iodobenzoic acid as by‑product; carried out in dichloromethane at ambient temperature, stoichiometric amount of BI‑OH is used.

Catalytic hydrogenation (transfer hydrogenation) of naphthalene to decalin; Pd/C catalyzes the addition of hydrogen (generated from H₂ gas and/or formic acid) to fully saturate both aromatic rings, giving decalin; typical conditions involve Pd/C in ethanol or acetic acid, 80–120 °C, 1–5 atm H₂ (or formic acid as H‑donor).

Catalytic hydrogenation of methylenecyclobutane to methylcyclobutane; H₂ adds across the exocyclic double bond under a metal catalyst (e.g., Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni); reaction performed in a solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate at room temperature to 50 °C under 1–3 atm H₂ pressure.

Acid-catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis; converts a nitrile to the corresponding carboxylic acid while releasing ammonia as ammonium salt. Key transformation is cleavage of the C≡N bond to form a –COOH group; nitrogen becomes NH4⁺. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous HCl (often 6 M) for several hours. Solvent is water (sometimes containing a co‑solvent such as ethanol). No additional catalyst required.

E2 dehydrohalogenation (elimination) of bromocyclobutane with potassium tert‑butoxide, serving to generate the strained alkene cyclobutene. The strong, sterically hindered base abstracts the β‑hydrogen, expelling bromide as KBr and forming tert‑butanol as the conjugate acid; typically carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMSO or DMF at 50‑100 °C under anhydrous conditions.

Nucleophilic ring‑opening of ethylene oxide by phenethylamine, yielding a β‑amino alcohol (2‑(2‑phenylethylamino)ethanol). The amine attacks the less hindered carbon of the epoxide, opening the ring and forming a new C–N bond; the resulting alkoxide is protonated to give the alcohol. Typical conditions: phenethylamine (1–2 equiv) with excess ethylene oxide gas or solution, in a polar aprotic solvent such as THF or methanol, at 0–25 °C; a base (e.g., NaHCO₃) may be added to neutralize the generated acid. Reaction is carried out under inert atmosphere to avoid polymerization of the epoxide.

Trans‑nitrosation between S‑nitroso‑L‑cysteine and N‑acetyl‑penicillamine. The nitric oxide (NO) group is transferred from the cysteine thiol‑nitrosothiol to the penicillamine thiol, yielding free L‑cysteine and S‑nitroso‑N‑acetyl‑penicillamine. Performed in aqueous buffer (pH 6‑8) at 0‑25 °C; the reaction proceeds spontaneously and does not require additional catalysts, although mild reductants can be used to drive equilibrium.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification) of hexyl acetate to furnish hexanol and acetic acid. In acidic hydrolysis the mixture is refluxed with aqueous HCl; in basic hydrolysis NaOH is used, followed by acid work‑up to protonate the acetate. Water (often mixed with ethanol) is the solvent and the reaction proceeds at reflux.

Chloromethane + sodium hydroxide -> methanol + sodium chloride: alkaline hydrolysis (SN2 substitution) of a primary halide; purpose is synthesis of methanol from methyl chloride; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of OH⁻ on the methyl carbon forming CH3OH and NaCl; typical conditions are aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) refluxed for several hours; solvent is water, sometimes mixed with ethanol; no additional catalyst required.

Metathesis/ion‑exchange reaction of calcium citrate with potassium hydroxide, yielding soluble potassium citrate and precipitating calcium hydroxide. The reaction is performed in aqueous medium at room temperature, often with gentle heating to improve dissolution; no catalyst needed.

High‑temperature oxidation (combustion) of chromium(III) sulfide with molecular oxygen, converting sulfide to chromium(III) oxide and sulfur to sulfur dioxide. Conducted in a furnace or tube furnace in flowing air at temperatures above 600 °C; solid‑state reaction, no solvent or catalyst required.

Halogen displacement (redox) reaction: Chlorine oxidizes iodide in barium iodide, producing iodine gas and barium chloride. Usually performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; no special catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed ether hydrolysis: Sodium hydroxide cleaves the C–O bond of furfuryl methyl ether, yielding methanol and furfuryl alcohol. Typical conditions are refluxing aqueous NaOH (often 1 M) for several hours; solvent can be water or a water‑ethanol mixture.

Electrophilic bromination of a quinone: Molecular bromine adds to the 2‑position of 1,4‑naphthoquinone, forming 2‑bromo‑1,4‑naphthoquinone and releasing hydrogen bromide. Conducted in an inert organic solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride or chloroform) at 0 °C to room temperature; no catalyst required.

Solid‑state redox reaction; Cr(VI) oxide oxidizes iron metal to Fe2O3 while Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr2O3; typically heated in a high‑temperature furnace (≈800 °C) in the solid phase; no solvent, may be conducted in air or under inert atmosphere; no separate catalyst.

Base‑catalyzed Claisen‑Schmidt (aldol) condensation to a chalcone: 4‑Hydroxy‑3‑methoxyacetophenone condenses with 2‑hydroxybenzaldehyde in the presence of potassium carbonate, giving the α,β‑unsaturated ketone Licochalcone A. Reaction is usually run in ethanol or methanol at reflux for several hours under nitrogen atmosphere.

Catalytic hydrogenation/reduction of succinic anhydride: Hydrogen gas reduces and opens the anhydride ring to afford 1,4‑butanediol. Typical conditions: 50–100 atm H₂, 80–150 °C, Raney Ni or Ru/Al₂O₃ catalyst, in water or an alcohol solvent.

General type: double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Purpose: to isolate nickel(II) hydroxide as a solid precipitate from a soluble nickel salt. Key transformation: NiSO₄(aq) + 2 NaOH(aq) → Ni(OH)₂(s) ↓ + Na₂SO₄(aq). Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature; excess NaOH ensures complete precipitation. No catalyst needed. Common solvent: water.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of ethyl trans‑2‑butenoate to trans‑2‑butenoic acid; purpose is to cleave the ester back to the free carboxylic acid; key transformation is nucleophilic addition of water to the carbonyl, releasing ethanol; typical conditions: reflux in aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M H₂SO₄) or aqueous HCl, sometimes with a co‑solvent such as ethanol; the reaction proceeds under acidic catalysis until the ester is fully converted.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation: In aqueous solution, nickel sulfate reacts with sodium tungstate to form insoluble nickel tungstate (NiWO₄) and sodium sulfate remains in solution. The reaction is carried out at ambient temperature with stirring; no additional reagents are required.

Transesterification (ester exchange); purpose is to convert p‑hydroxybenzoic acid into its propyl ester (propyl paraben) while generating acetic acid. Key transformation: the carboxylic acid group of p‑hydroxybenzoic acid replaces the acetyl group of propyl acetate, forming propyl p‑hydroxybenzoate and acetic acid. Typical conditions: reflux in a non‑nucleophilic solvent (toluene or xylene) with removal of acetic acid by azeotropic distillation; acid catalyst such as p‑toluenesulfonic acid or catalytic amount of sulfuric acid; inert atmosphere not required.

Lithiation‑followed‑by‑carboxylation; purpose is to introduce a carboxyl group at the 4‑position of thiazole. Key transformation: n‑BuLi performs a lithium‑halogen exchange on 4‑bromothiazole to give 4‑lithiothiazole, which then reacts with CO₂ to afford 4‑thiazolecarboxylic acid; LiBr is formed as a stoichiometric by‑product. Typical conditions: dry THF, −78 °C to 0 °C under nitrogen or argon, slow addition of CO₂ gas or dry ice; quench with aqueous NH₄Cl. No additional catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic bromination; purpose is to install a third bromine atom at the remaining unsubstituted position of 2,4‑dibromoanisole. Key transformation: Br₂ adds to the 6‑position of the aromatic ring via an SEAr mechanism, giving 2,4,6‑tribromoanisole. Typical conditions: Br₂ (1 equiv) in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, often in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst (FeBr₃ or AlCl₃) at 0 °C to rt; reaction quenched with aqueous Na₂S₂O₃.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) to form a cyanate; purpose is to generate ethyl cyanate from cyanogen bromide. Key transformation: ethoxide attacks the carbon of Br‑C≡N, displacing bromide and forming ethyl cyanate (Et‑OCN); NaBr is the inorganic by‑product. Typical conditions: sodium ethoxide generated in ethanol or dry THF, addition of cyanogen bromide at 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere; reaction proceeds without additional catalyst.

2-(2-hydroxyethoxy)acetaldehyde is reduced to 2-(2-hydroxyethoxy)ethanol using sodium borohydride. The purpose is to convert the aldehyde group to a primary alcohol. Key transformation involves hydrogen transfer from the borohydride. Reaction conditions typically occur in a protic solvent like ethanol or methanol at room temperature.

Acyl‑chloride amide formation (Schotten‑Baumann reaction); purpose is to synthesize N,N‑diethyl‑m‑toluamide (DEET). Key transformation: the amine nitrogen attacks the carbonyl carbon of 3‑methylbenzoyl chloride, displacing chloride to give the amide; HCl is liberated (often scavenged by a base). Typical conditions: dilute solution in dichloromethane or THF, temperature 0 °C to rt, presence of a base such as pyridine, triethylamine, or NaHCO₃ to neutralize HCl; reaction under nitrogen.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an aldehyde; purpose is to reduce the aldehyde functional group to a primary alcohol, producing perillyl alcohol. Key transformation: addition of H2 across the C=O bond of perillaldehyde to give the corresponding alcohol. Typical conditions: H2 gas (1–3 atm) with 5–10 % Pd/C catalyst, in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol, at room temperature to gentle reflux; reaction time 1–4 h.

Acid–base neutralization; calcium oxide (quicklime) reacts with acetic acid in water to form calcium acetate and water; typically performed at ambient temperature in aqueous solution, exothermic, no catalyst needed.

Solid‑state carburization of molybdenum; purpose is to produce molybdenum carbide (e.g., Mo₂C) for use as a hard material or catalyst. Key transformation: methane decomposes on the metal surface, delivering carbon that incorporates into the Mo lattice while hydrogen is released (CH₄ → C + 2 H₂). Typical conditions: high temperature (≥1000 °C, often 1200–1300 °C) under a flow of CH₄ (or CH₄/H₂ mixture) in a tubular furnace; no solvent, and the reaction is carried out in an inert or reducing atmosphere to avoid oxidation.

Hydrolysis of lithium methyl carbonate with water to afford lithium hydroxide, methanol and carbon dioxide. Carried out in aqueous medium, usually with mild heating to accelerate evolution of CO2. Water is both reactant and solvent.

Oxidation of primary alcohols to aldehydes using TEMPO/NaOCl. This is a TEMPO‑mediated aerobic oxidation (often called the “NaOCl/TEMPO” system). Purpose: convert the two hydroxymethyl groups of 2,5‑bis(hydroxymethyl)furan into formyl groups to give 2,5‑diformylfuran. Key transformation: R‑CH2OH → R‑CHO under mild, aqueous conditions. Typical conditions: buffered aqueous solution (pH 8–10), NaOCl (household bleach) as stoichiometric oxidant, catalytic TEMPO (≈5 mol %). Optional co‑catalyst NaBr to accelerate. Reaction is performed at 0 °C to room temperature, often under air. Common solvent: water or water/acetone mixture.

Oxidative electrophilic iodination of 8‑hydroxyquinoline. General type: electrophilic aromatic substitution (halogenation) using I₂/HO₂ in acidic medium. Purpose: install two iodine atoms at the 5‑ and 7‑positions to afford 5,7‑diiodo‑8‑hydroxyquinoline. Key transformation: generation of the electrophilic iodine species I⁺ (from I₂ oxidized by H₂O₂) which attacks the activated quinoline ring. Typical conditions: dilute H₂SO₄ (1–2 M) as solvent and acid promoter, aqueous H₂O₂ (30 %) as oxidant, stoichiometric I₂, temperature 0 °C to 25 °C. Reaction is usually carried out in water or aqueous sulfuric acid; no additional catalyst needed.

N‑hydroxylation of phthalimide with peracetic acid. General type: oxidation (oxygen transfer) of an imide nitrogen to the N‑hydroxy derivative. Purpose: prepare N‑hydroxyphthalimide, a useful hydroxylamine precursor. Key transformation: Phthalimide + peracetic acid → N‑hydroxyphthalimide + acetic acid. Typical conditions: low temperature (0–5 °C) to control over‑oxidation, dilute solution of peracetic acid in acetic acid or dichloromethane, inert atmosphere. Reaction often proceeds without metal catalyst; the peracid itself is the oxidant.

Acidic decomposition of aluminium selenide with nitric acid. General type: redox/acid‑metal selenide reaction (acid digestion). Purpose: liberate hydrogen selenide gas and convert aluminium to its nitrate salt. Key transformation: Al₂Se₃ + 6 HNO₃ → 2 Al(NO₃)₃ + 3 H₂Se (g). Typical conditions: dilute HNO₃ (≈2 M), temperature kept low (0–25 °C) to avoid rapid H₂Se release, reaction performed in a sealed or well‑ventilated apparatus. No catalyst required; aqueous medium.

Nucleophilic ring‑opening of ethylene oxide by 2‑mercaptoethanol. General type: nucleophilic addition (alkoxide/thiolate attack) to an epoxide. Purpose: synthesize bis(2‑hydroxyethyl) sulfide, a thioether diol. Key transformation: HS‑CH₂‑CH₂‑OH attacks the less hindered carbon of ethylene oxide, forming –S‑(CH₂‑CH₂‑OH)₂. Typical conditions: basic medium (e.g., NaOH or K₂CO₃) to deprotonate the thiol, aqueous or alcoholic solvent, temperature 25–80 °C. Reaction often proceeds smoothly without additional catalyst; excess ethylene oxide drives completion.

Type: dehydration of an oxime to a nitrile (elimination). Purpose: generate a nitrile from the corresponding oxime. Key transformation: loss of water from N‑butylidenehydroxylamine forms the C≡N triple bond of butanenitrile. Typical conditions: heating with strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or dehydrating agents such as POCl₃, P₂O₅, or ZnCl₂, often neat or in a high‑boiling non‑polar solvent (toluene, xylene) at 150–200 °C.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between potassium chromate and magnesium nitrate in water. General type: precipitation/ion‑exchange reaction. Purpose: exchange cations to form soluble potassium nitrate and sparingly soluble magnesium chromate, which precipitates. Key transformation: K₂CrO₄ + Mg(NO₃)₂ → 2 KNO₃ (aq) + MgCrO₄ (s). Typical conditions: aqueous solution at room temperature, often stirring for 30 min to allow MgCrO₄ to precipitate. The solid is filtered off; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑base double displacement (neutralisation) in aqueous solution: phosphoric acid protonates selenite ion, producing selenous acid (H₂SeO₃) and sodium phosphate (Na₃PO₄); performed by mixing the reagents in water at ambient temperature, no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic addition of an acetylide to an aldehyde (alkynylation): acetylene is deprotonated by a strong base (e.g., NaNH₂ or KOH) to give the acetylide ion, which adds to benzaldehyde and after protonation yields phenylpropargyl alcohol; carried out in an anhydrous polar aprotic solvent such as THF or ether at 0‑25 °C; base acts as the only reagent.

Leuckart‑Wallach reductive amination of 4‑chlorophenylacetone with formamide; thermal conversion of a ketone to the corresponding N‑methyl amine. Typically heated neat or in excess formamide at 150–200 °C for several hours; no external catalyst needed. Water is eliminated and the product, 4‑chloromethamphetamine, is obtained after work‑up and purification.

Acid‑catalysed nitrosation forming an N‑nitrosamine: sodium nitrite reacts with acetic acid to generate nitrous acid, which nitrosates dimethylamine to produce N‑nitrosodimethylamine, water and sodium acetate; conducted in aqueous acidic medium, typically at 0‑5 °C to control rate; no catalyst required.

Oxidation (N‑oxidation); converts the tertiary amine trimethylamine into its N‑oxide, a useful intermediate or protecting group. Key transformation: N→N‑oxide addition of an oxygen atom. Typically performed with aqueous hydrogen peroxide (30 % H₂O₂) at 0‑25 °C, often in water or a water‑compatible organic solvent (e.g., THF) under mildly basic or neutral pH; no additional catalyst required.

Acyl‑substitution (amide formation) between formyl chloride and diethylamine: the acid chloride reacts with the secondary amine to give diethylformamide and hydrogen chloride; performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, usually at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; HCl may be scavenged by a base, no additional catalyst.

Nitrosation (nitroso transfer) using nitroso acetate. Purpose: form an N‑nitroso aromatic amine. Key transformation: the nitroso group (–NO) is transferred from acetyl nitrite to aniline, producing N‑nitrosoaniline and releasing acetic acid. Typical conditions: ambient to 0 °C, inert solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, stoichiometric nitroso acetate, often with a mild base (e.g., pyridine) to scavenge acid. Reaction proceeds under nitrogen atmosphere to avoid oxidation.

Tin(II) chloride‑mediated reduction of an aryl azide (Staudinger‑type): in the presence of excess HCl, SnCl₂ reduces 2,6‑dimethylphenyl azide to 2,6‑dimethylaniline, releasing N₂ gas and oxidizing Sn(II) to Sn(IV) as SnCl₄; carried out in aqueous (or aqueous/organic) medium at ambient or reflux temperature; no other catalyst required.

Acidic dissolution of silicon; purpose: generate volatile silicon tetrafluoride and hydrogen gas; key transformation: Si is fluorinated by HF, producing SiF₄ gas and reducing protons to H₂; typical conditions: reaction with concentrated aqueous HF (≈48 % w/w) at room temperature or slight heating; often performed in a PTFE or glass vessel; no external catalyst, though ammonium bifluoride can increase rate.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation. Choline iodide reacts with soluble silver sulfate in aqueous solution; Ag⁺ exchanges with choline⁺ to form insoluble silver iodide precipitate, leaving choline sulfate in solution. Typically carried out at room temperature in water; no catalyst required; product filtered and washed.

Redox/acid‑base reaction; used to generate chlorine gas from household bleach; hypochlorite ion is oxidized to Cl₂ while reduced to Cl⁻, producing NaCl and H₂O; typically performed by adding cold dilute HCl to an aqueous NaOCl solution at ≤25 °C in a fume hood; water is the solvent; no catalyst required.

Oxidation reaction. Potassium permanganate in water oxidizes 1,10‑phenanthroline5,6‑positions to give 1,10‑phenanthroline‑5,6‑dione. Usually performed in mildly acidic or neutral aqueous media, heating gently to reflux; KMnO₄ acts as oxidant, water is solvent; reaction quenched with a reducing agent or by filtration of MnO₂.

Condensation (dehydrative dimerization) of bromic acid: two molecules of HBrO₃ lose water to form dibromine pentoxide (Br₂O₅). The process requires low temperature (0‑5 °C) to avoid explosive decomposition and is usually performed in a sealed glass apparatus; no catalyst is needed.
Acid-base reaction; converts sodium carboxylate salt to carboxylic acid via protonation; sulfuric acid serves as the proton donor; typically occurs under aqueous conditions with heat.

Aqueous double‑replacement (metathesis) reaction between barium nitrate and sodium metaborate. Dissolve both salts in water, stir at ambient temperature; insoluble barium metaborate precipitates while sodium nitrate remains in solution. The solid is filtered, washed, and dried to isolate Ba(BO₂)₂.

Copper‑catalyzed oxidative coupling (Chan‑Lam type). Phenylboronic acid reacts with copper(II) acetate in pyridine under an oxygen atmosphere to give phenyl acetate, with boric acid formed as the boron by‑product. Typical conditions: pyridine or mixed pyridine/solvent, O₂ balloon or air, room‑to‑moderate temperature, catalytic amount of Cu(OAc)₂; no additional base is required.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction). Nitrobenzene is reduced by hydrogen gas over palladium on carbon in the presence of hydrochloric acid, converting the nitro group to an amine which is protonated to give benzenamine hydrochloride (anilinium chloride). Conducted in aqueous HCl or mixed HCl/ethanol, at 1–5 atm H₂, ambient to 50 °C; Pd/C is the catalyst.

Fluorination of hafnium dioxide; forms volatile hafnium tetrafluoride and water; HfO2 + 4 HF → HfF4 + 2 H2O; typically carried out in aqueous HF solution at 200–400 °C or in gaseous HF at elevated temperature; no catalyst; reaction vessel must resist HF.

Dehydration of succinic acid using phosphorus pentoxide; P₂O₅ acts as a powerful dehydrating agent, converting the dicarboxylic acid to succinic anhydride with evolution of water; heated (120–150 °C) in the presence of excess P₂O₅ under nitrogen; solid‑state or in a minimal amount of inert solvent (e.g., dry toluene).

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (thiolate displacement) of dichloromethane with phenyl mercaptan; base deprotonates PhSH to PhS⁻, which attacks CH₂Cl₂ to give phenyl chloromethyl sulfide (PhS‑CH₂Cl) and Cl⁻; the liberated HCl is neutralized by the base. Performed at 0 °C–rt in an aprotic solvent such as THF or dichloromethane using a mild inorganic base (e.g., K₂CO₃, NaHCO₃) or organic base (triethylamine). No catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization of permanganic acid (HMnO₄) with cesium bicarbonate; proton transfer forms cesium permanganate (CsMnO₄) while the bicarbonate decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O. Conducted in aqueous solution, typically at 0–25 °C, with stirring; no additional reagents or catalysts are needed.

Salt formation (acid‑base reaction) between the basic quinoxaline amine (5‑bromo‑6‑(2‑imidazolin‑2‑ylamino)quinoxaline) and tartaric to give brimonidine tartrate and water. Reaction is carried out in a polar protic solvent such as ethanol or isopropanol, often with gentle heating (50–80 °C) to promote crystallization of the tartrate salt; no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (ester cleavage) of bornyl acetate with water to afford borneol and acetic acid. Typically refluxed in aqueous HCl or a dilute mineral acid (1–3 M) in a co‑solvent like THF or dioxane to improve solubility; reaction time ranges from 1–4 h. No additional catalyst beyond the acid is needed.

Oxidation of vanillyl alcohol to vanillin with pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC); PCC selectively oxidizes the primary benzylic alcohol to the corresponding aldehyde without over‑oxidation to the acid; reactions are typically conducted in anhydrous dichloromethane at room temperature under nitrogen; the by‑product is reduced chromium species (Cr(III)) complexed with pyridine; no extra catalyst is required.

Hydrolysis of an amide (neutral or acid‑catalyzed) where formamide reacts with water to yield formic acid and ammonia. The reaction proceeds via cleavage of the C–N bond; it is typically accelerated by heating the aqueous mixture at elevated temperature (e.g., 150‑200 °C) and may be catalyzed by a small amount of acid or base.

Halogenation of a tertiary alcohol (2‑methyl‑2‑butanol) with phosphorus pentachloride (PCl₅); the alcohol oxygen attacks PCl₅, generating the alkyl chloride (2‑chloro‑2‑methylbutane), phosphorus oxychloride (POCl₃) and hydrogen chloride (HCl). Performed under anhydrous conditions at 0 °C to rt in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform; the reaction is typically done in a dry inert atmosphere, no external catalyst.

Acid‑salt double displacement (metathesis) neutralization; used to prepare zinc chloride from zinc acetate. Key transformation: chloride ions replace acetate ions, giving ZnCl₂ and acetic acid. Conducted by treating an aqueous solution of zinc acetate with hydrochloric acid, often with gentle heating to ensure complete reaction. No catalyst; water as solvent.

E2 elimination (base‑induced dehydrohalogenation) using bulky tert‑butoxide; potassium tert‑butoxide abstracts a β‑hydrogen leading to formation of 1‑butene, potassium iodide and tert‑butanol as by‑product; purpose is to generate the terminal alkene; usually performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMSO or THF at moderate temperature (0 °C to reflux); strong, non‑nucleophilic base serves as both reagent and catalyst.

Thermal decomposition of 1,3‑dioxetanedione to two molecules of carbon dioxide; the strained peroxide ring undergoes concerted bond cleavage, releasing CO₂ gas and exothermic energy. Occurs spontaneously at ambient temperature or can be initiated by slight heating or UV light; no catalyst or solvent is required.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr); used to introduce a thiol group at C‑6 of the purine ring to prepare the antimetabolite 6‑mercaptopurine. The sulfide anion (HS⁻) from NaSH attacks the electron‑deficient C‑6 of 6‑chloropurine, displacing chloride. Typically carried out in aqueous ethanol or DMF at reflux (80‑100 °C) with a slight excess of NaSH; no catalyst required; NaCl precipitates and the product is isolated after neutralisation and crystallisation.

Gas‑solid acid‑base reaction (sulfidation); purpose is to generate caesium sulfide; caesium oxide reacts with hydrogen sulfide gas to form caesium sulfide and water; performed by passing H2S over heated Cs2O (≈200‑300 °C) in an inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Hydrogen reduction of a metal oxide; employed to obtain metallic cobalt from cobalt(II) oxide; CoO is reduced by H2 to Co metal, and hydrogen is oxidized to water; reaction carried out in a flow of hydrogen gas at 400–800 °C in a tube furnace or similar apparatus; solid‑gas reaction, no solvent or catalyst is typically used.

SN2 hydrolysis of a primary alkyl bromide; aqueous sodium hydroxide attacks 1‑bromooctane to give 1‑octanol and NaBr; generally refluxed in water or water/ethanol mixture; the reaction proceeds cleanly because the substrate is primary and unhindered.

Acid‑base neutralization analogous to (3) but with potassium hydroxide; yields potassium arsenate (K₃AsO₄ or K₂HAsO₄); key steps: As₂O₅ + H₂O → 2 H₃AsO₄, then 3 KOH → K₃AsO₄ + 3 H₂O; performed in aqueous medium, often by dissolving As₂O₅ in hot water then adding solid KOH while stirring; temperature 60–90 °C; water solvent, no catalyst.

Direct solid‑state combination (high‑temperature synthesis) of tin and selenium to afford tin(IV) selenide (SnSe₂), a layered semiconductor material. Elemental Sn and 2 equiv Se are ground together and heated under an inert atmosphere (Ar or N₂) at 400‑600 °C for several hours in a sealed quartz tube or furnace; no solvent or catalyst is employed.

Acid‑base reaction of calcium hydride with hydrogen bromide; calcium hydride acts as a strong base, abstracting a proton to give calcium bromide and evolve hydrogen gas; performed in anhydrous conditions, often in a dry inert solvent such as diethyl ether or THF at room temperature or with gentle heating; no catalyst.

Amidation. Reaction of 4-hydroxybenzoic acid with ammonia to form an amide. Conditions: heating under reflux, excess ammonia. Solvent: water or aqueous ammonia. Key transformation: replacement of the hydroxyl group with a -NH2 group.

Radical oxidation of hydroquinone by a hydroxyl radical to form para‑benzoquinone; OH· abstracts a hydrogen atom from hydroquinone, yielding water and p‑quinone; same type as reaction 2; aqueous phase, ambient conditions; no catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol); converts glycolaldehyde (HOCH₂‑CHO) to ethylene glycol (HOCH₂‑CH₂OH). Commonly performed with H₂ (1‑3 atm) over Raney Ni, Pd/C, or PtO₂ in aqueous ethanol or water at 50‑100 °C; reaction proceeds via aldehyde reduction to the diol. The mixture is filtered to remove catalyst and the product is purified by distillation.

Kumada‑type cross‑coupling (aryl‑aryl bond formation) between 4‑bromobiphenyl and phenylmagnesium bromide to give p‑terphenyl. Usually catalysed by NiCl₂·dppp, Pd(PPh₃)₄ or a related Pd(0) complex (5‑10 mol %) in dry THF under nitrogen at 0‑25 °C. After addition of the Grignard reagent, the mixture is stirred until completion, quenched with aqueous NH₄Cl, and the magnesium bromide salt is removed; the crude product is purified by recrystallisation or chromatography.

Palladium(II)‑catalysed aerobic oxidation of α‑pinene to 2‑pinen‑7‑one. Pd(OAc)₂ (5‑10 mol %) activates molecular oxygen as the oxidant; the reaction is run in an aprotic polar solvent such as acetonitrile or DMSO at 70‑90 °C under an O₂ balloon or slight positive pressure. The process selectively inserts an oxygen atom at the C‑7 position, delivering the ketone after work‑up and removal of palladium residues.

Reagent‑level halogen exchange/acid chloride formation. Phosphorus pentachloride reacts with trifluoroacetic anhydride at 0‑5 °C in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform, generating phosphorus oxychloride (POCl₃) and two equivalents of trifluoroacetyl chloride (CF₃COCl). The reaction is exothermic; the mixture is stirred under inert gas (N₂) and the volatile products are removed by distillation.

Halogenation (iodination) of a diol via in situ generated hydrogen iodide; red phosphorus reduces iodine to HI which then substitutes the two hydroxyl groups of ethylene glycol to give 1,2‑diiodoethane, with phosphorous acid formed as the oxidized phosphorus by‑product. Typically performed under reflux in an inert organic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane, often with a Dean–Stark trap to remove water.

N‑oxidation of pyridine with DMDO; purpose: form pyridine N‑oxide from pyridine; key transformation: pyridine + DMDO → pyridine N‑oxide + acetone; typical conditions: 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere; common solvent: dichloromethane or chloroform; DMDO generated in situ from acetone and oxone.

Direct combination (synthesis) oxidation of samarium metal by bromine; furnishes samarium tribromide. Samarium is exposed to Br₂ gas at low to moderate temperature (0–150 °C) in a dry, inert‑gas setup to control the exotherm. The product, SmBr₃, precipitates as a solid; no solvent or catalyst is employed.

Acid–base neutralization of a metal oxide with hydrofluoric acid; fluoride replaces oxide, yielding gallium(III) fluoride and water; typically performed in aqueous HF at room temperature or mild heating, no additional catalyst required.

Dehydrative chlorination (acyl‑chloride formation) of a carboxylic acid using phosphorus pentachloride. PCl5 converts methacrylic acid into methacryloyl chloride, releasing hydrogen chloride and phosphoryl chloride (POCl₃) as gaseous by‑products. Conducted anhydrously in solvents like dry CH₂Cl₂ or toluene at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration of 8‑hydroxyquinoline using a mixed nitric‑sulfuric acid (nitrating) mixture to afford nitroxoline (5‑nitro‑8‑hydroxyquinoline). The reaction proceeds via the nitronium ion (NO₂⁺) generated in situ; water is liberated. Carried out at low temperature (0–5 °C) then warmed to 50–70 °C, with conc. H₂SO₄ as solvent and excess HNO₃ as nitrating agent.

Benzyne addition (nucleophilic aromatic substitution via elimination‑addition) enabling amination of bromobenzene to aniline. Sodium amide abstracts a proton ortho to bromine, generating a benzyne intermediate that is trapped by NH₂⁻ to give aniline; NaBr is a by‑product. Conducted in liquid ammonia (–33 °C) or sealed tube at 70–80 °C, using NaNH₂ as both base and nucleophile; no additional catalyst.

Condensation (anhydride formation) of fluorosulfonic acid with sulfur trioxide to produce fluorosulfonic anhydride (FSO₂‑O‑SO₂F). The process is a dehydration reaction; excess SO₃ or removal of water drives formation of the anhydride. Performed at low temperature (−30 °C to 0 °C) under dry, inert atmosphere, often in the liquid SO₃ medium without additional solvent.

Halogen exchange/oxidative fluorination: elemental fluorine oxidizes niobium pentachloride to niobium(V) fluoride, liberating chlorine gas. No solvent is used; the gases are mixed in a flow reactor at 200–400 °C, with careful control of stoichiometry and containment due to the highly reactive F₂.

Acid‑catalyzed ether cleavage (hydrolysis) of tert‑butyl ethyl ether with aqueous hydrochloric acid, yielding ethanol and tert‑butanol (2‑methyl‑2‑propanol). The reaction proceeds via protonation of the ether oxygen followed by C‑O bond cleavage. Conducted by refluxing the ether in aqueous HCl (typically 6 M) for several hours; water acts as the solvent.

Acid‑catalyzed depolymerisation of 1,3,5‑trioxane to formaldehyde; hydrolysis of the cyclic trimer in aqueous sulfuric acid, typically heating the mixture (50–80 °C) in water to generate formaldehyde and water.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation); pyrophosphoric acid is neutralized by sodium carbonate to give disodium pyrophosphate with evolution of CO₂ and H₂O; performed in aqueous solution, typically at room temperature to gentle heating, with stirring; water is the solvent and no additional catalyst is required.

Acid‑base metathesis (no redox change) converting sodium iodate to iodic acid with formation of sodium sulfate; performed in aqueous solution of dilute H₂SO₄ at room temperature; no special catalyst required.

Fischer esterification of acrylic acid with cyclohexanol to give cyclohexyl acrylate and water; acid‑catalysed (e.g., a few drops of H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH), reflux in an inert organic solvent such as toluene or benzene with a Dean‑Stark trap to remove water.

Metathesis precipitation; aqueous cadmium(II) nitrate is mixed with sodium phosphate, resulting in cadmium phosphate solid precipitate and sodium nitrate in solution; typically performed at ambient temperature, no catalyst needed.

Acid chloride formation with phosphorus trichloride; converts (E)-but‑2‑enoic acid to (E)-but‑2‑enoyl chloride, producing phosphorous acid (H₃PO₃) as by‑product; reaction proceeds via nucleophilic attack of the carboxyl oxygen on PCl₃; usually carried out in anhydrous CH₂Cl₂ or toluene at 0 °C to rt; pyridine or triethylamine often added to scavenge HCl.

Acyl substitution (esterification) of propionic anhydride with methanol; purpose is to synthesize methyl propionate while generating propionic acid; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of methanol on the anhydride carbonyl forming an ester and a carboxylic acid; typical conditions: reflux methanol (often the solvent) at 60‑70 °C, optionally with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or base to accelerate; no special solvent needed beyond methanol.

A double displacement (metathesis) reaction swapping ions between dysprosium(III) sulfate and calcium chloride to form dysprosium(III) chloride and calcium sulfate. Occurs in aqueous solution at ambient temperature. Calcium sulfate precipitates if solubility limits are exceeded.

Redox reaction in acidic medium where nitrous acid oxidises iodide to iodine while being reduced to nitric oxide; carried out in cold aqueous solution containing HCl, KI and freshly prepared HNO₂; no external catalyst needed, reaction proceeds at 0–5 °C.

Zinc‑mediated reduction of pentachloronitrobenzene to pentachloroaniline in glacial acetic acid; zinc dust acts as the reductant, generating zinc acetate as by‑product; reflux the mixture for several hours under nitrogen; solvent is acetic acid, no additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (esterification of an acyl chloride). Ethanol attacks nicotinoyl chloride to give ethyl pyridine‑3‑carboxylate, releasing HCl. Typically performed in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to rt with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to neutralize HCl.

Catalytic hydrogenation of cyclobutene to cyclobutane; performed under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) in the presence of a heterogeneous metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni; solvent can be ethanol, methanol or ether; reaction typically runs at ambient temperature to 50 °C.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution; cyanide ion replaces the bromide on 6‑bromo‑1‑hexanol to afford 6‑cyano‑1‑hexanol; typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at ambient temperature; sodium bromide precipitates or remains soluble.

Friedel‑Crafts alkylation; methyl chloride generates a methyl cation in the presence of AlCl₃ which adds to 1‑methylnaphthalene giving 1,4‑dimethylnaphthalene; carried out under anhydrous conditions using AlCl₃ (often 1–2 equiv) in a non‑protic solvent like dichloromethane or carbon disulfide, at 0 °C to reflux, under nitrogen.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; potassium iodide exchanges anions with lead(II) sulfate producing insoluble lead(II) iodide and soluble potassium sulfate; conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; no catalyst required.

Oxidative dehydrogenation using IBX (o‑iodoxybenzoic acid); IBX oxidises norketamine to dehydronorketamine while being reduced to o‑iodobenzoic acid; usually carried out in DMSO or DMF at 20–40 °C, stoichiometric IBX, under inert atmosphere; by‑product is o‑iodobenzoic acid.

Mercuric‑mediated desulfurization; purpose is to restore uracil from 4‑thiouracil by hydrolytic removal of sulfur; key transformation is C=S → C=O with concurrent formation of insoluble HgS; typically performed by stirring 4‑thiouracil with aqueous HgCl2 (or Hg(OAc)2) at 40–60 °C, often in a water/pyridine mixture, followed by filtration to remove the mercury sulfide precipitate.

Chemical reduction of chloroauric acid by sodium borohydride to precipitate elemental gold; concurrent formation of sodium chloride, boric acid, and hydrogen gas; carried out in aqueous solution (often cold water or dilute ethanol/water) under inert atmosphere or with rapid stirring; NaBH4 acts as the reducing agent.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (carbamoylation); the primary hydrazine nitrogen of 1‑phenylethylhydrazine attacks ethyl chloroformate forming ethyl 2‑(1‑phenylethyl)hydrazine‑carboxylate and releasing HCl; performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt, with a base (e.g., triethylamine) to scavenge HCl.

Ozonolysis of an enol ether; 2‑methoxypropene reacts with ozone, cleaving the C=C bond to give formaldehyde and methyl acetate; the reaction is run at low temperature (‑78 °C) in an inert solvent like CH₂Cl₂, followed by a reductive work‑up (e.g., dimethyl sulfide) to afford the carbonyl fragments.

Redox oxidation; fluorination of Pu(III) to Pu(IV); F2 oxidizes PuF3 to PuF4 releasing heat; typically performed in a dry fluorinating furnace at 500‑600 °C under anhydrous conditions, no solvent, often in a flow of inert gas.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 2‑methylfuran to 2‑methyltetrahydrofuran. Conducted in a hydrogen atmosphere (1–5 atm) with a catalyst such as Pd/C, Raney Ni, or Pt‑O₂ in a solvent like ethanol or THF at 25–80 °C. After completion, the reaction mixture is filtered to remove the catalyst and the product is isolated by distillation or extraction.

Acid‑base precipitation/neutralization; hydroxide ion deprotonates ammonium ion and precipitates nickel(II) hydroxide while forming sodium sulfate in solution; performed in aqueous solution at room temperature with excess NaOH, vigorous stirring; no special solvent or catalyst required.

Palladium‑catalyzed Buchwald‑Hartwig amination of 2‑chloro‑1,3,5‑trimethylbenzene with ammonia. Purpose: replace an aryl chloride with an amino group to afford 2‑amino‑1,3,5‑trimethylbenzene. Key transformations: oxidative addition of Pd(0) into C–Cl bond, transmetallation with ammonia (generated in situ), reductive elimination to form C–N bond, releasing HCl. Typical conditions: 2‑mol % Pd(OAc)₂, 4‑mol % tri‑tert‑butylphosphine, NaOtBu as base, ammonia (often as NH₃ gas or in liquid NH₃ solution), solvent such as toluene or dioxane, heated to 80–120 °C under inert atmosphere. Common solvents: toluene, dioxane, or THF.

Hydrolysis/dissociation equilibrium; ammonium bifluoride (NH4HF2) reacts with water to give ammonium fluoride (NH4F) and hydrofluoric acid (HF); the reaction is a simple acid‑base dissociation in aqueous solution; proceeds readily at room temperature; no catalyst; performed in water as solvent.

Acid‑base neutralization; hydrofluoroboric acid reacts with lithium carbonate to generate lithium tetrafluoroborate salt with evolution of CO₂ and H₂O; conducted in aqueous solution, usually at 0‑25 °C to control gas release; no catalyst needed.

Bicarbonate neutralization; sodium bicarbonate reacts with cyclooctylamine·HCl to liberate CO₂ and H₂O while forming free cyclooctylamine and NaCl; carried out in aqueous medium at ambient temperature with gentle stirring; no catalyst required.

β‑Elimination (E2) of 2‑iodo‑3‑methylbutane with the bulky, non‑nucleophilic base potassium tert‑butoxide to give the more substituted alkene 2‑methyl‑2‑butene. The strong base abstracts a β‑hydrogen while the C–I bond breaks in a concerted step, producing KI as the by‑product. Typical conditions: dry THF or DMF, 0 °C to reflux, under nitrogen; stoichiometric or slight excess of KOt‑Bu. No additional catalyst is needed.

Acid‑metal reaction; benzoic acid reacts with metallic magnesium to generate hydrogen gas and the magnesium salt of benzoic acid (magnesium benzoate). The metal is oxidized to Mg²⁺ while the acidic proton is reduced to H₂. Typically carried out in anhydrous ether or THF under reflux or gentle heating; no additional catalyst required.

Enolization (reverse keto‑enol tautomerization); formation of vinyl alcohol from acetaldehyde. Usually carried out under basic conditions (e.g., NaOH or KOH, 0–5 °C) to generate the enolate, which protonates to give the enol. A polar protic solvent such as methanol/water is common; the equilibrium heavily favors acetaldehyde, so the reaction is used mainly for mechanistic studies.

Reductive amination (hydrogenation) of 3,4‑methylenedioxyphenylacetone with ethylamine using palladium on carbon under H₂. The carbonyl is converted to an imine with ethylamine, which is then reduced in situ to give methylenedioxy‑N‑ethyl‑amphetamine (MDEA) and water. Common conditions: 5 atm H₂ Pd/C (5–10 % wt), solvent such as ethanol or methanol, 25–50 °C.

Enzymatic deamination (hydrolytic deamination) of the antifungal agent flucytosine (5‑fluorocytosine) to produce 5‑fluorouracil and ammonia. Catalyzed by cytosine deaminase in aqueous buffer, typically at physiological pH (≈7.4) and ambient temperature.

Aqueous double‑replacement (metathesis) reaction between trisodium phosphate and calcium hydroxide. Phosphate anions exchange with calcium to form insoluble calcium phosphate precipitate while sodium ions combine with hydroxide to give sodium hydroxide in solution. Performed in water at room temperature with stirring; no special catalyst needed.

Acid‑base (salt hydrolysis) reaction of ammonium acetate with NaOH; purpose is generation of ammonia gas; OH⁻ deprotonates NH₄⁺ to give NH₃, while Na⁺ combines with acetate to form sodium acetate and water; performed in aqueous solution at room temperature or mild heating, no catalyst needed.

Selenium dioxide oxidation of camphor to bornane‑2,3‑dione. SeO₂ selectively oxidizes the allylic C‑2 and C‑3 positions of the bicyclic ketone, converting the methylene groups to carbonyls and yielding the 2,3‑diketone. Reaction is usually run in refluxing dioxane or acetic acid, using stoichiometric SeO₂; the work‑up includes filtration of selenium precipitate.

Electrophilic aromatic chlorination of toluene catalyzed by iron(III) chloride. FeCl₃ activates Cl₂ to generate Cl⁺, which substitutes the aromatic ring preferentially at ortho and para positions relative to the methyl group, giving ortho‑ and para‑chlorotoluene; HCl is released as a by‑product. Typical conditions: FeCl₃ (1020 mol %), Cl₂ gas, solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride, 0–25 °C.

Fluorination (free‑radical substitution); purpose is to add a third fluorine to produce trifluoromethane and HF; key transformation CH2F2 + F2 → CHF3 + HF; carried out at low temperature with excess F2 in the gas phase or inert solvent; no catalyst required.

Phenol‑formaldehyde condensation (electrophilic aromatic alkylation) forming a bisphenol; formaldehyde acts as electrophile linking two 2,6‑dimethylphenol units; typically carried out in acidic medium (HCl or H2SO4) at 0‑50 °C in a polar protic solvent such as water or methanol, sometimes under basic conditions for phenol‑formaldehyde resins.

Ozonolysis of an allyl side chain followed by reductive work‑up. Cleaves the C=C of 5‑propenyl‑benzo‑1,3‑dioxole to give 3,4‑methylenedioxy‑benzaldehyde. Ozone is bubbled through a solution of the substrate in dry CH2Cl2 at –78 °C (dry ice/acetone bath). After completion, a reductive work‑up (e.g., dimethyl sulfide, Zn/AcOH, or PPh3) converts the ozonide to the aldehyde. The reaction mixture is warmed, filtered, and the aldehyde isolated by extraction and distillation.

[3+2] cycloaddition of an azide to a nitrile (tetrazole synthesis); purpose is to build the 1,5‑disubstituted tetrazole ring of pentylenetetrazole, a heterocycle used in research and explosives; key transformation is nucleophilic addition of the azide ion to the nitrile carbon followed by cyclization and protonation to give the tetrazole, with NaCl and water as by‑products; typical conditions involve refluxing the nitrile, NaN₃, and NH₄Cl in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, often 80‑120 °C for several hours; no metal catalyst is required.

Reductive amination of phenylpropanal with ammonia using sodium cyanoborohydride; imine formed in situ is reduced to the primary amine, giving 3‑phenylpropylamine; performed in methanol or ethanol with a catalytic amount of acetic acid at ambient temperature, NaBH3CN as the mild hydride source.

Acid‑catalyzed intramolecular cyclization of the monoterpene myrcene to the bicyclic terpene sabinene; proceeds via a cationic cascade that forms the cyclobutane‑containing ring system; typically uses a Lewis acid such as BF3·OEt2 or TiCl4 in dichloromethane at –78 °C to 0 °C, then quenched.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification between n‑butanol and ethyl acetate, exchanging the alkoxy groups to give butyl acetate and ethanol; commonly run with catalytic sodium methoxide or sulfuric acid under reflux in excess butanol (or ethanol) to drive equilibrium toward products.

Oxidation (redox) reaction. Hydrogen peroxide oxidizes the selenide anion in barium selenide to the selenite anion, producing barium selenite and water: BaSe + H2O2 → BaSeO3 + H2O. Carried out in aqueous solution, often at 0–25 °C, sometimes with slight acid or neutral pH; H2O2 serves as the oxidant.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification of 2‑propoxyethyl acetate with methanol to afford methyl acetate and 2‑propoxyethanol; purpose is exchange of the alkoxy group on the ester; the reaction proceeds via methoxide attack on the carbonyl, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to exchange the alcohol moieties; usually performed with catalytic sodium methoxide or potassium carbonate in excess methanol at 50‑80 °C for several hours; removal of the by‑product ester (methyl acetate) drives the equilibrium.

α‑Bromination of butanal using N‑bromosuccinimide (NBS); generates the α‑bromoaldehyde (2‑bromobutanal) with succinimide as by‑product; performed in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane under light or with a radical initiator (AIBN) at room temperature, often with a catalytic amount of acid to activate NBS.

Sulfate ester hydrolysis; indoxyl sulfate cleaves in aqueous conditions to produce indoxyl and sulfuric acid. Typically requires acidic conditions and heat. Common in biological systems during detoxification or degradation.

High‑temperature redox oxidation of strontium sulfide with concentrated nitric acid; sulfide is oxidized to sulfate (forming sulfuric acid) while nitrate is reduced to nitrogen dioxide; reaction is conducted in a sealed or refluxing vessel at 150‑200 °C, producing strontium nitrate, water, SO4^2‑ species and NO2 gas.

Acid- or base‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis; converts N-(2‑hydroxyethyl)acetamide into acetic acid and 2‑aminoethanol; performed in aqueous medium, usually with HCl, NaOH or heat (80‑150 °C); no special solvent needed, water serves as both reagent and solvent.

Salt metathesis to generate tetramethylammonium fluoride from cesium fluoride and tetramethylammonium bromide. Mix the two solids in anhydrous acetonitrile (or other polar aprotic solvent) at room temperature, stir until complete exchange; insoluble cesium bromide precipitates and is removed by filtration. The filtrate contains tetramethylammonium fluoride, which can be isolated by solvent evaporation under inert atmosphere.

Direct combination (halogenation) reaction; thorium metal reacts with iodine gas to afford thorium tetraiodide (ThI₄). Conducted at elevated temperature (≈500‑600 °C) under dry, inert conditions, often in a sealed quartz ampoule; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic addition of sulfite to formaldehyde; sodium metabisulfite reacts with aqueous formaldehyde to form sodium bisulfite and sodium hydroxymethanesulfonate (sodium formaldehyde sulfoxylate); proceeds in water at room temperature to 50 °C; no additional catalyst required.

Haloform (iodoform) reaction of a methyl‑aryl ketone; iodine in aqueous NaOH oxidizes the methyl carbonyl group of 1‑(4‑phenylphenyl)ethanone, yielding iodoform (CHI₃) and the carboxylate which upon acid work‑up gives 4‑phenylbenzoic acid; typical conditions are NaOH (10‑20 % w/v), I₂, 0‑25 °C to reflux, aqueous medium.

Ozonolysis (oxidative cleavage) of hept‑2‑ene: ozone adds to the C=C double bond forming a molozonide that fragments to give acetaldehyde and pentanal after reductive work‑up (e.g., dimethyl sulfide). Conducted in dry dichloromethane or chloroform at –78 °C to 0 °C, followed by gentle warming during work‑up.

Direct combination (synthesis) reaction; formation of an alkali metal halide. Cesium metal reacts vigorously with chlorine gas to give cesium chloride; highly exothermic. Typically carried out in a dry, inert‑gas atmosphere at room temperature to modest heating (≈50–100 °C) without solvent or catalyst.

High‑temperature reduction (hydrogen reduction) of a rare‑earth oxide to the metal. Pr₂O₃ is reduced by H₂, which is oxidized to H₂O while Pr³⁺ is reduced to Pr⁰. Performed in a flow of dry hydrogen gas at 900‑1100 °C, typically in a quartz or alumina tube furnace. No additional catalyst; inert carrier gas (Ar) may be used to prevent oxidation.

Redox halogen exchange and reduction of Re(V) to Re(III); hydrogen bromide reacts with rhenium(V) chloride, producing rhenium(III) bromide, hydrogen chloride, and elemental bromine; typically conducted under reflux in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dry acetonitrile, with careful temperature control to manage the evolution of Br₂.

Catalytic ammonia decomposition (thermal decomposition); used to generate hydrogen and nitrogen gases; NH3 is split into H2 and N2 via a metal catalyst (e.g., Ni, Ru, Fe) at 500‑700 °C under a flow of inert gas or reduced pressure; typically conducted in a tubular reactor with no solvent.

Alkyl halide amination (SN2 substitution); primary bromocyclobutane reacts with ammonia to give cyclobutylamine while the liberated HBr is neutralized by a second equivalent of ammonia forming ammonium bromide; performed by refluxing the alkyl bromide in excess liquid ammonia or aqueous NH3 (often in ethanol or methanol) at 50‑100 °C; excess ammonia drives the reaction and suppresses secondary amine formation.

Nucleophilic substitution of tert‑butyl bromide with cyanide ion (SN1 pathway) to afford tert‑butyl cyanide; KCN is used in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMSO, DMF or acetone, heated to 60‑80 °C; potassium bromide precipitates; introduces a nitrile functional group.

Acid-base neutralization; preparation of sodium phosphinite; proton transfer from phosphinous acid to hydroxide forms water and phosphinite salt; aqueous solution, ambient or mild heating; water solvent.

Nucleophilic substitution (ammonolysis) of allyl acetate; ammonia displaces the acetate group to give allylamine and acetic acid; usually performed by heating a mixture of allyl acetate and excess ammonia in an alcoholic or aqueous solvent (e.g., ethanol) under reflux.

Double displacement (ion‑exchange) reaction; aqueous Na2SO4 reacts with CrCl3·6H2O to give NaCl in solution and chromium(III) sulfate (Cr2(SO4)3) with water; performed in water at ambient temperature, no catalyst.

Complete combustion of diethyl ether; diethyl ether (C4H10O) reacts with excess oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and water; initiated by a flame or spark, occurring at ambient pressure with a plentiful supply of O2; no solvent or catalyst is required; the reaction is highly exothermic and proceeds rapidly.

N‑Alkylation of a secondary amine (SN2 reaction); N‑methyltryptamine is deprotonated by potassium carbonate and attacks allyl bromide, forming N‑methyl‑N‑allyltryptamine while KBr precipitates; carried out in an aprotic polar solvent such as dry DMF or acetonitrile at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; potassium carbonate acts as a mild base and scavenges HBr.

Neutralization of ammonium tetrafluoroborate with sodium hydroxide to afford sodium tetrafluoroborate, ammonia and water. Reaction type: acid‑base (salt metathesis) conversion; purpose: obtain NaBF₄ and release volatile NH₃; key transformation: NH₄⁺ proton transferred to OH⁻ forming NH₃ and H₂O while BF₄⁻ pairs with Na⁺; conditions: aqueous solution, room temperature or mild heating to drive off NH₃, water as solvent.

Base‑catalyzed condensation (Aldol‑type) of acetone with chloral; trichloroacetaldehyde (chloral) reacts with acetone in the presence of calcium hydroxide to give chlorobutanol (a tertiary trichloromethyl alcohol) plus water; performed in aqueous Ca(OH)2 solution, typically at reflux or ambient temperature with stirring; calcium hydroxide neutralizes the generated HCl and drives the condensation forward.

Metathesis/precipitation – double displacement between calcium azide and copper(II) sulfate produces copper(II) azide and calcium sulfate. Often used to prepare insoluble copper azide for analytical or preparative purposes. Performed in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; the low solubilities of Cu(N₃)₂ and CaSO₄ cause both solids to precipitate, which are then filtered.

Redox reaction used to generate chlorine dioxide gas; sodium chlorate is reduced by hydrogen peroxide in acidic medium, while hydrogen peroxide is oxidized to water; typically performed in aqueous solution with dilute sulfuric acid at 0‑5 °C to control ClO₂ evolution; no catalyst required, water is the solvent.

Reductive dehalogenation (metal‑mediated reduction) of 1,2‑dibromo‑3‑chloropropane with zinc metal, producing allyl chloride through elimination of two bromine atoms that form zinc bromide; carried out in refluxing ethanol or acetic acid under inert atmosphere; zinc dust is the reductant, no additional catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (esterification) of menthol with isovaleroyl chloride to give menthyl isovalerate and HCl; reaction is performed under anhydrous conditions, often in dichloromethane or pyridine (which acts as base and solvent) at 0 °C to room temperature; pyridine or triethylamine scavenges the generated HCl.

Oxidative conversion of iron(II) oxide to iron(III) sulfate in sulfuric acid with molecular oxygen as oxidant; FeO dissolves to give FeSO₄ which is oxidized by O₂ to Fe₂(SO₄)₃, producing water; the process is done in aqueous H₂SO₄, typically with heating and air or oxygen bubbling; no special catalyst required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between cobalt(II) chloride and ammonium acetate yielding cobalt(II) acetate and ammonium chloride; carried out in water, often with gentle heating to ensure complete ion exchange; no catalyst needed.

Reduction of TEMPO to the corresponding hydroxylamine with sodium borohydride; restores the reduced form of the nitroxyl species. NaBH₄ delivers hydride to the N‑O• group, yielding 4‑hydroxy‑2,2,6,6‑tetramethylpiperidine and NaBO₂ (or related borate) as by‑product. Conditions: methanol or THF as solvent, 0 °C to room temperature, 1–2 equiv NaBH₄, reaction complete within minutes to an hour.

Salt metathesis reaction between barium chloride and calcium sulfite forming calcium chloride and barium sulfite; performed in aqueous solution, usually at ambient temperature; the insoluble barium sulfite precipitates out, driving the reaction; no catalyst is required.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (nitration); purpose is to install a nitro group on pyrene. Key transformation: aromatic C–H replaced by C–NO₂ producing 1‑nitropyrene and nitric acid as by‑product. Typical conditions: anhydrous, low temperature (0–25 °C), dinitrogen pentoxide as nitrating agent, solvent such as glacial acetic acid or nitrobenzene; no external catalyst needed.

Acetylation (esterification) of an alcohol with acetic anhydride. Key transformation: cyclopropanol + (CH3CO)2O → cyclopropyl acetate + acetic acid. Usually performed at 0 °C to rt in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine, which also serves as base to scavenge the generated acid; catalytic amounts of DMAP may be added to accelerate the reaction.

Redox oxidation of elemental iodine by concentrated nitric acid; purpose is to convert I₂ to iodic acid while reducing HNO₃ to NO₂. Key transformation: I₂ + HNO₃ → HIO₃ + NO₂ + H₂O. Typical conditions: concentrated HNO₃ (≈ 68 %), temperature 0–20 °C to control gas evolution, performed in glassware resistant to strong acids; no catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification) of isoamyl acetate; purpose is to cleave the ester to the corresponding alcohol. Key transformation: isoamyl acetate + OH⁻ → 3‑methyl‑1‑butanol + acetate ion (K⁺). Typical conditions: aqueous KOH (1–2 M), reflux 1–2 h, often in a water/ethanol mixture; after reaction the mixture is acidified to liberate the alcohol.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification) of methyl benzoate; purpose is to generate benzoate salt and methanol. Key transformation: methyl benzoate + OH⁻ → methanol + benzoate ion (K⁺). Typical conditions: aqueous KOH, reflux 1 h, solvent water or water/ethanol; acid work‑up gives benzoic acid if desired.

Redox fluorination of scandium sulfide; elemental fluorine oxidizes Sc₂S₃ (or ScS) to scandium fluoride while sulfur is converted to sulfur dioxide; reaction proceeds at elevated temperature (200–400 °C) in a dry, inert atmosphere, no solvent; fluorine acts as both oxidant and fluorinating agent.

Redox coupling between tetrachloro‑1,4‑benzoquinone and dipyrromethane; purpose is to oxidize dipyrromethane to dipyrrin and reduce the quinone to the corresponding hydroquinone. Key transformation: tetrachloro‑quinone + dipyrromethane → tetrachloro‑hydroquinone + dipyrrin (two‑electron transfer). Typical conditions: reflux in ethanol or acetonitrile, often with a mild acid (e.g., acetic acid) to facilitate proton transfers; temperature 60‑80 °C.

Acid‑base neutralization of a basic metal oxide; hydrochloric acid dissolves bismuth oxide to give the oxychloride salt and water. Typically performed in aqueous HCl, often with gentle heating; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Ozonolysis of 1,6‑heptadiene; oxidative cleavage of the two C=C bonds to afford carbonyl fragments. Purpose: convert the diene into smaller aldehydes/ketones. Key transformation: each double bond is broken by ozone, yielding formaldehyde from the terminal alkenes and pentane‑1,5‑dial from the internal fragment. Typical conditions: solution of the diene in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride at –78 °C to 0 °C under an ozone atmosphere, followed by reductive work‑up (e.g., dimethyl sulfide, Zn/AcOH) to isolate the aldehydes. No additional catalyst is required.

Metal‑acid reduction of nitro groups to amines; tin metal in excess hydrochloric acid reduces the two nitro groups of 2,4‑dinitrophenol to give 2,4‑diaminophenol, while tin is oxidized to tin(IV) chloride and water is formed. Usually carried out by refluxing the substrate with Sn powder in concentrated aqueous HCl; water is the reaction medium and no additional catalyst is needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an allene; molecular hydrogen adds across the cumulated double bonds of allene to afford propene. Performed under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) in the presence of a transition‑metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney nickel, often in a protic or aprotic solvent (e.g., ethanol or THF) at room temperature or slightly elevated temperature.

Rosenmund–von Braun cyanation (nucleophilic substitution): copper(I) cyanide replaces the bromide of 1‑bromo‑4‑methylbenzene with CN⁻, giving 4‑methylbenzonitrile and CuBr reaction is carried out in DMF or DMSO, heated to reflux under nitrogen, sometimes with added KCN to improve yield.

Fischer esterification of a β‑keto acid; 3‑oxopropanoic acid reacts with methanol under acid catalysis to give methyl 3‑oxopropanoate (a methyl β‑keto ester) and water. Typical conditions involve refluxing methanol with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., concentrated H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) and removal of water to drive the equilibrium; no special catalyst beyond the acid is required.

Generation of hexafluorophosphoric acid by reaction of HF with phosphorus pentoxide; excess anhydrous HF reacts with P₂O₅, a strong dehydrating agent, to produce water and two equivalents of HPF₆. Conducted in anhydrous conditions, often at low, using excess HF as both reagent and solvent; no additional catalyst is employed.

Ester aminolysis (amidation): methylamine attacks the carbonyl of ethyl hexanoate, displacing ethanol and forming N‑methyl hexanamide. Typically performed with excess amine at reflux in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., ethanol or toluene); removal of the formed alcohol drives the equilibrium.

Acid‑base neutralization/precipitation; lead(II) acetate reacts with sodium hydroxide to give lead(II) hydroxide precipitate and sodium acetate in solution, along with water. Performed in water at ambient temperature; no catalyst needed.

Wolff–Kishner reduction: hydrazine condenses with the ketone to give a hydrazone, which under strong basic conditions (KOH) temperature (≈200 °C) in a high‑boiling solvent such as ethylene glycol decomposes, eliminating nitrogen and yielding 3‑methyl‑1‑phenylbutane. The reaction removes the carbonyl group, converting it to a methylene.

Nitrosylation to form an alkyl nitrite: nitrosyl tetrafluoroborate (NO⁺ BF₄⁻) reacts with isopropyl alcohol, transferring the nitrosyl group to produce isopropyl nitrite and hydrogen tetrafluoroborate. Conducted at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent like dichloromethane under inert atmosphere; the acid by‑product is neutralized by the solvent or added base if needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation: aqueous hydroiodic acid reacts with lead(II) nitrate, exchanging anions to precipitate insoluble lead(II) iodide (PbI₂) while forming nitric acid in solution. Carried out at ambient temperature in water; filtration isolates the yellow PbI₂ solid.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification); converts the methyl ester into the carboxylate salt and methanol; typically performed with aqueous KOH (1–2 equiv) at reflux (often in ethanol/water); the reaction proceeds via nucleophilic attack of OH⁻ on the carbonyl, giving potassium decanoate and methanol.

Base‑promoted methylation of urea: dimethyl sulfate alkylates the nitrogen atoms of urea in the presence of sodium hydroxide, yielding N,N′‑dimethylurea and sulfate by‑products. Typical conditions use aqueous or mixed water/acetone medium, 0 °C to 25 °C, with careful control to avoid over‑methylation or side reactions.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation; introduction of an isovaleryl group onto benzene to give 3‑methyl‑1‑phenylbutan‑1‑one. The acyl chloride reacts with AlCl3 (Lewis acid) to generate an acylium ion which electrophilically substitutes a hydrogen on the aromatic ring. Typically performed under anhydrous conditions in a non‑protic solvent such as CH2Cl2 or CS2 at 0 °C to reflux, followed by aqueous work‑up.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) to form a nitrile: potassium cyanide attacks the primary carbon of 3‑phenylpropyl chloride, displacing chloride and generating 3‑phenylpropanenitrile (with KCl as by‑product). Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 50–80 °C; the reaction proceeds cleanly for primary halides.

Gem‑dichlorination of an aldehyde with thionyl chloride; converts acetaldehyde to 1,1‑dichloroethane, releasing SO₂ and HCl gases. Usually run in anhydrous CH₂Cl₂ or CCl₄, refluxing or at rt, with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to trap H; inert atmosphere is common.

Halogen exchange (metathesis) reaction converting hafnium(IV) iodide to hafnium(IV) chloride; purpose is synthesis of HfCl4. Key transformation: Cl2 replaces I− ligands on Hf, releasing I2. Typically conducted in a sealed tube or refluxing vessel at elevated temperature (150‑250 °C) under an inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is required, solid HfI4 may be mixed directly with gaseous Cl2.

Transesterification; exchanges the methyl group for an ethyl group on the salicylate ester. Key transformation: methyl ester O‑CH₃ is replaced by ethyl O‑CH₂CH₃, producing ethyl salicylate and methanol. Typical condition: reflux in excess ethanol with catalytic H₂SO₄ or p‑toluenesulfonic acid, 2–6 h; ethanol serves as both reactant and solvent.

Phosphorylation (esterification) of phosphorus oxychloride with 2‑ethylhexanol to form tris(2‑ethylhexyl) phosphate. Pyridine acts as a base and solvent, scavenging the generated HCl. Reaction is usually performed at 0 °C to room temperature in dichloromethane or toluene under nitrogen, then warmed to reflux to drive completion. No additional catalyst is needed; the key steps are nucleophilic attack of the alcohol on POCl3 and displacement of chloride ions.

Reductive deiodination (hydrogenolysis) of perfluorohexyl iodide to perfluorohexane. The C–I bond is reduced by H₂ in the presence of a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, Raney nickel, or PtO₂. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂ pressure, 50‑150 °C, solvent like ethanol or THF, inert atmosphere. The reaction yields perfluorohexane and hydrogen iodide (which is usually trapped by a base).

Staudinger reduction of a 3′‑azido nucleoside using triphenylphosphine and water. The azide is converted to the corresponding amine (3′‑amino‑2′,3′‑dideoxyuridine) while triphenylphosphine is oxidized to triphenylphosphine oxide. Conducted in a mixed organic–aqueous solvent (e.g., THF/H₂O) at room temperature or mild heating; inert atmosphere is optional. No catalyst is required.

Sonogashira cross‑coupling between iodobenzene and trimethylsilylacetylene to afford phenylethynyltrimethylsilane. Catalyzed by Pd(II) (often generated in situ from PdCl₂ with phosphine ligand) and CuI, with triethylamine as base. Typical conditions: inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar), solvent such as THF, DMF or MeCN, 50‑80 °C for several hours. The reaction forms a carbon‑carbon sp²–sp bond linking the phenyl group to the TMS‑protected alkyne.

Iodoform (haloform) reaction of 2‑hexanol; iodine in aqueous NaOH oxidizes the secondary alcohol to the corresponding ketone, which undergoes triiodination and cleavage to give iodoform (CHI₃) and sodium pentanoate; performed at 0–25 °C in aqueous solution, excess I₂ and NaOH are required.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation); converts cyclamic acid to its sodium salt, a more water‑soluble sweetener. Proton transfer from the acid to hydroxide yields water and sodium cyclamate. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic addition of hydrazine to an isocyanate (formation of a semicarbazide); phenyl isocyanate reacts with hydrazine to give phenylsemicarbazide via attack of the –NH2 on the electrophilic carbon of the –N=C=O group, forming a urea‑type linkage. Usually carried out in anhydrous polar solvents such as ethanol or THF at 0 °C to room temperature, often under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst needed.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (Friedel‑Crafts chlorination); chlorine, activated by the Lewis acid AlCl3, substitutes a hydrogen on benzene to give chlorobenzene, with HCl generated as by‑product. Conducted under anhydrous conditions, typically at 0–5 °C then warmed to room temperature, using AlCl3 as catalyst and a non‑protic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride, CS2, or nitrobenzene.

Redox metal displacement (reduction of Pd(II) to Pd(0)); elemental copper reduces dichloro(1,5‑cyclooctadiene)palladium(II) to palladium metal while forming copper(I) chloride and liberating the cyclooctadiene ligand. The reaction is used to generate Pd(0) in situ for catalytic processes. Performed in aprotic solvents such as THF or toluene under inert atmosphere, often with gentle heating (reflux).

Aerobic oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone using heterogeneous photocatalysis; cyclopentanol is oxidized to cyclopentanone in the presence of molecular oxygen and TiO2 under UV irradiation. TiO2 acts as the photocatalyst, generating reactive oxygen species that effect the oxidation. Typical conditions: suspension of TiO2 in a solvent like acetonitrile or ethanol, O2 bubbling, UV lamp, ambient to moderate temperature.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction in aqueous solution; exchanges anions to produce silver sulfate and ammonium nitrate. Key transformation: 2 Ag⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → Ag₂SO₄, (NH₄)⁺ + 2 NO₃⁻ → (NH₄)NO₃. Conducted by mixing aqueous solutions of AgNO₃ and (NH₄)₂SO₄ at room temperature with stirring; water is the medium, no catalyst required.

Double nucleophilic substitution (SN2 hydrolysis of a dihalide); 1,4‑dichlorobutane reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide, each chloride being displaced by hydroxide to afford 1,4‑butanediol and sodium chloride. Conducted in aqueous or aqueous‑ethanol medium under reflux, often with excess NaOH to drive the reaction to completion; no catalyst required.

Double displacement/acid‑base exchange reaction. Purpose: replace acetate ligands on copper(II) with fluoride to generate soluble copper(II) fluoride and free acetic acid. Key transformation: Cu(OAc)2 + 2 HF → CuF2 + 2 HOAc. Typical conditions: performed in anhydrous solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane at 0–25 °C, using excess gaseous or aqueous HF under an inert atmosphere. No catalyst is required.

Double displacement precipitation reaction. Purpose: precipitate cobalt(II) carbonate while forming soluble ammonium sulfate. Key transformation: CoSO4 + (NH4)2CO3 → CoCO3↓ + (NH4)2SO4. Typical conditions: aqueous solutions of the two salts are mixed at room temperature with stirring; the insoluble carbonate precipitates and is isolated by filtration. No catalyst; water is the solvent.

Formation of an acid chloride from a carboxylic acid (reagent‑mediated activation). Purpose: convert 4‑tert‑butylbenzoic acid into the corresponding acid chloride for further acylation chemistry. Key transformation: 4‑tert‑butyl‑C6H4CO2H + SOCl2 → 4‑tert‑butyl‑C6H4COCl + SO2 + HCl. Typical conditions: react the acid with a slight excess of thionyl chloride in anhydrous dichloromethane or pyridine, initially at 0 °C then allowed to warm to reflux (≈70 °C) for 30 min to 2 h. Pyridine or a tertiary amine is often used as a base to scavenger HCl. No additional catalyst required.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis) forming lead telluride; aqueous lead(II) perchlorate reacts with sodium telluride to precipitate insoluble PbTe while sodium perchlorate remains in solution; usually carried out at room temperature in water with stirring; no special catalyst needed.

Alpha‑halogenation of a ketone (electrophilic addition to the enol form). Purpose: install a bromine atom at the α‑position of acetone to give bromoacetone. Key transformation: CH3COCH3 + Br2 → CH3COCH2Br + HBr. Typical conditions: bromine is added dropwise to acetone solution in carbon tetrachloride or chloroform at 0 °C to ambient temperature, often under light or with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., H2SO4) to promote enol formation. Solvent is a non‑nucleophilic, inert halogenated solvent; no metal catalyst is required.

Nitrile‑to‑amidine conversion (amidination); benzonitrile reacts with methylamine to give N′‑methylbenzenecarboximidamide; the amine adds to the electrophilic nitrile carbon forming an imidate intermediate that tautomerizes to the amidine; usually carried out in ethanol or another polar protic solvent under reflux, often with a catalytic amount of acid to facilitate proton transfers.

Acid‑base neutralization reaction. Purpose: generate the potassium salt of acetic acid and water. Key transformation: CH3COOH + KOH → CH3COOK + H2O. Typical conditions: aqueous solutions of acetic acid and potassium hydroxide are mixed at room temperature with stirring until neutralization is complete (pH ≈ 7). No catalyst; water is the solvent.

Acid‑base salt metathesis; purpose: liberate free gluconic acid from calcium gluconate and form calcium chloride; key transformation: Ca(gluconate)₂ + 2 HCl → 2 gluconic acid + CaCl₂; typical conditions: aqueous solution, ambient temperature, excess concentrated HCl, vigorous stirring until complete dissolution, no catalyst.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification); NaOH hydrolyzes phenyl salicylate to phenol and sodium salicylate; typically performed in aqueous or aqueous‑ethanol solution under reflux for 1–2 h; no additional catalyst required.

Palladium‑catalyzed Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling (mono‑arylation); phenylboronic acid couples with one iodo substituent of 1,2‑diiodobenzene in the presence of Pd(OAc)2, triphenylphosphine ligand and Cs2CO3 base to give 2‑iodobiphenyl while the other iodine remains, generating CsI as by‑product; commonly run at 80–120 °C in polar aprotic solvents such as toluene, dioxane or DMF under inert atmosphere.

Oxidative conversion of a catechol to a quinone using sodium periodate; NaIO4 oxidizes 1,4‑dihydroxynaphthalene to 1,4‑naphthoquinone in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic media, usually at 0–25 °C; periodate is reduced to iodate/iodide; no catalyst needed; purpose is to introduce the quinone functionality.

Halogen exchange (fluorination) where elemental fluorine substitutes chlorine atoms on hexachlorocyclotriphosphazene to give hexafluorocyclotriphosphazene and chlorine gas; typically performed under anhydrous conditions, often in liquid HF or a fluorinating medium at elevated temperature, with nickel or copper vessels to tolerate corrosive F2.

Dehydrative chlorination of a phenol using thionyl chloride; meta‑cresol reacts with SOCl2 in a dry organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) or pyridine at 0 °C to reflux to form 3‑methyl chlorobenzene; gaseous HCl and SO2 are liberated; pyridine or a tertiary amine often serves as base/scavenger.

Fischer esterification of a triol with acetic acid; trimethylolpropane reacts with excess acetic acid in the presence of an acid catalyst such as H2SO4 under reflux, forming trimethylolpropane triacetate and water; water is removed (Dean‑Stark trap) to drive the equilibrium; glacial acetic acid can serve as solvent; purpose is protection of the three hydroxyl groups as acetate esters.

Double displacement (acid‑base neutralization). Used to prepare ammonium dichromate by exchanging K⁺ and NH₄⁺ ions. Key transformation: 2 NH₄OH + K₂Cr₂O₇ → 2 KOH + (NH₄)₂Cr₂O₇. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the solvent; no catalyst required.

Oxidation (dehydrogenation) of fluorene with DDQ (2,3‑dichloro‑5,6‑dicyano‑1,4‑benzoquinone). Converts fluorene to fluorenone by removing two benzylic hydrogens; DDQ is reduced to its hydroquinone form. Typically carried out in dry aromatic solvent (toluene or CH₂Cl₂) under reflux or at 0–80 °C, often under nitrogen; no additional catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amidation) of dicyclohexylamine with acetic anhydride. Forms N,N‑dicyclohexylacetamide and liberates one equivalent of acetic acid.
