Halogenation (free‑radical substitution) of a Si‑H bond; purpose: replace one hydrogen on methylsilane with chlorine to give methylchlorosilane; Cl₂ abstracts a hydrogen atom from CH₃SiH₃, forming HCl and CH₃SiClH₂; usually performed under inert atmosphere, in anhydrous, non‑polar solvent such as chlorobenzene or toluene, with UV light or a radical initiator; no metal catalyst.

Single‑displacement/halogen exchange (redox) reaction; purpose: use chlorine’s stronger oxidizing power to liberate bromine from barium bromide; Cl₂ oxidizes Br⁻ to Br₂ while being reduced to Cl⁻, yielding BaCl₂ and Br₂ vapor; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst; water is the solvent and bromine evolves as a gas.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling (palladium‑catalyzed aryl‑aryl bond formation); purpose: construct the biaryl 2‑phenylbenzoic acid from 2‑iodobenzoic acid and phenylboronic acid; key steps: oxidative addition of Pd(0) into C–I bond, transmetalation with phenyl‑B(OH)₂, reductive elimination to form the new C‑C bond; typical conditions: 1–5 mol % Pd(PPh₃)₄ or Pd(dppf)Cl₂, base such as K₂CO₃ or Na₂CO₃, mixed solvent (toluene/water or dioxane/water), 80–100 °C under nitrogen; no additional catalyst beyond the Pd complex.

Isomerization (geometric) of itaconic acid to citraconic acid; converts the trans‑methylene double bond to the cis configuration. Typically performed by heating the acid with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or a metal catalyst such as Pd/C at 100–150 °C. No external reagents required; solvent can be toluene or the melt itself.

Redox oxidation: Concentrated nitric acid oxidizes Fe(II) to Fe(III) producing ferric nitrate, water and nitrogen dioxide gas. Typically carried out by mixing the reagents and heating under reflux; the reaction medium is the nitric acid itself and no external catalyst is required.

Acetylation of an alcohol (esterification): Acetic anhydride transfers an acetyl group to the hydroxyl of methyl 5‑hydroxyhexanoate, yielding methyl 5‑acetoxyhexanoate and acetic acid as by‑product. Conducted at 0 °C to room temperature in an inert organic solvent (e.g., pyridine or dichloromethane) with a base to scavenge the generated acid.

Acyl chloride esterification (acylation) – conversion of (E)-hex‑2‑en‑1‑ol to (E)-hex‑2‑enyl acetate using acetyl chloride, with evolution of HCl. Usually performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, in the presence of a base (pyridine, triethylamine) to scavenge the liberated HCl and promote ester formation.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction): Myristicin is hydrogenated over palladium on carbon, saturating the allylic double bond to give dihydromyristicin. Performed in a solvent such as ethanol or methanol under 1–5 atm H₂ at ambient or mild temperature; Pd/C acts as the catalyst.

Metathesis/acid‑base double displacement: Magnesium stearate reacts with aqueous ammonium hydroxide, forming insoluble magnesium hydroxide precipitate and soluble ammonium stearate. The reaction proceeds at room temperature in water; no catalyst is needed.

General type: nucleophilic substitution (alcohol → alkyl bromide). Purpose: convert primary alcohol to 2‑bromoethyl acetate. Key transformation: OH is displaced by Br, generating phosphorous acid (H₃PO₃) as by‑product. Typical conditions: add PBr₃ dropwise to a solution of the alcohol at 0 °C, then allow the mixture to warm to rt (often under N₂). Common solvents/catalysts: dry CH₂Cl₂, CCl₄ or ether; no external base required, though pyridine can be used to absorb HBr.

Direct condensation of ethylamine with glycolic acid to afford N‑ethyl‑2‑hydroxyacetamide with loss of water. Reaction type: simple amidation (carboxylic acid‑amine coupling). Usually performed at elevated temperature (150–200 °C) in a high‑boiling solvent such as toluene or xylene, or under reduced pressure with azeotropic removal of water; inert atmosphere may be used.

Hydroamination (addition of ammonia to an alkene): 1‑Dodecene reacts with ammonia in the presence of a metal catalyst (e.g., Raney nickel, Rh, or Co) to give dodecylamine. Conducted at elevated temperature (150–250 °C) and high NH₃ pressure (several bar) in the gas or liquid phase; the metal surface facilitates the N–C bond formation.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an aldehyde: 5‑Methylfurfural is reduced over palladium on carbon to 5‑methylfurfuryl alcohol. The reaction is carried out in ethanol or methanol under 1–3 atm H₂ at room temperature or slight heating; Pd/C serves as the hydrogenation catalyst.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling; forms a C‑C bond between the aryl bromide of 3‑bromofuran and the arylboronic acid of 4‑methoxyphenylboronic acid to give 3‑(4‑methoxyphenyl)furan; typically performed with 1–5 mol % Pd catalyst (e.g., Pd(PPh₃)₄, PdCl₂(dppf)), a base such as K₂CO₃ or Cs₂CO₃, in a mixed organic/aqueous solvent (toluene/H₂O, dioxane/H₂O, or THF/H₂O) at 80–100 °C under inert atmosphere.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (Friedel‑Crafts alkylation) of phenol onto cyclohexanone to give 1,1‑bis(4‑hydroxyphenyl)cyclohexane; acid or Lewis‑acid catalyst (e.g., H₂SO₄, BF₃·OEt₂) activates the carbonyl, allowing two phenol molecules to add to the same carbon; typically reflux in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as carbon disulfide, chloroform or nitrobenzene; water removed to drive equilibrium.

Olefin metathesis (cross‑metathesis) between propene and isobutene to exchange alkyl fragments, yielding ethylene and 2‑methyl‑2‑butene; catalyzed by a transition‑metal carbene complex (e.g., Grubbs‑type Ru catalyst) in an inert solvent such as dichloromethane or toluene, typically 40–80 °C under nitrogen or argon.

Simple halide metathesis (double displacement) in which ZnCl₂ and KF exchange anions to form KCl and ZnF₂; can be carried out in aqueous solution or molten salts; the insoluble ZnF₂ precipitates, driving the reaction forward; no special catalyst required, ambient temperature often sufficient.

Eschweiler‑Clarke methylation of 4‑aminophenol; the primary amine reacts with formaldehyde and formic acid, generating an iminium intermediate that is reduced by formic acid, converting the –NH₂ group to a –N(CH₃)₂ group and releasing CO₂ and H₂O; usually performed by refluxing the substrate in a mixture of methanol/water (or ethanol) with excess formaldehyde (often as paraformaldehyde) and formic acid for several hours.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution forming a chloroformate; menthol reacts with phosgene, the alcohol attacks the carbonyl carbon, releasing chloride and forming menthyl chloroformate plus HCl; carried out in dry dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to rt, using an amine base (pyridine or triethylamine) to absorb HCl and maintain anhydrous conditions.

Acid‑base reaction with gas evolution (carbonate decomposition). Silver carbonate is protonated by methanesulfonic acid, producing silver methanesulfonate, carbon dioxide gas, and water. Conducted in methanol or aqueous medium under reflux; the evolution of CO₂ drives the reaction forward. No catalyst is needed.

Acid‑base salt formation; the basic amine function of propafenone is protonated by hydrochloric acid to give propafenone hydrochloride; the reaction is done by dissolving propafenone in a polar solvent such as ethanol or methanol, adding aqueous HCl (or HCl gas) at 0–25 °C, then isolating the solid salt by filtration or evaporation; no catalyst required.

Reduction of an acyl chloride with lithium aluminium hydride: LiAlH₄ reduces 4‑methylpentanoyl chloride to 4‑methyl‑1‑pentanol (primary alcohol); carried out in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere, quenching excess hydride with careful addition of water then dilute acid to afford the alcohol.

Copper‑catalyzed Ullmann ether synthesis; purpose is formation of an aryl‑oxygen bond to give 3‑phenoxypyridine. Phenol is deprotonated by potassium carbonate, the phenoxide attacks 3‑bromopyridine in the presence of CuI as catalyst. Typical conditions: DMSO as solvent, 100–150 °C under nitrogen, 5–10 mol % CuI, sometimes an additional ligand. By‑products are CuBr and KBr.

Fluorination of a binary semiconductor; indium arsenide reacts violently with fluorine gas to form indium trifluoride (InF₃) and arsenic trifluoride (AsF₃) (or higher fluorides if excess F₂ is present). The reaction is highly exothermic and is performed in a fluorine‑compatible reactor (e.g., nickel or Monel) at room temperature to moderate heating, with an inert carrier gas (N₂ or He). No catalyst is employed; moisture must be excluded.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis); purpose is to exchange the anions and precipitate insoluble BaSO₄. Aqueous solutions of Ba(NO₃)₂ and Rb₂SO₄ are mixed at ambient temperature with stirring; BaSO₄ precipitates and is filtered, while RbNO₃ remains in solution.

Reaction type: further oxidation of a sulfoxide to a sulfone; purpose: conversion to a more oxidized sulfur species for downstream chemistry; key transformation: a second equivalent of hydrogen peroxide transfers an oxygen atom to the sulfoxide sulfur, yielding allyl phenyl sulfone and water; typical conditions: excess H2O2 (30 %) in MeCN or methanol, 0–40 °C, optionally with a catalyst (molybdate, vanadyl acetylacetonate) to promote complete oxidation.

Oxidation of arsine by hydrogen peroxide in aqueous solution; converts AsH₃ (arsenic ‑3) to arsenic trioxide (As₂O₃, arsenic +3) with water as by‑product. Typically performed at room temperature in dilute aqueous medium using excess H₂O₂; no catalyst required, water is the solvent.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of ethyl bromide with hydroxide; purpose is conversion of the alkyl halide to ethanol. Tetramethylammonium hydroxide provides OH⁻ in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMSO or aqueous MeCN) at 0 °C to reflux. Ethanol and tetramethylammonium bromide are formed.

Acyl chloride formation from acetic anhydride and hydrogen chloride; purpose is generation of acetyl chloride. Anhydrous Ac₂O is treated with gaseous or aqueous HCl (often as a solution in dry pyridine) at 0–25 °C under inert atmosphere. The reaction yields acetyl chloride and acetic acid; removal of HCl gas drives the equilibrium.

Electrophilic aromatic chlorination of 2,4‑dichlorophenol; purpose is to install additional chlorine atoms to give 2,3,4,5‑tetrachlorophenol. The reaction is carried out by bubbling Cl₂ gas through a solution of the phenol in a non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., CCl₄ or CHCl₃) at 0–25 °C, often catalyzed by FeCl₃ or AlCl₃. Multiple chlorination steps occur via the phenoxide activating the ring.

NaBH₄ reduction of a ketone; purpose is conversion of 3‑octanone to the secondary alcohol 3‑octanol. The ketone is dissolved in methanol, ethanol, or THF and NaBH₄ (1–2 equiv) is added at 0 °C to ambient temperature, stirring until completion. The reaction is quenched with water and the product is isolated after work‑up.

Acid–salt metathesis; reaction of barium acetate with nitric acid yields barium nitrate and acetic acid; carried out in water, often with gentle heating to promote dissolution and mixing; no catalyst is employed.

Metal‑base dissolution (amphoteric metal reaction). Gallium dissolves in hot concentrated NaOH to form soluble sodium gallate (Na[Ga(OH)4] or NaGaO2) while releasing H2 gas. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (~10 M), heated near reflux (≈80‑100 °C). No catalyst required; reaction is performed in a glass vessel under stirring.

Double displacement with thermal decomposition; heated Ca(OH)2 reacts with BeCl2 to form CaCl2 and precipitate Be(OH)2; performed by heating a mixture of the solid salts or their aqueous solutions to drive off water; water may be present as solvent; no catalyst required.

SN2 O‑methylation of genistein phenolic hydroxyls with methyl iodide in the presence of a base (e.g., K2CO3 or NaH) in an aprotic solvent such as DMF or acetone; purpose is to convert genistein into the more lipophilic flavonoid ononetin; reaction proceeds at 0 °C to reflux, HI formed is neutralized by the base.

Oxidative conversion of the ethyl side chain of 1‑ethyl‑3‑methoxybenzene to a carboxylic acid using potassium permanganate in aqueous or aqueous‑acetone medium; type is a strong oxidation/oxidative cleavage; heated under reflux in alkaline or neutral conditions, then acidified to isolate 3‑methoxybenzoic acid; CO₂ and H₂O are formed as gaseous/solvent by‑products.

Zinc reduction of 4‑nitro‑1,1′‑biphenyl to 4‑aminobiphenyl in acetic acid (Bechamp‑type reduction); Zn dust serves as the reductant, the reaction is carried out under reflux in glacial AcOH, generating Zn(OAc)₂ and water; purpose is conversion of a nitro group to an aniline.

Nucleophilic substitution of arsenic trichloride with phenyl lithium to give phenyl dichloroarsine; performed at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) in anhydrous THF or diethyl ether under inert atmosphere; LiCl is formed as a by‑product; the reaction introduces an aryl group onto arsenic.

Double displacement/precipitation reaction; converts soluble scandium nitrate to insoluble scandium carbonate for purification or downstream processing. An aqueous solution of scandium nitrate is mixed with an aqueous solution of sodium carbonate, usually at room temperature or with mild heating. Sc2(CO3)3 precipitates, while NaNO3 stays in solution. No catalyst; water is the medium; the solid is filtered, washed and dried.

Aqueous base precipitation; Ho2(SO4)3 + 6 NH3·H2O → 2 Ho(OH)3(s) + 3 (NH4)2SO4(aq); reaction in water with excess aqueous ammonia, often with gentle heating; holmium hydroxide precipitates while ammonium sulfate remains in solution; no catalyst needed.

Oxidation of 9,10‑anthracenediol to 9,10‑anthraquinone using hydrogen peroxide catalyzed by FeCl₃ (Fenton‑type oxidation); typically conducted in water or a water/acetone mixture at ambient temperature with a few mol % FeCl₃; water is the only stoichiometric by‑product.

Condensation of pyrrole‑2‑carboxylic acid with ammonia to afford pyrrole‑2‑carboxamide; usually requires activation of the acid (e.g., conversion to the acid chloride with SOCl₂ or use of a coupling reagent such as DCC) and is carried out in dry aprotic solvent (THF, DMF) at 80‑120 °C under inert atmosphere, with removal of water; purpose is formation of a primary amide.

General type: Friedländer quinoline synthesis (condensation‑cyclization). Purpose: construction of the heterocyclic core 4‑hydroxyquinoline from an o‑aminophenol and a β‑ketoester. Key transformations: nucleophilic attack of the amino group on the carbonyl of methyl acetoacetate, followed by cyclization, dehydration, and decarboxylation; the ester groups are eliminated as methanol and carbon dioxide. Typical conditions: strong acid catalyst (e.g., polyphosphoric acid, H2SO4) at 150–200 °C under inert atmosphere. Common solvents/catalysts: polyphosphoric acid itself acts as solvent; alternatively, acetic acid with catalytic HCl can be used.

General type: catalytic hydrogenation (reductive desulfonylation). Purpose: conversion of a sulfone (tetrahydrothiophene‑1,1‑dioxide) to the corresponding thioether (tetrahydrothiophene). Key transformations: Raney nickel catalyzes the uptake of two equivalents of H2, reducing the S=O bonds to S–H and ultimately to S, with formation of two molecules of water. Typical conditions: H2 pressure 1–5 atm, Raney Ni (activated), temperature 50–150 °C, often in ethanol or water as solvent. Solvent: ethanol, isopropanol, or aqueous media.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution; carbamate synthesis. Phenyl chloroformate reacts with N,N-dimethylamine to afford N,N-dimethyl phenylcarbamate and HCl (often trapped as a salt). The reaction is usually performed in dry dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt, with an added base such as triethylamine or excess amine to neutralize HCl. Employed for protecting amine functions or preparing phenyl‑carbamate building blocks.

Geometric isomerization of a trans‑alkene to the cis‑alkene (fumaric acid → maleic acid); purpose is to obtain the more reactive cis isomer. Key transformation: rotation around the C=C bond facilitated by acid catalysis or photochemical/thermal activation. Typical conditions: aqueous acidic medium (e.g., 0.1 M HCl) at 60–100 °C, or UV irradiation in the presence of a photosensitizer; catalytic amounts of mineral acid or a solid acid (e.g., zeolite) can also be employed.

General type: Mitsunobu coupling (ether formation via nucleophilic substitution). Purpose: synthesis of a symmetric ether (di‑isopropyl ether) from a secondary alcohol under inversion‑free conditions. Key transformations: triphenylphosphine reacts with diethyl azodicarboxylate (DEAD) to generate a phosphonium intermediate; the alkoxide derived from 2‑propanol attacks this intermediate, displacing the hydrazine dicarboxylate and forming the ether while producing triphenylphosphine oxide and diethyl hydrazine dicarboxylate as by‑products. Typical conditions: anhydrous THF or dichloromethane, 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere (N2). Solvent/catalyst: PPh₃ and DEAD are stoichiometric reagents; no additional catalyst required.

General type: transesterification (ester exchange). Purpose: preparation of isopropyl lactate, a biodegradable solvent, from methyl lactate. Key transformations: nucleophilic attack of isopropanol on the carbonyl carbon of methyl lactate displaces methanol, generating the new isopropyl ester. Typical conditions: reflux in a polar aprotic solvent (toluene, xylene) or bulk; removal of methanol (e.g., azeotropic distillation) drives equilibrium to product. Catalysts: acidic (p‑toluenesulfonic acid, H₂SO₄) or basic (NaOMe, K₂CO₃) can be employed; enzyme (lipase) is an alternative for milder conditions.

General type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2) alkylation of a telluride anion. Purpose: synthesis of dimethyl telluride, a volatile organotellurium compound. Key transformations: Na₂Te (generated in situ from sodium telluride) attacks methyl bromide at the carbon bearing the leaving bromide, forming a C–Te bond; a second equivalent of methyl bromide reacts with the intermediate to give the symmetric dimethyl telluride, with NaBr as by‑product. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO, or THF; ambient to gentle heating (25–80 °C); inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation of telluride. No additional catalyst required.

General type: phosphorothioate phosphorylation (Williamson‑type ether synthesis on phosphorus). Purpose: preparation of the organophosphate insecticide fenthion. Key transformations: K₂CO₃ deprotonates 4‑nitro‑3‑methylphenol to generate the phenoxide, which attacks the electrophilic phosphorus of O,O‑dimethyl phosphorochloridothioate, displacing chloride; carbonate decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O, and KCl is formed as a salt. Typical conditions: dry aprotic solvent (acetone, THF, or dichloromethane), reflux or gentle heating (50–80 °C), inert atmosphere (N₂) to prevent oxidation of the thio‑phosphate. Common reagents: potassium carbonate as base, the phosphorochloridothioate as electrophile; no metal catalyst is required.

Carboxylation of urea with carbon dioxide to form allophanic acid (carbamic acid; also called ureidoformic acid). Reaction proceeds under CO₂ pressure (1–5 atm) in aqueous or alcoholic medium, often at ambient or slightly elevated temperature; no catalyst is required.

Salt metathesis (precipitation) between silver nitrite and hydrochloric acid; AgNO₂ reacts with HCl in aqueous solution to form soluble nitrous acid (HNO₂) and insoluble silver chloride precipitate; performed at room temperature in water, no special catalyst required.

Oxidative cleavage (KMnO4 oxidation); purpose is to convert the two benzylic methyl groups of ortho‑xylene into carboxyl groups yielding phthalic (o‑benzenedicarboxylic) acid; key transformation: CH3 → CO2H on each aromatic carbon; typically performed with hot aqueous potassium permanganate in basic medium, followed by acid work‑up; MnO2 precipitates as a by‑product.

Acid‑base protonolysis of a Grignard reagent; purpose is to quench methylmagnesium chloride and generate the corresponding hydrocarbon; key transformation: Mg–CH3 bond is protonated to give methane and MgCl2; carried out in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature, followed by aqueous work‑up.

Ceric ammonium nitrate (CAN) oxidative demethylation; purpose: generate phenolic eugenol from methyleugenol under mild aqueous conditions; key transformation: Ar‑OCH₃ + CAN → Ar‑OH + formaldehyde + reduced Ce(III); typical conditions: aqueous/acetonitrile (1:1), room temperature, 1–2 equiv CAN, pH neutral to slightly acidic; catalyst: CAN (oxidant).

Ester aminolysis (amide formation) where methyl 3‑(methylthio)propionate reacts with ammonia; ammonia attacks the carbonyl, displacing methanol and yielding 3‑(methylthio)propion; performed under reflux in a sealed tube or high‑pressure reactor, often in excess liquid NH₃ or aqueous ammonia; no catalyst required; temperature ~100–150 °C.

Acid‑catalyzed oxidation of sulfur dioxide by hydrogen peroxide in aqueous sulfuric acid to produce dithionic acid (H₂S₂O₆) and water; performed at low temperature (0–5 °C) in dilute acid solution; H₂O₂ acts as oxidant.

Metathesis/precipitation (neutralization) reaction; purpose is to isolate insoluble chromium(III) hydroxide; key transformation: CrCl3 + 3 RbOH → Cr(OH)3 (solid) + 3 RbCl (in solution); performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the Cr(OH)3 precipitate is filtered off.

Oxidative chlorination (halogenolysis) of platinum silicide; purpose is to convert the silicon component to volatile SiCl4 and oxidize platinum to PtCl4; key transformation: PtSi + 4 Cl2 → SiCl4 (gas) + PtCl4 (solid or sublimed); requires heating (typically several hundred °C) under a flow of chlorine gas; no solvent is used.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 2‑butyne‑1,4‑diol using H₂ (1–5 atm) over Pd/C or Raney Ni in a protic solvent (e.g., ethanol or methanol) at 25–80 °C; reduces the C≡C triple bond to a C–C single bond, converting the diol into saturated 1,4‑butanediol. Reaction type: reduction (hydrogenation); purpose: saturate alkyne to give a useful diol.

Oxidative cleavage of the C=C side chain of 4‑hydroxy‑3,5‑dimethoxycinnamic acid with aqueous KMnO₄ under reflux in alkaline medium; the unsaturated side chain is fully oxidized to a carboxyl group, yielding syringic acid (4‑hydroxy‑3,5‑dimethoxybenzoic acid). Reaction type: oxidative degradation; purpose: shorten phenylpropanoid to benzoic‑acid derivative.

Acid‑catalyzed skeletal isomerization of 1,1‑dimethylcyclohexane to 1,2‑dimethylcyclohexane; typically performed with strong mineral acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or solid acid catalysts (AlCl₃, zeolites) at elevated temperatures (150‑250 °C). Reaction type: alkyl‑shift isomerization; purpose: relocate a methyl group to obtain the positional isomer.

Transfer hydrogenation of 4‑(4‑hydroxyphenyl)but‑3‑en‑2‑one using Pd/C and ammonium formate as the hydrogen source in methanol (or ethanol) at room temperature to reflux; the α,β‑unsaturated double bond is reduced while the carbonyl remains intact, affording 4‑(4‑hydroxyphenyl)‑2‑butanone. Reaction type: catalytic reduction (transfer hydrogenation); purpose: saturate the alkene in a keto‑aryl substrate.

Acylation (esterification) of n‑propyl alcohol with acetic anhydride catalyzed by DMAP (0.05–0.1 equiv) in anhydrous dichloromethane (or THF) at 0 °C to ambient temperature; the alcohol attacks the anhydride to give propyl acetate with acetic acid as the by‑product. Reaction type: acyl substitution (esterification); purpose: synthesis of propyl acetate.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis (saponification) of 1‑ethynylcyclohexyl acetate using NaOH (1 equiv) in aqueous/organic solvent (e.g., water/THF or ethanol) under reflux; the ester is converted to 1‑ethynylcyclohexanol and sodium acetate. Reaction type: ester hydrolysis; purpose: deprotect acetate to liberate the free alcohol.

Transesterification (SN2 nucleophilic substitution) between methanol and isopropyl methanesulfonate; methanol attacks the sulfonate ester, exchanging the alkoxy groups to give isopropyl alcohol and methyl methanesulfonate. Typically performed by refluxing the sulfonate ester in excess methanol, often with a catalytic amount of a base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) or acid (e.g., catalytic H₂SO₄) to accelerate the reaction.

Double displacement acid‑base reaction; hydrochloric acid protonates acetate to acetic acid and yields soluble neodymium chloride. Conducted in aqueous solution, typically at room temperature with stirring; no catalyst.

Strong‑reduction of an ester (pentyl formate) with lithium aluminium hydride; LiAlH₄ delivers hydride to the carbonyl, cleaving the C–O bond and producing the corresponding primary alcohols, pentanol (from the alkoxy fragment) and methanol (from the acyl fragment). Conducted under anhydrous conditions in dry ether or THF, usually at 0 °C to reflux, under nitrogen or argon atmosphere.

Neutral (or acid‑catalyzed) ester hydrolysis; water attacks the carbonyl of pent‑4‑enyl acetate to give pent‑4‑en‑1‑ol and acetic acid. Reaction proceeds slowly at ambient temperature; rate is increased with a catalytic amount of mineral acid (e.g., H₂SO₄, 0.1 M) and heating (50–80 °C) in aqueous medium.

Acid‑base metathesis/precipitation reaction; aqueous sulfuric acid reacts with soluble barium perchlorate, exchanging anions to generate perchloric acid in solution and insoluble barium sulfate, which precipitates. Carried out at ambient temperature in water; no catalyst required; the solid BaSO₄ is filtered off to isolate HClO₄.

MnO₂ oxidation of furfuryl alcohol; the benzylic alcohol is converted to 2‑furaldehyde (furfural) while MnO₂ is reduced to MnO and water is formed. Typical conditions are stirring the alcohol with excess activated MnO₂ in a dry aprotic solvent (e.g., chloroform or toluene) at 25‑50 °C, sometimes with gentle heating. Purpose is selective aldehyde synthesis for biomass‑derived chemicals.

Complete combustion of 2,7‑dimethyloctane; molecular oxygen oxidizes the hydrocarbon to carbon dioxide and water, releasing heat and light. Requires a flame or spark and excess O₂ (air) at high temperature; occurs in the gas phase, no solvent or catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (esterification) of 3‑bromopropanoyl chloride with methanol; the alcohol attacks the acyl chloride, forming methyl 3‑bromopropanoate and releasing hydrogen chloride. Typically performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, in the presence of a base (e.g., pyridine, triethylamine) to scavenge HCl.

Double‑displacement (acid‑base) reaction between sulfuric acid and calcium hydrogen phosphate; the strong acid protonates the phosphate, releasing phosphoric acid, while calcium ions combine with sulfate to precipitate calcium sulfate. Conducted in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to promote solid formation; no additional catalysts required.

Direct combination (synthesis) reaction forming zinc sulfide from elemental zinc and sulfur; performed by mixing the powders and heating strongly (300‑600 °C) in an inert or air atmosphere; solid‑state reaction, no solvent needed.

Ligand exchange / complexation of gallium(III) sulfate with maltol to afford gallium maltolate complex; aqueous solution of Ga₂(SO₄)₃ mixed with excess maltol (often as sodium maltolate) at mildly acidic to neutral pH and gentle heating (50–80 °C); precipitated gallium maltolate is isolated, and sulfuric acid is released into the solution.

Electrophilic etherification with hypofluorous ester. Purpose: preparation of methyl‑trifluoromethoxy ether, a fluorinated solvent or intermediate. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of methanol O‑atom on the electrophilic CF₃O‑ group of trifluoromethyl hypofluorite (CF₃O‑OF), forming CH₃OCF₃ and releasing HF. Typical conditions: low temperature (‑20 °C to 0 °C) in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform, inert atmosphere (N₂), often with a mild base (pyridine or triethylamine) to scavenge HF. Reaction time: 30 min to 1 h.

Base‑catalyzed aldol/Claisen‑Schmidt condensation followed by intramolecular cyclization (flavanone synthesis). Purpose: construction of the flavanone scaffold (4′‑hydroxyflavanone). Key transformations: (a) condensation of 4‑hydroxybenzaldehyde with acetophenone under NaOH to give a chalcone intermediate; (b) Michael‑type intramolecular cyclization of the chalcone to a 2‑phenyl‑chroman‑4‑one ring system. Typical conditions: 10–20 % aqueous NaOH in ethanol or methanol, 0 °C addition then reflux 2–4 h. Work‑up involves acidification to precipitate the flavanone. Solvent: ethanol/methanol; catalyst: NaOH (base).

Reductive amination (Schiff‑base formation and NaBH₃CN reduction). Purpose: N‑alkylation of a secondary amine to give N,N‑dibenzyl aniline. Key transformations: condensation of benzaldehyde with N‑benzyl aniline to generate an imine, followed by selective reduction of the C=N bond by sodium cyanoborohydride to afford the tertiary amine. Typical conditions: methanol or ethanol solution, catalytic acetic acid (or pyridinium buffer) to promote imine formation, NaBH₃CN (1.2–1.5 equiv), 0 °C to rt, 2–6 h. Solvent: MeOH/EtOH; catalyst/base: acetic acid (mild acid).

Hydration/formal acid formation from metal oxide. Purpose: preparation of tungstic acid (H₂WO₄) for further inorganic syntheses or as a catalyst precursor. Key transformation: addition of water to tungsten trioxide to generate the hydrated oxide, H₂WO₄, which precipitates as a white solid. Typical conditions: excess distilled water, heating to reflux (≈100 °C) for 1–2 h; the solution may be cooled to induce crystallization. No special catalysts required; solvent is water.

Double‑displacement/acid‑base reaction forming a metal thiocyanate. Purpose: synthesis of cobalt(II) thiocyanate, a coordination compound used in pigment and analytical chemistry. Key transformation: CoO reacts with ammonium thiocyanate, protonating the oxide to water while the thiocyanate anion coordinates to Co²⁺, yielding Co(SCN)₂, NH₃, and H₂O. Typical conditions: aqueous suspension of CoO mixed with excess NH₄SCN, heated to 80–100 °C for 30–60 min. Solvent: water; sometimes a small amount of ethanol is added to improve solubility.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis) of alkali‑metal bromide with silver nitrate; employed to isolate insoluble silver bromide and generate soluble lithium nitrate. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature; the mixture is stirred until a white AgBr precipitate forms, which is then filtered. No catalyst is required.

Double displacement (metathesis) acid‑base reaction; aqueous mixture of sulfuric acid and cobalt(II) phosphate yields soluble cobalt(II) sulfate and phosphoric acid; typically performed in water with heating to dissolve the phosphate, no special catalyst required.

Oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid; 2‑amino‑2‑methylpropanal is oxidized by H₂O₂ (often in aqueous basic medium) to give 2‑amino‑2‑methylpropanoic acid; reaction proceeds at room temperature, pH 7‑9, sometimes with a catalytic amount of transition‑metal catalyst (e.g., Fe or Mn) but can occur without; water is the solvent.

Acyl substitution / esterification (acetylation) of a primary alcohol; acetic anhydride transfers an acetyl group to diethylene glycol monoethyl ether producing the corresponding acetate ester and acetic acid; usually carried out neat or in a low‑boiling solvent (e.g., pyridine) at 0 °C to reflux, often with a catalytic amount of DMAP or pyridine as base/solvent.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification; exchanges the methyl ester of benzoic acid for a phenyl ester, producing phenyl benzoate and methanol. Typically performed with excess phenol and a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H2SO4 or p‑TsOH) under reflux. Removal of methanol (e.g., azeotropic distillation) drives the equilibrium to the right. Solvent can be toluene or the phenol itself.

Double displacement precipitation (metathesis) in aqueous solution; sodium carbonate reacts with manganese sulfate to precipitate insoluble manganese carbonate while sodium sulfate remains in solution; performed at ambient temperature with stirring, no catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution of a secondary alcohol with hydroiodic acid; an SN1 process that yields 3‑iodopentane and water; usually performed by refluxing the alcohol in concentrated HI (often 48 % aqueous) possibly with catalytic red phosphorus to regenerate HI and suppress oxidation; the reaction proceeds under acidic conditions without added solvent or catalyst.

Hydrohalogenolysis of beryllium carbide with hydrogen bromide; HBr (gaseous or aqueous) reacts with BeC₂ at elevated temperature (~200–300 °C) to cleave the C≡C bond, generating methane (CH₄) and beryllium bromide (BeBr₂); reaction typically carried out in a sealed vessel or flow of HBr gas; safety precautions required due to toxicity of beryllium compounds.

Strong hydride reduction of a dicarboxylic acid; purpose is to reduce both carboxyl groups of glutaric acid to primary alcohols, yielding pentane‑1,5‑diol. LiAlH₄ delivers hydride to each carbonyl, generating the corresponding alkoxide which is protonated on work‑up. Conducted in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) under nitrogen at reflux; after completion the reaction is quenched with cautious addition of water then dilute acid to afford the diol.

Double‑displacement/acid‑base exchange between tetrafluoroboric acid and ammonium sulfate yielding ammonium tetrafluoroborate and sulfuric acid; conducted in aqueous medium, often with gentle heating or reflux to ensure complete reaction and crystallization of NH4BF4; no catalyst, water as solvent.

Catalytic hydrogenation of but‑2‑yn‑1‑ol to butan‑1‑ol. The alkyne triple bond is reduced to a saturated C–C single bond while the primary alcohol group remains unchanged. Typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm), 5–10 % Pd/C or Raney Ni catalyst, room temperature to 50 °C, in ethanol or THF; no other reagents required.

Acid–base dissolution of silicate. Perchloric acid protonates sodium silicate (Na2SiO3) to generate sodium perchlorate (NaClO4), silicic acid (H4SiO4) which polymerizes to silica gel, and water. Typically carried out in dilute aqueous HClO4 at 0–25 °C with vigorous stirring; the silica precipitate can be filtered, and the perchlorate remains in solution.

Copper‑catalyzed Ullmann ether coupling (aryl‑aryl ether formation); 2,4‑dichlorophenol reacts with 1‑bromo‑2,4‑dichlorobenzene in the presence of copper powder or CuI and a base (e.g., K₂CO₃) to afford chlorobenzilate (a diaryl ether) with HBr as by‑product; typical conditions are 150–200 °C in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or NMP under inert atmosphere.

High‑temperature carbonylation reduction of a metal oxide to a metal carbonyl; carbon monoxide reduces RuO₂ to triruthenium dodecacarbonyl while being oxidized to CO₂; performed at 200–250 °C under several atmospheres of CO pressure, often in a sealed reactor without solvent; no added catalyst beyond the oxide itself.

Acid‑metal displacement (redox) reaction; concentrated aqueous HCl attacks barium aluminide, oxidizing aluminum and barium to their chlorides while reducing protons to H₂ gas. Typical conditions: reflux in water or dilute HCl solution; no catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an α,β‑unsaturated carboxylic acid. Purpose: saturation of the C=C bond to give the fully saturated acid. The C=C of but‑3‑enoic acid is reduced to a C‑C single bond while the carboxyl group remains unchanged, yielding butyric acid. Typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm) over 10 % Pd/C in an alcoholic solvent (ethanol or methanol) at 25–80 °C; no additional reagents.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation). The carboxylic acid is deprotonated by potassium hydroxide to give the potassium carboxylate and water. Used to convert 3‑methylbutanoic acid into a water‑soluble salt for purification or for subsequent reactions. Typically carried out in aqueous or aqueous‑ethanol solution at ambient temperature with equimolar reagents; no special catalyst is required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) acid‑base neutralization; calcium acetate reacts with glycolic acid to exchange the cations, producing calcium glycolate (a calcium salt) and acetic acid as the by‑product. Usually carried out in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to evolve acetic acid; no catalyst needed.

General type: skeletal isomerization (alkane isomerization). Purpose: increase branching to improve fuel octane rating. Key transformation: rearrangement of the carbon skeleton of heptane to produce the more branched isomer 2‑methylhexane (C7H16). Typical conditions: moderate temperatures (200–350 °C) with acidic zeolite or metal‑acid bifunctional catalysts (e.g., Pt/ZSM‑5). Common solvents/catalysts: solid acid or metal‑acid catalysts; reaction performed in the gas phase without solvent.

Condensation (oxime formation): Propionaldehyde reacts with hydroxylamine to give the oxime (N‑propylidenehydroxylamine) and water. Nucleophilic addition of NH2OH to the carbonyl followed by loss of water. Typically carried out in ethanol or methanol at 0 °C to reflux, often using hydroxylamine·HCl with a base (e.g., pyridine) to neutralize HCl.

Carbonation reaction; purpose is to convert basic iron(II) oxide into iron(II) carbonate for mineral carbonation or material synthesis; key transformation is the incorporation of CO₂ into the oxide lattice forming a carbonate; typically carried out in an aqueous slurry or under elevated CO₂ pressure (1–10 MPa) at 150–300 °C; water serves as solvent, no catalyst required.

Double‑displacement precipitation reaction; mercury(II) sulfate and sodium selenide exchange anions, forming insoluble mercury(II) selenide precipitate and soluble sodium sulfate. Performed in aqueous medium at ambient temperature; the precipitate is filtered off; no catalyst required.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis) reaction; cobalt(II) chloride reacts with sodium tungstate to give cobalt(II) tungstate precipitate and sodium chloride in solution. Conducted in water, sometimes with mild heating to ensure dissolution before cooling to induce precipitation; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑base decomposition (neutralization) reaction; potassium hydroxide neutralizes ammonium cyanide, liberating ammonia gas, forming water, and generating potassium cyanide salt. Usually carried out in aqueous solution at low to moderate temperature to capture NH₃ gas; no catalyst required.

Reductive conversion of osmium tetroxide (OsO₄) by hydrogen gas to osmium dioxide (OsO₂) with water as by‑product. Carried out at elevated temperature (150–300 °C) in the gas phase or in a high‑boiling inert solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride); hydrogen serves as the reducing agent, no additional catalyst required.

Metathesis/acid‑base exchange reaction; ammonia reacts with urea nitrate, displacing nitric acid to form ammonium nitrate while freeing urea. Conducted in aqueous solution, often at low temperature to control exotherm; no catalyst needed.

E2 elimination (dehydrohalogenation); converts a tertiary alkyl bromide to a more substituted alkene by removal of HBr. Used to generate 2,3‑dimethyl‑2‑butene. Typically performed with a strong, bulky base such as potassium tert‑butoxide in an aprotic solvent (e.g., THF, DMSO) at 0 °C to reflux, often under inert atmosphere.

Halogen exchange (acyl‑halide substitution); acetyl chloride reacts with hydrogen iodide to give acetyl iodide and hydrogen chloride. The reaction is a nucleophilic substitution of chloride by iodide and is performed under anhydrous conditions, often in a non‑protic solvent such as dry dichloromethane or chloroform, at 0 °C to rt. Excess HI drives the equilibrium toward acetyl iodide; HCl gas is evolved.

Condensation of a carboxylic acid with its acid chloride to form a symmetric acid anhydride, releasing HCl. Generates pivalic anhydride for use as an acylating agent. Commonly carried out in a non‑nucleophilic base (pyridine or triethylamine) as HCl scavenger, in dichloromethane or THF, at 0 °C to room temperature.

Enzymatic methyl transfer – phenylethanolamine N‑methyltransferase (PNMT) transfers a methyl group from S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine to the primary amine of norepinephrine, yielding epinephrine and S‑adenosyl‑L‑homocysteine; a key step in catecholamine biosynthesis; carried out in aqueous physiological buffer (pH 7.5), often with Mg²⁺ as cofactor, at 37 °C.

Type: oxime formation (condensation). Purpose: convert aldehyde to corresponding oxime. Key transformation: furan‑2‑carbaldehyde + NH₂OH → (E)‑N‑(furan‑2‑ylmethylidene)hydroxylamine + H₂O. Typical conditions: hydroxylamine hydrochloride or free NH₂OH (1–1.2 equiv) in methanol or ethanol, buffered with pyridine or acetate (pH 5‑6), reflux or rt for 1–6 h; removal of water drives equilibrium.

Nitrosyl bromide mediated esterification of an alcohol to give an alkyl nitrite, with concomitant liberation of HBr. Produces n‑butyl nitrite, a nitrite ester used in organic synthesis or as flavor additive. Usually run in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform at low temperature (0 °C to 25 °C); a base (e.g., pyridine) may be added to neutralize HBr.

Oxidative intramolecular C–N couplingoxidative cyclization) of 2‑aminobiphenyl to afford phenanthridine, a heteroaromatic scaffold. Sodium persulfate acts as the oxidant, generating sodium bisulfate as by‑product. Typical conditions: aqueous Na2S2O8 (or in mixed organic–water solvent such as AcOH/H2O), heated to reflux (80–120 °C) for several hours; no transition‑metal catalyst required.

Oxidation of an aldehyde: Potassium dichromate (K₂Cr₂O₇) in acidic medium (typically H₂SO₄) oxidizes 2,2‑dimethylpropanal to 2,2‑dimethylpropanoic acid. Conducted at room temperature to reflux in aqueous sulfuric acid; the Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr³⁺, and the aldehydic carbon is converted to a carboxyl group.

Strong hydride reduction of a dialdehyde to the corresponding 1,5‑diol. LiAlH4 donates hydride to both aldehyde carbonyls, yielding 1,5‑pentanediol after aqueous work‑up. Conducted in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) under nitrogen, initially at 0 °C then warmed to reflux; quench with careful addition of water then dilute acid.

Electrophilic addition (acid‑catalyzed hydration) of 3‑methylpent‑2‑ene to give 3‑methylpentan‑3‑ol; Markovnikov addition of water across the double bond; typically performed with dilute H₂SO₄ or H₃PO₄ in aqueous solution, heating to reflux; solvent is water or aqueous acid.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt metathesis) of hydrazine dihydrochloride with potassium hydroxide to liberate free hydrazine. Forms water and potassium chloride as by‑products. Performed in aqueous solution, typically at ambient temperature with excess KOH; the mixture is filtered to remove KCl and the hydrazine is isolated from the filtrate.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (oxidative chlorination) of phenol using sodium hypochlorite (HOCl) to install a para‑chloro substituent; purpose is synthesis of 4‑chlorophenol; key transformation is substitution of H by Cl on the aromatic ring with formation of water and NaCl; typically carried out in aqueous alkaline solution at 0‑25 °C, often with vigorous stirring; water is the solvent and no additional catalyst is required.

High‑temperature solid‑state reaction (thermal synthesis) of calcium metasilicate from calcium carbonate and silicon dioxide; purpose is production of calcium silicate (used in cements and refractories); key transformation is decarboxylation of CaCO₃ releasing CO₂ and combination of CaO with SiO₂ to give CaSiO₃; performed by grinding the powders together and heating to 1100–1300 °C in a furnace under dry conditions; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Base‑mediated acylation (esterification) of ethyl 4‑hydroxybutanoate with acetyl chloride; purpose is protection of the alcohol as an acetate; key transformation is conversion of the hydroxyl group to an acetoxy group with generation of triethylammonium chloride; typically run in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; triethylamine acts as the base and HCl scavenger.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation); salicylic acid is deprotonated by sodium carbonate producing the water‑soluble sodium salicylate salt with evolution of CO₂; typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient or gently heated temperature, water being the solvent, and the reaction proceeds to completion with stirring.

Mild oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde using Dess‑Martin periodinane; purpose is synthesis of perillaldehyde from perillyl alcohol; key transformation is conversion of the –CH₂OH group to –CHO while preserving other functionalities; usually performed in dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; Dess‑Martin periodinane is used in stoichiometric amount as the oxidant, no additional catalyst is needed.

LAH reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol; pyridine‑4‑carboxylic acid is reduced to pyridin‑4‑ylmethanol; typical procedure uses 1–2 equiv lithium aluminium hydride in dry ether (THF or Et₂O) at 0 °C to room temperature, followed by reflux if needed; reaction is quenched carefully with water then dilute NaOH; no additional catalyst is required.

Acyl‑chloride formation; oxalyl chloride converts 2‑chlorobutanoic acid to 2‑chlorobutyryl chloride, releasing CO, CO₂ and HCl gases; carried out in dry CH₂Cl₂ at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a catalytic amount of DMF; inert atmosphere.

Neutralization (acid‑base) reaction: nitrous acid reacts with ammonia to produce ammonium nitrite (NH₄NO₂). Performed in aqueous solution, typically kept below 30 °C because the salt decomposes at higher temperature. Provides a source of nitrite for diazotization or other nitrosation processes.

Catalytic ring‑opening transesterification of ethylene carbonate by ethanol (ethanolysis); purpose is production of ethylene glycol mono‑ethyl ether with concurrent release of CO₂; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of ethanol on the cyclic carbonate, breaking the C–O bond and forming the linear glycol ether; commonly carried out neat or in a high‑boiling solvent at 150–200 °C in the presence of a base catalyst such as potassium carbonate or a metal alkoxide; no external solvent is required, and the base serves as the catalyst.

Electrophilic addition of hydrogen bromide to an alkene (Markovnikov addition). HBr adds across the double bond of 1‑pentene, with the proton attaching to the terminal carbon and bromide to the internal carbon, affording 2‑bromopentane. Common conditions: solution in dichloromethane or ether, often at 0 °C to room temperature; no catalyst needed unless anti‑Markovnikov product is desired.

Acid‑base/metathesis reaction of sodium dicyanoaurate(I) with hydrochloric acid, forming gold(I) chloride, sodium chloride, and releasing hydrogen cyanide gas; carried out in aqueous solution, kept cool (0‑5 °C) to minimize HCN evolution, no catalyst needed.

Hydrolysis of dimethyl phosphate back to the mono‑ester; acid‑ or base‑catalyzed cleavage of a phosphate ester bond; typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient or elevated temperature, using dilute mineral acid or a mild base to generate methyl dihydrogen phosphate and methanol.

Chlorination of zirconium carbide; a high‑temperature gas‑phase halogenation used to produce carbon tetrachloride and zirconium tetrachloride. Key transformation: replacement of carbide C–Zr bonds by C–Cl (forming CCl4) and formation of ZrCl4. Typical conditions: dry Cl2 gas passed over ZrC at 400–600 °C under inert atmosphere; no solvent, solid‑gas reaction.

Acidic decomposition of magnesium antimonide; a strong‑acid metal displacement reaction that generates hydrogen gas and soluble metal sulfates. Key transformation: Mg–Sb bonds are broken by H2SO4, yielding H2, MgSO4 and antimony(III) sulfate (Sb2(SO4)3). Typical conditions: reflux of powdered Mg3Sb2 (or MgSb) in concentrated aqueous H2SO4, heating 80–120 °C; excess acid and aqueous medium; no special catalyst.

Catalytic reductive amination of a ketone with ammonia; 4phenylbutan‑2‑one reacts with gaseous H₂ in the presence of a hydrogenation catalyst (e.g., Raney Ni, Pd/C or PtO₂) and ammonia to give 4‑phenylbutan‑2‑amine and water; usually performed in an alcohol solvent such as ethanol or methanol, at 1–5 atm H₂ pressure, 50–100 °C under reflux.

Acid‑mediated precipitation of bismuth oxyiodide; reaction of Bi2O3 (or Bi2O2) with hydroiodic acid to give BiOI solid and water. Key transformation: oxide is protonated and iodide replaces oxide to form Bi–OI bonds, producing insoluble BiOI. Typical conditions: aqueous HI (6–12 M) added to finely powdered Bi2O3 at 50–80 °C; stirring under reflux; product isolated by filtration; no catalyst required.

Carbamate (Boc) protection of the amine group; an amine protection reaction where L‑proline hydrochloride is converted to N‑tert‑butoxycarbonyl‑L‑proline using di‑tert‑butyl dicarbonate (Boc2O) as the protecting reagent and triethylamine as base to neutralize HCl; typically performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution of 3‑chloropyridine with aqueous ammonia; substitution of the chlorine atom by an amino group to afford 3‑aminopyridine. Key transformation: Cl is displaced by NH3 on the pyridine ring. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous NH3 (or NH4OH) possibly with a polar aprotic co‑solvent (e.g., ethanol) at 100–120 °C for several hours; pressure may be increased for better conversion; no catalyst needed.

Reductive amination (Leuckart–Wallach reaction) of a β‑keto‑aryl compound with ammonium formate to give a phenethylamine. Ammonium formate supplies both ammonia (for imine formation) and formic acid as the reducing agent, which reduces the imine to the amine while releasing CO₂ and H₂O. The reaction is conducted by heating the ketone with excess ammonium formate (typically 5–10 equiv) in a polar protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol, often in a sealed tube at 150–200 °C for several hours. The product is the corresponding amphetamine analogue; gaseous CO₂ and water are by‑products.

Ester formation from an alcohol and an acyl chloride; heptanol attacks acetyl chloride, releasing HCl and yielding heptyl acetate. Conducted at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent (CH₂Cl₂ or THF) in the presence of a base (pyridine, triethylamine, or 2,6‑lutidine) to neutralize the generated HCl; reaction completes within minutes to an hour.

Base‑catalyzed ring opening of ethylene oxide by 2‑methoxyethanol; formation of a di‑ether (2‑(2‑methoxyethoxy)ethanol). Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of the alcohol oxygen on the less‑substituted carbon of the epoxide, opening the three‑membered ring and forming an ether linkage. Typical conditions: excess 2‑methoxyethanol as solvent, catalytic amount of NaOH or KOH (1–5 mol %), temperature 50–80 °C under inert atmosphere; product isolated after neutralization and distillation.

Thermal decomposition of thallium(I) chlorate; heating the metal chlorate causes it to break down, releasing oxygen gas and forming thallium(I) chloride as the solid residue. Typically performed by strong heating (often above 200 °C) in a dry, inert apparatus; no solvent required.

Reaction type: sulfonate ester formation (mesylation) using an external base; purpose: same as above—to activate the alcohol; key transformation: triethylamine abstracts the HCl generated from methanesulfonyl chloride, yielding 2‑ethoxypropyl methanesulfonate and triethylammonium chloride; typical conditions: 0 °C to rt in dry dichloromethane or THF, 2 equiv triethylamine, inert atmosphere optional.

Hydride reduction of an oxime to a primary amine; acetaldehyde oxime is reduced by sodium borohydride (often in methanol or ethanol, sometimes with a catalytic amount of transition‑metal salt such as NiCl₂) to afford ethylamine, with concomitant formation of borate by‑products; the reaction is typically run at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere.

Acid‑base neutralization with gas evolution; citric acid (triprotic) reacts with three equivalents of lithium hydride, deprotonating each carboxylic acid to give lithium citrate and releasing three equivalents of hydrogen gas. The reaction is carried out in dry, aprotic solvents (e.g., THF or diethyl ether) under inert atmosphere to avoid moisture, typically at ambient temperature.

Base‑mediated hydrolysis (saponification) of a salt; aqueous sodium hydroxide hydrolyzes Etilefrine pivalate, liberating the free base Etilefrine and forming sodium pivalate. The mixture is heated gently (50–80 °C) in water or a water‑ethanol blend; after completion, the product is isolated by extraction or acidification.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene; 2,3‑dimethyl‑1‑butene is saturated with hydrogen in the presence of a metal catalyst (commonly Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney nickel) to afford 2,3‑dimethylbutane. Typical conditions are 1–5 atm H₂, room temperature to 50 °C, in solvents such as ethanol, methanol, or ethyl acetate.

Selective reduction of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol using sodium borohydride; converts the aldehyde group of 4‑chlorobenzaldehyde to a benzylic alcohol; 4‑Cl‑C6H4‑CHO + NaBH4 → 4‑Cl‑C6H4‑CH2OH; usually performed in methanol or ethanol (or a mixed protic solvent) at 0 °C to room temperature; NaBH4 acts as the hydride source, no additional catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr); ammonia replaces the chlorine at the 4‑position of 2,4‑dichloropyrimidine to give 4‑amino‑2‑chloropyrimidine. Typically performed with excess liquid ammonia or aqueous NH3 solution, refluxing in ethanol, dioxane or DMF (120‑150 °C) for several hours; no catalyst required. Purpose: introduce an amino substituent onto a heteroaryl ring.

Oxidation‑reduction; preparation of potassium permanganate by oxidising Mn(IV) oxide in alkaline solution with oxygen. MnO2 is dissolved in aqueous KOH, O2 gas is passed over the solution at 70‑100 °C (often under pressure). The key transformation is Mn(IV) → Mn(VII) forming KMnO4 and water. Typical conditions: aqueous KOH, O2 atmosphere, moderate heating; no additional catalyst required.

Baeyer‑Villiger oxidation of a ketone; 4‑heptanone reacts with meta‑chloroperbenzoic acid (m‑CPBA), inserting an oxygen adjacent to the carbonyl and rearranging to give propyl butanoate (an ester) while the peracid is reduced to m‑chlorobenzoic acid. The reaction is performed at 0 °C to room temperature in dichloromethane or chloroform, often with a buffer to neutralize generated acid.

Oxidation of an aromatic aldehyde to a carboxylic acid using chromic acid (Jones oxidation); the aldehyde carbonyl is converted to a carboxyl group. Typically performed in a mixture of aqueous sulfuric acid and acetone at 0–25 °C; chromic acid acts as the oxidant and no additional catalyst is required.

Birch reduction of anthracene; sodium metal in liquid ammonia with ethanol as a proton source reduces the central 9,10‑double bond of anthracene to give 9,10‑dihydroanthracene. The reaction proceeds at –33 °C under anhydrous conditions; liquid ammonia is the solvent and ethanol supplies the necessary protons.

Deprotonation (acid‑base) of imidazole with NaH; NaH abstracts the N–H proton to give the sodium salt (imidazolate) and H2 gas. Performed in dry aprotic solvent (THF, DMF) under inert atmosphere, 0 °C to rt; no catalyst required.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation); the carboxylic acid reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide sodium carboxylate salt and water; simple proton transfer from acid to hydroxide; carried out at room temperature in water; no special catalyst; stoichiometric NaOH (1 equiv) is sufficient.

This is an oxidation reaction, used to convert alcohols to carboxylic acids. Key transformation is the oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid. Typical conditions include aqueous basic medium at room temperature or slightly elevated. Common solvents are water, with sodium hypochlorite as the oxidizing agent.

Sandmeyer‑type diazotization‑sulphide substitution: para‑aminobenzoic acid is diazotized with NaNO₂/HCl at 0‑5 °C to give the diazonium salt, which is displaced by Na₂S (or NaSH) to afford 4‑mercaptobenzoic acid; nitrogen gas, NaCl and water are produced as by‑products.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation of toluene with acetyl chloride using aluminum chloride; an electrophilic acylium ion attacks the aromatic ring, yielding a mixture of ortho‑ and para‑methylacetophenone while hydrogen chloride is released. Conducted anhydrously with AlCl₃ (1–1.5 equiv) in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane, nitrobenzene or carbon disulfide, typically at 0 °C to reflux.

Acid‑base (acid dissolution) reaction; bismuth(III) oxide reacts with hydrochloric acid to form bismuth trichloride and water; typically performed in aqueous HCl with gentle heating; no special catalyst required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction in aqueous solution; silver acetate reacts with hydrochloric acid to produce insoluble silver chloride precipitate and acetic acid; typically carried out at room temperature in water; no catalyst required.

Reaction between strontium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid: Neutralization (acid-base double displacement). Produces strontium chloride and water. Purpose: neutralizing hydrochloric acid. Key transformation: H+ (from HCl) reacts with OH- (from Sr(OH)2) to form H2O; Sr²+ combines with Cl- to form SrCl2. Typically occurs in aqueous solution at room temperature, no catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of octyl acetate; water in the presence of a strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) cleaves the ester bond to afford acetic acid and octanol. The reaction is carried out under reflux in aqueous acidic medium; no special catalyst beyond the acid is needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) hydrolysis of methyl iodide with solid potassium hydroxide; analogous to reaction 3, yielding methanol and potassium iodide; carried out under similar conditions (80‑120 °C, solid KOH, polar protic solvent) with the more reactive iodide leaving group giving a faster reaction than the bromide analogue.

Aerobic oxidation of 1,4‑butanediol to succinic acid; molecular oxygen oxidizes both primary alcohol groups to carboxylic acids in the presence of a metal catalyst such as Pt/Al₂O₃, Pd, or Au. Typical conditions involve elevated temperature (150–200 °C), oxygen pressure (1–5 MPa), and an aqueous or mixed solvent system.

Double displacement (precipitation) reaction; purpose is to exchange anions and isolate copper(II) carbonate as an insoluble solid. Key transformation: CuSO4·5H2O + Na2CO3 → CuCO3 (precipitate) + Na2SO4 (soluble) + water from hydration. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, ambient temperature, stirring; no special catalyst. Common solvent: water.

Acid–base metathesis between hydrochloric acid and lithium metaborate; protonation of the metaborate ion produces boric acid while lithium ions combine with chloride to form lithium chloride. The reaction proceeds in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no additional reagents are required.

Alkene isomerization (double‑bond migration). 3‑Octene is rearranged to the more substituted 2‑octene. The transformation can be catalyzed by acidic media (e.g., a few drops of H₂SO₄) or by transition‑metal complexes such as Ni, Pd, or Rh on a solid support, usually at 100–150 °C in an inert solvent like toluene or under solvent‑free conditions. The reaction proceeds via a carbocation or metal‑hydride intermediate.

Acid‑chloride formation: treatment of ammonium benzoate with phosphorus pentachloride converts the benzoate anion into benzoyl chloride while generating phosphorus oxychloride and ammonium chloride; typically performed in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride at 0 °C to room temperature under an inert atmosphere.

Nucleophilic ring‑opening of ethylene carbonate by ethylenediamine: one amine nitrogen attacks the cyclic carbonate, opening the ring and attaching a 2‑hydroxyethyl group to the diamine, releasing carbon dioxide; carried out by heating the neat reactants or in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF) without added catalyst.

Chromium(VI) oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde: potassium dichromate in concentrated sulfuric acid oxidizes 1‑octanol to octanal, producing water, potassium sulfate and chromium(III) sulfate as by‑products; the reaction is performed in aqueous acidic medium, usually at 50–80 °C, with vigorous stirring.

Acidic decomposition of diazomethane to give a methyl ester: diazomethane reacts with perchloric acid, liberating nitrogen gas and forming methyl perchlorate via protonation of the diazo compound and capture of the perchlorate anion; conducted at low temperature (0 °C to ‑20 °C) in an inert organic solvent such as diethyl ether, with strict safety precautions.

Acid‑catalyzed nucleophilic substitution of a secondary alcohol (SN1/SN2 mixture, Lucas test conditions); protonation of 2‑propanol by HCl generates a good leaving group (water) which is displaced by chloride to give 2‑chloropropane. Key transformation: conversion of the hydroxyl group to a chloride, releasing water. Typical conditions: excess concentrated HCl gas or aqueous HCl, reflux; often ZnCl₂ (Lucas reagent) is added to accelerate the SN1 pathway for secondary alcohols. No external catalyst beyond the acid.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of phenacetin to regenerate 4‑ethoxyaniline and acetic acid; purpose: cleavage of amide bond; key transformation: amide → amine + carboxylic acid; typically refluxed in aqueous HCl (1‑2 M) or dilute mineral acid at 100 °C for several hours; solvent: water or water‑ethanol mixture.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification: 2‑phenylethanol attacks ethyl acetate, exchanging the alkoxy groups to afford 2‑phenylethyl acetate and ethanol; typically run under reflux in excess ethyl acetate using a catalytic amount of sulfuric acid, p‑toluenesulfonic acid, or a base such as sodium ethoxide.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis of 3,4‑dimethoxyphenylacetonitrile with aqueous NaOH under reflux, converting the nitrile to the corresponding sodium carboxylate; acid work‑up yields 3,4‑dimethoxybenzoic acid and releases ammonia (as NH₃); solvent water (often with ethanol).

Double displacement/acid‑base reaction: trichloroneodymium (NdCl₃) reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid to form neodymium sulfate (Nd₂(SO₄)₃) and gaseous hydrochloric acid. Typically performed in aqueous medium or melt, heated to evolve HCl; no catalyst required, water as solvent.

Acid–base neutralization: ammonia (NH₃) protonates tetrafluoroboric acid (HBF₄) yielding ammonium tetrafluoroborate (NH₄BF₄). Carried out in water at ambient temperature; product crystallizes on cooling; no catalyst needed.

Oximation of propanal with hydroxylamine to give the oxime (C=NOH); carried out in ethanol or aqueous medium using hydroxylamine·HCl together with a base such as pyridine or NaOAc, at 0–25 °C under neutral to mildly acidic conditions; purpose is carbonyl protection or preparation for Beckmann rearrangement.

Acid‑base metathesis: zinc oxide reacts with D‑gluconic acid to give zinc gluconate and water. Conducted in water or aqueous ethanol with gentle heating to dissolve ZnO; pH control may be used; no catalyst.

Prilezhaev epoxidation of styrene with perbenzoic acid; yields styrene oxide and benzoic acid via oxygen transfer to the alkene; same usual conditions as reaction 3 (CH₂Cl₂, 0 °C to rt, stoichiometric peracid).

Heterocycle‑forming condensation (Fischer pyrazole synthesis): hydrazine condenses with 2,3‑pentanedione, cyclizing to 2,5‑dimethylpyrazole while releasing two molecules of water. Typical conditions: reflux in ethanol or methanol, often with a catalytic amount of acetic acid; inert atmosphere optional.

Double displacement/fluoride exchange: hydrofluoric acid reacts with cobalt(II) sulfate to precipitate cobalt(II) fluoride and produce sulfuric acid. Usually performed in aqueous solution at low to moderate temperature; excess HF drives the reaction; no catalyst, careful HF handling required.

Redox oxidation: chlorine gas oxidizes gold(I) chloride (AuCl) to gold(III) chloride (AuCl₃). Conducted in a dry, non‑aqueous halogenated solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride or nitrosyl chloride) at 0–25 °C; no additional catalyst, inert atmosphere employed to exclude moisture.

Catalytic hydrogenation; reduces the nitro group of 3‑methyl‑4‑nitrophenol to an amine giving 3‑methyl‑4‑aminophenol and water. Typically performed with H₂ gas (1–5 atm) over Pd/C in an alcoholic solvent (e.g., EtOH or MeOH) at room temperature to reflux, sometimes with a small amount of acid to keep the phenol protonated.

Oxidative halogenation (halogen exchange); Sn(II) bromide is oxidized by Br₂ to Sn(IV) bromide, forming tetrabromostannane (SnBr₄). Conducted in anhydrous, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride, chloroform or dichloromethane, under an inert atmosphere at 0 °C to ambient temperature.

Base‑promoted hydrolysis (alkyl nitrate saponification); n‑butyl nitrate reacts with NaOH to give n‑butanol and sodium nitrate. Usually carried out in aqueous NaOH (often 1 M) with reflux heating (≈80–100 °C); the reaction proceeds efficiently without added catalyst.

Chemical reduction of an aromatic nitro group; aqueous sodium dithionite (Na₂S₂O₄) reduces methyl 5‑nitro‑2‑hydroxybenzoate to methyl 5‑amino‑2‑hydroxybenzoate, producing water and sodium sulf as by‑products. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, pH 7–9, temperature 50–80 °C, and excess dithionite; no additional catalyst required.

Double‑displacement precipitation; FeCl₃ reacts with tribasic potassium phosphate in water to precipitate iron(III) phosphate (FePO₄) while forming soluble KCl. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; the solid product is isolated by filtration and washing.

Direct solid‑state combination (synthesis) of a metal chalcogenide; elemental molybdenum reacts with selenium to afford molybdenum diselenide (MoSe₂). Usually carried out in a sealed quartz ampoule or furnace at 400–800 °C under argon or vacuum to prevent oxidation; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Oxidation of methimazole to carbimazole; methimazole is oxidized by hydrogen peroxide in the presence of a catalytic amount of sodium tungstate (Na₂WO₄) to give carbimazole and water; the reaction proceeds in aqueous medium at ambient temperature, often buffered to pH 7–9 to maintain catalyst activity.

Aqueous double‑displacement precipitation: thulium(III) chloride reacts with sodium hydroxide forming thulium(III) hydroxide precipitate and sodium chloride in solution. Performed in aqueous medium, often at room temperature with stoichiometric or slight excess NaOH; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Type: catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation) of an alkyl chloride. Purpose: convert a primary alkyl chloride to the corresponding alkane and generate HCl, often used for deprotection or simplification of halogenated substrates. Key transformation: C–Cl bond cleaved, hydrogen added to carbon to give isopentane; chloride captured asCl. Typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm) over a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, Raney Ni, or PtO₂, in an inert solvent (e.g., ethanol, THF, or dichloromethane) at 25–80 °C. No additional reagents required beyond the catalyst.

Type: alkaline hydrolytic degradation of cellulose. Purpose: break down polymeric cellulose into low‑molecular‑weight, water‑soluble acids for waste treatment or feedstock preparation. Key transformation: β‑1,4‑glycosidic linkages cleaved under strong base, yielding β‑glucoisosaccharinic acid (a C₆ acid) and oxidation of terminal glucose units to sodium gluconate. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (0.5–5 M), temperature 120–200 °C, often under sealed pressure‑vessel or autoclave for several hours. No metal catalyst; reaction proceeds via base‑catalyzed depolymerization and oxidation.

Peroxide‑mediated ester hydrolysis; methylparaben undergoes hydrolysis by the hydrogen peroxide released from sodium percarbonate, yielding p‑hydroxybenzoic acid, methanol and water; typically carried out in a water‑acetone mixture at 40–80 °C, sometimes with a small amount of base (e.g., Na₂CO₃) to accelerate the reaction.

Type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an alkyl bromide by cyanide. Purpose: introduce a nitrile group onto a benzylic carbon, forming 2‑nitrophenylacetonitrile. Key transformation: bromide displaced by CN⁻, forming C≡N bond; Na⁺ pairs with liberated Br⁻ to give NaBr. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO, or acetone; temperature 0 °C to reflux (often 25–60 °C) to favor SN2 and avoid elimination; stoichiometric NaCN (often slight excess). Reaction may be carried out under nitrogen to prevent oxidation of cyanide.

Photo‑oxidation (allylic oxidation) of perillene to perillyl aldehyde; perillene is exposed to O₂ under UV light in the presence of a photosensitizer (e.g., Rose Bengal) in an organic solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ or MeCN, converting an allylic C‑H bond to an aldehyde to give perillyl aldehyde; reaction carried out at ambient temperature with continuous irradiation.

Condensation (amidation) of a carboxylic acid with isopropylhydrazine to form a hydrazide (ipriona zid) with loss of water; typically carried out by activating the acid (e.g., using DCC, EDC, or converting to an acid chloride) in refluxing ethanol or methanol, sometimes with a catalytic acid to promote coupling.

Type: Friedel‑s alkylation (electrophilic aromatic substitution). Purpose: install a methyl substituent on benzene to afford toluene. Key transformation: methyl cation generated from methyl iodide and AlCl₃ attacks the aromatic ring, followed by deprotonation; HI is formed as by‑product. Typical conditions: anhydrous AlCl₃ (1–2 equiv) in a dry, non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane, carbon tetrachloride, or CS₂; reaction performed under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) at 0 °C to reflux (≈40 °C) for 1–2 h. Excess AlCl₃ is quenched with ice‑water after completion.

Type: esterification of an phenol with an acid chloride (acylation). Purpose: synthesize phenyl methacrylate, a monomer for polymerization. Key transformation: phenolic O attacks the carbonyl carbon of methacryloyl chloride, displacing chloride; HCl is scavenged by a base. Typical conditions: dry dichloromethane or THF, base such as pyridine, triethylamine, or N‑methylmorpholine (1–1.5 equiv) to capture HCl, temperature 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere. Reaction usually completes within 30 min to 2 h, after which work‑up removes the base‑HCl salt.

High‑temperature oxidation (combustion) of tin(IV) sulfide. SnS2 + O2 → SnO2 + SO2. Conducted in a furnace at >500 °C in air or oxygen stream; solid‑state reaction produces tin(IV) oxide and sulfur dioxide gas.

Type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an alkyl halide by a thiol to form a thioether; purpose: synthesis of a symmetrical sulfide; key transformation: sulfur of ethanethiol attacks ethyl iodide, creating a C–S bond and releasing HI; typical conditions: dry polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetone or DMF) at reflux, often with a base such as pyridine or sodium carbonate to neutralize the generated HI; no catalyst required.

Oxidation of a 1,2‑diol using ceric ammonium nitrate (CAN); cleaves ethylene glycol to give glyoxal, with concurrent reduction of Ce(IV) to Ce(III) and formation of nitric acid; CAN + HOCH2CH2OH → OHC‑CHO + Ce(NO3)3·NH4NO3 + HNO3 + H2O; performed in water or water‑acetonitrile mixtures at 0‑25 °C; CAN is the sole oxidant/catalyst.

Type: catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol; purpose: convert citronellal to citronellol; key transformation: addition of H₂ across the carbonyl C=O (and optionally the C=C) to give the corresponding alcohol; typical conditions: 1 atm H₂, palladium on carbon (5–10 % Pd) as catalyst, room temperature to 50 °C, solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, inert atmosphere.

Type: carbodiimide‑mediated esterification (Steglich esterification); purpose: prepare isobutyl acetate from acetic acid and isobutyl alcohol under mild, non‑acidic conditions; key transformation: DIC activates the carboxylic acid to an O‑acylurea, which is then attacked by the alcohol, yielding the ester and N,N‑diisopropylurea as by‑product; typical conditions: dichloromethane (or THF) at 0 °C then room temperature, often with catalytic DMAP, no external coupling reagents beyond DIC.

Type: Strecker‑type synthesis of an α‑amino acid (sarcosine, N‑methylglycine); purpose: build sarcosine from C₁ precursors; key transformation: formaldehyde condenses with methylamine to form an imine, cyanide adds to give an α‑aminonitrile, and aqueous hydrolysis converts the nitrile to a carboxylate while releasing ammonia; typical conditions: aqueous solution, pH 7–9, 0–25 °C for imine/cyanohydrin formation, followed by acid or neutral hydrolysis at reflux to complete the conversion.

Type: reductive amination of a ketone with an amine using sodium cyanoborohydride; purpose: synthesize 3,4‑methylenedioxy‑N‑isopropylamphetamine; key transformation: ketone (3,4‑methylenedioxyphenylacetone) forms an imine with isopropylamine, which is then reduced by NaCNBH₃ to the secondary amine; typical conditions: methanol or dichloromethane as solvent, mildly acidic medium (pH ≈ 5–6, often with acetic acid), 0 °C to room temperature, stoichiometric NaCNBH₃, inert atmosphere.

Type: redox displacement (amalgam reduction) of elemental arsenic by sodium amalgam; purpose: generate sodium arsenide (Na₃As) for further synthetic use; key transformation: sodium atoms in the amalgam donate electrons to arsenic, forming arsenide anion while metallic mercury is liberated; typical conditions: powdered arsenic reacted with sodium‑mercury amalgam under anhydrous, inert atmosphere (e.g., nitrogen or argon), usually at low temperature (0–25 °C) in a dry ether or THF medium; mercury is produced as a by‑product.

Thermal decarboxylation; anthranilic acid loses carbon dioxide to afford aniline; carried out by heating the solid acid at high temperature (≈200–300 °C) often under inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is necessary, the reaction is driven by heat.

Oxidative syn‑dihydroxylation of an alkene; dilute KMnO4 in cold aqueous solution (0‑5 °C) adds two hydroxyl groups to trans‑2‑butene to give the cis‑vicinal diol butane‑2,3‑diol; purpose is conversion of C=C to a 1,2‑diol; water is the solvent, no additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) – the nitrogen of morpholine attacks the primary carbon of chloroethane, displacing chloride to give N‑ethylmorpholine; the released HCl is usually neutralized by a base or removed as a gas. Typical conditions: reflux in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF, often with an inorganic base (e.g., K₂CO₃) to trap HCl.

Same oxaziridine‑mediated epoxidation applied to styrene; the oxaziridine transfers an oxygen atom to the C=C bond of styrene, producing styrene oxide and hydroxylamine. Conducted at room temperature in dichloromethane or acetonitrile; the reaction proceeds without metal catalysts, sometimes with a catalytic amount of triethylamine to facilitate nitrogen deprotonation.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) – hydroxide ion from sodium hydroxide replaces the chlorine atom on 2‑chlorobenzimidazole, yielding 2‑hydroxybenzimidazole. Usually carried out in aqueous NaOH (or NaOH/ethanol) with heating (70–100 °C) to promote substitution; no special catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic halogenation of azulene. Purpose: install a chlorine substituent at the 1‑position (most activated site). Key transformation: azulene + Cl2 → 1‑chloroazulene + HCl. Typical conditions: Cl2 gas bubbled through a solution of azulene in an inert, non‑protic solvent (CHCl3, CCl4, or CS2) at 0 °C to rt; often no Lewis acid catalyst is needed because azulene is highly activated, but FeCl3 or AlCl3 can be used to increase rate. Reaction is usually quenched with aqueous Na2SO3 to remove excess chlorine.

Acid–base/ion‑exchange reaction – potassium hydroxide deprotonates ammonium bifluoride (NH₄HF₂), producing water and the two fluoride salts, potassium fluoride and ammonium fluoride. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst needed.

Acid–base reaction of strontium sulfide with sulfuric acid; yields insoluble strontium sulfate and hydrogen sulfide gas. SrS is added to dilute H2SO4 (or concentrated acid) in water, often with gentle heating, forming a precipitate of SrSO4 and releasing H2S.

Acid–base displacement and carbonate decomposition; nitric acid protonates the basic bismuth subcarbonate, releasing CO₂ and forming bismuth subnitrate; typically performed in aqueous solution at mild heating (40‑80 °C) with stirring; water serves as solvent and excess acid drives the reaction to completion.

Heterocycle‑forming cyclocondensation – the thiol and aldehyde functions of 2‑mercaptoacetaldehyde react with the cyano group of cyanoacetic acid to generate a thiazoline ring, giving 2‑aminothiazoline‑4‑carboxylic acid with loss of water. Typically run in ethanol or methanol under reflux; mild acidic or neutral conditions (e.g., acetic acid) may be added to promote cyclization.

N‑acylation of piperazine with acetyl chloride to afford N‑acetylpiperazine (1‑piperazin‑1‑yl ethanone) and HCl. The nucleophilic secondary amine attacks the carbonyl of acetyl chloride, displacing chloride. Reaction is typically done in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt, using a base such as triethylamine or pyridine (1–2 equiv) to trap the generated HCl.

General type: double displacement (acid–base metathesis) in aqueous solution. Purpose: conversion of ammonium aluminum sulfate into useful chloride salts and recovery of sulfuric acid. Key transformation: exchange of chloride anions from HCl with sulfate anions of the ammonium aluminum sulfate, yielding AlCl₃, NH₄Cl and H₂SO₄. Typical conditions: dissolve the salts in water, add concentrated HCl slowly while stirring at 0–25 °C, then warm to reflux if needed to drive the reaction to completion. No special catalyst; water serves as the solvent.

Acid–base neutralization of the hydrochloride salt of 4‑hydroxymethylpiperidine with aqueous sodium hydroxide; the strong base deprotonates the ammonium ion, liberating the free amine and forming water and sodium chloride. Conducted in water or mixed aqueous/organic solvent at 0‑25 °C; no catalyst required; the amine is usually extracted into an organic layer after basification.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (hydrogenolytic dehalogenation) of benzyl chloride to toluene using palladium on carbon under hydrogen pressure. The C–Cl bond is reduced, releasing hydrogen chloride as a by‑product. Typical conditions: H₂ 1–5 atm, Pd/C (5–10 wt %), solvent such as ethanol, methanol or THF, temperature 25–80 °C; often a base (e.g., triethylamine) is added to neutralize HCl.

Selective reduction of pyridine‑4‑carboxaldehyde to pyridine‑4‑ylmethanol using sodium borohydride. Purpose: obtain the primary alcohol from the aldehyde. Key transformation: hydride transfer from NaBH₄ to the carbonyl carbon, forming an alcohol. Typical conditions: NaBH₄ (1.0–1.5 equiv) in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to rt; reaction quenched with water; no catalyst.
